## Khuddaka Nikāya
## Itivuttaka-aṭṭhakathā
## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
## Introduction to the Text (Ganthārambhakathā)

I pay homage to the Protector, possessed of great compassion, who has reached the further shore of the ocean of the knowable, and who teaches through subtle, profound, and diverse methods.

I pay homage to that supreme Dhamma, worshipped by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, endowed with the three knowledges and fifteen conducts, by which [beings] emerge from the three worlds.

I pay homage to that Noble Saṅgha, endowed with virtues such as morality, established in the paths and fruits, and who are the incomparable field for the seeds of merit.

Whatever merit is produced by thus paying homage to the Triple Gem, may I, by its power, be free from obstacles in all places.

The Great Sage has taught [the Dhamma] in various divisions such as the 'Ones' (Ekaka), specifically illustrating the abandonment of greed and so forth.

The Elder Dhamma-reciters, great sages who sought virtues such as morality, collected the discourses and formed the words and syllables known as the 'Itivuttaka'.

In former times, those who had mastery [over the five masteries] recited together in the Khuddaka Nikāya that which is named 'Itivuttaka', consisting of a profound sequence of meanings and words.

Because the depth of this Itivuttaka is to be fathomed only by those of profound wisdom [Arahants], it is indeed difficult for me to compose an explanation of its meaning.
2:
Since the teaching of the Teacher together with its commentary still exists, and the decisions of the lion-like former teachers still stand, therefore, relying on those [decisions], delving into the five Nikāyas, and depending on the method of the ancient commentaries (Porāṇaṭṭhakathā), I shall compose the Itivuttaka-vaṇṇanā (Commentary on the Itivuttaka) to the best of my ability. It will follow the tradition of the dwellers of the Mahāvihāra, being very pure, uncomplicated, and containing subtle decisions on meaning, while carefully avoiding meanings that appear repeatedly. Thus, desiring the long endurance of the True Dhamma, may the virtuous listen to my words as I analyze the meaning of that Itivuttaka.

In this Itivuttaka text, it is organized into four divisions (Nipātas): the Book of Ones (Ekaka-nipāta), the Book of Twos (Duka-nipāta), the Book of Threes (Tika-nipāta), and the Book of Fours (Catukka-nipāta). Among the three Piṭakas—Vinaya Piṭaka, Suttanta Piṭaka, and Abhidhamma Piṭaka—it is included in the Suttanta Piṭaka. Among the five Nikāyas—Dīgha Nikāya, Majjhima Nikāya, Saṃyutta Nikāya, Aṅguttara Nikāya, and Khuddaka Nikāya—it is included in the Khuddaka Nikāya. Among the nine limbs of the Teacher’s instruction (anga)—Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla—it constitutes the Itivuttaka limb.

The Treasurer of the Dhamma, the Venerable Ānanda, declared: "I received eighty-two thousand from the Buddha and two thousand from the monks; thus eighty-four thousand teachings are current in my mind." Among these eighty-four thousand Dhamma-groups (dhammakkhandha), the Itivuttaka is composed of a few Dhamma-groups. In terms of the number of discourses (suttas), it is composed of 112 suttas in total: 27 suttas in the Ekaka-nipāta, 22 suttas in the Duka-nipāta, 50 suttas in the Tika-nipāta, and 13 suttas in the Catukka-nipāta. Among the divisions of this text, the Ekaka-nipāta is the first. Among the groups (vaggas), the Pāṭibhoga-vagga is the first. Among the discourses, the Lobha-sutta is the first. At the beginning of that Lobha-sutta, the introduction (nidāna) beginning with "Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā" (This was said by the Blessed One), spoken by the Venerable Ānanda at the time of the First Great Council, is the beginning. That First Great Council is indeed incorporated into the Vinaya Piṭaka. The sequence of words spoken here for the sake of proficiency in the introduction...
3:
There is a sequence of words intended for proficiency in the introduction of the Itivuttaka Commentary. Since that sequence of words has already been explained in detail in the Dīgha Nikāya Commentary named Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, it should be understood according to the method stated in that commentary.

## Explanation of the Introduction

There is the introduction beginning with 'Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā' and the sutta beginning with 'Ekadhammaṃ bhikkhave pajahatha'. In that introduction and sutta, words such as 'vuttaṃ' and 'bhagavatā' are nouns (nāmapada). The word 'iti' is an indeclinable (nipātapada). In the word 'pajahathāti', 'pa' is a prefix (upasagga) and 'jahatha' is a verb (ākhyāta). In this manner, the analysis of words should be understood in all places.

In terms of meaning, the word 'vutta'—whether with a prefix or without—is seen in such meanings as sowing, leveling the ground for sowing, shaving hair, livelihood, being released from bonds, being established as sacred speech, studying or reciting, and speaking. For instance:

'The cows of one who does not betray friends multiply; the seed sown in his field sprouts; he enjoys the fruit of what was sown.'

In such passages, it occurs in the sense of sowing. In passages such as 'No ca kho paṭivuttaṃ', it occurs in the sense of leveling the ground for sowing with eight plowshares and so forth. In passages such as 'Kāpaṭiko māṇavo daharo vuttasiro', it occurs in the sense of shaving hair. In passages such as 'Pannalomo paradattavutto migabhūtena cetasā viharati', it occurs in the sense of livelihood. In passages such as 'Seyyathāpi nāma paṇḍupalāso bandhanā pavutto abhabbo haritattāya', it occurs in the sense of being released from bonds (falling off). In passages such as 'Yesamidaṃ etarahi brāhmaṇā porāṇaṃ mantapadaṃ gītaṃ pavuttaṃ samihitaṃ', it occurs in the sense of being established as sacred speech. In the world, it is well-known in the sense of studying or reciting in such contexts as 'Vutto gaṇo, vutto pārāyano'. In passages such as 'Vuttaṃ kho panetaṃ bhagavatā dhammadāyādā me bhikkhave bhavatha mā āmisadāyādā', it occurs in the sense of speaking. Here too, it should be understood in the sense of speaking. Therefore, 'vutta' carries the meaning of 'said', 'spoken', or 'taught'.
4:
The second word 'vutta', however, should be understood in the sense of both 'spoken' and 'practiced'. The particle 'hi' is an indeclinable (nipāta) used in the sense of certainty or clarity. This particle now illustrates the clarity of the Blessed One's teaching in the sutta that is about to be spoken. Indeed, indeclinables used in proximity to expressive words clarify the meaning to be conveyed.

Regarding the word 'etaṃ' (this):
'He who has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, perceives with right wisdom the Four Noble Truths.
Suffering, the origin of suffering, the overcoming of suffering, and the Noble Eightfold Path leading to the cessation of suffering.
This indeed is the safe refuge, this is the supreme refuge; having come to this refuge, one is released from all suffering.' (Dhp. 190-192)
In such passages, it appears in the sense of something already mentioned and immediately present.

'Monks, when a worldling speaks in praise of the Tathāgata, he would speak of this which is trifling, minor, and a mere matter of virtue.' (DN 1.7)
In such passages, however, it appears in the sense of something about to be mentioned and immediately present. In this text also, it should be understood only in the sense of what is about to be mentioned. The Treasurer of the Dhamma, Venerable Ānanda, having placed in his mind the sutta to be recited by way of the Council (Saṅgāyana), spoke the word 'etaṃ' at that time.

In the word 'bhagavatā', 'bhagavā' is a term of respect. In the world, people call a teacher 'bhagavā'. The Tathāgata is the Teacher of all beings because He is distinguished by all virtues; therefore, He should be known as 'Bhagavā'. The ancient teachers also said:
'The word Bhagavā is the most excellent; the word Bhagavā is supreme. He is the Teacher endowed with reverence; therefore, He is called Bhagavā.'

A word expressing the most excellent is called 'most excellent' because it is associated with the most excellent qualities. Alternatively, 'vuccati' means 'vacana' (word), referring to the meaning. Therefore, 'the word Bhagavā is the most excellent' means that the meaning expressed by this word 'Bhagavā' is the most excellent. The same method applies to the phrase 'the word Bhagavā is supreme'. 'Gāravayutta' means being endowed with the state of being a teacher (garu) due to the possession of the qualities of a teacher. Or, He is called 'gāravayutta' because He is exceedingly worthy of being treated with respect (garukaraṇa); it means one who is worthy of reverence. Thus, this name 'Bhagavā' is a designation for the person who is supreme among beings, distinguished by virtues, a teacher, and worthy of reverence.

Furthermore—He is called Bhagavā because He possesses fortune (bhaga) such as sovereignty; He is accustomed to associating with (bhajī) the superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma); He possesses (vanta) the four requisites and virtues; He is one who has analyzed and taught (vibhattavā) the Dhamma; He has destroyed (bhagga) evils such as lust; therefore, He is called Bhagavā.
5:
Because He possesses fortune, associates, has portions, has analyzed, has performed the destruction of evil, is a teacher, is fortunate, and because He has well-developed Himself through many methods and has reached the end of existence, He is called 'Bhagavā'.

According to the method found in the Niddesa: 'He is called Bhagavā because He is fortunate (bhāgyavā), has destroyed evil (bhaggavā), is endowed with the six glories (bhagehi yutto), has analyzed the Dhamma (vibhattavā), associates with virtues (bhattavā), has discarded craving (vantagamano), and has done so throughout his existences (bhavesu).'

The meaning of the word 'Bhagavā' is explained by the power of this verse. That meaning is explained in every aspect in the Visuddhimagga, in the section on the Recollection of the Buddha (Buddhānussati-niddesa); it should be understood exactly as stated there.

Another method: He is Bhagavā because He has portions (bhāgavā); He is Bhagavā because He has practiced (bhatavā); He is Bhagavā because He has desired the portions (bhāge vanī); He is Bhagavā because He has associated with glory (bhage vanī); He is Bhagavā because He has followers who associate with Him (bhattavā); He is Bhagavā because He has vomited glory (bhage vamī); He is Bhagavā because He has vomited the portions (bhāge vamī).

'The Victorious Buddha is called Bhagavā because He has portions, has practiced, has desired the portions, has associated with glory, has followers who associate with Him, has vomited glory, and likewise has vomited the portions.'

In that context, how is He Bhagavā because He has portions? The aggregates of Dhamma and divisions of virtue, such as virtue (sīla) and so on, which are not shared with others and are unsurpassed, exist and are found in the Tathāgata. Specifically, He possesses: virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, knowledge and vision of liberation, shame, fear of wrongdoing, faith, energy, mindfulness, clear comprehension, purification of virtue, purification of mind, purification of view, serenity, insight, the 3 roots of the wholesome, the 3 right conducts, the 3 right thoughts, the 3 faultless perceptions, the 3 elements, the 4 foundations of mindfulness, the 4 right efforts, the 4 bases of power, the 4 noble paths, the 4 noble fruits, the 4 analytical insights, the 4 knowledges of defining the modes of birth, the 4 lineages of the noble ones, the 4 intrepidities, the 5 factors of striving, the 5-fold right concentration, the 5-fold right concentration with knowledge, the 5 faculties, the 5 powers, the 5 elements of deliverance, the 5 knowledges of the spheres of liberation, the 5 perceptions that ripen liberation, the 6 bases of recollection, the 6 grounds for respect, the 6 elements of deliverance, the 6 constant abidings, the 6 unsurpassed things, the 6 [knowledges] that are causes for penetration...
6:
The 6 types of wisdom partaking of penetration, the 6 supernormal powers (abhiññā), the 6 unshared knowledges (asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa), the 7 factors of non-decline (aparihāniya-dhamma), the 7 noble treasures (ariya-dhana), the 7 factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), the 7 qualities of a good person (sappurisa-dhamma), the 7 grounds for wearing away (nijjara-vatthu), the 7 perceptions (saññā), the 7 teachings on persons worthy of offerings (dakkhiṇeyya-puggala), the 7 teachings on the powers of those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava-bala), the 8 teachings on the causes for obtaining wisdom, the 8 rightnesses (sammatta), the 8 transcendences of worldly conditions, the 8 grounds for effort (ārambha-vatthu), the 8 teachings on inopportune moments (akkhaṇa), the 8 thoughts of a great man (mahāpurisa-vitakka), the 8 teachings on the bases of transcendence (abhibhāyatana), the 8 liberations (vimokkha), the 9 dhammas rooted in wise attention (yoniso-manasikāra), the 9 factors of effort for purity (pārisuddhi-padhāniyaṅga), the 9 teachings on the abodes of beings (sattāvāsa), the 9 ways of removing resentment (āghāta-paṭivinaya), the 9 perceptions, the 9 teachings on diversity (nānatta), the 9 teachings on successive abodes (anupubba-vihāra), the 10 dhammas that make for a protector (nāthakaraṇa-dhamma), the 10 bases of kasina (kasiṇāyatana), the 10 courses of wholesome action (kusala-kammapatha), the 10 rightnesses, the 10 noble abodes (ariyavāsa), the 10 dhammas of an adept (asekha-dhamma), the 10 powers of a Tathāgata (tathāgata-bala), the 11 benefits of loving-kindness (mettā-nisaṃsa), the 12 aspects of the Wheel of Dhamma (dhammacakka-ākāra), the 13 benefits of ascetic practices (dhutaṅga-guṇa), the 14 Buddha-knowledges (buddha-ñāṇa), the 15 dhammas that ripen liberation (vimutti-paripācanīya-dhamma), the 16-fold mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati), the 16 dhammas that do not cause remorse (aparantapanīya-dhamma), the 18 Buddha-dhammas, the 19 knowledges of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa), the 44 grounds for knowledge (ñāṇa-vatthu), the 50 knowledges of rise and fall (udayabbaya-ñāṇa), more than 50 wholesome dhammas, the 77 grounds for knowledge (ñāṇa-vatthu), the Great Vajira Knowledge that ranges over two hundred and forty thousand koṭis of attainments, the knowledge of reviewing the investigation of the Infinite Method of the Samantapaṭṭhāna, and the knowledge of discerning the inclinations etc. of infinite beings in infinite world systems (āsayādivibhāvana-ñāṇa)—these and other infinite, immeasurable, unshared, and unsurpassed groups of qualities (guṇabhāga) exist and are found in Him. Therefore, because He possesses these various groups of qualities as described, He should be called "Bhāgavā". By shortening the 'ā' to 'a', He is called "Bhagavā". Thus, He is first called "Bhagavā" because He possesses groups of qualities.

"Because all groups of qualities like virtue etc. exist without remainder in the Sugata, therefore He is called Bhagavā."

How is He "Bhagavā" because of accumulating (bhata) qualities? There are the 10 perfections (pāramī), the 10 sub-perfections (upapāramī), and the 10 ultimate perfections (paramattha-pāramī) fulfilled by the Great Bodhisattas who, for the benefit of the whole world, combined the eight factors such as human existence and made the Great Resolve (mahābhinīhāra) for Right Self-Enlightenment. These are the perfection of giving, the perfection of virtue, renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truthfulness, resolution, loving-kindness, and equanimity.
7:
In brief, there are the thirty perfections, the four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu), the four resolutions (adhiṭṭhāna), the five great sacrifices (mahāpariccāga) consisting of the sacrifice of self, eyes, wealth, kingdom, and children and wife; previous application (pubbayoga), previous conduct (pubbacariyā), preaching the Dhamma (dhammakkhāna), conduct for the benefit of the world (lokattha-cariyā), conduct for the benefit of relatives (ñātattha-cariyā), and conduct for the benefit of Buddhahood (buddhattha-cariyā). These and other dhammas that make one a Buddha are the requisites of merit (puñña-sambhāra) and requisites of knowledge (ñāṇa-sambhāra). From the time of making the Great Resolve for four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons, these dhammas were not of the nature of decline, defilement, or mere stagnation, but were indeed always of the nature of distinction (visesabhāgiya). Because He has accumulated (bhata) and gathered (sambhata) these (as the foundation for Omniscience and the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship) respectfully, constantly, and without remainder, He is called "Bhatavā". By linguistic rule, changing the letter 't' to 'g', He is called "Bhagavā". Alternatively, He is called "Bhatavā" because He accumulated and fulfilled those aforementioned dhammas that make one a Buddha in the manner described; thus, being "Bhatavā", He is "Bhagavā".

"Because the Protector accumulated all the requisites like the perfection of giving for the sake of enlightenment, therefore He is also known as Bhagavā."

How is He "Bhagavā" because of frequenting (vanī) parts (bhāga)? Because He constantly and fully frequented, associated with, and practiced the parts of attainments used daily, numbering two million four hundred thousand koṭis, both for the benefit of the world and for His own pleasant dwelling in this life, He is called "Bhagavā" as one who frequents parts. Alternatively, regarding the dhammas to be known (abhiññeyya) such as wholesome dhammas and the aggregates, He frequented the four types of penetration (abhisamaya) in brief; and in detail, the many parts to be fully known (pariññeyya) such as "the eye is to be fully known ... old age and death are to be fully known"; the parts to be abandoned (pahātabba) such as "the origin of the eye is to be abandoned ... the origin of old age and death is to be abandoned"; the parts to be realized (sacchikātabba) such as "the cessation of the eye is to be realized ... the cessation of old age and death is to be realized"; and the many various parts to be developed (bhāvetabba) such as "the practice leading to the cessation of the eye is to be developed ... the four foundations of mindfulness are to be developed". He frequented these dhammas by way of objective focus, development, and association as appropriate. Thus, He is called "Bhagavā" because He frequented these parts. Alternatively, the groups of dhammas (dhammakkhandha) such as virtue are groups of qualities (guṇabhāga) shared with the disciples; He desired (vanī) with great compassion, thinking, "How may I establish these groups of qualities in the continuities of beings to be tamed?" Because the Tathāgata, the Blessed One, [frequented] the parts of the abhiññeyya attainments...
8:
That aspiration of the Blessed One also brought about the desired benefit. In this way, because he aspired to the portions (bhāga) of qualities such as virtue (sīla) and so forth, he is called "Bhagavā".

"Because the Tathāgata, for the welfare of beings, associated with and aspired to the portions of qualities consisting of the knowable things (ñeyya) and attainments (samāpatti), therefore the Blessed One is called 'Bhagavā'."

How is he called "Bhagavā" because of associating with portions (bhaga)? Briefly stated, mundane (lokiya) and supramundane (lokuttara) successes (sampatti) are called "bhaga" because they are associated with by those who have performed prior merit and are endowed with effort, according to their own wealth. Among those successes, regarding mundane successes, the Tathāgata, previously as a Bodhisatta before attaining omniscience, associated with and cultivated mundane successes that were superior to others. Established in those mundane successes, he gathered the qualities that make one a Buddha and brought to maturity the factors of enlightenment. After becoming a Buddha, however, he associated with and cultivated those supramundane successes which are connected with faultless happiness and are not shared with others. In detail, he associated with and cultivated many various portions (bhaga) not shared with others, by way of regional kingship, sovereignty, the success of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti), the success of a king of devas, and so forth; and by way of superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) such as jhāna, liberation (vimokkha), concentration (samādhi), attainment (samāpatti), knowledge and vision (ñāṇadassana), development of the path (magga-bhāvanā), and the realization of the fruit (phala-sacchikiriyā). Thus, he is called "Bhagavā" because he associated with these portions.

"Whatever many mundane successes and supramundane successes there are in the world, the Fully Enlightened One associated with them all; therefore he is known as 'Bhagavā'."

How is he called "Bhagavā" because of having devoted followers (bhattavā)? There are many followers who devotedly associate with the Blessed One; therefore he is called "Bhagavā". Indeed, the Tathāgata is supreme among all beings because he is endowed with immeasurable and incomparable special qualities of power and virtue, such as the knowledge of Great Compassion (Mahākaruṇā) and Omniscience (Sabbaññutañāṇa); because he is of great benefit to the multitude of beings including devas and humans, being endowed with unsurpassed accomplishment of effort that is preceded by the removal of all harm and is dedicated to the provision of complete welfare and happiness; because he possesses a physical body (rūpakāya) adorned with unique special qualities not shared with others, such as the 32 marks of a Great Man (Mahāpurisalakkhaṇa), the 80 minor marks (anubyañjana), and the fathom-wide aura; because he is endowed with a very extensive and very pure sound of praise that pervades the three worlds, arising in the manner of "Thus indeed is that Blessed One..." through the attainment of true qualities; because he is well-established in qualities such as fewness of wishes (appicchatā) and contentment (santuṭṭhitā), which have reached the pinnacle of perfections (pāramī); because he is endowed with unsurpassed special qualities such as the Ten Powers (Dasabala) and the Fourfold Fearlessness (Catuvesārajja); because he brings about inspiration in every way for the beings of the world who belong to the four types of measurement (pamāṇa)—namely, those inspired by form (rūpappamāṇa), those inspired by sound (ghosappamāṇa), those inspired by austerity (lūkhappamāṇa), and those inspired by the Dhamma (dhammappamāṇa); because he is inspiring from all aspects, and because he is the object of immeasurable respect and devotion from devas and humans, he is the source of supreme love. Those devas and humans who abide in the instruction of that Blessed One are endowed with entering into confidence. To them, whether a monk or a brahmin...
9:
One who has faith in the Dhamma is called 'Dhammapasanna'. Thus, for the beings of the world who judge by the four measures, because he brings inspiration in every way and is inspiring in all aspects (samantapāsādika), he is the object of respect, esteem, and reverence for immeasurable gods and humans, and the ground for supreme love and devotion. Those gods and humans who stand in the instruction of that Blessed One and are endowed with unshakable faith, their devotion cannot be hindered or destroyed by any monk, brahmin, god, Mara, or Brahma. Therefore, even if they must sacrifice their lives, they do not abandon their faith in that Buddha, nor do they transgress his authority because of their firm devotion. Thus it is said:

'The wise person who is grateful and appreciative, who has good friends, and is firm in devotion...'

And: 'Monks, just as the great ocean is stable and does not exceed its shore, so my disciples do not transgress the training rules I have prescribed for them, even for the sake of their lives.'

In this way, from the word 'Bhattavā', by the method of linguistics (nirutti), one 'ta' is dropped and the remaining 'ta' is changed to 'ga', thus he is called 'Bhagavā'.

'Because many beings are devoted to the Teacher, who is endowed with supreme qualities and seeks the welfare of the world, he is therefore called Bhagavā.'

How is he called 'Bhagavā' because he discarded fortunes like vomit? Even while the Blessed One was a Bodhisatta, fulfilling the perfections in previous lives, he vomited and discarded the fortunes (bhaga) known as glory, sovereignty, and fame without any lingering attachment, like a glob of spit. Thus, in his lives as Prince Somanassa, Prince Hatthipāla, the wise Ayoghara, the wise Mūgapakkha, King Cūḷasutasoma, and so on, by way of fulfilling the perfection of renunciation, there is no measure to the number of existences in which he renounced royal glory similar to that of the king of gods. Even in his final existence, he regarded the glory of a Universal Monarch already in his hand—sovereignty over the four continents similar to the lordship of the heavenly realms, and the retinue shining with the seven jewels which is the basis of a Universal Monarch's success—as not even worth a blade of grass, and without lingering attachment, he renounced it, went forth, and realized Supreme Enlightenment. Therefore, because he vomited and discarded these fortunes such as the glory of a Universal Monarch, he is called 'Bhagavā'. Alternatively, 'Bhā' is the name for stars; those that move in accordance with the stars are called 'Bhagā'. The aspects of beauty (sobhā) that depend on the special features of the world, such as Mount Sineru, Mount Yugandhara, the Northern Continent, and the Himālaya, which endure for an aeon—the Blessed One has also vomited that beautiful portion. Because he transcended the dwelling places of beings who usually live in those regions, he abandoned the lust (rāga) connected with those places. Because he vomited the beautiful portion, he is called 'Bhagavā'. Because the Blessed One abandoned the glory, retinue, sovereignty, and happiness of a Universal Monarch and the diversity of the world, he is called 'Bhagavā'. How is he called 'Bhagavā' because he vomited the groups of dhammas? There are groups of dhammas by way of aggregates and so on; in those groups, by way of form, feeling, and so on...
10:
The aspects of beauty (bhaga) that depend on the special features of the world, such as Mount Sineru, Mount Yugandhara, the Northern Continent, and the Himālaya, exist because they endure for an aeon. The Blessed One has vomited those beautiful portions because he transcended the dwelling places of beings who usually live in those regions, and because he abandoned the lust (rāga) connected with them. In this way, because he vomited the 'bhaga' (beauty/fortune), he is called 'Bhagavā'.

'Because the Blessed One abandoned the glory of a Universal Monarch, fame, sovereignty, happiness, and the world's diversity, the Sugata is therefore called Bhagavā.'

How is he called 'Bhagavā' because he vomited the portions (bhāga)? 'Bhāga' means portions or groups (koṭṭhāsa). These groups are manifold by way of aggregates (khandha), sense bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu); and therein by way of form (rūpa), feeling (vedanā), and so on; and by way of the past and so on. When the Blessed One reached the Deathless Nibbāna, having utterly cut off all proliferation (papañca), all yokes (yoga), all ties (gantha), and all fetters (saṃyojana), he vomited, discarded, and threw away those groups without lingering attachment, and he did not return to them. For this reason, the Blessed One, by way of analyzing the dhammas in succession, has utterly vomited and discarded all groups of dhammas without remainder—namely, all earth, water, fire, air, eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, mental objects, eye-consciousness ...pe... mind-consciousness, eye-contact ...pe... mind-contact, feeling born of eye-contact ...pe... feeling born of mind-contact, perception born of eye-contact ...pe... perception born of mind-contact, volition born of eye-contact ...pe... volition born of mind-contact, craving for forms ...pe... craving for mental objects, thought of forms ...pe... thought of mental objects, examination of forms ...pe... examination of mental objects—by way of renunciation without lingering attachment. Thus it is said:

'Ananda, it is impossible that the Tathāgata would return to that which has been relinquished, vomited, released, abandoned, and discarded.'

In this way, because he vomited the portions (bhāga), he is called 'Bhagavā'. Alternatively, he is called 'Bhagavā' because he vomited, discarded, and abandoned all wholesome and unwholesome, blameworthy and blameless, low and excellent, dark and bright states through the door of the Noble Path Knowledge, and he taught the Dhamma to others for the sake of such attainment. Thus it is also said:

'Monks, you should abandon even (wholesome) dhammas, let alone non-dhammas. Monks, I will teach you the Dhamma compared to a raft, for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping,' and so forth.
11:
In this way, He is called 'Bhagavā' because He has discarded the groups of phenomena such as the aggregates (khandha) and sense bases (āyatana). "The Great Sage (Mahesi), the Blessed One, is known as Bhagavā because He has vomited and discarded the various phenomena such as the aggregates, sense bases, and elements (dhātu), as well as the dark and bright (wholesome and unwholesome) states." Therefore, it is said: "The Victorious Buddha is called Bhagavā because He possesses qualities such as virtue (sīla), has accumulated the structure of the Path of Arahatship and Omniscience, and has poured forth the grace of virtue. He has partaken of mundane and supramundane attainments and has the fourfold assembly of followers. He is called Bhagavā because He has vomited and discarded mundane attainments as well as the groups of phenomena such as the aggregates and sense bases."

That Blessed One is called 'Araha' because He is remote from defilements, has killed the enemies that are the defilements without remainder, has destroyed the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra, is worthy of receiving the four requisites and so forth, and does not perform evil even in secret. This is only a brief explanation here; the detailed explanation should be understood as stated in the Visuddhimagga.

In this context, by the word 'Bhagavatā', showing His state of being fortunate, it expresses the perfection of the form-body (rūpakāya-sampatti) which is unique and adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man, the eighty minor marks, the fathom-wide aura, and the garland of rays (ketumālā), etc., as He possesses the store of merit accumulated throughout many incalculable aeons. By the word 'Arahatā', showing His abandonment of all defilements without remainder, it expresses the perfection of the Dhamma-body (dhammakāya-sampatti) which is inconceivable and immeasurable, including the ten powers (dasabala), the four intrepidities (vesārajja), the six uncommon knowledges (asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa), and the eighteen unique Buddha-qualities (āveṇika-buddhadhamma), etc., because He has attained Omniscience which has the destruction of taints (āsavakkhaya) as its proximate cause. Due to these two attributes, His state of being highly cherished by those of similar nature in the world, His state of being approachable by laypeople and monks, His ability to remove the physical and mental suffering of those who approach Him, His helpfulness through the gift of material things and the gift of Dhamma, and His ability to unite others with mundane and supramundane qualities are made manifest.

Likewise, by the word 'Bhagavatā', the perfection of conduct (caraṇa-sampadā) is shown by illustrating His endowment with special abidings such as the divine abidings (dibba-vihāra), which are the pinnacle of the caraṇa-dhammas. By the word 'Arahatā', the perfection of knowledge (vijjā-sampadā) is shown by illustrating His attainment of the knowledge of the destruction of taints, which is the pinnacle of all knowledges (vijjā). Alternatively, by the former term, His endowment with the latter two intrepidities is shown by His unerring analysis and teaching of the states that are obstacles and the states that lead out of saṃsāra. By the latter term, the fulfillment of the first two intrepidities is shown by illustrating His abandonment of defilements along with their residual traces (vāsanā). Furthermore, by the former term, the fulfillment of the Resolve on Truth, Resolve on Determination, and Resolve on Generosity is shown by illustrating the Blessed One's truth of promise, truth of speech, and truth of knowledge; His renunciation of sensual pleasures, mundane sovereignty, and offerings; and His renunciation of all defilements and kamma-formations (abhisaṅkhāra). By the second term, showing the attainment of Nibbāna, the stilling of all formations...
12:
...His endowment with the first two intrepidities is made manifest by illustrating His abandonment of defilements along with their residual traces (vāsanā).

Furthermore, by the former term, the fulfillment of the Resolve on Truth (sacca-adhiṭṭhāna) and the Resolve on Generosity (cāga-adhiṭṭhāna) is made manifest by illustrating the Tathāgata's truth of promise, truth of speech, and truth of knowledge, as well as His renunciation of sensual pleasures, mundane sovereignty, gains, and honors, and His renunciation of all defilements and kamma-formations (abhisaṅkhāra). By the second term, the fulfillment of the Resolve on Peace (upasama-adhiṭṭhāna) and the Resolve on Wisdom (paññā-adhiṭṭhāna) is made manifest by illustrating His attainment of Nibbāna, the stilling of all formations, and His Perfect Self-Enlightenment (sammāsambodhi). Indeed, when the Blessed One was a Bodhisatta and made His resolution for supramundane qualities, His Resolve on Truth reached fulfillment through His practice of all perfections (pāramī) according to His promise, joined with Great Compassion (mahākaruṇā). His Resolve on Generosity reached fulfillment through His renunciation of things contrary to the perfections. His Resolve on Peace reached fulfillment through the stilling of the mind by means of the qualities of the perfections. His Resolve on Wisdom reached fulfillment through His skill in means (upāya-kosalla) for the welfare of others, even through the perfections.

Furthermore, His Resolve on Truth reached fulfillment by giving without fail, as He had promised, "I will give to the seekers without deceiving them." His Resolve on Generosity reached fulfillment through the renunciation of the objects to be given. His Resolve on Peace reached fulfillment through the stilling of greed, hatred, delusion, and fear regarding the recipient, the gift, and the exhaustion of the gift. His Resolve on Wisdom reached fulfillment through giving appropriately, at the right time, and in the proper manner, and through the supremacy of His wisdom. In this same way, the fulfillment of the four resolves should be understood in the remaining perfections as well. Indeed, all perfections are produced by truth, manifested by generosity, augmented by peace, and purified by wisdom. For the Tathāgata who has thus accomplished the four resolves: purification of virtue (sīla-visuddhi) arises from the accomplishment of the Resolve on Truth; purification of livelihood (ājīva-visuddhi) arises from the accomplishment of the Resolve on Generosity; purification of mind (citta-visuddhi) arises from the accomplishment of the Resolve on Peace; and purification of view (diṭṭhi-visuddhi) arises from the accomplishment of the Resolve on Wisdom. Furthermore, because of reaching the Resolve on Truth, His virtue (sīla) can be known through living together; because of reaching the Resolve on Generosity, His purity (soceyya) can be known through dealings; because of reaching the Resolve on Peace, His fortitude (thāma) can be known in times of adversity; and because of reaching the Resolve on Wisdom, His wisdom (paññā) can be known through discussion.

Moreover, because of reaching the Resolve on Truth, He endures without anger; because of reaching the Resolve on Generosity, He partakes without greed; because of reaching the Resolve on Peace, He avoids without fear; and because of reaching the Resolve on Wisdom, He dispels without delusion.
13:
Furthermore, through the attainment of the Blessed One's foundation of truth (saccādhiṭṭhāna), the attainment of the bliss of renunciation (nekkhammasukha) is shown; through the attainment of the foundation of relinquishment (cāgādhiṭṭhāna), the attainment of the bliss of seclusion (pavivekasukha); through the attainment of the foundation of peace (upasamādhiṭṭhāna), the attainment of the bliss of tranquility (upasamasukha); and through the attainment of the foundation of wisdom (paññādhiṭṭhāna), the attainment of the bliss of enlightenment (sambodhisukha) is shown.

Alternatively, through the attainment of the foundation of truth, the attainment of joy and bliss born of seclusion is shown; through the attainment of the foundation of relinquishment, the attainment of joy and bliss born of concentration; through the attainment of the foundation of peace, the attainment of physical bliss born of the absence of joy (pīti); and through the attainment of the foundation of wisdom, the attainment of the bliss of equanimity born of the purity of mindfulness is shown. Furthermore, through the attainment of the foundation of truth, because of its non-deceptive nature, the association with the bliss of requisites characterized by the perfection of retinue is shown. Through the attainment of the foundation of relinquishment, because of the absence of greed, the association with natural bliss characterized by contentment is shown. Through the attainment of the foundation of peace, because of being unvanquished by the defilements, the association with causal bliss characterized by having performed meritorious deeds is shown. Through the attainment of the foundation of wisdom, because of the attainment of Nibbāna through the perfection of knowledge, the association with the bliss of the cessation of suffering characterized by the perfection of liberation (vimutti) is shown.

Furthermore, through the attainment of the foundation of truth, the accomplishment of the understanding and penetration of the noble aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha) is shown; through the attainment of the foundation of relinquishment, that of the noble aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha); through the attainment of the foundation of wisdom, that of the noble aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha); and through the attainment of the foundation of peace, the accomplishment of the understanding and penetration of the noble aggregate of liberation (vimuttikkhandha) is shown. Through the fulfillment of the foundation of truth, the accomplishment of spiritual power (tapa) is achieved; through the fulfillment of the foundation of relinquishment, the accomplishment of total renunciation; through the fulfillment of the foundation of peace, the accomplishment of the restraint of the sense faculties; through the fulfillment of the foundation of wisdom, the accomplishment of insight (buddhi); and through that very foundation of wisdom, the accomplishment of Nibbāna is achieved. Furthermore, through the fulfillment of the foundation of truth, the acquisition of the penetration of the Four Noble Truths is shown; through the fulfillment of the foundation of relinquishment, the acquisition of the four noble lineages (ariya-vaṃsa); through the fulfillment of the foundation of peace, the acquisition of the four noble abidings (ariya-vihāra); and through the fulfillment of the foundation of wisdom, the acquisition of the four noble modes of expression (ariya-vohāra) is shown.

Another method: By the word 'Bhagavatā' (by the Blessed One), the Great Compassion (mahākaruṇā) of the Tathāgata is manifested by showing the desire for the mundane and supramundane success of beings. By the word 'Arahatā' (by the Worthy One), the wisdom of abandonment (pahāna-paññā) is manifested by showing the perfection of abandonment (pahāna-sampatti). In this regard, through His wisdom, the Blessed One attained the Kingdom of Dhamma; through His compassion, He shares the Dhamma. Through His wisdom, He is weary of the suffering of saṃsāra; through His compassion, He endures the suffering of saṃsāra. Through His wisdom, He fully understands the suffering of others; through His compassion, He undertakes the remedying of others' suffering. Through His wisdom...
14:
Through His wisdom, He inclines toward Parinibbāna; through His compassion, He strives so that others may reach that Parinibbāna. Through His wisdom, He Himself crosses over the cycle of rebirth; through His compassion, He enables others to cross over. Through His wisdom, the state of Buddhahood is accomplished; through His compassion, the duties of a Buddha are accomplished. Alternatively, because of His compassion, He inclines toward the cycle of rebirth in His existence as a Bodhisatta; because of His wisdom, He finds no delight in that cycle of rebirth. Likewise, through His compassion, He does not harm others; through His wisdom, He Himself has no fear of others. When He protects others through His compassion, it amounts to protecting Himself; when He protects Himself through His wisdom, it amounts to protecting others. Likewise, because of His compassion, He does not torment others; because of His wisdom, He does not torment Himself. By thus not tormenting, He accomplishes the state of the fourth type of person among those who practice for their own benefit and so forth.

Likewise, because of His compassion, He is the refuge of the world; because of His wisdom, He is His own refuge. Because of His compassion, the Blessed One has a humble demeanor; because of His wisdom, He has an exalted demeanor. Likewise, because of His compassion, He brings about the welfare of all beings; yet, because He follows wisdom, it is not that His mind is not detached from all things (it is indeed detached). Because of His wisdom, His mind is detached from all phenomena; yet, because He follows compassion, it is not that He does not act for the welfare of all beings (He indeed acts). Just as the Blessed One's compassion is free from affection and grief, so too His wisdom is liberated from the conceit of 'I' (ahaṃkāra) and the conceit of 'mine' (mamaṃkāra). Thus, they should be understood as supremely pure, having been purified by each other. Between these two, the domain of wisdom is the Ten Powers (bala), and the domain of compassion is the Four Intrepidities (vesārajja). Among them, because He is endowed with the Powers, He is not vanquished by others; because He is endowed with the Intrepidities, He vanquishes others. Through the Powers, the perfection of the Teacher (satthu-sampadā) is accomplished; through the Intrepidities, the perfection of the Dispensation (sāsana-sampadā) is accomplished. Likewise, through the Powers, the Jewel of the Buddha is accomplished; through the Intrepidities, the Jewel of the Dhamma is accomplished. This is a mere indication of the application of the meaning of the two words 'Bhagavatā Arahatā' in this context.

Why, then, in this context, after saying 'vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā' (for this was said by the Blessed One), is the word 'vuttaṃ' (said) stated again? It is for the purpose of showing a definite determination (niyama) by rejecting hearsay (anussava). For example, when something is spoken by someone after hearing it from another, even if he speaks with knowledge, it was not spoken by him alone because it had also been spoken by another. And that statement is not only 'spoken' by him but also 'heard'. It is not so here. The Blessed One, without hearing from another, spoke only that Dhamma which He Himself attained through His self-evolved knowledge (sayambhū-ñāṇa). To show this distinction, the word 'vuttaṃ' is stated twice. This is what is meant: in saying 'this word was spoken by the Blessed One,' it means that word was spoken by the Blessed One alone, not by another; and it was indeed 'spoken' (from direct realization), not 'heard' (from another). Since the additional word conveys another meaning, there is no fault of tautology (punarutti). This method should also be understood in the words that follow.
15:
Similarly, the word "vuttaṃ" (it was said) is stated twice to show the absence of prior preparation. Indeed, because the Blessed One is the Fully Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha), he teaches the Dhamma according to the disposition of the assembled audience through spontaneous intuition (paṭibhāna) arising at that moment; for the Blessed One, there is no task of prior preparation as there might be for acts like giving (dāna) and so forth. Therefore, this following meaning is shown: "The Blessed One has truly spoken this word; moreover, it was not spoken through prior preparation, nor was it arrived at through mere reasoning or followed by investigation. Rather, it was spoken spontaneously in accordance with the disposition of those to be guided (veneyya)."

Alternatively, "vuttaṃ" is stated twice to show that the word is irreversible. Whatever word the Blessed One has spoken, it is indeed spoken; it cannot be refuted by anyone because of its perfection in phrasing (akkharasampatti) and its perfection in meaning (atthasampatti). Has it not been stated thus: "This unsurpassed Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakka) was set in motion by the Blessed One at the Deer Park in Isipatana, near Bārāṇasī, and it cannot be turned back (or stopped) by any recluse or brahmin," and so forth?

It has also been stated elsewhere: "Monks, if a recluse or a brahmin should come here and say, 'This is not the Noble Truth of Suffering (Dukkha Ariyasacca) as proclaimed by the recluse Gotama; I will set aside this Noble Truth of Suffering and proclaim another Noble Truth of Suffering,' such a thing is impossible," and so forth. Therefore, "vuttaṃ" is stated twice also to show the state of the word being irreversible.

In another way, "vuttaṃ" is stated twice to show that it fulfills the benefit of the listeners. Whatever is spoken by one who is not omniscient, who does not know the disposition and so forth of others, or is spoken in an improper place or at an improper time—even if that word is true—it may be called "unsaid" (avutta) because of its inability to fulfill the benefit of the listeners, let alone if it were untrue. But the Blessed One, because of his state as the Fully Enlightened One, speaks with full knowledge of the disposition and so forth of others, the proper place and time, and the fulfillment of the benefit. Since it definitely fulfills the intended benefit of the listeners, it is indeed "spoken" (vutta); there is no sense in which it could be considered "unsaid." Therefore, "vuttaṃ" is stated twice also to show that it fulfills the benefit of the listeners.

Furthermore, just as something is not called "heard" (suta) if its meaning is not understood or if it is not practiced for the sake of suchness, so too, a word is not called "spoken" (vutta) if it is not properly received. As for the word of the Blessed One, the fourfold assembly receives it well...
16:
(The fourfold assembly) having received it, they practice according to that teaching. Therefore, "vuttaṃ" is stated twice also to show the state of being properly received.

Alternatively, "vuttaṃ" is stated twice to show that the word is not contradictory to the Noble Ones (Ariyas). Indeed, just as the Blessed One teaches without deviation concerning states such as wholesome and unwholesome, blameworthy and blameless, and concerning conventional and ultimate truths in their aspects of arising and ceasing, so too the Noble Ones, such as the General of the Dhamma (Dhammasenāpati), follow and teach only the Blessed One's instruction, whether during his lifetime or after his Parinibbāna; there is no divergence of views therein. Therefore, it is stated thus to show the state of the word being uncontradicted by the Noble Ones: "It was spoken by the Arahant, and subsequently, it was also spoken by the Noble Saṅgha of Arahants."

In another way, "vuttaṃ" is stated twice to show that it follows the method spoken by previous Fully Enlightened Ones. Although there are differences in terms of birth, clan, and lifespan, there is no difference among the Buddhas in their teaching of the Dhamma, just as there is no difference in their qualities such as the Ten Powers (Dasabala). They speak without contradiction between one another and between their own earlier and later words. Therefore, "vuttaṃ" is stated twice also to show that it follows the method spoken by previous Buddhas and by himself in other discourses (suttas), as in: "Just as it was spoken by the Buddhas of the past and by himself previously, so too it is spoken now by our Blessed One, the Arahant." By this, the absence of contradiction in the Buddhas' teaching in all respects is illustrated.

Alternatively, this second word "vuttaṃ" should be understood as a statement of the fact that it was spoken by the Arahant. This is what is meant: "This was spoken by the Blessed One, and it was also spoken by the Arahant—namely, the word now being spoken, 'Monks, one thing...'" and so forth.

In another way, this second word "vuttaṃ" should be understood not in the sense of "speaking," but in the sense of "sowing" (vapana). By this, it shows: "This was spoken by the Blessed One, and it was not merely spoken or merely told; rather, the root of merit (kusalamūla) was sown in the hearts of those to be guided (veneyya)."

Alternatively, this second word "vuttaṃ" has the sense of "conduct" or "practice" (vattana). This is its meaning: "This was spoken by the Blessed One, the Arahant, and it was not merely spoken, but that very essence of meaning was practiced (vutta/carita)." By this, it shows: "As the Blessed One speaks, so he acts" (Yathāvādī tathākārī).

In another way, it means: "It was spoken by the Blessed One; the spoken word was uttered by the one who is fit to speak (the Arahant)."
17:
Alternatively, the word "vutta" (said) is spoken with reference to the indication of the brief discourse; then again, the word "vutta" is spoken with reference to the illustration of the detailed discourse. Indeed, the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma both in brief and in detail. Alternatively, after saying "vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā" (For this was said by the Blessed One), the word "vuttaṃ" (said) is spoken again for the purpose of showing that there is no wrongly spoken word in the Blessed One. Because the Blessed One's verbal actions always follow knowledge, and because He has abandoned all faults along with their latent tendencies and possesses unerring speech, there is never any such thing as a wrongly spoken word for Him.

In the world, some people, either through forgetfulness or ignorance, say something and then, upon regaining their memory, act as if what was said before was not said, or they revise it; the Blessed One is not like that. The Blessed One is always concentrated. He possesses the quality of non-disappearance (of mindfulness) and the quality of non-delusion. With the analytical insight of perspicuity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā) associated with omniscience, He brings forth the meaning. Through special faculties that are exceptionally pure and unique, arising from the accumulation of immeasurable merit gathered over an infinite time, He manifests the Four Noble Truths—the essence to be heard, the supreme hearing (savananuttariya)—like raining down the rain of the Deathless upon those who listen, serving as a tonic for the sense of hearing. He speaks words in accordance with the natural language (sabhāvanirutti) and the dispositions of those to be led (veneyya), with a voice as sweet as the song of the Karavīka bird. In such teaching, there is not even a hair's breadth of error; how then could there be an opportunity for a wrongly spoken word? Therefore, to show that "what was said by the Blessed One is indeed said, and is never unsaid or wrongly said," after saying "vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā," it is said again "vuttam-arahatā" (said by the Arahant). Thus, there is no fault of repetition (punaruttidosa) here. In this way, the purposefulness of the repeated word in this Pali text should be understood.

In the phrase "iti me sutaṃ," this word "iti" has many various meanings such as cause (hetu), conclusion (parisamāpana), beginning (ādi), synonym (padatthavipariyāya), manner (pakāra), indication (nidassana), determination (avadhāraṇa), and so forth. Thus, this word "iti" is seen in the sense of cause in such passages as: "Monks, it is deformed (ruppati), therefore it is called form (rūpa)." It is seen in the sense of conclusion in such passages as: "Therefore, monks, be heirs of the Dhamma, not heirs of material things. I have compassion for you: How may my disciples be heirs of the Dhamma, and not heirs of material things?" It is seen in the sense of beginning in such passages as: "Thus (iti) or thus (iti), he abstains from watching such shows which are a thorn to the dispensation." It is seen in the sense of synonym in such passages as: "Māgaṇḍiya is the designation, name, concept, usage, name, naming, naming-process, language, syllable, and expression of that brahmin." It is seen in the sense of manner in such passages as: "In this manner (iti), monks, the fool is fearful, the wise man is not fearful; the fool is calamitous, the wise man is not calamitous; the fool is with affliction (upasagga)..."
18:
"...the wise man is without affliction." In such passages, it is in the sense of manner (pakāra). In passages such as: "Kaccāna, 'everything exists' is one extreme; Kaccāna, 'everything does not exist' is the second extreme," it is in the sense of indication (nidassana). In passages such as: "Ānanda, if it is asked, 'Are there aging and death due to this condition?' it should be answered, 'There are.' If it is asked, 'Due to what condition are there aging and death?' it should be answered, 'Aging and death are due to the condition of birth,'" it is in the sense of determination (avadhāraṇa) and ascertainment (sanniṭṭhāna). In this context, this word "iti" should be understood in the senses of manner, indication, and determination.

Among those three meanings, the word "iti" in the sense of manner (pakāra) shows this meaning: Who is capable of fully knowing in every way the word of the Blessed One, which is subtle through various methods, arising from many dispositions (ajjhāsaya), endowed with meaning and phrasing, possessing various miracles, profound in Dhamma, meaning, teaching, and penetration, and reaching the ear-path of all beings in accordance with their respective languages? However, even while generating the desire to hear with all one's might, it is stated as: "In this manner I heard; I too heard in one manner."

In this context, the methods known as the method of unity (ekatta), the method of diversity (nānatta), the method of non-activity (abyāpāra), and the method of the nature of things (evaṃdhammatā), as well as the methods known as the Nandiyāvaṭṭa, Tipukkhala, Sīhavikkīḷita, Disālocana, and Aṅkusa, are called "various methods" (nānānaya) because they are diverse and manifold according to the division of objects and so forth. Alternatively, the ways of the Pali (pāḷigati) are called methods (naya). These are called "various methods" because they are diverse and manifold by way of designation (paññatti) and secondary designation (anupaññatti), etc.; by way of being part of defilement (saṃkilesabhāgiya), being mundane (lokiya), or a mixture of both, etc.; by way of the wholesome (kusala), etc.; by way of the aggregates (khandha), etc.; by way of compendium (saṅgaha), etc.; by way of being liberated by occasion (samayavimutta), etc.; by way of establishment (ṭhapanā), etc.; by way of the roots of the wholesome (kusalamūla), etc.; and by way of the Triads of the Paṭṭhāna (tikapaṭṭhāna), etc. Because it is subtle through these various methods, it is called "nānānayanipuṇa" (subtle through various methods).

Disposition (āsaya) is itself "ajjhāsaya." That disposition is of many kinds by way of the division of the eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi), etc., and by way of the division of having little dust in the eyes (apparajakkha), etc. Alternatively, one's own disposition (attajjhāsaya), etc., is itself "many dispositions" (anekajjhāsaya). Because those many dispositions are the cause of the arising (samuṭṭhāna) of that word, it is called "anekajjhāsayasamuṭṭhāna."

It is called "atthabyañjanasampanna" (endowed with meaning and phrasing) because it is endowed with the fulfillment of meaning such as the wholesome, etc., and the fulfillment of phrasing that clarifies that meaning; and because it is endowed with the six terms of meaning: brief indication (saṅkāsana), detailed explanation (pakāsana), opening up (vivaraṇa), analysis (vibhajana), making plain (uttānīkaraṇa), and designation (paññatti); and with the six terms of phrasing: syllable (akkhara), word (pada), phrasing (byañjana), mode (ākāra), language (nirutti), and description (niddesa).
19:
Because there are various or manifold miracles (pāṭihāriya) by way of the miracle of psychic power (iddhipāṭihāriya), the miracle of mind-reading (ādesanāpāṭihāriya), and the miracle of instruction (anusāsanīpāṭihāriya), and by way of the various objects (visaya) of each of those miracles, it is called 'Vividhapāṭihāriya' (Various Miracles).

In the word 'pāṭihāriya', although it has the meaning of 'pāṭihāriya' because it removes opposition or because it dispels defilements such as lust (rāga), there are no opposing factors such as lust to be removed in the Blessed One. Even in worldlings (puthujjanas), when the mind is free from impurities, endowed with the eight qualities, and has destroyed opposition, the various modes of psychic power (iddhividha) can occur. Therefore, it is not possible to use the term 'pāṭihāriya' in this context based on the conventional usage occurring in such psychic powers. However, because the defilements in the mental continuities of the trainable beings (veneyya) who are the objects of the Great Compassionate One's [teaching] are the opposing factors, it is called 'pāṭihāriya' because it removes those defilements. Alternatively, it is called 'pāṭihāriya' because it removes the ascetics of other sects (titthiyas) who are opponents of the Blessed One and the Dispensation (Sāsana). Indeed, those [titthiyas] are removed and dispelled by the miracles of psychic power, mind-reading, and instruction, through the removal of their wrong views (micchādiṭṭhi) and through their inability to demonstrate their own views.

The word 'paṭi' has the meaning of 'pacchā' (after). Therefore, it is called 'paṭihāriya' because it is made to occur after (pacchā) the task to be done has been performed in a concentrated mind free from impurities. Or, 'paṭihāriya' means the removal [of defilements in others] after (pacchā) one's own defilements have been removed by the fourth jhāna and the Path (magga). The miracles of psychic power, mind-reading, and instruction are also made to occur again for the benefit of beings by a person who is free from impurities and has completed the task; since the removal of defilements in the continuities of others occurs after one's own defilements have been removed, they are called 'pāṭihāriya'. 'Paṭihāriya' itself is 'pāṭihāriya'. Or, each individual [miracle] occurring in the collection of miracles of psychic power, mind-reading, and instruction is called 'pāṭihāriya'. Or, the fourth jhāna and the Path are called 'paṭihāriya' because they remove opposition; it is called 'pāṭihāriya' because it arises in that fourth jhāna and Path, or because it occurs with that as its cause, or because it comes from that.

However, the profundity of Dhamma, meaning (attha), teaching (desanā), and penetration (paṭivedha)—referred to as the sequence of the Pali, the sequence of meaning, the preaching, and the realization of that teaching; or referred to as the designation and penetration of cause, effect, and both—is profound. Just as the great ocean is difficult to plunge into and offers no footing for small animals like hares that have not accumulated the necessary strength, these teachings are difficult to plunge into and difficult to find a footing in. Therefore, because it is endowed with these four types of profundity, it is called 'Dhamma-attha-desanā-paṭivedha-gambhīra' (Profound in Dhamma, meaning, teaching, and penetration).

Even though the single sound of the Blessed One's Dhamma teaching occurs in a single moment, it enables beings of various languages to understand it according to their own respective languages, without any before or after, leading to the attainment of the meaning. The majesty of the Buddhas is inconceivable (acinteyya).
20:
Indeed, it should be understood that by the majesty of the Buddhas (buddhānubhāva), [the teaching] reaches the path of the ear (sotapatha) of all beings in accordance with their own respective languages.

With the sense of indication (nidassana), [the Elder Ānanda] indicates the entire sutta to be spoken now, saying, "Thus have I heard; I too have heard in this way," thereby freeing himself [from self-exaltation] by implying, "I am not the self-enlightened one (sayambhū); I did not realize this [Dhamma] by myself."

With the sense of determination (avadhāraṇa), the Blessed One said, "Monks, among my monk disciples who are very learned (bahussuta), Ānanda is the foremost; among those who possess wisdom, mindfulness, and resolution, and among those who are attendants, Ānanda is the foremost." Likewise, the General of the Dhamma (Venerable Sāriputta) praised him, saying, "The Venerable Ānanda is skilled in the meaning (attha), skilled in the Dhamma, skilled in the phrasing (byañjana), skilled in the linguistics (nirutti), and skilled in the sequence [of the teaching]." In accordance with being so praised, [the Elder Ānanda] wishes to show his own power of retention (dhāraṇabala) and thus generates a desire to listen in beings, [implying]: "Thus have I heard; and that hearing is exactly like this, neither less nor more in meaning or phrasing, and not otherwise." "Not otherwise" means not other than the manner in which it was heard from the presence of the Blessed One; it does not mean [not other than] the manner in which it was taught by the Blessed One. For the Blessed One's teaching has inconceivable majesty, and it is not possible to know that teaching in every aspect—this is the intended meaning. Only the non-contradiction with the manner in which it was heard is called the power of retention (dhāraṇabala). In this context, the exclusion of another meaning is not intended, because both meanings have the same object. Otherwise, it would follow that the Elder was either [entirely] capable or incapable of receiving the Blessed One's teaching in every aspect.

The word 'me' is found in three senses. Specifically, in such passages as "Gāthābhigītaṃ me abhojaneyyaṃ," it has the sense of "mayā" (by me). In such passages as "Sādhu me, bhante, bhagavā saṅkhittena dhammaṃ desetu," it has the sense of "mayhaṃ" (to/for me). In such passages as "Dhammadāyādā me, bhikkhave, bhavatha," it has the sense of "mama" (my/of me). In this context, however, it is appropriate in both senses: "mayā sutaṃ" (heard by me) and "mama sutaṃ" (my hearing).

Furthermore, since that which is not another is called the self (atta), and because it occurs in one's own continuity referred to as one's internal self, even if the word 'me' is seen in only one sense [of self], there still exists this distinction of meanings known as the specific cases of the instrumental (karaṇa) and the dative (sampadāna), etc. Therefore, he said, "The word 'me' is found in three senses."
21:
The word "sutaṃ" has many various meanings, whether with a prefix or without, such as going, becoming famous, being wet, accumulating, practicing repeatedly, being cognizable by ear-consciousness, and being known sequentially as sounds reach the ear-door. In truth, although a prefix (upasagga) specifically modifies a verb, because it illuminates the meaning even when present, it is the word "suta" itself that expresses those respective meanings. Therefore, in extracting the meaning of the word "suta" without a prefix, words with prefixes are also cited as examples.

Among those meanings, in passages such as "senāya pasuto" (he goes with an army), it means "one who goes." In passages such as "sutadhammassa passato" (one who sees the famous Dhamma), it means "one who possesses the famous Dhamma." In passages such as "avassutā avassutassa" (a lustful woman for a lustful man), it means "one who is wet (with defilements)." In passages such as "tumhehi puññaṃ pasutaṃ anappakaṃ" (you have accumulated much merit), it means "accumulated." In passages such as "ye jhānappasutā dhīrā" (those wise ones who are devoted to Jhana), it means "those who practice repeatedly in Jhana." In passages such as "diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ mutaṃ," it means "cognized by ear-consciousness." In passages such as "sutadharo sutasannicayo," it means "one who remembers the Dhamma known sequentially as sounds reach the ear-door." In this sentence "Evaṃ me sutaṃ," however, the meaning of this word "suta" is "noted and retained by reflecting sequentially on the sounds reaching the ear-door" or "the act of noting."

If the word "me" means "by me" (mayā), the meaning is: "Thus has it been noted by me through the ear-door." If it means "of me" (mama), the meaning is: "Thus is the noting of me through the ear-door."

Thus, among these three words, since the word "iti" used in conjunction with the word "suta" illuminates the act of hearing, the word "iti" indicates the function of consciousness such as ear-consciousness, and the word "me" indicates the person endowed with the aforementioned consciousness. All sentences are accompanied by the sense of the word "eva" (only/certainly) because they have the benefit of emphasis (avadhāraṇa). Therefore, the word "sutaṃ" indicates noting without deficiency or distortion by rejecting the state of not hearing. Indeed, just as what is heard deserves to be called "only what was heard," such good hearing is noting without deficiency and noting without distortion. Alternatively, because a word expresses its meaning by excluding the meaning of other words, the word "sutaṃ" means "it is not non-hearing." Therefore, the word "sutaṃ" rejects non-hearing and indicates noting without deficiency or distortion.

This is what is meant: "Thus I have heard; it was not seen, it was not realized by self-enlightened knowledge (sayambhū-ñāṇa), it was not obtained by any other means; rather, it was only heard, and that hearing was indeed heard well." Or, when the word "iti" has the sense of emphasis (avadhāraṇa), this interpretation of the meaning belongs to the word "suta" which regards that word "iti"...
22:
The interpretation of meaning in the word "iti" having the sense of emphasis (avadhāraṇa) is appropriate; therefore, the meaning of the word "suta" which regards that word "iti" should be the sense of certainty (niyama). In this way, it should be understood as rejecting non-hearing and indicating noting without deficiency and noting without distortion. Thus, it should be noted that the interpretation of the three words is made through the cause of hearing and the distinction of hearing.

Furthermore, the word "iti" should be understood as having the sense of "manner" (ākāra), expressing the occurrence of the object in various ways because of grasping various meanings and sounds in the cognitive process (vīthi) that occurs following the sounds reaching the ear-door. The word "me" is the revelation of oneself. The word "sutaṃ" is the revelation of the Dhamma, because the aforementioned cognitive process takes the scriptural Dhamma (pariyatti-dhamma) as its object. The summary here is: "Through the cognitive process which is the cause and which occurs in the object in various ways, I have done nothing else; I have only heard this Dhamma."

Furthermore, the word "iti" should be understood as having the sense of "illustration" (nidassana), expressing the meaning to be pointed out. This is because there is no absence of the state of being pointed out for the meaning to be pointed out. Therefore, by the word "iti," it should be understood that the entire discourse (sutta) is repeatedly reflected upon. The word "me" is the revelation of the person. The word "sutaṃ" is the revelation of the person's function. The reason is that the act of hearing obtained by the word "suta" is connected with the continuity of hearing-consciousness, and in that continuity of consciousness, there is the conventional designation of a "person." This is because the act of hearing cannot be obtained in a continuity of phenomena (dhamma) devoid of the conventional designation of a person. The summary meaning of that Pali is: "Whatever sutta I shall point out, that sutta has been thus heard by me."

Furthermore, the word "iti" should be understood as having the sense of "manner" (ākāra), expressing the occurrence of that mental continuum in various modes, because that mental continuum grasps various meanings and sounds due to its occurrence in various objects. The reason is that this designation "iti" is a conceptual manner (ākāra-paññatti), having the nature of making things known by depending on the respective modes of occurrence of phenomena. The word "me" is the designation of the agent (kattar). The word "sutaṃ" is the designation of the object (visaya). Indeed, the Dhamma that is heard is the station of occurrence by way of the act of hearing for the person who is the agent of the act of hearing. By this much, the grasping and determination in the object by the agent endowed with that mental continuum, through the mental continuum occurring in various ways, is shown.

Alternatively, the word "iti" is the designation of the person's function. The reason is that, by the word "iti" which expresses the manner of grasping, the illustration, or the determination of the Dhammas that have been heard, the bearing of those manners and so forth is the activity (byāpāra) of the continuity of phenomena which occurs depending on the conventional designation of a "person"...
23:
A function is indeed indicated. "Sutaṃ" (heard) is the indication of the function of consciousness (viññāṇa). Even for the Personalists (Puggalavādins), the act of hearing is not independent of consciousness. The word "me" is the indication of the person associated with the dual function. Indeed, the occurrence of the word "me" definitely has a specific being (satta) as its object. It should be understood that the function of consciousness is also integrated by making that specific being the object. The summary here is: "Sutaṃ" (I have heard) is the summary of the person endowed with consciousness which has the act of hearing called "I," and who possesses the designation of the function of hearing obtained through the power of consciousness.

Furthermore, the designations "iti" (thus) and "me" (by me) are concepts of the non-existent (avijjamāna-paññatti) in terms of ultimate reality (paramattha). Indeed, all meanings to be understood must be approached through the medium of designation. All designations are included within the six types of designations, such as the concept of the existent (vijjamāna-paññatti). Therefore, it is not an unreal meaning like magic or a mirage, nor is it an inferior meaning like that which is to be taken from hearsay. That ultimate nature, characterized by transformation (ruppana) and experiencing (anubhavana), such as form and sound, exists by way of ultimate reality. However, that which is called "iti" and "me," such as modes (ākāra) and so on, which are not of ultimate nature and are not found in the sense of ultimate reality, is called the concept of the non-existent (avijjamāna-paññatti). In this context, where could that indication which might be received as "iti" or "me" exist in the ultimate sense? The designation "sutaṃ" is a concept of the existent (vijjamāna-paññatti). This is because that which is cognized by the ear exists in the ultimate sense.

Furthermore, the word "iti" is a derivative concept (upādā-paññatti) by way of reflecting again on those modes of attention and so on, depending on the phenomena that have come into the range of the ear. The word "me" is a derivative concept (upādā-paññatti) because it is spoken depending on the aggregates (khandhas) included in one's own continuity, distinguished by such factors as agency. The word "sutaṃ" is a comparative concept (upanidhā-paññatti) because it is spoken in comparison to what is seen and so on. Even though the term "suta" occurs in the sound-base (saddāyatana) which is devoid of the nature of the seen and so on, just as "second" or "third" depends on "first," it is to be understood as "that which is not independent of the seen, the sensed, and the cognized is 'heard'"; thus, it is spoken in comparison to the seen and so on. The meaning is expressed as "sutaṃ" to show it is "not unheard."

In this context, by the word "iti," the Venerable Ānanda shows non-confusion (asammoha). Indeed, the various aspects of the meaning that have been penetrated are reflected upon here by the Venerable Ānanda with the word "iti"; thereby, his non-confusion is shown. For one who is confused is not capable of penetrating various aspects. The meanings of the Suttas, which are of various kinds and difficult to penetrate by way of the abandonment of greed and so on...
24:
(The Venerable Ānanda) indicates. By the word "sutaṃ," he shows non-forgetfulness (asammosa). This is because the manner of hearing is shown as it really is. For if the teaching heard by someone is forgotten, he cannot later admit, "I have heard it." Thus, through this non-confusion or absence of confusion, or through the wisdom (paññā) arising at the time of hearing, the wisdom of the subsequent time is established; likewise, through non-forgetfulness, mindfulness (sati) is established. In that establishment, with mindfulness preceded by wisdom, one is capable of retaining the phrasing (byañjana). Because the aspect of the phrasing to be penetrated is not very profound, and since the only thing to be done there is to remember it as heard, the exertion of mindfulness is predominant. Wisdom, though preceding it, remains in a subordinate role. With wisdom preceded by mindfulness, one is capable of penetrating the meaning (attha). Because the aspect of the meaning to be penetrated is profound, the exertion of wisdom is predominant. Mindfulness, though preceding it, remains in a subordinate role. By being endowed with both these capabilities, one is able to preserve the treasury of the Dhamma, which is complete in meaning and phrasing; thus, the status of "Treasurer of the Dhamma" (Dhamma-bhaṇḍāgārika) is established.

Another method: By the word "iti," he shows wise attention (yoniso manasikāra). This is because the aspects, indications, and meanings of retention expressed by that word "iti," as well as the words to be mentioned hereafter which illuminate the penetration of various aspects, have the unerring True Dhamma as their object. For one who does not attend wisely, the penetration of various aspects is not possible. By the word "sutaṃ," he shows non-distraction (avikkhepa). The hearing of the Sutta to be spoken, which has come to the occasion by way of the inquiry into the origin (nidāna), is not possible without composure, for there is no hearing for one with a distracted mind. Indeed, even if a distracted person is spoken to with all perfection, he says, "I did not hear it; please say it again." In this context, through wise attention, he accomplishes right self-direction (atta-sammā-paṇidhi) and the state of having performed merit in the past (pubbe-kata-puññatā). This is because for one who has not directed himself rightly or has not performed merit in the past, that wise attention is absent. Through non-distraction, he accomplishes the hearing of the True Dhamma and association with the virtuous (sappurisa-upanissaya). This is because for one who has not heard and is devoid of association with the virtuous, that non-distraction is absent. For a distracted person is unable to listen to the True Dhamma, and for one who does not associate with the virtuous, there is no hearing.

Another method: It is said, "For that mental continuity in which the grasping of various meanings and phrasings occurs due to the occurrence of various modes, there is an indication by way of various modes." And because that Venerable Ānanda, by way of defining the distinctions of meaning and phrasing of the Buddha's words, and by plunging into the perfection of the entire Dispensation, became the cause for fulfilling the welfare of others without remainder...
25:
Such a noble manner is not possible for one whose mind is ill-directed or who has not performed merit in the past. Therefore, by this noble manner expressed as 'Iti', he shows his own endowment with the last two wheels (cakka-dvaya). By the connection with hearing expressed as 'Sutaṃ', he shows his endowment with the first two wheels. This is because hearing is not possible for one living in an unsuitable locality or for one devoid of association with the virtuous. Thus, through the accomplishment of the last two wheels of the Venerable Ānanda, the purity of his inclination (āsaya-suddhi) is accomplished. One who has a well-directed mind and has performed merit in the past possesses a pure inclination, because of being far from the defilements that cause impurity of inclination.

Indeed, it is true; therefore it was said:
"A well-directed mind can do for one even more than what [parents and relatives] can do."
"Ānanda, you have performed merit; apply yourself to meditation; you will soon be free from taints (anāsava)," He said.

Through the accomplishment of the first two wheels, purity of application (payoga-suddhi) occurs. By living in a suitable locality and associating with the virtuous, pure application arises even through following the example of the virtuous. Due to that purity of inclination, skill in knowing the attainment (adhigama) is accomplished, because of having previously purified the defilements such as craving (taṇhā) and wrong view (diṭṭhi). Due to the purity of application, skill in the scriptural tradition (āgama) is accomplished. Indeed, one with extremely pure application of body and speech, being free from remorse and thus having an undistracted mind, becomes confident in the scriptures (pariyatti). Thus, the words of the Venerable Ānanda—who is pure in application and inclination, and endowed with the scriptural tradition and attainment—are like the dawn before the sun rises, or like wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) for wholesome states. Since they are worthy of being the precursor to the Buddha's words, he placed the introduction (nidāna) in its proper place, saying "Iti me sutaṃ" and so forth.

Another way: By this word 'Iti', in the manner previously mentioned as indicating various types of penetration, he shows his own possession of the analytical insights of meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā) and perspicuity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā).
