By this word 'Sutaṃ', either because of its proximity to the word 'Iti' or because of its regard for what is to be said, he shows his possession of the analytical insights of Dhamma (dhamma-paṭisambhidā) and language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā) by indicating the penetration of the various aspects of what is to be heard. By speaking this word 'Iti', he shows: "These teachings have been reflected upon by me with the mind and well-penetrated by wisdom." For the scriptural teachings (pariyatti-dhamma) are reflected upon with the mind in such a way as: "Here virtue is taught, here concentration, here wisdom; there are this many sequences (anusandhi)," and so forth. Having well-defined the material and immaterial phenomena mentioned here and there—such as "This is matter, this much is matter"—through wisdom known as 'acceptance through reflecting on the Dhamma' (dhamma-nijjhāna-khanti) or 'full understanding of the known' (ñāta-pariññā), which is accompanied by successive hearing and contemplation, they are penetrated and bring about the welfare and happiness of oneself and others. By speaking the word 'Sutaṃ' which shows the effort of hearing, he shows that many teachings that are to be heard have been heard, retained, and practiced verbally.
26:
He shows: "Many teachings have been heard by me, retained, and practiced verbally." Indeed, the hearing, retaining, and practicing of the scriptural Dhamma are connected to the application of the ear. By both of these, he shows the perfection of meaning and phrasing (attha-vyañjana) through the Dhamma being well-expounded, thereby generating respect in hearing. If one does not respectfully hear the Dhamma that is perfect in meaning and phrasing, one may be excluded from great welfare. Therefore, having generated respect, the Dhamma should be heard respectfully.

By this entire statement "Iti me sutaṃ", the Venerable Ānanda, not assuming the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata as his own creation, transcends the level of the unworthy (asappurisa) and, by acknowledging his status as a disciple, enters the level of the virtuous (sappurisa). Likewise, he raises his mind from the false Dhamma and establishes it in the True Dhamma (Saddhamma). By showing "This was merely heard by me; it is the word of the Blessed One himself," he frees himself from blame, points to the Teacher, entrusts the words of the Conqueror (Jina), and establishes the Eye of Dhamma (Dhamma-netti).

Furthermore, by the words "Iti me sutaṃ", not claiming it as his own production but revealing the Buddha's words heard previously, [he implies]: "I received this in the presence of the Blessed One—who is intrepid due to the four kinds of intrepidity (vesārajja), who possesses the ten powers (dasabala), who stands in the supreme position (āsabha-ṭṭhāna), who utters the lion's roar (sīhanāda), who is the most excellent of all beings, the Lord of Dhamma, the King of Dhamma, who has the Dhamma as his lamp, who has the Dhamma as his refuge, the Turner of the Wheel of the Noble True Dhamma, the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha)." He destroys the lack of faith of all devas and humans in this Dhamma-Vinaya, [showing] that no doubt or uncertainty should be entertained regarding the meaning, the Dhamma, the words, or the phrasing, and he generates the perfection of faith. Therefore, it is said:

"The disciple of Gotama, the Venerable Ānanda,
Speaking these words 'Iti me sutaṃ',
Destroys lack of faith in the Dispensation,
And causes the growth of the perfection of faith."

Here, it may be asked: "Why is the introduction (nidāna) not spoken by referring to the time and place as in other suttas, such as 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ, ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā' and so forth?" Other teachers say: It is because it was not [originally] spoken by the Elder [Ānanda]. Indeed, this introduction was not first spoken by the Venerable Ānanda. It was first spoken to the five hundred women led by Sāmāvatī by the noble female disciple Khujjuttarā, who was placed by the Blessed One in the foremost position (etadagga) among laywomen of great learning, and who was a trainee (sekha) who had attained the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā).
27: In this regard, the sequential narrative (anupubbīkathā) is as follows: One hundred thousand aeons ago from this present Bhadda-kappa, the Perfectly Enlightened One named Padumuttara appeared in the world. Having set in motion the noble Wheel of Dhamma, He resided in the city of Haṃsāvatī. Then one day, a certain noble daughter in Haṃsāvatī went to the monastery along with other laywomen to listen to the Teacher's Dhamma discourse. Seeing the Teacher appoint a certain laywoman to the foremost position (etadagga) among those of great learning (bahussuta), she performed meritorious deeds and made a resolution for that same position. The Teacher also prophesied: 'In the future, she will become the foremost among the learned laywomen disciples of the Perfectly Enlightened One named Gotama.' Having performed meritorious deeds throughout her life, she was reborn in the celestial realm and then again in the human realm. Thus, wandering through the celestial and human realms, one hundred thousand aeons passed. Then, in this Bhadda-kappa, during the time of our Blessed One, she passed away from the celestial realm and took rebirth in the womb of a slave woman in the house of Ghosaka the treasurer, and they named her Uttarā. Because she was hunchbacked at birth, she became known as Khujjuttarā. Later, when Ghosaka the treasurer gave her to Queen Sāmāvatī, the consort of King Utena, she lived in King Utena's palace as Sāmāvatī's attendant. At that time, the treasurers Ghosaka, Kukkuṭa, and Pāvārika in Kosambī built three monasteries dedicated to the Blessed One. When the Tathāgata, wandering through the countryside, arrived at the city of Kosambī, they offered the monasteries to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha and provided great alms for about a month. Then it occurred to them: 'The Buddhas are compassionate toward all beings in the world; let us give others an opportunity as well.' Thus, they allowed the citizens of Kosambī to offer alms. From then on, the citizens gave great alms according to their streets and groups. Then one day, the Teacher, surrounded by the community of monks, sat in the house of the chief florist. At that moment, Khujjuttarā went to that house, taking eight kahāpaṇas to buy flowers for Sāmāvatī. Seeing her, the chief florist said, 'Dear daughter Uttarā, today there is no time to give you flowers yet. I am serving the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. You too, please assist in the service; by doing so, you will be freed from performing the tasks of others.' Then Khujjuttarā performed voluntary service (veyyāvacca) at the place where the Buddhas were taking their meal. She learned and memorized all the Dhamma spoken by the Teacher while He was seated nearby, and after listening to the discourse of appreciation (anumodanā), she was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala).
28: On other days, Khujjuttarā used to give only four kahāpaṇas and take the flowers. However, on that day, because she had realized the Truth, she did not allow her mind to dwell on the property of others. She gave all eight kahāpaṇas, filled the basket, took the flowers, and went to Sāmāvatī. Then Sāmāvatī asked her, 'Dear Uttarā, on other days you did not bring so many flowers, but today there are very many. Has the King become exceptionally pleased with us?' Because she was incapable of telling a lie, Khujjuttarā did not hide what she had done in the past and told everything. When asked, 'Why did you bring so many today?' she replied, 'Today I listened to the Dhamma of the Perfectly Enlightened One and realized the Deathless (amata); therefore, I will no longer deceive you.' Hearing this, Sāmāvatī did not threaten her by saying, 'You wicked slave, give back the money you have taken for so long.' Instead, being urged by past causes, she said, 'Mother, let us also drink the Deathless Dhamma that you have drunk.' Khujjuttarā said, 'If that is so, let me bathe.' Thus, she was bathed with sixteen jars of scented water and given two fine cloth garments. She dressed in one and draped the other over her shoulder. Having had a seat prepared, she sat upon it, took a beautiful fan, and addressed the five hundred women who were sitting on lower seats. Established in the analytical knowledges of a trainee (sekha-paṭisambhidā), she preached the Dhamma to those women in the very manner taught by the Teacher. At the end of the discourse, all those women were established in the fruit of Stream-entry. All of them bowed to Khujjuttarā and said, 'Mother, from today onwards, do not perform any lowly tasks. Please remain in the position of our mother and our teacher.' Thus, they placed her in a position of great respect. Why was she born as a slave? It is said that during the time of Kassapa Buddha, she was born as the daughter of a treasurer in Bārāṇasī. When an Arahant nun came to her family's house for support, she made the nun perform a task, saying, 'Venerable lady, give me this jewelry box.' The elder nun thought, 'If I do not give it, this treasurer's daughter will harbor resentment and be reborn in hell. If I give it, she will be reborn as a slave to others. Slavery is better than the torment of hell.' Out of compassion, she did as the treasurer's daughter said. Due to that kamma, Khujjuttarā was born as a slave to others for five hundred births. Why was she hunchbacked? It is said that in a time when no Buddha had appeared, while living in the palace of the King of Bārāṇasī, she saw a Paccekabuddha who visited the royal house and was slightly hunchbacked...
29:
Wishing to mock the women she lived with, she showed a hunchbacked posture in a playful manner. Therefore, she was born with a hunchbacked body.

What good deed did she perform to become wise? It is said that before the Buddha appeared, while this Khujjuttarā was living in the palace of the King of Bārāṇasī, she saw eight Paccekabuddhas turning their bowls in their hands because they were filled with hot milk-rice (received from the palace). Then, she offered her own eight ivory bracelets, saying, "Please place the bowls on these and take them." The Paccekabuddhas did so and looked at them. She said, "These are offered only for you, Venerable Sirs; please take them and go." They went to the Nandamūlaka cave. Even today, those bracelets remain undamaged. Due to the result of that merit, Khujjuttarā became wise.

Then, the five hundred women headed by Sāmāvatī said, "Mother, please go to the Teacher every day, listen to the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, and teach it to us." Khujjuttarā did so, and later she became a bearer of the Tipiṭaka. Therefore, the Teacher placed her in the foremost position, saying, "Monks, among my laywomen disciples who are of great learning, Khujjuttarā is the foremost." Thus, Khujjuttarā, the noble disciple who was placed in the foremost position by the Teacher for her great learning and who had attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), would go to the Teacher from time to time while he was staying in Kosambī. After listening to the Dhamma, she would return to the inner palace and preach the Dhamma as she had heard it to the five hundred noble disciples headed by Sāmāvatī, according to the manner taught by the Teacher. In preaching thus, to free herself from blame and to make clear that she had heard it directly from the Teacher, she introduced the prologue: "This was indeed said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant; so I have heard" (Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā, vuttamarahatāti me sutaṃ).

Since she heard it in the presence of the Blessed One in that very city of Kosambī and preached it to those women on that same day, there was no special purpose in indicating the time and place by saying, "At one time the Blessed One was staying in Kosambī," because it was so well-known. The bhikkhunīs also learned these suttas from her. Thus, through the lineage, the prologue introduced by her became well-known among the bhikkhus as well. Later, after the parinibbāna of the Tathāgata, the Venerable Ānanda, sitting in the midst of the group of masters (vasi) headed by Mahākassapa in the Saddhamma Hall at the Sattapaṇṇi Cave built by King Ajātasattu, while reciting the Dhamma, [introduced] these suttas...
30:
It is said that the Venerable Ānanda, removing the duality of the prologue, introduced the prologue exactly in the manner presented by Khujjuttarā.

Some teachers expand on this in many ways. What is the use of such expansion? Furthermore, the teachers of the Council (saṅgītikāras) recited the Dhamma and Vinaya through various methods. The Great Elders who recited the Dhamma knew the Buddha's approval. Knowing well the manner in which the Dhamma and Vinaya should be recited, they placed the prologue in some places as "Thus have I heard" (Evaṃ me sutaṃ), in some places as "At that time" (Tena samayena), and in some places by way of verse. In some places, they did not place any prologue at all but recited the Dhamma and Vinaya by way of grouping into vaggas, etc. In doing so, they recited this Itivuttaka by placing the prologue as "This was indeed said" (Vuttañhetaṃ), etc. Just as this ninefold word of the Buddha (navaṅga-buddhasāsana) exists by way of Sutta, Geyya, etc., so it is for all the Perfectly Enlightened Ones. There is a saying that for those Buddhas, Sutta and Geyya were very few. In that context, to show that it is the Itivuttaka division, no other reason is evident except for this statement: "This was indeed said... so I have heard." Therefore, the commentators said, "The one hundred and twelve suttas that proceed in the manner of 'This was indeed said by the Blessed One' are called Itivuttaka." Thus, it should be understood that the Dhamma-reciters who knew the Teacher's intention, as well as the noble disciple (Khujjuttarā), placed the prologue in this very manner to make known that these suttas belong to the Itivuttaka division.

However, why is the prologue included when reciting the Dhamma and Vinaya? Should not only the words spoken by the Blessed One be recited? To answer that: it is for the purpose of the stability of the teaching, its non-disappearance, and its credibility. For a teaching that is established by indicating the time, place, speaker, and the audience lasts long, does not disappear, and is credible, just like a legal decision (vohāra-vinicchaya) bound by time, place, agent, cause, and sign. That is why, when the Venerable Mahākassapa asked about the place and so on of the Brahmajāla Sutta, Mūlapariyāya Sutta, etc., the Treasurer of the Dhamma, Venerable Ānanda, in giving the answers, spoke the prologue starting with "Thus have I heard." In this Itivuttaka, the reason for not taking the place and time has already been stated.

Alternatively, the prologue is spoken to show the perfection (sampatti) of the Teacher. For the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the state of being a Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) is established because he has no prior composition, inference, tradition, or logic. Because...
31:
Alternatively, the introductory words are spoken for the purpose of demonstrating the perfection of the Blessed One. Indeed, for the Blessed One, who possesses a sublime gait like the previous Buddhas, the state of knowing all things by Himself is established because there is no prior composition, no reflection by inference, and no thinking by way of tradition. Truly, for the Blessed One, there is no use for prior composition and so forth. Because His knowledge acts without obstruction in all matters and because He is the sole authority regarding the fivefold knowable things (ñeyyadhamma), and likewise, because there is no stinginess of the 'teacher's fist' (ācariyamuṭṭhi) regarding the Dhamma and no resentment towards the disciples of the Dispensation, His state as an Arahant is established. For these things do not occur at all in a Fully Enlightened One who is an Arahant. Therefore, the Blessed One, being perfectly pure, acts for the benefit of others.

In this way, the first two confidences (vesārajja) are established through the Buddha's pure states, which indicate the absolute absence of ignorance and craving—those defilements of the teacher that ruin the perfection of view and virtue—and which manifest the perfection of knowledge (ñāṇa-sampadā) and the perfection of abandonment (pahāna-sampadā). Furthermore, the latter two confidences are established through the state of non-confusion regarding things that are obstacles and things that lead to liberation. Thus, the Blessed One's possession of the four confidences and His practice for the benefit of Himself and others are revealed by the introductory words. This is because He demonstrates the Dhamma teaching with a presence of mind that arises spontaneously (ṭhānuppattika-paṭibhāna) according to the inclinations of the audience present in various places. In this specific context, however, it should be applied as demonstrating the teaching after having effected the abandonment of sensual desire and ill will without remainder. Therefore, it is said: 'The introductory words are spoken for the purpose of demonstrating the perfection of the Teacher.' In this regard, the manifestation of the meaning already mentioned through the words 'Bhagavatā Arahatā' has already been shown below.

Likewise, the introductory words are spoken for the purpose of demonstrating the perfection of the Dispensation (Sāsana). For the Blessed One, whose every action is embraced by wisdom and compassion, there is no practice that is useless or merely for His own benefit. Therefore, every action of the Fully Enlightened One—bodily, verbal, and mental—which occurs solely for the benefit of others and is to be described, is called 'Sāsana' (Instruction) because it has the sense of instructing beings according to what is appropriate for their welfare in this life, the next life, and the ultimate goal; it is not a poetic composition (kabba-racanā). This conduct of the Teacher is revealed appropriately in various places through introductory words by indicating the time, the place, the teacher, and the audience. In this context, it should be applied by indicating the teacher and the audience. Therefore, it is said: 'The introductory words are spoken for the purpose of demonstrating the perfection of the Dispensation.'

Furthermore, the introductory words are spoken for the purpose of showing the authority of the Dispensation by demonstrating the authority of the Teacher. And His state of being an authority should be understood as manifested by these words 'Bhagavatā Arahatā' according to the method mentioned below. What has been said here is merely a primary illustration of the purpose of the introductory words.

## The Explanation of the Introduction is finished.
32:
## 1. The Book of Ones (Ekaka Nipāta)
## 1. The First Chapter (Paṭhama Vagga)
## 1. Commentary on the Lobha Sutta

Now, the opportunity has arrived to explain the Sutta laid down by the Blessed One in the manner beginning with: 'Bhikkhus, abandon one thing.' Since that explanation of the meaning becomes clear only when spoken after investigating the occasion for the delivery of the Sutta, we shall first investigate the delivery of the Sutta. There are four occasions for the delivery of a Sutta: (1) by one's own inclination (attajjhāsaya), (2) by the inclination of others (parajjhāsaya), (3) by way of a question (pucchāvasika), and (4) on account of a specific occurrence (atthuppattika).

Just as the Suttas, though they have many hundreds and thousands of divisions, do not exceed the sixteenfold nature according to the systematic method (paṭṭhāna-naya) such as the 'partaking of defilement' (saṃkilesabhāgiya) and so forth, so too they do not exceed the fourfold nature by way of the delivery of the Sutta such as 'one's own inclination' and so forth.

In that regard, the division of mixing 'one's own inclination' and 'the occurrence of an incident' with 'the inclination of others' and 'by way of a question' is possible. This is because the connection between inclination and question can occur as: 'one's own inclination and the inclination of others,' 'one's own inclination and by way of a question,' 'on account of an incident and the inclination of others,' and 'on account of an incident and by way of a question.' Thus, although the division of mixing 'on account of an incident' with 'one's own inclination' is also possible, because there is no mixing of 'on account of an incident' with 'one's own inclination' and so forth that stand at the beginning, the exhaustive systematic method is not possible. Alternatively, it should be understood that the four deliveries of the Sutta are stated by way of the root deliveries, because the remaining deliveries of the Sutta that arise are included within them.

In this regard, this is the word-meaning (vacinattha): It is called 'nikkhēpa' because it is laid down (nikkhipīyati). The Sutta itself is the delivery, thus 'sutta-nikkhēpa'. Or, the act of laying down is 'nikkhēpa'; the laying down of the Sutta is 'sutta-nikkhēpa', which means the teaching of the Sutta. One's own inclination is 'attajjhāsaya'; it is called 'attajjhāsaya' because that [inclination] exists as a cause for Him [the Buddha], or because His own inclination belongs to Him. The same method applies to 'parajjhāsaya' (the inclination of others). The influence of a question is 'pucchāvasa'; it is called 'pucchāvasika' because that influence of a question exists for this person. The arising of the matter which is the basis for the teaching of the Sutta is 'atthuppatti'. That same 'atthuppatti' is called 'aṭṭhuppatti' by changing the letter 'th' to 'ṭh'. Because that arising of the matter exists for this Sutta...
33:
It is called aṭṭhuppattika because it has the meaning of arising from an occasion. Alternatively, it is called nikkhepa because the Sutta is presented (placed) by this means; attajjhāsaya and so forth are the same. In this specific sense, one's own inclination is called attajjhāsaya. The inclination of others is called parajjhāsaya. It is called pucchā because it is asked; the meaning to be asked is pucchā. The speech of those receiving the Dhamma that proceeds by way of a question is pucchāvasa; that same pucchāvasa is called pucchāvasika in the masculine gender, in consideration of the word nikkhepa. Similarly, the arising of the meaning from an occasion is itself called aṭṭhuppattika. Thus should the meaning be understood in this context.

Furthermore, because it is independent of causes such as the maturation of others' faculties (indriya), the separate presentation of a Sutta by the Buddha's own inclination (attajjhāsaya) is appropriate, as it is a teaching delivered solely for the purpose of establishing the lineage of the Dhamma by His own inclination. Since the teachings delivered by the inclination of others (parajjhāsaya) and by way of a question (pucchāvasika) are delivered when the inclinations and questions of others—which are the causes for the teaching—arise, how can they be included without conflict in the occasion-based teaching (aṭṭhuppattika)? Or, since the question-based and occasion-based teachings are delivered in accordance with the inclination of others, how can they be included without conflict in the inclination of others (parajjhāsaya)? This should not be questioned. Because only the arising of a cause for teaching a Sutta that is free from others' aspirations (abhinīhāra), inquiries, and so forth is taken as aṭṭhuppatti, parajjhāsaya and pucchāvasika are taken separately. For this reason, in the Brahmajāla Sutta, Dhammadāyāda Sutta, and so forth, the cause of the teaching, such as the arising of praise, blame, or material requisites, is called aṭṭhuppatti. A Sutta taught by making the inclination alone the cause, without regarding others' questions, is called parajjhāsaya. A Sutta taught by the power of a question is called pucchāvasika. This meaning is clear.

Those Suttas which the Blessed One teaches solely by His own inclination, without being requested by others—such as the Ākaṅkheyya Sutta, Tuvaṭṭaka Sutta, and so forth—their presentation is called attajjhāsaya.

However, those Suttas which are taught by the power of others' inclination, after observing their inclination, preference, aspiration, and capacity for realization—such as, "The qualities of Rāhula that ripen toward liberation have matured; what if I were to further discipline Rāhula in the destruction of the taints (the fruit of Arahantship)?"—such as the Rāhulovāda Sutta, Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, and so forth, their presentation is called parajjhāsaya.

Approaching the Blessed One, devas, humans, the four assemblies, and the four castes ask questions in various ways: "Venerable Sir, they are called 'factors of enlightenment, factors of enlightenment'..."
34:
"...they are called 'hindrances, hindrances'," and so forth. When thus questioned, those Suttas taught by the Blessed One, such as the Bojjhaṅga Saṃyutta, etc., their presentation (nikkhepa) is called "presentation by way of a question" (pucchāvasika nikkhepa).

Those Suttas taught in dependence on an occasion that has arisen, such as the Dhammadāyāda Sutta, Puttamaṃsūpama Sutta, Dārukkhandhūpama Sutta, and so forth, their presentation is called "occasion-based presentation" (aṭṭhuppattika nikkhepa).

Thus, among these four types of Sutta presentations, the presentation of this Sutta is called "presentation by the inclination of others" (parajjhāsaya nikkhepa). Indeed, this Sutta was presented by the power of the inclination of others. By whose inclination? By the inclination of those individuals who see the danger in greed (lobha). However, some teachers say it is "presentation by one's own inclination" (attajjhāsaya nikkhepa).

In that context, in the phrases such as "Bhikkhus, one thing (eka dhammaṃ)," the word eka (one) exists in the sense of "another" (añña) in such places as: "Some say, 'The self and the world are eternal; only this is true, any other is empty,'" and so forth. It exists in the sense of "noble" (seṭṭha) in such places as: "Unification of mind (cetaso ekodibhāva)," and so forth. It exists in the sense of "solitary" (asahāya) in such places as: "One who dwells alone and secluded (eko vūpakaṭṭho)," and so forth. It exists in the sense of "number" (saṅkhyā) in such places as: "Bhikkhus, there is only one moment and opportunity for living the holy life," and so forth. Here too, it should be understood only in the sense of number.

The word dhamma is seen in the senses of scripture (pariyatti), truth (sacca), concentration (samādhi), wisdom (paññā), nature (pakati), merit (puñña), offense (āpatti), emptiness (suññatā), the knowable (ñeyya), intrinsic nature (sabhāva), and so forth. Thus, the meaning of this word dhamma should be understood as scripture (pariyatti) in such places as: "In this Dispensation, a bhikkhu learns the Dhamma," and so forth. It should be understood as truth (sacca) in such places as: "One who has seen the Truth (diṭṭhadhammo)," and so forth. It should be understood as concentration (samādhi) in such places as: "Those Blessed Ones possessed such concentration," and so forth. It should be understood as wisdom (paññā) in such places as: "One who possesses truth, wisdom, steadfastness, and generosity does not sorrow after passing away," and so forth. It should be understood as nature (pakati) in such places as: "Bhikkhus, such a desire arises in beings subject to birth," and so forth. It should be understood as merit (puñña) in such places as: "The Dhamma indeed protects the one who practices the Dhamma," and so forth. It should be understood as offense (āpatti) in such places as: "One should be charged with one of the three offenses: a pārājika, a saṅghādisesa, or a pācittiya," and so forth. It should be understood as emptiness (suññatā) in such places as: "At that time, phenomena (dhammā) exist," and so forth. It should be understood as the knowable (ñeyya) in such places as: "All knowable things (sabbā dhammā) appear in all aspects before the gateway of the knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One," and so forth. It should be understood as intrinsic nature (sabhāva) in such places as: "Wholesome states (kusalā dhammā), unwholesome states (akusalā dhammā)," and so forth.
35:
The meaning here is also simply a nature (sabhāva). Therefore, 'eka-dhammaṃ' means a single nature that is the cause of defilement. Because it is both one and a nature, it is called 'eka-dhamma'; that one nature (is what is meant).

'Bhikkhave' is the addressing of the monks. For what purpose does the Blessed One address the monks when teaching the Dhamma? Why does he not teach the Dhamma directly? It is for the purpose of arousing mindfulness. This is because monks may be sitting while thinking of other things, reflecting on the Dhamma, or applying their minds to a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). If the Dhamma were taught without first addressing them, they would not be able to discern, 'What is the cause of this teaching? What is its condition?' However, when addressed, they are able to establish mindfulness and discern. Therefore, he addresses them as 'Bhikkhave' to arouse mindfulness. By using this word, which is established through their possession of qualities such as the character of a monk and virtue, he expresses a mode of living practiced by both the lowly and the noble, thereby subduing restlessness and dejection. With the word 'Bhikkhave', preceded by a glance from eyes and a heart softened by the pervading of compassion, he causes them to face him. By that word, which indicates the desire to speak, he generates in them the desire to listen. By that very word in the sense of addressing, he urges them to listen well and attend carefully. This is because the perfection of the Dispensation (sāsana) depends on listening well and attending carefully.

Why does he address only the monks when there are other devas and humans included in the assembly? It is because of their being the eldest, the most excellent, the nearest, and always present. Although the Blessed One's Dhamma teaching is common to the entire assembly, the monks are the eldest because they were the first to appear; they are the most excellent because, starting with their state of homelessness, they follow the Teacher's conduct and are the recipients of the entire Dispensation; they are the nearest because they sit in close proximity; and they are always present because they move about in the Teacher's presence. Furthermore, those monks are like vessels for the Dhamma teaching because of their existence in practice according to the instruction. Specifically, because this teaching was given with reference to certain monks, he addressed only those monks.

In this word 'pajahatha', abandonment (pahāna) is of five kinds: abandonment by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-pahāna), abandonment by suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna), abandonment by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna), abandonment by tranquilization (paṭippassaddhi-pahāna), and abandonment by escape (nissaraṇa-pahāna). Among these five, just as darkness is abandoned by the light of a lamp, there is the abandonment of greed etc. by non-greed etc. because they are opposites, and the abandonment of various harms by insight knowledges such as the discernment of mind and matter. To wit: the abandonment of the stain of greed by generosity; the abandonment of immorality such as killing by virtue; the abandonment of lack of faith etc. by faith etc.; the abandonment of the view of self (sakkāya-diṭṭhi) by the discernment of mind and matter; the abandonment of the view of no-cause and the view of wrong-cause by the grasping of conditions; the abandonment of doubt by the subsequent overcoming of doubt; the abandonment of the perception of 'I' and 'mine' by the comprehension of groups (kalāpa-sammasana)...
36:
...the abandonment of the obsession with 'I' and 'mine' (by the discernment of mind and matter); the abandonment of the perception of the path in what is not the path by the defining of path and non-path; the abandonment of the view of annihilation (uccheda-diṭṭhi) by the vision of arising; the abandonment of the view of eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi) by the vision of passing away; the abandonment of the perception of fearlessness in fearful things by the vision of fear; the abandonment of the perception of gratification by the vision of danger; the abandonment of the perception of delight by the contemplation of disenchantment; the abandonment of the desire not to be released by the knowledge of the desire for deliverance (muñcitukamyatā-ñāṇa); the abandonment of non-equanimity by the knowledge of equanimity (upekkhā-ñāṇa); the abandonment of the state of being contrary to the Dhamma by conformity (anuloma); the abandonment of the state of being contrary to Nibbāna; the abandonment of the grasping of the signs of formations by change-of-lineage (gotrabhū). This is called abandonment by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-pahāna).

The abandonment of various factors such as the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) by means of concentration, divided into access (upacāra) and attainment (appanā), which prevents their occurrence—like pushing away moss on the surface of water with a pot—is called abandonment by suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna). The cutting off of the group of defilements belonging to the side of origination (samudaya) so that they never occur again, as stated in the manner of 'for the abandonment of views' etc. in one's own continuity by one who possesses the respective path due to the development of the four Noble Paths, is called abandonment by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna). The complete tranquilization of defilements at the moment of Fruition (phala) is called abandonment by tranquilization (paṭippassaddhi-pahāna). Nibbāna, which is the abandonment of all conditioned things because it is the escape from all conditioned things, is called abandonment by escape (nissaraṇa-pahāna). Among these five kinds of abandonment, since the abandonment that brings about the state of a Non-returner (anāgāmika) is intended here, it should be understood as abandonment by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna). Therefore, 'pajahatha' (abandon) means 'give up, cut off at the root'.

'Ahaṃ' (I) is the Blessed One referring to himself. The word 'vo' is seen in the senses of the nominative, accusative, instrumental, genitive, expletive (padapūraṇa), and dative cases. Indeed: in sentences such as 'Anuruddhas... are you (vo) united and rejoicing?', it appears in the nominative sense. In sentences such as 'Go, monks, I dismiss you (vo)', it appears in the accusative sense. In sentences such as 'You (vo) should not live in my presence', it appears in the instrumental sense. In sentences such as 'Sāriputta, the speech of all of you (vo) is excellent', it appears in the genitive sense. In sentences such as 'Those noble ones who (vo) are of pure bodily action', it appears as an expletive (padapūraṇa). In sentences such as 'Monks, I will teach the Vanapattha discourse to you (vo)', it appears in the dative sense. Here too, it should be understood only in the dative sense.

'Pāṭibhogo' means a guarantor (paṭibhū). He is one who, depending on the debtor for the creditor, or depending on the creditor as a representative of the debtor, takes the creditor's property from that person...
37:
It is called *paṭibhoga* because it protects by guarding; *paṭibhoga* is the same as *pāṭibhoga*. *Anāgāmitā* means for the sake of the state of an *anāgāmī* (non-returner). Indeed, one is called an *anāgāmī* because of not returning to the sense-sphere (*kāmabhava*) by way of taking rebirth. That third path together with its fruit, by the attainment of which one is called an *anāgāmī*, is named *anāgāmitā*. Thus, the Blessed One, skilled in disciplining those to be tamed, showed the attainment of the third path in accordance with the inclinations of those to be tamed, making it firm by a quick means, merely by the fulfillment of a single Dhamma, just as a Fully Enlightened Buddha does. Indeed, the defilements to be abandoned by the third path, such as the fetter of aversion (*paṭighasaṃyojana*) which belongs to a different stage, do not exceed the abandonment of sensual lust (*kāmarāga*).

Why does the Blessed One place himself in the position of a guarantor (*pāṭibhoga*) here? It is for the purpose of generating effort in those monks for the attainment of the path of non-returning. For the Blessed One sees: "When I say, 'Monks, abandon one thing; I am your guarantor for non-returning,' these monks will surely be able to abandon that one thing and reach the third stage (the path of non-returning)." Since the Lord of Dhamma first said, "I am the guarantor," the monks will become energetic and think, "We must practice for that purpose." Therefore, to generate effort, he placed himself as a guarantor for their state of non-returning for the sake of the state of an *anāgāmī*.

In the phrase "Which one thing?" (*katamaṃ ekadhammaṃ*), "which" (*katamaṃ*) is an interrogative word. There are five kinds of questions (*pucchā*): the question to illuminate what is not seen (*adiṭṭhajotanāpucchā*), the question to compare what is seen (*diṭṭhasaṃsandanāpucchā*), the question to cut off doubt (*vimaticchedanāpucchā*), the question to gain consent (*anumatipucchā*), and the question from a desire to explain (*kathetukamyatāpucchā*). Among those five, when a characteristic is naturally unknown, unseen, unweighed, unjudged, unmanifest, and unclarified, asking a question for the sake of knowing, seeing, weighing, judging, manifesting, and clarifying it is called *adiṭṭhajotanāpucchā*. When a characteristic is naturally known, seen, weighed, judged, manifest, and clarified, asking a question for the sake of comparing it with other wise people is called *diṭṭhasaṃsandanāpucchā*. When one naturally falls into doubt and indecision, thinking, "Is it thus, or not? What is it? How is it?", asking a question to cut off that doubt is called *vimaticchedanāpucchā*. The Blessed One asking a question to gain consent, such as, "What do you think, monks, is form permanent or impermanent?" is called *anumatipucchā*. The Blessed One asking a question from a desire to explain to the monks, "Monks, there are these four nutriments..."
38:
"...for the maintenance of beings that have come into being or for the assistance of those seeking a new existence. What are the four?" (SN 2.11)—this is a question from a desire to explain (*kathetukamyatāpucchā*).

Among those five questions, the first three do not exist for the Buddhas. Why? Because there is nothing conditioned (*saṅkhata*) in the three periods of time, or unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*) beyond the three periods, that is unseen, unweighed, unjudged, unmanifest, or unclarified by the Fully Enlightened Buddhas. Therefore, they have no *adiṭṭhajotanāpucchā*. Since there is no need for them to compare what they have realized through their own knowledge with any other recluse, brahmin, deva, Mara, or Brahma, they also have no *diṭṭhasaṃsandanāpucchā*. Since the Blessed Buddhas are free from "how and why" (*akathaṃkathī*), have crossed over doubt, and are rid of uncertainty regarding all phenomena, they have no *vimaticchedanāpucchā*. The other two kinds of questions do exist. Among them, this one should be understood as a *kathetukamyatāpucchā*.

Now, wishing to show the meaning asked by that question in its specific form, he said: "Monks, one thing, greed..." In that context, it is called greed (*lobha*) because associated states lust by means of it, or it lusts by itself, or it is merely the act of lusting. This greed has the characteristic of clinging to an object like monkey-glue; its function is sticking to the object like a piece of meat thrown into a hot pan; it is manifested as not letting go like the staining of oil-soot; its proximate cause is seeing enjoyment in things that are fetters. Greed, growing as the river of craving, should be understood as taking hold of a being in whom it has arisen and carrying them to the states of deprivation (*apāya*), just as a swift-flowing river carries an object to the great ocean. Although this word "greed" (*lobha*) is a general term for all greed, here it should be understood as referring to sensual lust (*kāmarāga*). For that [sensual lust] is what is to be abandoned by the path of non-returning.

Addressing them again as "Monks" is to generate respect for the Dhamma in those who are present to receive it. By the words "Abandon [it]," the breakthrough by abandoning (*pahānābhisamaya*) is prescribed. This occurs only together with the breakthroughs of full understanding (*pariññā*), realization (*sacchikiriyā*), and development (*bhāvanā*), not separately. Thus, all four functions of right view based on the Four Noble Truths are already performed. When he says "Abandon greed," because they share the same state of being abandoned, the abandonment of hatred (*dosa*) and so on is also effectively stated. Similarly, when the breakthrough by abandoning, which is the function of right view regarding the truth of origin (*samudayasacca*), is stated, the functions regarding the truth of origin of the remaining path factors like right intention (*sammāsaṅkappa*), which are its co-operating causes, are also effectively stated. Thus, the activity of the Noble Path is complete.
39:
In this context, it should be understood that the function (of the Noble Path) is being taught. In this manner, the function of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma), such as the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), should also be understood as being taught here, expanded as appropriate.

Furthermore, by the words "Abandon greed," the full understanding of abandoning (pahānapariññā) is stated. That full understanding of abandoning is based on the full understanding of investigation (tīraṇapariññā), and the full understanding of investigation is based on the full understanding of the known (ñātapariññā). Therefore, through their inseparable nature, all three types of full understanding are made known. In this way, it should be understood that the meditation on the Four Truths (catusacca-kammaṭṭhāna) is fully presented here together with the fruit. Alternatively, by the words "Abandon greed," the purification by knowledge and vision (ñāṇadassana-visuddhi) is taught together with the fruit. That purification by knowledge and vision depends on the purification by knowledge and vision of the way (paṭipadā-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi)... and depends on the purification of mind (citta-visuddhi) and purification of virtue (sīla-visuddhi). Therefore, it should be understood that all seven purifications are manifested together with the fruit by way of immediacy.

In this way, one who wishes to abandon greed by fulfilling the three types of full understanding through the development of these successive purifications should consider the faults of greed through various sutta passages such as:

"Greed gives rise to harm; greed agitates the mind. This danger arisen from within, the people do not understand."

"The greedy person does not know his own benefit; the greedy person does not see the Dhamma. When greed overcomes a man, there is then a state of utter darkness." (Itivuttaka 88)

"Friends, a person who is lustful, overcome by passion, with a mind obsessed, kills living beings, takes what is not given, breaks into houses, commits robbery, plunders single houses, waits in ambush on the road, goes to another's wife, and speaks falsehood. For those recluses and brahmins who do not know, do not see, and do not experience, and who follow after craving, that action of theirs is merely the trembling and quivering of one who is distressed." (Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.54)

"A man with craving as his companion, wandering for a long time in saṃsāra, does not transcend the cycle of rebirth, which consists of this state and other states." (Itivuttaka 15, 105)

"There is no fire like passion; there is no fault like hatred." (Dhammapada 202, 251)

"I burn with sensual passion; my mind is fiercely on fire." (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.212)

"Those who are infatuated with passion fall into the stream (of saṃsāra) like a spider falling into the web it has made itself." (Dhammapada 347)

One should practice to abandon that greed by contemplating its faults through various methods using such sutta passages. Alternatively, these six things lead to the abandonment of sensual desire (kāmarāga): learning the sign of foulness (asubhanimitta), application of meditation on foulness, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, good friendship, and suitable talk. Let me expand on this. Sensual desire is abandoned for one who learns the ten types of signs of foulness. Sensual desire is also abandoned for one who repeatedly applies the meditation on foulness—whether on a conscious corpse by way of the development of mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati), or on an unconscious corpse by way of the bloated state and so on. Sensual desire is also abandoned for one whose doors are closed with the door-panel of mindfulness by way of restraint of the sense faculties. Sensual desire is also abandoned for one who knows moderation in eating by having the habit of sustaining oneself by drinking water when there is still room for four or five mouthfuls. Therefore, it is said: "One should drink water instead of eating four or five mouthfuls; this is sufficient for the comfortable living of a monk with a mind directed toward Nibbāna."

Sensual desire is also abandoned for one who associates with good friends who delight in the development of the meditation on foulness. Sensual desire is also abandoned by speaking suitable talk related to the ten types of foulness while standing, sitting, etc. Therefore, the Blessed One taught: "Monks, there is the sign of foulness; frequently applying wise attention (yonisomanasikāra) to that sign of foulness is for the non-arising of unarisen sensual desire and for the abandoning of arisen sensual desire."

In this context, the practitioner who strives to abandon greed, known as sensual desire, in the preliminary stage, develops insight (vipassanā) and completely cuts off that greed with the Third Path. Therefore, it was taught: "Monks, abandon one thing, greed; I am your surety for the state of Non-returner (anāgāmitā)."
40:
Following the sequence of such sutta passages, one should practice to abandon greed by contemplating its disadvantages through various methods.

Furthermore, six things lead to the abandonment of sensual desire (kāmarāga): learning the sign of foulness, application of meditation on foulness, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, good friendship, and suitable talk. Sensual desire is abandoned for one who learns the ten types of signs of foulness; for one who is devoted to the application of meditation on foulness—whether on a conscious corpse by way of the development of mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati), or on an unconscious corpse by way of the bloated state and so on; for one whose doors are closed with the door-panel of mindfulness by way of restraint in the sense faculties with the mind as the sixth; and for one who is moderate in eating, having the habit of sustaining oneself by drinking water when there is still room for four or five mouthfuls. Therefore, (the Elder Sāriputta) said:

"Having not eaten four or five mouthfuls,
One should drink water.
For a monk with a resolute mind,
This is sufficient for living in comfort."

Sensual desire is abandoned for one who associates with good friends who delight in the development of the meditation on foulness, and by speaking suitable talk related to the ten types of foulness while standing, sitting, etc. Therefore, the Blessed One taught: "Monks, there is the sign of foulness; frequently applying wise attention to that sign of foulness is for the non-arising of unarisen sensual desire and for the abandoning of arisen sensual desire."

In this way, one who practices to abandon greed, known as sensual desire, in the preliminary stage, develops insight and completely cuts off that greed with the Third Path. Therefore, it was taught: "Monks, abandon one thing, greed; I am your surety for the state of Non-returner."

In this context, there is a question: "Regarding the statement that greed is abandoned, which greed is abandoned? Is it past greed, or future greed, or present greed?" To speak briefly on this: first, past greed is not abandoned, nor is future greed abandoned, because those past and future greeds do not exist. What has ceased or what has not yet arisen cannot be said to "exist," and the effort (to abandon them) would be fruitless. If present greed were to be abandoned, even then the effort would be fruitless because present greed has the nature of vanishing by its own momentum, and the development of the Path would become defiled.
41:
The development of the path would occur, or greed would exist without being associated with the mind; this method is not desired. It is said that greed of the past, future, and present is not abandoned by the aforementioned method. For example, just as in this world, if a man were to cut a young tree that has not yet borne fruit at its root with an axe, the fruits that would have arisen had the tree not been cut do not arise because the tree has been cut; even so, greed that is liable to arise if the Noble Path is not attained does not arise because the cause has been destroyed by the attainment of the Noble Path. In the commentaries, this greed is called 'arisen from obtaining a ground' (bhūmiladdhuppanna). The five aggregates, which are the objects of insight, are called 'ground' (bhūmi) because they are the place where it arises. Because it arises having obtained an opportunity in that ground, it is called 'arisen from obtaining a ground'. It is also called 'arisen from being seized by an object' (ārammaṇādhiɡɡahituppanna), 'arisen from not being suppressed' (avikkhambhituppanna), and 'arisen from not being uprooted' (asamūhatuppanna).

'Therein' (tattha) means in that sutta. 'This' (etaṃ) means this matter. Now it is spoken by way of verse composition. When it is said 'thus it is said,' who says it? It is said by the Blessed One himself. Although there are verses composed by the Elders of the Council in other such places, here the Blessed One himself, summarizing the meaning already spoken, spoke the verse according to the inclination of those individuals who delight in verses.

In that verse, 'by which greed beings are greedy, they go to a miserable state' refers to those who are greedy through that greed which has the characteristic of grasping an object and, for that very reason, has the function of intense attachment, being greedy and clinging to the internal and external sense bases. The word 'se' is merely a particle. Grammarians, however, desire the augment of the letter 'se' in such places. Because of being greedy in that way, without performing even a slight amount of good conduct among bodily good conduct and so on, but having accumulated bodily misconduct and so on, beings—who have acquired the name 'satta' because of their attachment to forms and so on—reach, by way of taking rebirth, the miserable states (duɡɡati) known as hell, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts, because these are the places where suffering arises.

'Having known that greed rightly, those who see clearly abandon it' means having known that aforementioned greed rightly, without distortion, through the reason and method, by means of the wisdom known as full understanding of the known (ñātapariññā) and full understanding by investigation (tīraṇapariññā), in these aspects: by way of its nature, its origin, its cessation, its gratification, its danger, and the escape from it. Because they see the five aggregates of clinging, such as form and so on, through various aspects such as impermanence, those called 'insightful ones' (vipassī) abandon the remaining defilements through the Path-knowledge preceded by insight-knowledge, by way of abandoning by eradication (samucchedappahāna), and they do not allow them to arise again in their own continuity.
42:
'Having abandoned it, they never come to this world again' means that having abandoned that greed along with the remaining defilements which have the single sense of being abandoned together, through the Path of Non-returning (anāɡāmimaɡɡa), they never again come to this world, known as the sensual realm, by way of taking rebirth, because the lower fetters (orambhāɡiyāni saṃyojanāni) have been well abandoned. Thus the Blessed One concluded the teaching with the Fruit of Non-returning.

'This meaning also' refers to the meaning revealed by this sutta from the beginning of the introduction until the end of the verse. The word 'api' (also) has the sense of inclusive connection with the meaning of the sutta that is about to be spoken. The rest is just as previously stated. In this sutta, the Truth of the Origin (samudayasacca) is mentioned in its own form; the Truth of the Path (maɡɡasacca) is mentioned by way of the instruction on abandoning. The other two truths should also be determined because they are the causes of those two truths. In the verse, however, the truths of Suffering, Origin, and Path are known according to the literal words; the other truth (Cessation) should be determined. This same method applies to the suttas following this one.

## In the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya named Paramatthadīpanī,
## the explanation of the first sutta in the Itivuttaka is finished.
## 2. Dosasutta-vaṇṇanā

'This was said... greed (dosa)' is the second sutta. Therein, what follows is the explanation of new terms. Just as in this sutta, we shall provide only the explanation of new terms in all the suttas following this one.

Since this sutta was taught for the purpose of subsiding anger, having observed the inclination of individuals who have much anger, it is said: 'Monks, abandon one thing: hate (dosa).'

In that statement, 'hate' (dosa) refers to the malice (āɡhāta) that arises from any of the nineteen grounds of malice: the nine grounds of malice mentioned in the Suttas by way of 'He has done me harm' and so on, the nine grounds of malice established by way of their opposites such as 'He has not done me good' and so on, making eighteen, together with the nineteenth ground which is groundless anger towards a tree stump, a thorn, and so on. For beings are corrupted by it, or it itself is corrupt, or it is merely the act of corrupting; thus it is called 'dosa'. It has the characteristic of fierceness like a struck cobra. It has the function of spreading like the falling of poison, or it has the function of burning its own support like a forest fire.
43:
Anger has the manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) of offending like an enemy who has gained an opportunity. It has the aforementioned grounds for resentment (āghātavatthu) as its proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna). It should be regarded like putrid urine mixed with poison.

"Pajahatha" means to abandon or cut them off completely. Regarding that abandonment, it is stated thus:

"Monks, there are these five ways of removing resentment (āghātapāṭivinaya) by which a monk should entirely dispel resentment that has arisen toward anyone. What five? Monks, in whatever person resentment should arise, one should develop loving-kindness (mettā) toward that person... compassion (karuṇā)... equanimity (upekkhā); one should disregard that person and pay no attention to him. In this way, resentment toward that person should be dispelled. Monks, in whatever person resentment should arise, one should resolve upon the fact that this person is the owner of his kamma: 'This venerable one is the owner of his kamma, the heir to his kamma... so it will be.'" In this way, the five ways of removing resentment have been taught.

"Friends, there are these five ways of removing resentment by which a monk should entirely dispel resentment that has arisen toward anyone. What five? Here, friends, some person is of impure bodily conduct but of pure verbal conduct. Friends, resentment toward such a person should also be dispelled," and so forth, the five ways of removing resentment have been taught. One should reflect and dispel resentment by any of these methods of removing resentment.

Furthermore, there is this instruction of the Teacher: "Monks, even if bandits were to sever you limb by limb with a double-handled saw, anyone who cherished ill-will in his mind would not be a follower of my teaching."

"One who retaliates with anger against an angry person is, for that very reason, worse than the first. One who does not retaliate with anger against an angry person wins a battle that is hard to win."

"He practices for the benefit of both, his own and the other's, who, knowing that the other is angry, remains mindful and becomes calm."
44:
"Monks, these seven things, which are desired by an enemy and bring about an enemy's purpose, come upon an angry woman or man. What seven? Here, monks, an enemy wishes for his enemy: 'O, may this person be ugly!' For what reason? Monks, an enemy does not rejoice in an enemy's beauty. Monks, this person who is angry, overcome by anger, conquered by anger, even though he is well-bathed, well-anointed, with hair and beard trimmed, and dressed in white clothes, he is still ugly because he is overcome by anger. Monks, this is the first thing desired by an enemy and brought about by an enemy that comes upon an angry woman or man.

"Furthermore, monks, an enemy wishes for his enemy: 'O, may this person sleep in suffering!' ... 'May he not have much wealth!' ... 'May he not have possessions!' ... 'May he not have fame!' ... 'May he not have friends!' ... 'May he, with the breakup of the body, after death, be reborn in the plane of misery, the bad destination, the lower world, hell!' For what reason? Monks, an enemy does not rejoice in an enemy's going to a good destination. Monks, this person who is angry, overcome by anger, conquered by anger, conducts himself badly in body, conducts himself badly in speech, and conducts himself badly in mind. Having conducted himself badly in body, speech, and mind, with the breakup of the body, after death... he is reborn in hell because he was overcome by anger."

An angry person does not know the benefit,
An angry person does not see the Dhamma.

One should abandon anger, one should abandon pride,
One should transcend all fetters.

Anger gives birth to misfortune,
Anger agitates the mind.

Having cut off anger, one sleeps happily;
Having cut off anger, one does not sorrow.
O Brahmins, anger has a poisoned root and a honeyed tip.
45:
“O wise one of vast wisdom like the earth, forgive this one fault. The wise do not have anger as their strength.” By such means, one should reflect on the disadvantages of anger and the benefits of abandoning anger through the aforementioned opposite qualities. Having abandoned anger in the preliminary stage by means of abandoning by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-pahāna) and so forth, and having exerted effort in insight (vipassanā), one should completely cut off and abandon all anger with the Third Path. This is the exhortation to those monks regarding the abandonment of anger. Therefore, He said: “Monks, abandon the one thing: anger.” “Duṭṭhāse” means those who are corrupted due to having a mind defiled by ill-will. The rest of what should be said here is the same as the method stated in the commentary on the first sutta.

## The Commentary on the Second Sutta is finished.

## 3. Mohasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the third sutta, “moha” means ignorance (aññāṇa). That delusion is ignorance regarding suffering, ignorance regarding the origin of suffering, ignorance regarding the cessation of suffering, and ignorance regarding the practice leading to the cessation of suffering. Although it has many divisions through such analysis, it is called “moha” because it deludes, or it deludes by itself, or it is merely the act of deluding. It should be understood as having the characteristic of blindness of the mind or the characteristic of ignorance; its function is non-penetration or the function of covering the true nature of the object; its manifestation is wrong practice or the manifestation of darkness; its proximate cause is unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra); and it is the root of all unwholesome states.

In this sutta also, regarding the word “pajahatha” (abandon):
“The deluded person does not know the benefit; the deluded person does not see the Dhamma. When delusion overcomes a person, then there is utter darkness.” (Itivuttaka 88),
“Delusion gives rise to harm... (pe) ...” (Itivuttaka 88),
“Monks, ignorance is the precursor to the attainment of unwholesome states.” (Itivuttaka 40),
“The world, bound by delusion, appears as if it were substantial (fit for unwholesome deeds).” (Udāna 70),

“Delusion is a cause for the arising of kamma.”
“Brahmin, a person whose mind is overcome and obsessed by delusion increases the fear and enmity belonging to the present life, and increases the fear and enmity belonging to the future life.” By such means, and by the way that “whatever state is produced by the defilements such as sensual desire, in meaning all that is rooted in delusion,” one should reflect on the disadvantages of delusion and the benefits of abandoning delusion, which is the opposite of it. Just as in the sequence of abandoning sensual desire and so forth, having abandoned delusion in the preliminary stage by means of substitution of opposites and so forth, one should abandon it by means of completely cutting off delusion—which has the same basis as greed and anger as previously mentioned—with the Third Path. This is how the meaning should be understood. Indeed, it should be known that in this sutta, only the delusion that is to be abandoned by the Path of Non-Returning (anāgāmi-magga) is intended. “Mūḷhāse” means those who are deluded, being confused about wholesome and unwholesome, blameworthy and blameless, and about their own benefit and harm. The remaining words are as previously stated.
46:
'Delusion is the root for the arising of kamma' (Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.34). 'Brahmin, one who is confused, overcome by delusion, and whose mind is possessed, creates danger and enmity in the present life, and creates danger and enmity in the future life'—by such methods, and also by considering, 'Whatever state is to be produced by the defilements such as sensual desire, all that is fundamentally caused by delusion,' one contemplates the faults of delusion and the benefits of abandoning delusion, which is its opposite. Just as one abandons sensual desire and so forth, one should understand the meaning as: abandoning delusion in the preliminary stage by way of partial abandoning (tadaṅga) and so forth, and then abandoning delusion—which shares the same basis as the aforementioned greed and hatred—by way of total eradication (samuccheda) through the Third Path (the Path of Non-returning). Indeed, in this sutta, only the delusion that is to be destroyed by the Path of Non-returning is intended. 'Mūḷhāse' refers to those who are confused about their own benefit and harm, categorized as wholesome and unwholesome, blameworthy and blameless, and so forth. The rest is just as previously explained.

## The Explanation of the Third Sutta is Finished.

## 4. Kodhasuttavaṇṇanā

In the fourth sutta, 'kodha' means hatred (dosa). Hatred itself is spoken of in this way according to the inclination of individuals who understand it more easily through the synonym 'kodha' (anger). Therefore, the meaning here should be understood in the same way as stated in the second sutta. Furthermore, it should be understood that anger (kodha) has the characteristic of being angry, the function of creating enmity, the manifestation as the state of the mind's corruption, and it should be regarded as the state of the mind's putridity. This distinction should also be known.

## The Explanation of the Fourth Sutta is Finished.

## 5. Makkhasuttavaṇṇanā

In the fifth sutta, 'makkha' means the denigration of others' virtues. Although this state first soils one's own hand, like someone who picks up excrement to strike another, it is called 'denigrating others' virtues (paraguṇamakkhana)' because it is brought about with the intention of denigrating the virtues of others. Likewise, it destroys the virtues of others just as one wipes away water from the body of a person who has bathed. Or, it is called 'makkha' because it destroys the great virtues performed by others. That state of makkha has the characteristic of denigrating others' virtues, the function of destroying those virtues, and the manifestation as concealing virtues. In terms of meaning, it should be regarded as the arising of a mind accompanied by displeasure (domanassa) that occurs in the manner of denigrating others' virtues. 'Pajahatha' means: having contemplated the various forms of hatred mentioned in that sutta, as well as the faults and the benefits of abandoning that contempt (makkha) by the aforementioned method, one abandons it in the preliminary stage by way of partial abandoning (tadaṅga-pahāna) and so forth, then develops insight (vipassanā), and should understand the meaning as: 'Eradicate the contempt (makkha) without remainder by the Third Path.' 'Makkhāse' refers to those who denigrate the virtues of others...
47:
Indeed, that denigration (makkha) wipes away the virtues of others just as one wipes away water from the body of a person who has bathed; it cleanses them away, it destroys them. Alternatively, it is called denigration because it destroys or suppresses even the great favors done by others. That denigration has the characteristic of smearing (wiping out) the virtues of others, the function of destroying those virtues, and the manifestation of concealing those virtues. In terms of ultimate meaning, it should be understood as the arising of a mind accompanied by displeasure (domanassa) which occurs in the manner of smearing the virtues of others.

Regarding the word "pajahatha" (abandon), it means: having reflected upon the various types of anger (dosa) mentioned in that sutta, the faults of anger in the manner already stated, and the benefits of abandoning that denigration, one should abandon it in the preliminary stage by way of substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-pahāna) and so forth, and by exerting oneself in insight meditation (vipassanā), cut it off without remainder through the Third Path (the Path of Non-returning).

Regarding "makkhāse," it means those who smear the virtues of others, those who are denigrators of others' virtues, and for that very reason, they are those whose own virtues are also destroyed. The remaining terms are to be understood in the manner already stated.

## The Commentary on the Fifth Sutta is Finished.

## 6. Mānasutta-vaṇṇanā (Commentary on the Sutta on Conceit)

In the sixth sutta, "māna" (conceit) refers to the uplifting of the mind based on birth and so forth. Indeed, one considers with that mind in the manner of "I am superior," etc., or the mind itself considers, or it is called conceit because it is an act of honoring or uplifting. That conceit is of three kinds: the conceit "I am superior," the conceit "I am equal," and the conceit "I am inferior."

Furthermore, it is of nine kinds: for one who is superior, the conceits "I am superior," "I am equal," and "I am inferior"; for one who is equal, the conceits "I am superior," "I am equal," and "I am inferior"; and for one who is inferior, the conceits "I am superior," "I am equal," and "I am inferior." Despite these nine types, it should be understood as having the characteristic of loftiness, the function of ego-making (ahaṃkāra) or the function of uplifting, the manifestation of puffing up or the manifestation of vainglory (ketukamyatā), and the proximate cause of greed dissociated from wrong view (diṭṭhi-vippayutta-lobha); it is like a state of madness.

Regarding "pajahatha," it means: having reflected upon the faults of all that conceit—such as being the cause for exalting oneself and disparaging others, being the cause for not performing acts of respect, welcoming, saluting with joined palms, and proper duties toward those worthy of honor, and being the cause for falling into negligence through intoxication with birth, intoxication with manhood, and so forth—and having reflected upon the benefits of being free from conceit as its opposite, one should establish a humble mind toward fellow practitioners like an outcaste (caṇḍāla) who has entered a royal assembly. In the preliminary stage, one abandons that conceit by way of substitution of opposites and so forth, develops insight meditation, and by the Path of Non-returning...
48:
...it means: cut it off completely. For in this context, only the conceit that is to be abandoned by the Path of Non-returning is intended. "Mattāse" refers to those who wander about uplifting themselves, intoxicated by the conceit that is the cause of falling into negligence, such as intoxication with birth, intoxication with manhood, and so forth. The remaining terms are to be understood in the manner already stated.

In these six suttas or verses in sequence, the teaching is concluded by leading to the Fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmi-phala). Among those Non-returners, there are five types by way of their place of rebirth: Aviha, Atappa, Sudassa, Sudassī, and Akaniṭṭha. Those born in the Aviha realm are called Aviha. Just as those Aviha residents are of five types—the one who attains Nibbāna in the interval (antarā-parinibbāyī), the one who attains Nibbāna after landing (upahacca-parinibbāyī), the one who attains Nibbāna without exertion (asaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī), the one who attains Nibbāna with exertion (sasaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī), and the one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm (uddhaṃsota-akaniṭṭhagāmī)—so too are the residents of Atappa, Sudassa, and Sudassī of five types each. However, in the Akaniṭṭha realm, the "upstream-goer to Akaniṭṭha" is absent.

Among them, one who is born in realms such as Aviha and, without exceeding the middle of the lifespan, attains the Fruit of Arahatship and passes away into Nibbāna through the extinguishing of defilements is called an "antarā-parinibbāyī." One who is born in realms such as Aviha and passes away into Nibbāna only after exceeding the middle of the lifespan, such as five hundred aeons and so forth from the beginning, is called an "upahacca-parinibbāyī." One who passes away into Nibbāna without instigation, without making excessive effort, and with little pain or difficulty is called an "asaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī." One who passes away into Nibbāna with instigation, having to make excessive effort, and with pain, toil, and difficulty is called a "sasaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī." The other is called "uddhaṃsota" (upstream-streamer) because of the nature of flowing upwards in realms such as Aviha, or because he has an upward-tending stream of craving, stream of saṃsāra, or stream of the Path. One who is born in realms such as Aviha and, being unable to reach Arahatship, stays there until the end of the lifespan and then goes to the Akaniṭṭha realm by way of the sequence of rebirths is called an "akaniṭṭhagāmī."

In this matter, it should be understood that there is a fourfold classification: one who is both an upstream-streamer and an Akaniṭṭha-goer; one who is an upstream-streamer but not an Akaniṭṭha-goer; one who is not an upstream-streamer but is an Akaniṭṭha-goer; and one who is neither an upstream-streamer nor an Akaniṭṭha-goer. How? One who, starting from the Aviha realm, purifies (passes through) the four celestial realms in sequence and reaches the Akaniṭṭha realm to attain Nibbāna is called an "uddhaṃsota-akaniṭṭhagāmī." One who purifies the three lower celestial realms and attains Nibbāna while staying in the Sudassī realm is called an "uddhaṃsota who is not an akaniṭṭhagāmī." One who goes directly from this realm to the Akaniṭṭha realm and attains Nibbāna is called "not an uddhaṃsota but an akaniṭṭhagāmī." One who attains Nibbāna right in any of the four lower celestial realms is called "neither an uddhaṃsota nor an akaniṭṭhagāmī."
49:
Among those Non-returners (Anāgāmīs), there are three types of 'attainers of Nibbāna in the interval' (antarāparinibbāyī): one who is reborn in the Aviha realm and attains Nibbāna after more than a hundred aeons (kappa), one who attains Nibbāna at the end of two hundred aeons, and one who attains Nibbāna before reaching five hundred aeons. It has also been said: "Immediately after being reborn, or before reaching the middle of the lifespan (he attains Nibbāna)." By the word 'vā' (or), one who has just reached the middle of the lifespan is also included. Thus, there are three types of antarāparinibbāyī, one upahaccaparinibbāyī (attainer of Nibbāna after being reborn), and one uddhaṃsota (one who goes upstream). Among them, there are five asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī (attainers of Nibbāna without exertion) and five sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī (attainers of Nibbāna with exertion), making ten. Similarly, in the Atappa, Sudassa, and Sudassī realms, there are ten each, totaling forty. In the Akaniṭṭha realm, however, because there is no uddhaṃsota person, there are three types of antarāparinibbāyī and one upahaccaparinibbāyī (making four); thus there are four asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī and four sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī, making eight. In this way, there are forty-eight types of Non-returners (Anāgāmīs). It should be understood that all these persons are included in these suttas by general terms without specific distinction.

## The Commentary on the Sixth Sutta is finished.

## 7. Sabbapariññā Sutta Commentary

In the seventh, the Sabba Sutta, 'sabba' means without remainder. This word 'sabba' is a term that expresses the absence of remainder. That word indicates the absence of remainder for whatever term it is connected with. For example, as in "all form, all feeling, in all things included in the personality (sakkāya)." That word 'sabba' is of two kinds by way of being limited (sappadesa) and unlimited (nippadesa). Thus, this word 'sabba' is seen used in four contexts: the 'all-all' (sabbasabba), the 'partial-all' (padesasabba), the 'all of the sense bases' (āyatanasabba), and the 'all of the personality' (sakkāyasabba). Among those four, in passages such as "All things (sabbe dhammā) in every way come into the range of the knowledge-door of the Blessed Buddha," it occurs in the sense of 'all-all' (sabbasabba). In passages such as "Sāriputta, the speech of all of you is well-spoken in its own way," it occurs in the sense of 'partial-all' (padesasabba). In this passage, "Monks, I will teach you the all: the eye and forms... the mind and mental objects," it occurs in the sense of 'all of the sense bases' (āyatanasabba). In passages such as "Monks, I will teach you the discourse on the root of all things," it occurs in the sense of 'all of the personality' (sakkāyasabba). Among those four, the word 'sabba' occurring in the sense of 'all-all' has an unlimited (nippadesa) scope. The word 'sabba' occurring in the other three...
50: ...has a limited (sappadesa) scope. Here, however, it should be understood in the sense of 'all of the personality' (sakkāyasabba). The reason is that in this sutta, the things belonging to the three planes of existence, which are the objects of insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa), are taken as 'all' without remainder. 'Anabhijānaṃ' means not knowing with direct knowledge (abhiññā), not knowing with distinguished knowledge, the things that should be directly known in their undistorted nature, such as: "These things are wholesome, these things are unwholesome, these things are blameworthy, these things are blameless," and "These are the five aggregates, these are the twelve sense bases, these are the eighteen elements, this is the noble truth of suffering, this is the noble truth of the origin of suffering," and so on. 'Aparijānaṃ' means not fully understanding (parijānana). If a person fully understands all things belonging to the three planes, he does so through the three types of full understanding (pariññā): full understanding of the known (ñātapariññā), full understanding by investigation (tīraṇapariññā), and full understanding by abandoning (pahānapariññā). Among those three, what is full understanding of the known (ñātapariññā)? It is the defining of all mind and matter (nāmarūpa) belonging to the three planes by way of characteristic (lakkhaṇa), function (rasa), manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna), and proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna), as: "This is matter; matter is only this much, not more than this. This is mind; mind is only this much, not more than this," distinguishing matter such as the primary elements and sensitive matter, and mind such as contact and so on. The grasping of the causes of that mind and matter, such as ignorance (avijjā) and so on, is called full understanding of the known (ñātapariññā). What is full understanding by investigation (tīraṇapariññā)? Having thus known them, the investigating and contemplating of all those things of mind and matter in forty-two modes, such as impermanent (anicca), suffering (dukkha), and disease (roga), is called full understanding by investigation (tīraṇapariññā). What is full understanding by abandoning (pahānapariññā)? Having thus investigated, the abandoning of desire and lust (chandarāga) for all mind and matter by means of the highest Path (aggamagga) is called full understanding by abandoning (pahānapariññā). Purification of view (diṭṭhivisuddhi) and purification by overcoming doubt (kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhi) are also called full understanding of the known (ñātapariññā). Purification by knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path (maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhi), purification by knowledge and vision of the way (paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhi), and the wisdom starting from the knowledge of comprehension (sammasana-ñāṇa) up to the end of the knowledge of conformity (anuloma-ñāṇa) are called full understanding by investigation (tīraṇapariññā). Abandoning by the Noble Path is full understanding by abandoning (pahānapariññā). If a person fully understands the all, he does so through these three types of full understanding. In this sutta, however, because fading of lust (virāga) and abandoning (pahāna) are taken separately, full understanding should be understood only by way of full understanding of the known and full understanding by investigation. It is with reference to one who does not fully understand in this way that 'aparijānaṃ' is said. In that context, 'cittaṃ avirājayaṃ' means not causing one's own mental continuum to be free from lust in those things that should be directly known and fully understood; not developing the contemplation of fading away (virāgānupassanā) so that lust does not arise in them. 'Appajahaṃ' means not [abandoning] the round of defilements (kilesavaṭṭa) that should be abandoned in those things by means of Path-wisdom accompanied by insight-wisdom...
51:
Not abandoning without remainder. As it is explained here, direct knowledge (abhijānana) and so forth should also be understood by way of the mixed path (missaka-magga). Indeed, in the preliminary stage, one fulfills direct knowledge and so forth gradually through the full understanding of the known (ñāta-pariññā) and the full understanding by investigation (tīraṇa-pariññā).
