At the time of the Path, a single knowledge arises, accomplishing all that through the function of a single moment, perceiving all things belonging to the three planes (tebhūmaka-dhamma). "Incapable of the destruction of suffering" (abhabbo dukkhakkhayāya) means not fit for, not capable of, Nibbāna, which is the exhaustion of the entire round of suffering.

In the phrase "And all indeed" (sabbañca kho), the word "ca" is used in the sense of distinction (vyatireka), and the word "kho" is used in the sense of emphasis (avadhāraṇa). By these two words, it shows the distinction obtained from direct knowledge and so forth, as well as the certain cause for the destruction of suffering. What should be said regarding direct knowledge and so forth has already been stated. However, while it was stated by way of prohibition in that sutta, here it should be understood by way of prescription (vidhāna). This is the difference. Furthermore, "they directly know" (abhijānanti) means one who directly knows the entire identity (sakkāya), known as the five aggregates of clinging, both by its nature and its cause, by way of bringing it before knowledge. By grasping the aspect of non-existence and so forth, one fully understands (parijānanta) that identity by defining it through characteristics such as impermanence and so forth. "They become dispassionate" (virājayanti) means making one's mind dispassionate through the power of knowledges such as the knowledge of fear (bhaya-ñāṇa), the knowledge of danger (ādīnava-ñāṇa), and the knowledge of disenchantment (nibbidā-ñāṇa), which arise through the thorough penetration of impermanence and so forth, not allowing even an atom of lust to arise therein. "They abandon" (pajahanti) means completely cutting off and abandoning the round of defilements (kilesa-vaṭṭa) belonging to the side of the origin (samudaya) by means of the Path-wisdom (magga-paññā) accompanied by insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī vipassanā). "Capable of the destruction of suffering" (bhabbo dukkhakkhayāya) means that because the entire round of kamma (kamma-vaṭṭa) is exhausted precisely by abandoning the stains of defilements in this way, one is certainly fit to reach the Nibbāna element without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu), which is the exhaustion of the entire round of suffering in saṃsāra, or the exhaustion of the round of resultants (vipāka-vaṭṭa) without remainder. This is how the meaning should be understood.

"He who, having known all from every aspect" (yo sabbaṃ sabbato ñatvā) means the practitioner (yogī) who has undertaken the practice and begun insight, having known all things of the three planes in their entirety, by way of the division of aggregates such as wholesome and so forth, and by way of the division of oppression such as suffering and so forth. Alternatively, "from every aspect" (sabbato) means knowing through all modes, such as the characteristics of hardness, contact, etc., and through impermanence, etc., and penetrating with the Path-knowledge preceded by insight, or simply knowing through insight-knowledge. "Is not attached to anything" (sabbatthesu na rajjati) means he does not lust after any identity-dhammas, which are divided into many types by way of the past and so forth; he does not produce lust because of the attainment of the Noble Path. By this, showing the absence of his clinging through craving, and because of that [craving] being the cause, the three types of grasping through view and conceit—"This is mine, this I am, this is my self"...
52:
...it also shows the absence of the three types of wrong grasping. In the phrase "sa ve", "sa" is merely a particle (nipāta). "Ve" is a particle in the sense of clarity or certainty (ekāṃsa). "Full understanding of all" (sabbapariññā) means because of fully understanding everything, because of fully understanding all that was mentioned by way of penetration (abhisamaya). "He" (so) refers to the aforementioned practitioner or the Noble One (ariya). "Has transcended all suffering" (sabbadukkhamupaccagā) means he has gone beyond, has transcended, the entire round of suffering.

## The Commentary on the Seventh Sutta is finished.

## 8. Commentary on the Māna-pariññā Sutta

In the eighth sutta, there is nothing unusual; the teaching proceeds solely by way of conceit (māna). In the verses, "This generation is possessed by conceit" (mānupetā ayaṃ pajā) means these beings, called "generation" (pajā) because they are generated by kamma and defilements, are possessed by, or have approached, conceit which has the characteristic of imagining (maññana). "Bound by the tie of conceit, delighting in existence" (mānaganthā bhave ratā) means they are tied by conceit and bound by the fetter of conceit even in individual existences (attabhāva) such as worms, insects, and grasshoppers. Because of that very connection, through the power of I-making (ahaṅkāra) cultivated for a long time, they are frequent in their adherence to formations (saṅkhāra) as "This is mine," and through the power of perversion (vipallāsa) such as [perceiving] the permanent, the pleasant, and the self in those formations, they delight in the sensual existence (kāmabhava) and so forth.

"Not fully understanding conceit" (mānaṃ aparijānantā) means because they do not fully understand conceit through the three types of full understanding (pariññā). Or, it means they cannot transcend it with the knowledge of the Path of Arahantship. Some teachers recite it as "mānaṃ apariññāya." "They are goers to renewed existence" (āgantāro punabbhavaṃ) means they arrive at a future state of rebirth (upapatti-bhava). Or, because of repeated becoming, they are those who go to saṃsāra, known as renewed existence (punabbhava), by way of revolving from one life to another; they are not liberated from existence.

"But those who, having abandoned conceit, are liberated in the destruction of conceit" (ye ca mānaṃ pahantvāna, vimuttā mānasankhaye) means those who, having entirely abandoned conceit through the Path of Arahantship, are well-liberated through the liberation from all defilements that stand together with it, either in the Fruit of Arahantship or in Nibbāna, which is the absolute destruction of conceit. "They are conquerors of the tie of conceit, they have transcended all suffering" (te mānaganthābhibhuno, sabbadukkhamupaccaguṃ) means those Arahants whose fetters of existence are exhausted, having overcome the tie of conceit (the fetter of conceit) by the abandonment through cutting off (samuccheda-pahāna), remain having transcended the round of suffering without remainder. Thus, in this eighth sutta, as well as in the seventh sutta, the Fruit of Arahantship is proclaimed.

## The Commentary on the Eighth Sutta is finished.

11-13. In the second chapter as well, the first three suttas are just as previously explained; likewise, the reason for teaching them in this way has also been stated.

## 4. Commentary on the Sutta on the Hindrance of Ignorance

In the fourth sutta—among the words beginning with "Nāhaṃ, bhikkhave," the letter "na" has the meaning of negation (prohibition). "Ahaṃ" refers to the Blessed One referring to himself. "Aññaṃ" means something other than the hindrance of ignorance (avijjā-nīvaraṇa) which is about to be mentioned. "Ekanīvaraṇampi" means even a single hindrance. In the word "samanupassāmi," there are two kinds of contemplation (samanupassanā): contemplation through wrong view (diṭṭhi-samanupassanā) and contemplation through knowledge (ñāṇa-samanupassanā). Among these, the contemplation that appears as "He contemplates form as self" etc., is called contemplation through wrong view. However, the contemplation that appears as "He contemplates as impermanent, not as permanent" etc., is called contemplation through knowledge (ñāṇa-samanupassanā). Here, contemplation through knowledge is intended. The word "samanupassāmi" should be seen in connection with the letter "na." This means: "Monks, even when I, with the 'all-seeing eye' known as the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), look at all phenomena like an emblic myrobalan (āmalaka) placed in the palm of the hand, I do not see even one other hindrance..."

"By which hindrance beings, being enveloped, wander and roam for a long time" means: because that phenomenon has the nature of a hindrance, for the sake of knowing, seeing, and penetrating the nature of the Dhamma by that hindrance...
54:
...by making it invisible, covering it, and enveloping it, beings hindered by the darkness of that state wander and roam throughout the beginningless Saṃsāra for immeasurable aeons, in large and small existences, by way of repeated rebirths. Alternatively, wandering (sandhāvana) is the act of moving from one object to another, and roaming (saṃsaraṇa) is the act of moving from one existence to another. Or, wandering is due to the strength of the defilements, and roaming is due to their weakness. Or, wandering is within a single birth by way of momentary death (khaṇika-maraṇa), and roaming is through many births by way of conventional death (vohāra-maraṇa). Or, wandering is by the power of the mind—for has it not been said, "his mind wanders"?—and roaming is by the power of kamma. Thus, the distinction between wandering and roaming should be understood.

"Yathayidaṃ" means "yathā idaṃ." The letter "ya" is a euphonic conjunction, and it becomes short (rassa) by the power of the conjunction. In the term "avijjā-nīvaraṇa," because it is improper to fulfill, bodily misconduct and so forth are called "avindiya" (not to be found/attained); it means they should not be obtained. Because one finds that which is not to be found, it is called "avijjā" (ignorance). Conversely, bodily good conduct and so forth are called "vindiya" (to be found); because one does not find that which is to be found, it is called "avijjā." It is also called "avijjā" because it makes one not know the fourfold meanings taught by way of the oppression, etc., of suffering: the meaning of "heap" for the aggregates (khandha), the meaning of "base" for the sense-bases (āyatana), the meaning of "emptiness" for the elements (dhātu), the meaning of "predominance" for the faculties (indriya), and the true meaning of the truths (sacca). Or, it is called "avijjā" because it makes beings run in the endless Saṃsāra. Or, it is called "avijjā" because it occurs in things like women and men which do not exist in the ultimate sense (paramattha), and does not occur in things like the aggregates which do exist. Furthermore, it is called "avijjā" because it covers the bases and objects of eye-consciousness, etc., and the phenomena of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) and the dependently arisen (paṭiccasamuppanna). Since ignorance itself is a hindrance, it is called the hindrance of ignorance (avijjā-nīvaraṇa).

"Monks, beings hindered by the hindrance of ignorance wander and roam for a long time"—this statement is made to reinforce the previous one. Or, the previous statement, "Monks, just as this hindrance of ignorance," was spoken by way of showing an illustration, while this statement is spoken by way of showing the power of the hindrance. Why is only ignorance mentioned here in this way and not other states? Because by covering the fault, it is the specific cause for sensual desire (kāmacchanda) and so forth. This is true; in an object whose fault is covered by that ignorance, sensual desire and so forth arise.

## The verse beginning with "Natthanyo" is spoken by way of summarizing the meanings already mentioned and those not yet mentioned. In that verse, "nivutā" means obstructed, entangled, or covered. "Ahorattaṃ" means day and night, which means at all times.
55:
In such a way that beings, covered by delusion known as the hindrance of ignorance (avijjā-nīvaraṇa), do not know even the easily understandable Dhamma and wander in saṃsāra, it should be understood that there is no other single state or single hindrance like it. As for those noble disciples (ariya-sāvaka), having abandoned delusion in the beginning through the abandonment by substitution (tadaṅga-pahāna) and so forth, or having abandoned the delusion to be abandoned by each respective path through the lower paths (magga), they have completely cut off the mass of delusion called the mass of darkness without remainder, having shattered it with the diamond-like knowledge of the highest path. Those Arahants—

“The succession of aggregates,
And of elements and bases,
Occurring uninterruptedly,
Is called saṃsāra”. —

They no longer wander or roam in this saṃsāra so described. For what reason? Because the cause of saṃsāra does not exist for those Arahants. Since ignorance, which is the root cause of saṃsāra, has been completely cut off for those Arahants, it no longer exists.

## The Commentary on the Fourth Sutta is finished.

## 5. Commentary on the Taṇhāsaṃyojana Sutta

In the fifth sutta, it is called a 'fetter' (saṃyojana) because it binds that person who possesses craving with sufferings, or kamma with its results, or in the realms (bhava), origins (yoni), destinations (gati), stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti), and abodes of beings (sattāvāsa) with future existences and so forth. It is called 'craving' (taṇhā) in the sense of longing (taṇhāyana). It is called taṇhā because it itself trembles greatly, or because beings tremble by means of it. 'Bound' (saññuttā) means tied to the objects of attachment such as the eye and so forth. The rest is exactly as previously explained.

In fact, in this context, ignorance also has the nature of a fetter, and craving also has the nature of a hindrance. However, to show this distinction—that craving binds beings to existences which have faults covered by ignorance—ignorance was spoken of as a hindrance in the previous sutta, and craving as a fetter in this sutta. Alternatively, it is to show the predominance of the hindrance and the fetter. Just as ignorance is the chief and forerunner of the defiling states in its capacity as a hindrance, so craving is their chief and forerunner in its capacity as a fetter. Therefore, to show their predominance based on that craving, these states were taught in this way in the two suttas. Furthermore, especially because ignorance [obstructs] the bliss of Nibbāna...
56:
Because it obstructs, it is called a 'hindrance' (nīvaraṇa); because craving binds beings with the suffering of saṃsāra, it is called a 'fetter' (saṃyojana).

Alternatively, these two states are taught in two ways because they cause obstacles to seeing (vijjā) and going (caraṇa), or because they are the opposites of vijjā and caraṇa. Indeed, ignorance, being the direct opposite of knowledge (vijjā), especially causes obstacles to the seeing of Nibbāna and to non-perverted seeing. Craving, being the direct opposite of the states of conduct (caraṇa), causes obstacles to going, that is, to right practice (sammā-paṭipadā). Thus, the uninstructed worldling (assutavā puthujjana), covered and blinded by ignorance and obstructed and bound by craving, cannot transcend the wilderness of saṃsāra, just as a bound blind man cannot transcend a great wilderness. These two are also taught in two ways to show the two causes for the occurrence of misfortune (anattha). A person fallen into ignorance, in accordance with being a fool, loses his benefit and brings about his own misfortune, like an unskilled sick person performing unsuitable actions. Even while knowing, a fool, in accordance with being a fool, loses his benefit and brings about misfortune, like a sick person who, though knowing, indulges in what is unsuitable. The Makkaṭālepōpama Sutta proves this point.

These two are also taught in two ways to show the root causes of Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). Especially because of the strength of delusion (sammoha), the field of ignorance is the past time; because of the strength of longing (patthanā), the field of craving is the future time. Indeed, the fool, having much delusion, sorrows over the past; for him, 'with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise' and so forth should be connected. One with much longing yearns for the future; for him, 'with craving as condition, clinging arises' and so forth should be connected. Thus, it should be understood that the root causes are shown in their respective order by the bringing forward of the past and the linking of the future.

In the verses, 'with craving as his companion' (taṇhā-dutiya) means one who has craving as a companion. Indeed, just as the perception of water in a mirage in a waterless wilderness acts as a companion to a thirsty person, so craving, by way of showing what is enjoyable, acts as a companion to a being oppressed by suffering that is difficult to cure, making them wander without weariness in existences. Therefore, craving is called the 'companion' of a man (a being). If it is asked, "Are not other defilements also conditions for the production of new existence?", that is true; however, they are not special conditions in the way craving is. That is true; that craving [with] wholesome states...
57: Craving is called the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering (Samudaya Sacca) because it is the special cause for the arising of existence, distinct from unwholesome states and wholesome states of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara), and through wholesome states of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) and so forth. 'This state and the state of being otherwise' (itthabhāva-aññathābhāva) means the state of being this human and the state of being another creature. Samsara, which ends with the state of being this human and the state of being another creature, is called 'this state and the state of being otherwise.' In this phrase, 'this state' (itthabhāva) is the human state, and 'the state of being otherwise' (aññathābhāva) refers to the abodes of the remaining beings. Alternatively, the present existence (attabhāva) of various beings is 'this state,' and the future existence is 'the state of being otherwise.' Or, an existence of such a nature is 'this state,' and an existence not of such a nature is 'the state of being otherwise.' One cannot transcend the sequence of aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), and bases (āyatana), which is samsara, described as 'this state and the state of being otherwise.' Knowing this danger (ādīnava), and having known craving as the danger—the origin (samudaya) and cause of the arising of all suffering in the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa-dukkha)—this is the meaning. Alternatively, 'knowing this danger' means knowing the danger or fault of being unable to transcend this aforementioned samsara. Knowing craving, by the method mentioned, as the primary cause of the suffering in the round of rebirth. A monk who, through the three full understandings (pariññā), develops insight (vipassanā) and abandons craving through the sequence of the paths, becomes one whose craving is entirely gone (vītataṇhā) by the Path of Arahantship. Because of that state of being free from craving, he is 'without grasping' (anādāno) because of the absence of even a single one of the four types of grasping (upādāna), or because of the absence of grasping known as future rebirth (paṭisandhi). Reaching the abundance of mindfulness and acting with mindfulness in all matters, the monk who has destroyed the defilements (kilesa) should wander; or it means he should depart from the occurrence of formations (saṅkhāra) through the final Nibbāna of the aggregates (khandha-parinibbāna). ## The Explanation of the Fifth Sutta is Finished. ## 6. Explanation of the First Sekha Sutta In the sixth sutta, regarding the word 'sekha' (trainee), for what reason is one called a trainee? One is called a trainee because of the attainment of the qualities of a trainee (sekkha-dhamma). It was said: 'To what extent, venerable sir, is one a trainee?' 'Here, monk, a monk is endowed with the right view of a trainee... endowed with the right concentration of a trainee. To this extent, monk, is one a trainee.' Alternatively, one is called a trainee because one trains (sikkhati).
58: ...is endowed with right concentration. 'To this extent, monk, is one a trainee,' so it was said (in the Saṃyutta Nikāya). Alternatively, one is called a trainee (sekha) because one trains (sikkhati). This was also said: 'Monk, because one trains, therefore one is called a trainee. In what does one train? One trains in higher virtue (adhisīla), one trains in higher mind (adhicitta), and one trains in higher wisdom (adhipaññā). Monk, because one trains, therefore one is called a trainee,' so it was said (in the Aṅguttara Nikāya). Even a noble worldling (kalyāṇa-puthujjana) who fulfills the practice through the conforming way, being endowed with virtue, guarding the doors of the senses, knowing moderation in eating, being devoted to wakefulness, and being devoted to the development of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) in the first and last watches of the night, dwells thinking, 'Today or tomorrow, I shall attain one of the fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala).' Such a noble worldling is also called a trainee because he trains. In this context, it is not only the trainee who has penetrated (the truth) who is intended, but the noble worldling is also intended. One whose goal (mind) is not yet reached is called 'appattamānaso.' Regarding the word 'mānasa,' in the verse 'The snare of craving that wanders in the sky, that which wanders is mānasa,' craving (rāga) is called 'mānasa.' In 'cittaṃ mano mānasam,' it refers to the mind (citta). In 'The trainee whose goal is not yet reached (appattamānaso) may pass away, known among the people,' the fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala) is called 'mānasa.' Here also, only the fruit of Arahantship is intended. Therefore, it means 'for one who has not yet reached Arahantship.' 'Anuttaraṃ' means supreme or incomparable. 'Yogakkhema' means secure from the four yokes (yoga) and unassailed; here, only Arahantship is intended. Regarding 'patthayamānassa' (for one who desires), there are two kinds of desire: desire through craving (taṇhā-patthanā) and desire through wholesome wish (kusala-chanda-patthanā). In the verse 'For one who desires, there are cravings and tremblings in things imagined,' desire through craving is meant. 'The stream of the Evil One is cut, destroyed, and made like a hollow reed. O monks, be full of joy, and desire the secure Nibbāna.' In this verse, it is the desire through the wholesome wish to act (kattukamyatā-kusala-chanda) that is meant, and this alone is intended here. Therefore, 'patthayamānassa' means for one who wishes to go to that Nibbāna which is the end of the yokes, who is bent, inclined, and leaning towards it. 'Viharato' means for one who carries the existence (attabhāva) without falling, by cutting off the suffering of one posture with another posture. Alternatively...
59:
The meaning here should be understood through the method of explanation (niddesa) such as: "Abiding in faith, one attends to the thought: All conditioned things are impermanent." "Internal" (ajjhattika) means existing within one's own continuity. "Factor" (anga) means a cause. "Having done so" means having acted in this way. In the phrase "I do not see any other single factor," the summarized meaning is: "Monks, I do not see any other single cause arising within one's own continuity that is as greatly beneficial as this, namely, wise attention (yoniso manasikāra)." This is attention by way of means, attention by way of the right path, attention to impermanence and so on in the manner of impermanence, or the turning, repeated turning, advertence, and application of the mind in accordance with impermanence. This is wise attention.

Now, to show the power of wise attention, it is said: "Monks, when a monk attends wisely, he abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome." In that passage, "attending wisely" means exercising wise attention regarding the Four Noble Truths: "This is the Noble Truth of Suffering, this is the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, this is the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, this is the Noble Truth of the Way Leading to the Cessation of Suffering."

To explain the meaning therein: Although this sutta is given generally in terms of a person in training (sekha), I shall describe the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) briefly in connection with the four paths. A practitioner who has the Four Noble Truths as a meditation subject has previously learned the meditation subject of the Four Truths from a teacher thus: "The aggregates of the three planes, excluding craving, are suffering; craving is the origin; the non-occurrence of both is cessation; the path leading to cessation is the Truth of the Path." At a later time, when he has ascended to the path of insight (vipassanā-magga), he wisely attends to the aggregates of the three planes as "This is suffering"; he applies his mind through the right means and path, and practices insight. For here, insight is spoken of under the heading of "attention." He wisely attends to that craving from a previous life which is the producer of that suffering as "This is the origin of suffering." Since this suffering and this origin cease and do not occur upon reaching this state [Nibbāna], he wisely attends to that which is called Nibbāna as "This is the cessation of suffering." He wisely attends to the Eightfold Path that leads to cessation as "This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering"; he applies his mind through the right means and path, and practices insight.
60:
In this passage, the following is the method (upāya). Adherence (abhinivesa) occurs only in the aggregates, not in the state free from the round (Nibbāna). Therefore, the meaning is this: By the method beginning with "In this body there is the earth element, the water element," he grasps the four great elements and the derived matter following them, and defines them as "This is the material aggregate (rūpakkhandha)." While he is defining that, he defines the mental states (citta-cetasika) that have that material aggregate as their object as "These four are the immaterial aggregates (arūpakkhandha)." Then he defines them as "These five aggregates are suffering (dukkha)." These, in brief, are the two parts: mentality (nāma) and materiality (rūpa). This mentality-materiality arises with causes and conditions. He defines the causes and conditions, noting that ignorance (avijjā), existence (bhava), craving (taṇhā), and so on are its causes, and nutriment (āhāra) and so on are its conditions. Having defined the true nature, function, and characteristics of those conditions and the conditionally arisen phenomena, he applies the characteristic of impermanence (anicca-lakkhaṇa) thus: "These things, having not been, come to be; having come to be, they perish; therefore they are impermanent." He applies the characteristic of suffering (dukkha-lakkhaṇa) thus: "They are suffering because they are continuously oppressed by rise and fall." He applies the characteristic of non-self (anatta-lakkhaṇa) thus: "They are non-self because they are not subject to one's will."

While practicing insight by applying these three characteristics, when insight imperfections (vipassanūpakkilesa) such as effulgence (obhāsa) arise due to the arising of the knowledge of rise and fall (udayabbayāṇāṇa), he defines them as "not the path." He defines the knowledge of rise and fall itself as "the preliminary path that is the means to the Noble Path," thus distinguishing the path from the non-path (maggāmagga-vavatthāna). Then, producing the knowledge of rise and fall again, followed by the knowledge of dissolution (bhaṅgañāṇa) and so on in sequence, he reaches the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpattimagga) and the others. At that moment, he penetrates the Four Truths with a single penetration; he realizes them in a single realization. Therein, penetrating suffering through the penetration of full understanding (pariññā), and penetrating the origin through the penetration of abandoning (pahāna), he abandons all unwholesome states. Penetrating cessation through the penetration of realization (sacchikiriyā), and penetrating the path through the penetration of development (bhāvanā), he develops all wholesome states. For the Noble Path is wholesome (kusala) in the sense of destroying what is contemptible and so on in the primary sense. When that path is developed, all the faultless factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma) reach the fulfillment of development. Thus, by attending wisely, one abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome. So it has been said: "He wisely attends: This is suffering; he wisely attends: This is the origin of suffering," and so on. It is also said elsewhere: "Monks, for a monk who is possessed of wise attention, it is to be expected that he will develop the Noble Eightfold Path, that he will cultivate the Noble Eightfold Path."
61:
The summary of the meaning in the verse "Yoniso manasikāra" is as follows: One is called a trainee (sekha) because one trains in the training rules or has the habit of training. One is called a monk (bhikkhu) because one sees danger in the round of rebirths (saṃsāra). For that monk who is a trainee, for the attainment and realization of the supreme goal, Arahantship, there is no other quality as helpful as wise attention (yoniso manasikāra). Why is that? Because if one strives with the four right efforts (sammappadhāna), putting wise attention at the forefront, one can reach the end of suffering, Nibbāna, which is the complete exhaustion and end of the suffering of the round of defilements. Therefore, wise attention is of great help.

## The Commentary on the Sixth Sutta is finished.

## 7. Commentary on the Second Sekha Sutta

In the seventh sutta, "external" (bāhira) means occurring outside of one's own internal continuity. "Good friendship" (kalyāṇamittatā) means: for a person, there is a friend who is endowed with virtues such as morality, who removes suffering, who provides welfare, and who is helpful in every way; such a person is called a "good friend" (kalyāṇamitta). The state of having such a good friend is "good friendship" (kalyāṇamittatā). In this context, this good friend is naturally endowed with faith, virtue, learning, generosity, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. Among these eight, through the perfection of faith, he believes in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata (the knowledge of the path of Arahantship and omniscience). Because of that belief, he does not abandon seeking the welfare and happiness of beings, which is the cause of perfect enlightenment. Through the perfection of virtue, he is dear, respected, and venerable to his fellow practitioners; he is one who points out faults, reproaches evil, gives advice, and is patient under admonition. Through the perfection of learning, he is a speaker of deep discourses such as those on the aggregates (khandha), sense bases (āyatana), truths (sacca), and dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). Through the perfection of generosity, he has few wishes, is contented, secluded, and not entangled. Through the perfection of energy, he possesses energy exerted in the practice for the welfare of himself and others. Through the perfection of mindfulness, he has established mindfulness and is endowed with supreme mindfulness and prudence, able to remember and recall what was done and said long ago. Through the perfection of concentration, he is undistracted, with a composed and one-pointed mind. Through the perfection of wisdom, he knows things correctly without distortion.
62:
That person repeatedly investigates the courses of wholesome and unwholesome states with mindfulness, knows the welfare and happiness of beings as they truly are with wisdom, becomes one with an unswerving mind in that welfare with concentration, and restrains beings from what is not beneficial and joins them to what is truly beneficial with energy. Therefore, it is said (in the Nettippakaraṇa):

"Dear, respected, and venerable,
A speaker and patient in speech,
A speaker of deep discourse,
And not urging one in the wrong place."

"Monks, a monk who has a good friend abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome" means that a person with a good friend, by relying on that good friend, gives rise to the knowledge of the ownership of kamma (kammassakatā-ñāṇa) and increases the faith that has arisen. One who has developed faith approaches and listens to the Dhamma. Having heard that Dhamma, he gains faith in the Tathāgata. By gaining that faith, he abandons the life of a householder and follows the life of renunciation. He fulfills the fourfold purification of virtue (catu-pārisuddhi-sīla). He undertakes and practices the ascetic qualities (dhutaṅga) according to his strength. He becomes one who obtains the ten subjects of talk (kathāvatthu), lives with energy aroused, and is endowed with established mindfulness and clear comprehension. He is devoted to the practice of developing the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) in the first and last watches of the night. Before long, having intensified insight (vipassanā), he completely cuts off all unwholesome states through the attainment of the Noble Path (ariya-magga), and he develops all wholesome states, bringing them to the fulfillment of development (bhāvanā). For this was said by the Blessed One:

"Meghiya, for a monk who has a good friend, a good companion, a good associate, this is to be expected: that he will be virtuous, dwelling restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, endowed with proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults, and training in the training rules he has undertaken."

"For a monk who has a good friend... a good associate, this is to be expected: that such talk as is erasuresome (of defilements), suitable for opening up the mind, and which leads to absolute disenchantment... to Nibbāna—namely, talk on fewness of wishes, talk on contentment, talk on seclusion, talk on non-entanglement, talk on arousing energy, talk on virtue, talk on concentration... talk on the knowledge and vision of liberation—such talk he will obtain at will, without difficulty, and without trouble."
63:
It is to be expected of a bhikkhu who has a good friend, who is inclined towards a good friend, that he will be virtuous, that he will dwell restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults, and that he will undertake and train in the training rules. It is to be expected of a bhikkhu who has a good friend, who is inclined towards a good friend, that he will obtain at will, without difficulty or hardship, such talk as is truly effacing, conducive to opening the heart, and which leads to absolute disenchantment and to the benefit of Nibbāna—that is, talk on fewness of wishes, contentment, seclusion, non-association, arousal of energy, virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. It is to be expected of a bhikkhu who has a good friend, who is inclined towards a good friend, that he will dwell with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the undertaking of wholesome states, being steadfast and firm in his efforts, not laying down the burden of wholesome states.

It is to be expected of a bhikkhu who has a good friend, who is inclined towards a good friend, that he will be wise, possessing wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative, and which leads to the complete destruction of suffering (Udā. 31).

Thus, it should be understood that having a good friend (kalyāṇamittatā) is the cause for liberation from the entire suffering of the round of rebirths. For this very reason, the Buddha taught: "Ananda, it is by relying on me as a good friend that beings subject to birth are liberated from birth, and beings subject to aging are liberated from aging," and so forth (Saṃ. Ni. 1.129).

Therefore, it was said: "Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who has a good friend abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome."

In the verse, "sappatisso" means being with acceptance (patissava); thus he is called "sappatisso," meaning one who respectfully accepts the advice of a good friend and is easy to speak to (suvaco). Alternatively, "patisso" means one who establishes another in welfare and happiness, an advisor (ovādadāyaka). Because he dwells with that advisor with gravity and respect, he is called "sappatisso," being one who frequently shows respect to those worthy of respect. "Sagāravo" means being endowed with the six kinds of reverence (gārava). "Karaṃ mittānaṃ vacanaṃ" means following the advice of good friends and practicing according to that advice. "Sampajāno" means being endowed with clear comprehension (sampajañña) in the seven instances. "Patissato" means being mindful and acting with mindfulness capable of bringing the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) to growth. "Anupubbena" means by the sequence of purifications such as virtue, and therein by the sequence of insight (vipassanā) and the sequence of the Path (magga). "Sabbasaṃyojanakkhayaṃ" refers to the Fruit of Arahantship, which is the culmination of the Noble Path and is called the destruction of all fetters because it exhausts all fetters such as sensual lust, or it refers to Nibbāna itself, which is the object of that Arahantship. "Pāpuṇe" means he would reach or attain (adhigaccheyya). Thus, it should be understood that in these two suttas, the Teacher has identified the primary factor for the attainment of the Noble Path.

## The Commentary on the Seventh Sutta Ends.
64:
## 8. Saṅghabheda Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the eighth sutta, regarding the term "ekadhammo," what kind of discourse delivery (suttanikkhepa) is this? It is a discourse arisen from a specific occasion (aṭṭhuppatti). Here is the summary: Devadatta, having caused Prince Ajātasattu to adopt wrong views and having caused him to kill his father, King Bimbisāra, and having himself made efforts to kill the Buddha and caused a bruise by hurling a rock, was not yet notorious by those acts alone. However, he became notorious after releasing the elephant Nāḷāgiri. Then the great multitude raised a great outcry, saying, "A king is wandering about having committed such a wicked evil!" A great roar arose. Hearing this, the King cut off the five hundred pots of rice he used to offer and stopped going to attend on him. Even the city dwellers did not offer even a spoonful of alms-food to him when he approached their families.

Devadatta, having lost gain and honor and wishing to live by deceit, approached the Teacher and requested five points. The Blessed One rejected them, saying, "Enough, Devadatta. Let him who wishes be a forest-dweller," and so forth (Pārā. 409, Cūḷava. 343). Using those five points to convince foolish people who were impressed by austerity, he caused five hundred Vajjiputtaka monks to take the voting tickets, split the Saṅgha, and taking them with him, went to Gayāsīsa. Then the two Chief Disciples, by the command of the Teacher, went there, preached the Dhamma, established those monks in the noble fruits, and brought them back. For those monks who, favoring the view of Devadatta as he strove for a schism, remained supporting it and consented to the Saṅgha being split and having been split, that consent led to their harm and suffering for a long time.

Devadatta himself was soon overcome by disease and became severely ill. At the time of death, wishing to pay homage to the Teacher, he was being carried on a litter. While being placed down near the pond at Jetavana, the earth opened up, and he fell into the Avīci hell. His body was a hundred yojanas in size, and for the duration of an aeon, he was pierced by iron spikes the size of palm trunks. Five hundred families who were partisans of Devadatta and stood by his view were also reborn in hell along with their relatives. One day, the monks started a conversation in the Dhamma Hall: "Friends, Devadatta has committed a grave deed by splitting the Saṅgha." Then the Teacher, having come to the Dhamma Hall, asked, "Bhikkhus, for what conversation are you sitting here now?" When they replied, "For such and such a conversation," he spoke on the danger of splitting the Saṅgha...
65:
Wishing to show the danger of schism in the Saṅgha, he taught this sutta. However, some teachers say, "The Blessed One, having seen Devadatta and his followers destined for rebirth in hell in that manner, taught this sutta out of his own intention, wishing to show the danger of schism in the Saṅgha."

In that sutta, "ekadhammo" refers to a single unwholesome state that carries heavy consequences. "Loke" means in the world of beings. Regarding the phrase "uppajjamāno uppajjati" (arising, it arises), when disputes and so forth leading to schism arise in the Saṅgha, or when they speak by way of any of the eighteen grounds for schism such as "This is Dhamma, this is non-Dhamma," or when they make it known to generate preference for that matter, or when, having made it known, they cause the voting slips (salākā) to be taken—at such times, the schism in the Saṅgha is said to be "in the process of arising." However, when the voting slips have been taken and four or more monks perform a separate recitation of the Pātimokkha or a formal act of the Saṅgha (saṅghakamma), at that time the schism in the Saṅgha is said to have "arisen." Once that is done, the schism in the Saṅgha is said to have "occurred." Among these five causes for the schism of the Saṅgha—the formal act, the recitation, the assertion, the announcement, and the taking of voting slips—only the formal act or the recitation is the standard (decisive factor), while the assertion, the announcement, and the taking of voting slips are merely preliminary stages.

In the words beginning with "bahujanāhitāya" (for the harm of many), it is for the lack of benefit by preventing the attainment of the many folk such as jhāna and the Path (magga); for the lack of happiness by preventing the attainment of the heavenly realms; and for the lack of welfare by being the cause for rebirth in the states of woe (apāya). Alternatively, it should be understood as being for the lack of benefit by way of unwholesome states, and for the physical and mental suffering even if reborn in a happy destination (sugati) because of the total absence of even a slight benefit. The phrase "devamanussānaṃ" (of gods and humans) is a designation of the highest individuals among those called "the many folk."

Another method: "bahujanāhitāya" means for the lack of benefit of the great body of beings, for the lack of welfare in this life and the next. "Asukhāya" means for the lack of happiness in this life and the next, for the two kinds of suffering. "Anatthāya" means for the rejection of the ultimate goal (paramattha). Nibbāna alone is the ultimate goal; there is no goal higher than that. "Ahitāya" means for the rejection of the Path. There is no benefit higher than the Path that leads to Nibbāna. "Dukkhāya" means for the suffering of the round (vaṭṭadukkha) through missing the noble happiness (ariyasukha). Those who miss the noble happiness and are incapable of attaining it wander in the suffering of the round; there is no happiness higher than noble happiness. Indeed, it has been said: "This concentration is both happy in the present and has a happy result in the future."
66:
Now, having shown the nature of the schism in the Saṅgha (saṅghabheda), in order to reveal that it is the absolute cause of harm and so on, he said the words beginning with "Saṅghe kho pana, bhikkhave, bhinne." In that sutta, the word "bhinne" is in the locative case in the sense of cause. Just as in the phrase "adhanānaṃ dhane ananuppadīyamāne" (when wealth is not being given to the poor), it means "because of the cause of schism."

"Aññamaññaṃ bhaṇḍanāni" means the mutual quarreling and opposition between the four assemblies and the followers of the monk who causes the schism, saying "This is the Dhamma, this is not the Dhamma." Indeed, quarreling is the precursor to conflict. "Paribhāsā" means threatening by creating fear, saying "We will do such and such harm to you." "Parikkhepā" means casting aside from all sides by way of birth (caste) etc., and reviling and disparaging through the ten grounds for abuse (akkosavatthu). "Pariccajanā" means expulsion by way of performing the act of suspension (ukkhepanīyakamma) and so on. "Tattha" means in that schism of the Saṅgha, or in the quarreling etc., caused by that schism. "Appasannā" refers to those who do not understand the virtues of the Triple Gem. "Na pasīdanti" means they do not gain confidence in the manner one should gain confidence in monks, such as "They are practitioners of the Dhamma, practitioners of evenness," etc. Or, they do not consider the words of those monks as something to be listened to or believed. Furthermore, they simply lack confidence in the Dhamma and the Teacher. "Ekaccānaṃ aññathattaṃ" refers to the change from confidence to a state of lack of clarity in worldlings (puthujjana) whose faith is not yet firmly rooted.

In the verse, among the words beginning with "āpāyiko," he is "āpāyika" because he deserves to be reborn in the states of deprivation (apāya). Among those states, he is "nerayika" because he is reborn in the great hell known as Avīci. He is "kappaṭṭho" because he remains in that hell for a full intermediate eon (antarakappa). He is "vaggarato" because he delights in the group known as the schism of the Saṅgha. He is "adhamma" because of his unrighteous state. He is "adhammaṭṭho" because he stands in the unrighteousness known as the schism of the Saṅgha through the grounds that cause schism. "Yogakkhemā padhaṃsati" means he falls away and perishes from the welfare that is security from bondage (yogakkhema). Or rather, there is no need to even mention his fall from the fruit of Arahantship and Nibbāna, which are called yogakkhema because they are not oppressed by the four bondages (yoga). The "Saṅgha" is so called because of the sense of being united through the equality of view (diṭṭhi) and virtue (sīla). Because of being thus equal in view and virtue and being associated with the performance of major and minor acts together, it is called "samagga" (harmonious) and "sahita" (united). "Bhetvāna" means having divided the Saṅgha by the schism characterized as previously mentioned. "Kappaṃ" refers to the life-span eon (āyukappa). In this sutta, however, that eon is only an intermediate eon (antarakappa). "Nirayamhi" means in the great Avīci hell.

## End of the Commentary on the Eighth Sutta.
67:
## 9. Saṅghasāmaggīsutta-vaṇṇanā

In the commentary on the ninth sutta, the Saṅghasāmaggī Sutta, 'ekadhammo' refers to a single wholesome state, a faultless state. If a dispute should arise in the Saṅgha such as, 'This is the Dhamma, this is not the Dhamma,' then a wise person who loves the Dhamma should reflect thus: 'If this dispute grows, it is possible that it will lead to a crack in the Saṅgha or a schism in the Saṅgha.' If one is personally involved in that legal matter (adhikaraṇa) at the forefront, one should immediately withdraw from it, like one who has stepped on fire. If others are carrying out that legal matter but one is personally able to settle it, one should be energetic and travel even to a distant place to act in such a way that the legal matter is settled. If one is not personally able to do so, and that dispute continues to grow and is not settled, one should encourage suitable fellow practitioners who are desirous of training to settle that legal matter by whatever Dhamma, whatever Vinaya, and whatever instruction of the Teacher it may be settled.

The wholesome state of one who settles it in this way, which brings about concord in the Saṅgha, is what is intended by 'ekadhammo' in this sutta. By removing the defiling states (saṃkilesadhamma) that bring harm and suffering—which are liable to arise in the monks of both factions who are in a state of doubt, and in the bhikkhunīs, laymen, laywomen, and the guardian deities up to the Brahmas who follow those monks—and by being the cause for a great mass of merit and a flow of wholesome states, that state brings about the welfare and happiness of the world with its devas. Therefore, it was said: 'Monks, when one state arises in the world, it arises for the welfare of many,' and so forth. The meaning of those words should be understood as the opposite of what was said in the preceding sutta. 'Saṅghasāmaggī' means the state of concord of the Saṅgha, the absence of schism, the unity of legal acts (ekakammata), and the unity of the recitation of the Pātimokkha (ekuddesata).

In the verse, 'sukhā saṅghassa sāmaggī' (concord of the Saṅgha is blissful) is said because concord is a cause for happiness. It is like the saying, 'sukho buddhānamuppādo' (the arising of Buddhas is blissful). 'Samaggānañcanuggaho' means supporting the concord of those who are in harmony by rejoicing, acting in accordance with concord, and maintaining and providing support so that they do not abandon that concord. 'Saṅghaṃ samaggaṃ katvāna' means having made the divided Saṅgha or the Saṅgha that has reached a state of cracking united. 'Kappaṃ' means for the duration of a life-aeon (āyukappa). 'Saggamhi modati' means (rejoices) in the sense-sphere heaven.
68:
Surpassing other devas in ten attributes and experiencing divine bliss, he rejoices, greatly rejoices, sports, and plays according to his desires.

## The Commentary on the Ninth Sutta is Finished.

## 10. Paduṭṭhacittasutta-vaṇṇanā

What is the origin of the tenth sutta? It is simply an incidental origin. It is said that one day, while the monks were sitting assembled in the Dhamma hall, they started this discussion: "Friends, in this world, a certain person performs many meritorious deeds, another performs many evil deeds, and another performs a mixture of both. What will be the future destination of those who perform a mixture?" Then the Teacher, having come to the Dhamma hall and sat on the prepared noble Buddha-seat, heard that discussion and, wishing to show that "Monks, for one with a corrupted mind at the time of death, a miserable destination (duggati) is to be expected," he taught this sutta based on this occasion.

In that sutta, "idha" is a particle indicating place. That word "idha" is used in some places in reference to a location, as in: "To me, being a deva, staying right here (idheva)," and so forth. In some places, it is used in reference to the Dispensation (Sāsana), as in: "Monks, only in this Dispensation (idha) is there a recluse, here is the second recluse," and so forth. In some places, it is used as a mere filler of the verse, as in: "Monks, I (idha) have eaten and am satisfied," and so forth. In some places, it is used in reference to the world, as in: "The Tathāgata arises here (idha) in the world," and so forth. In this sutta also, it should be understood as "in the world." "Ekaccaṃ" means one or a certain one. "Puggalaṃ" means a being (satta). He is called "puggala" because he is filled with wholesome and unwholesome deeds and their results according to conditions, and because he "falls" (galana) by way of death. "Paduṭṭhacittaṃ" means having a mind corrupted by malice or ill-will (āghāta). Alternatively, "paduṭṭhacittaṃ" means having a mind made corrupt by defilements such as lust (rāga) and so forth. In this context, the word "ekaccaṃ" is an adjective for the person with a corrupted mind. It refers to a person for whom the kamma that gives rebirth has found an opportunity. It refers to a person near death whose mind cannot be turned back from the occurrence of unwholesome states and made to enter into wholesome states. "Evaṃ" shows the manner of what is about to be said. "Cetasā" means with one's own mind (by the knowledge of encompassing the minds of others). "Ceto" refers to the mind of that person. "Paricca" means having distinguished or delimited.
69:
I know. Is this not the domain of the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings according to their karma (yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa)? This is true; however, it is said in this way by the power of the unwholesome consciousness arising at that time.

'Imamhi cāyaṃ samaye' means at this time, or in this combination of conditions, if this person were to pass away in the later part of the javana process. This is the meaning. For there is no passing away at the moment of javana. 'Yathābhataṃ nikkhitto evaṃ niraye' means just as something brought is placed down, so too, by one's own karma, one is placed, indeed stationed, in hell. This is the meaning. 'Kāyassa bhedā' means due to the relinquishing of the acquired aggregates (upādinnakkhandha). 'Paraṃ maraṇā' means in the taking up of new aggregates immediately after that relinquishing. Alternatively, 'kāyassa bhedā' means due to the cessation of the life faculty (jīvitindriya). 'Paraṃ maraṇā' means after the death-consciousness (cuti).

All the words beginning with 'apāya' are synonyms for hell (niraya) itself. Hell is called 'apāya' because it is devoid of the happiness known as 'aya'. Or, it is called 'apāya' because it is devoid of the happiness designated as merit, which is the cause for heaven and liberation. It is called 'duggati' because it is the destination (gati) of suffering. Or, it is called 'duggati' because it is a destination produced by corrupt karma due to an abundance of hatred (dosa). It is called 'vinipāta' because those who habitually do evil fall into it involuntarily, or because they fall into it while their major and minor limbs are being destroyed. It is called 'niraya' in the sense of being devoid of gratification (nirassāda), because there is no happiness known as gratification in this hell.

Alternatively, by the word 'apāya', the animal realm is meant. The animal realm is called 'apāya' because it is excluded from the happy destinations (sugati); however, it is not called 'duggati' because great powerful beings like naga kings can exist there. By the word 'duggati', the realm of hungry ghosts (peta-visaya) is meant. That realm of hungry ghosts is called both 'apāya' and 'duggati' because it is excluded from the happy destinations and is a destination of suffering; however, it is not called 'vinipāta' because there is no falling into ruin like the asuras. By the word 'vinipāta', the host of asuras (asurakāya) is meant. That host of asuras is called both 'apāya' and 'duggati' by the aforementioned meanings, and it is also called 'vinipāta' because it has fallen away from all collections of prosperity. By the word 'niraya', only the various types of hell such as Avīci are meant. In this context, however, only hell is meant by all these terms. 'Upapajjanti' means they take rebirth (paṭisandhi).

Among the verses, the first verse was placed by the Elders who were the Recorders of the Dhamma (dhamma-saṅgāhaka) at the time of the Council. 'Ñatvāna' is a past participle (pubbakālakiriyā). This is because the explanation is preceded by knowledge. Alternatively, the word 'tvā' has a causal meaning. For example, just as it is said, 'Seeing the lion, fear arises,' it means 'because of knowing'.
70:
The meaning is: 'Buddho bhikkhūnaṃ santike' means the Buddha, the Knower of the Four Noble Truths, explained the meaning that will be spoken later in two verses to the monks who were in his presence. The remaining words are just as previously explained.

## The Commentary on the Tenth Sutta is finished.

## The Commentary on the Second Chapter is finished.

## 3. The Third Chapter

## 1. The Commentary on the Pasannacitta Sutta

In the first sutta of the third chapter, 'pasannacittaṃ' means one who has a clear mind through faith in the Triple Gem and faith in karma and its results. 'Sugati' is so called because it is a good destination, or because it is a destination of happiness. 'Sagga' (heaven) is so called because it is exceedingly noble due to being endowed with prosperity such as beautiful forms and so on. 'Loka' (world) is so called because the results of merit and demerit are seen in this world, or simply because of its nature of breaking up (lujjana). In this sutta, by the term 'sugati', the human realm (manussa-gati) is also included; by the term 'sagga', only the celestial realm (deva-gati) is included. The remaining words are just as previously explained below.

## The Commentary on the First Sutta is finished.

## 2. The Commentary on the Metta Sutta

In the second sutta, in the phrase 'mā bhikkhave puññānaṃ', 'mā' is a particle in the sense of prohibition. The word 'puñña' (merit) appears in the sense of the fruit of merit (puññaphala) in passages such as: 'Monks, due to the undertaking of wholesome states, this merit increases in this way.' It appears in the sense of good conduct in the sensual and fine-material spheres (kāma-rūpāvacara-sucarita) in passages such as: 'Monks, this person who is immersed in ignorance constructs the formation that is merit.' It appears in the sense of the rebirth-existence (upapatti-bhava) which is a distinction of the happy destinations in passages such as: 'Consciousness arrives at merit.' It appears in the sense of wholesome volition (kusala-cetanā) in passages such as: 'Monks, there are these three grounds for making merit: the ground for making merit consisting in giving, the ground for making merit consisting in virtue, and the ground for making merit consisting in mental development.' In this sutta, however, it should be understood as wholesome states belonging to the three planes (tebhūmaka-kusala-dhamma). In the word 'bhāyittha', fear (bhaya) is of two kinds: fear through knowledge (ñāṇa-bhaya) and fear through embarrassment or dread (sārajja-bhaya). Of these two, the fear that appears in the passage: 'Monks, even those devas who are long-lived, beautiful, full of happiness, and dwelling in high mansions...' is called fear through knowledge (ñāṇa-bhaya). Those devas, having heard the Dhamma teaching of the Buddha, for the most part, [fall into] fear and trembling...
71:
"Even those long-lived devas, having heard the Dhamma teaching of the Tathāgata, for the most part, fall into fear, terror, and great anxiety" and so forth (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.33)—the fear mentioned in such passages is fear through knowledge (ñāṇabhaya). "There was indeed fear, there was trepidation, there was hair-standing on end" and so forth (Dīgha Nikāya 2.318)—the fear mentioned in such passages is fear through timidity (sārajjabhaya). In this sutta as well, it is only fear through timidity.

The meaning here is: Monks, do not fear those merits which a monk should constantly practice, such as restraint of body and speech for a long time, fulfilling major and minor duties, eating at one sitting, sleeping alone, taming the faculties, restraining the mind through the dhutaṅga practices, possessing mindfulness and clear comprehension (sati-sampajañña), and initiating effort by way of devotion to meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna). Do not fall into fear or terror. Do not fear those merits that grant the happiness of Nibbāna in the future life out of fear of obstructing some happiness in the present life. This is the meaning. Here, the word "puññehi" in the genitive case (sāmi-vibhatti) is used in the sense of the ablative (nissakka).

Now, wishing to show the reason why one should not fear those merits, He spoke the words beginning with "Sukhassetaṃ." Therein, the word sukha (happiness/pleasure) appears in the sense of the root of happiness (sukhamūla) in such passages as: "Happy is the arising of the Buddhas; happy is the state of being free from passion in the world" (Dhammapada 194). It appears in the sense of a pleasant object (sukhārammaṇa) in such passages as: "Mahāli, form is a pleasant object, it results in happiness, it descends into happiness" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.60). It appears in the sense of a support for happiness (sukhapaccayatṭhāna) in such passages as: "Monks, it is not easy to describe how the heavenly realms are a support for happiness" (Majjhima Nikāya 3.255). It appears in the sense of a cause of happiness (sukhahetu) in such passages as: "The accumulation of merit is the cause of happiness" (Dhammapada 118). It appears in the sense of freedom from trouble (abyāpajja) in such passages as: "These qualities are for dwelling happily in the present life" (Majjhima Nikāya 1.82). It appears in the sense of Nibbāna in such passages as: "Nibbāna is the supreme happiness" (Dhammapada 204). It appears in the sense of pleasant feeling (sukhavedanā) in such passages as: "With the abandoning of pleasure..." (Cullaniddesa). It appears in the sense of equanimous feeling (upekkhāvedanā) in such passages as: "The peaceful state that is neither painful nor pleasant is spoken of as happiness itself" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.253). It appears in the sense of desired happiness (iṭṭhasukha) in such passages as: "Ānanda, I have taught two feelings by way of exposition: pleasant feeling and painful feeling" (Majjhima Nikāya 2.89). It appears in the sense of a happy result (sukhavipāka) in such passages as: "The result of merits is happiness" (Peṭakopadesa). In this sutta as well, it should be understood as the desired result (iṭṭhavipāka).

In the words beginning with "iṭṭhassa," the meaning should be understood as: "iṭṭha" (desired) because it is to be sought after and because it rejects what is undesired; "kanta" (lovely) because it is to be loved and because it enters the mind pleasingly; "piya" (dear) because it is to be cherished and because it satisfies the mind; and "manāpa" (agreeable) because it is to be honored and because it increases the mind's joy. The word "puññāni" in the phrase "yadidaṃ puññāni" is a designation (adhivacana) for the happy and desired result. Happiness itself...
72:
The word 'puñña' (merit) is the name for the desired and pleasant result. The statement 'sukhametaṃ yadidaṃ puññaṃ' (merit is a name for happiness) is spoken by way of abhedūpacāra (metaphorical identification), where the cause is identified with the effect. By thus identifying the cause with the effect, the Buddha encourages the performance of meritorious deeds, implying that upon hearing of the inevitable results of the merits performed and accumulated, one should perform merits diligently and respectfully; he also inspires respect for those meritorious actions in them.

Now, the Blessed One, wishing to make clear the matter by citing the most magnificent result of merit experienced over a long period, which was concealed by another birth and resulted from the meritorious deeds performed by himself during the time he was the teacher Sunetta, spoke the words beginning with "Abhijānāmi kho panāhaṃ" (I recall). In that passage, 'abhijānāmi' means I know with specially distinguished knowledge, I understand through direct realization. 'Dīgharattaṃ' means for a long time. 'Puññānaṃ' means of the wholesome states such as giving (dāna) and so forth. 'Satta vassāni' means for seven years. 'Mettacittaṃ' means a mind of loving-kindness; it is called 'mettā' because it loves, meaning it is affectionate. It is also called 'mettā' because it occurs towards a friend (mitta), or it is the conduct of a friend. According to its characteristics and so forth, it has the characteristic of occurring in the mode of wishing for welfare. Its function is to bring about welfare. Its manifestation is the removal of resentment. Its proximate cause is seeing the lovableness of beings. The subsiding of ill-will is its success, and the production of selfish affection is its failure. Because that mind possesses such loving-kindness, it is called 'mettacittaṃ'.

'Bhāvetvā' refers to the mind associated with loving-kindness; since concentration (samādhi) is spoken of by taking the mind as the head, it means having produced and developed the concentration of loving-kindness, which is the divine abode of loving-kindness (mettā-brahmavihāra). 'Satta saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭakappe' means for seven great aeons. By taking 'saṃvaṭṭa' (contraction) and 'vivaṭṭa' (expansion), those who abide during contraction and expansion are also included. 'Imaṃ lokaṃ' refers to the sense sphere (kāmaloka). 'Saṃvaṭṭamāne sudaṃ' means when [the world] is being destroyed; 'sudaṃ' is merely a particle. They also recite it as 'saṃvattamāne sudaṃ'. 'Kappe' means in the time. Time is spoken of by taking the aeon (kappa) as the head. When time is exhausted, the aeon is also exhausted. As it is said:
"Time consumes all beings, together with itself."

Since it is said "Ābhassarūpago homi" (I went to the Ābhassara realm), the arising of the aeon here should be understood by way of the destruction by fire (tejo-saṃvaṭṭa). 'Ābhassarūpago' means I go to the Ābhassara Brahma realm by way of taking rebirth there. 'Vivaṭṭamāne' means when it is being established, meaning when it is being born. 'Suññaṃ brahmavimānaṃ upapajjāmi' means I go to and arise in the Brahma palace that is empty because no being has yet been born there, which is the Brahma palace known as the first jhāna plane that arises at the beginning, by way of taking rebirth. 'Brahmā' is so called because he is noble compared to the beings of the sense sphere, because his qualities are developed in various ways, and because he is born from the divine abodes (brahmavihāra). He is 'Mahābrahmā' because he is greater than the Brahmā-pārisajja and Brahmā-purohita deities. Furthermore, because he stands having overcome them...
73:
Because he stands having overcome those Brahmā-pārisajja and Brahmā-purohita deities, he is called 'Abhibhū' (the Overlord). Because he cannot be overcome by those deities through any quality, he is called 'Anabhibhūta' (the Unconquered). The word 'aññadatthu' is a particle used in the sense of 'certainly'. 'Dassa' means one who has the habit of seeing; that Mahābrahmā is capable of seeing the past, future, and present, meaning 'I see what should be seen through higher knowledge (abhiññā)'. One should connect 'Vasavattī homi' (I am the wielder of power) as meaning 'I wield power over the minds of the remaining Brahmas and my own mind through the power of the development of the bases of psychic power (iddhipāda)'. At that time, it is said that the Bodhisatta, although he was a possessor of the eight attainments, looked towards the welfare of beings and the fulfillment of his own perfections (pāramī), and having produced attachment only to those two jhāna planes, he wandered repeatedly [in saṃsāra] by the power of the divine abode of loving-kindness. Therefore, it was said: "For seven years... (pe)... wielder of power."

Thus, the Blessed One, having shown the greatness of the result of merit in the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), now spoke the words beginning with "Chattiṃsakkhattuṃ" (thirty-six times) to show the same for merit in the sense sphere (kāmāvacara). In that passage, "Sakkō ahōsi" means that for thirty-six times, without being born elsewhere, he was continuously Sakka, the Lord of Devas, the King of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. In the words "Rājā ahōsi" and so forth, he is called 'Rājā' (King) because he delights the world with the four wonderful qualities and the four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu). He is called 'Cakkavatti' (Universal Monarch) because he causes the Wheel-treasure to turn, or because he proceeds by the four wheels of prosperity (sampatti-cakka) and causes others to proceed by them, or because the turning of the wheels of his postures exists for the welfare of others. Here, the word 'Rājā' is general, while 'Cakkavatti' is specific. He is 'Dhammika' because he acts according to the Dhamma, meaning he proceeds with justice and impartiality. He is 'Dhammarāja' because he became king having obtained kingship only through Dhamma. Alternatively, he is 'Dhammika' by practicing for the welfare of others, and 'Dhammarāja' by practicing for his own welfare. He is 'Cāturanta' because he is the lord of the four quarters, meaning the lord of the earth adorned with the four kinds of islands and bounded by the four oceans. He is 'Vijitāvī' (Victorious) because he conquered enemies such as anger internally, and all kings externally, without the use of force or weapons. He is 'Janapadatthāvariyappatta' because he has attained a state of permanence and stability in the country such that no one can move him from it, or because he has a country that has attained stability in him, being devoted to him, intent on its own work, steady, and unshakable.

He is 'Sattaratanasamannāgata' because he is endowed with these seven treasures: the Wheel-treasure, the Elephant-treasure, the Horse-treasure, the Gem-treasure, the Woman-treasure, the Householder-treasure, and the Counselor-treasure. Among them, the Universal Monarch conquers what is unconquered with the Wheel-treasure; he travels comfortably through what is conquered with the Elephant and Horse treasures; he protects what is conquered with the Counselor-treasure; and he enjoys the pleasure of use with the remaining treasures. And with the first, the Wheel-treasure, for that king...
74:
Possession of the power of effort (ussāha-satti) through association with the first jewel, the Wheel-jewel; possession of the power of counsel (manta-satti) through association with the last jewel, the eldest son jewel; and possession of the power of sovereignty (pabhū-satti) through association with the Elephant-jewel, the Horse-jewel, and the Householder-jewel are fully complete. Possession of the Woman-jewel and the Gem-jewel is the result of association with these three powers. That Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti) enjoys the pleasure of use (paribhoga-sukha) through the Woman-jewel and the Gem-jewel, and the pleasure of utility (upabhoga-sukha) through the remaining jewels. Specifically, for that Wheel-turning Monarch, the first three jewels are accomplished through the power of kamma born from the root of non-hatred (adosa-kusalamūla). The middle three jewels are accomplished through the power of kamma born from the root of non-greed (alobha-kusalamūla). The last one, the eldest son jewel, is accomplished through the power of kamma born from the root of non-delusion (amoha-kusalamūla). Padesarajja means sovereignty over a small country or region.

'Etadahosi' (this thought occurred) means that for the Wheel-turning Monarch reflecting on his own prosperity, at the time of being the final Wheel-turning Monarch, the thought arose: 'Of what kamma is this the fruit for me?' and so on. In every existence, this thought occurred as it was beneficial. In this context, the connection is made according to the time of being a Wheel-turning Monarch. 'Evammahiddhika' (of such great psychic power) means having such great power through the possession of the treasury and vehicles, led by the Gem-jewel, Elephant-jewel, etc., and through attaining stability in the country. 'Evammahānubhāva' (of such great majesty) means having such great majesty through the possession of the Wheel-jewel, etc., whereby he does not oppress anyone, his instructions are respectfully accepted by all kings with their heads bowed, and he travels through the air, etc. 'Dāna' (giving) means the relinquishing of offerable items such as alms-food and snacks. 'Dama' (restraint) means the taming of the sense faculties such as the eye, and the taming of defilements such as lust through the power of concentration (samādhi). 'Saṃyama' (self-control) means restraint of body and speech. In that context, the taming of defilements through the power of concentration is merit consisting in mental development (bhāvanāmaya-puñña). In this sutta, that merit is intended as the sublime state of loving-kindness (mettā-brahmavihāra). In that merit of loving-kindness, which is twofold as access (upacāra) and absorption (appanā), through the merit that has reached absorption, his rebirth occurred in the two aforementioned jhāna planes. Through the other three types of merit, it should be understood that he attained the state of a Wheel-turning Monarch and so on, as appropriate.

Thus, the Blessed One, having testified to himself and revealed the greatness of the fruits of merit, now wishing to show that same meaning in verse form, spoke the words beginning with 'Puññameva'. In that verse, 'Puññameva so sikkheyya' (one should train in merit alone) means that a man of good family who desires his own welfare should train in, establish, accumulate, and develop the three kinds of wholesome deeds called 'merit' (puñña), because they produce good results and because they purify one's own continuity. 'Āyataggaṃ' (of far-reaching excellence) is called so because it has extensive and noble fruits. Or, it is called āyatagga because it has pleasant and agreeable fruits that are excellent in the future. Or, it is called āyatagga because it is the most excellent (agga) through causes (āya) such as wise reflection (yoniso manasikāra).
75:
Āyataggaṃ. The letter 'ta' is a euphonic conjunction (padasandhikara). Alternatively, it is called āyatagga because it is excellent (agga) through the fruit of merit (āya). For that very reason, it has the meaning of increasing happiness or having happy results.

To the question 'What is that merit, and how should one train in it?', he said: 'One should develop giving, righteous living, and a mind of loving-kindness.' In that passage, 'samacariyā' (righteous living) means very pure virtue (sīla), which is the practice of bodily evenness, etc., having far avoided bodily unevenness, etc. 'Bhāvaye' (should develop) means one should produce and increase it in one's own continuity. 'Ete dhamme' (these qualities) refers to these qualities of good conduct such as giving. 'Sukhasamuddaye' (bringing happiness) shows that the benefits are happy, and the fruit of the benefits is also only happiness. 'Avyāpajjaṃ sukhaṃ lokaṃ' (a peaceful, happy world) means a world that is peaceful and free from suffering because it is devoid of sensual desire, ill-will, etc. As for the absence of oppressing others, it goes without saying. It is called 'sukha' (happy) because of the abundance of happiness through the power of meditative attainments (jhāna-samāpatti). A wise person, through the merit of jhāna, reaches the Brahma world which is exclusively happy, or through other merits, reaches a happy world known as a prosperous existence. Thus, in this sutta and the verses, only the prosperity within the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa-sampatti) is taught.

## The Commentary on the Second Sutta is finished.

## 3. Ubhayattha Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the third sutta, 'bhāvito' means produced and increased. 'Bahulīkato' means practiced repeatedly. 'Attho' means welfare (hita). It is called 'attha' because it should be approached and reached for the sake of welfare. 'Samadhigayha tiṭṭhati' means it remains well-grasped and not abandoned. 'Diṭṭhadhammikaṃ' (pertaining to this life) refers to the present existence as 'diṭṭhadhamma'; it has the meaning of occurring in that present life, belonging to this world. 'Samparāyikaṃ' (pertaining to the future life) refers to the future world as 'samparāya' because it is to be reached repeatedly according to one's deeds; it means occurring in that future world, belonging to the future world.

What is this benefit in the present life (diṭṭhadhammika-attha) and benefit in the future life (samparāyika-attha)? Briefly, the happiness in the present world and that which brings happiness in the present world now is called 'diṭṭhadhammika-attha'. What is that benefit? For laypeople, it includes things such as various wealth and possessions in this world, having an occupation free from confusion, managing health, skills and sciences associated with keeping things clean and pure, and having a well-supported retinue. For monks, it is the acquisition without difficulty of the requisites of life: robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicines for the sick, and the use of those requisites with reflection...
76:
Reflection on the use of requisites, avoidance, maintaining cleanliness of objects, fewness of wishes, contentment, seclusion, and non-association, and so forth. Living in a suitable locality, associating with good people, hearing the True Dhamma, and wise reflection—these should be understood as common to both types of benefits and appropriate for both.

In the term "appamāda," heedfulness should be understood as the opposite of negligence (pamāda). What is negligence? It is the mode of being negligent. Indeed, this was said by the Blessed One:

"Therein, what is negligence? It is the letting loose of the mind, or the producing of such letting loose, in regard to bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, mental misconduct, or the five strands of sensual pleasure; it is the lack of respect, lack of constancy, lack of persistence, sluggish behavior, laying aside of desire, laying aside of the task, non-practice, non-development, lack of frequent exercise, lack of determination, and lack of application in the development of wholesome states. Such negligence, being negligent, and the state of being negligent—this is called negligence." (Vibhaṅga).

Therefore, heedfulness (appamāda) should be understood as the opposite of the aforementioned negligence. In essence, it is the non-absence of mindfulness; this name is given to the state of having mindfulness constantly established. Other teachers, however, say: "The four immaterial aggregates proceeding in conjunction with mindfulness and clear comprehension are called heedfulness."

Regarding the statement "developed and frequently practiced," how should this heedfulness be developed? There is no separate, single meditation called "development of heedfulness." Any performance of merit or wholesome deed should be understood simply as the development of heedfulness. Specifically, starting from taking refuge, which is the basis for the cessation of the round of rebirths, and restraint in body and speech, all development of virtue (sīla), development of concentration (samādhi), development of wisdom (paññā), development of the wholesome, and development of the blameless should be understood as the development of heedfulness. Indeed, the word "appamāda" points to a great meaning and stands encompassing a great significance. A Dhamma preacher who brings the entire word of the Buddha from the Tipiṭaka and explains it by making it the meaning of the word "appamāda" should not be said to have "plunged in where there is no ford." Why? Because of the greatness of the word "appamāda." For this reason, the Fully Enlightened One, while lying down at the time of his Parinibbāna between the twin Sāla trees in Kusinārā, summarized what he himself had taught throughout the forty-five years since his Enlightenment...
77:
...showing the Dhamma by summarizing it into a single word, he gave the following advice to the monks: "Strive with heedfulness (appamādena sampādetha)." Thus it was said:

"Monks, just as the footprints of all land-dwelling animals are encompassed within the footprint of the elephant, and the elephant's footprint is called the foremost among them because of its great size; even so, monks, whatever wholesome states there are, all are rooted in heedfulness, all converge in heedfulness, and heedfulness is called the foremost among those states." (Majjhima Nikāya 1.300).

In the verses, "appamādaṃ pasaṃsanti" means: the wise, such as the Buddhas and others, praise, extol, and commend heedfulness in the performance of meritorious deeds like giving (dāna) and so forth. Why? Because the wise person who is heedful gains both types of benefits. What are those two benefits?
