He says: "The benefit to be obtained in the present life and the benefit to be obtained in the future life." Thus the connection of the words should be understood. Here too, "the benefit to be obtained in the present life" for a householder means the benefit to be obtained through methods such as farming and cattle-rearing, described in such ways as "blameless actions and unconfused occupations." For a renunciant, it should be understood as benefits such as freedom from remorse. "The benefit to be obtained in the future life" should be understood as referring only to the practice of the Dhamma (dhammacariya) for both [householders and renunciants].

"Atthābhisamaya" is so called because of the attainment of the welfare of both types of benefits. The meeting with what is to be obtained is called "samaya" (attainment). "Samaya" itself is "abhisamaya." Or, the meeting in a direct manner is "abhisamaya." Thus "abhisamaya" should be understood here. One is called "dhīra" (wise/steadfast) because of being endowed with fortitude (dhiti). In this Sutta, it should be understood that by the third use of the word "attha," the ultimate goal, Nibbāna, is also included. The rest is easy to understand. Thus, in this Sutta, only the fulfillment within the round of rebirths (vaṭṭasampatti) is taught. However, in the verse, the inclusion of liberation from the round (vivaṭṭa) should also be seen. Thus it was said:

Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless;
Negligence is the path to death.
The heedful do not die;
The negligent are as if already dead.

Having understood this distinction,
The wise, rejoicing in heedfulness,
Delight in the realm of the Noble Ones.
78:
“Those wise ones, meditative, persevering, always with firm effort, realize Nibbāna, the unsurpassed security from bondage.” (Dhammapada 21-23). Therefore, in this term “atthābhisamayā,” the meaning should also be understood by way of supramundane benefit.

## The Commentary on the Third Sutta is finished.

## 4. Commentary on the Aṭṭhipuñja Sutta

In the fourth sutta, regarding the term “ekapuggalassa,” the word “puggala” (person) is a conventional expression. Indeed, the teaching of the Blessed Buddha is twofold: conventional teaching (sammuti-desanā) and ultimate teaching (paramattha-desanā). Among these, teachings such as “person, being, woman, man, khattiya, brahmin, deva, Māra” are called conventional teaching. Teachings such as “impermanence, suffering, non-self, aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), sense bases (āyatana), foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna)” are called ultimate teaching. Between these two, the Blessed Buddha teaches the conventional teaching to those beings who are capable of attaining distinction by hearing the teaching through the power of convention. However, he teaches the ultimate teaching to those beings who are capable of attaining distinction by hearing the teaching through the power of the ultimate sense.

In this matter, there is this analogy: Just as a teacher skilled in local dialects and capable of explaining the meaning of the three Vedas teaches in the Tamil language to those students who can understand the meaning when spoken in Tamil. To those who can understand in the Andhra language or any other, he teaches in those respective languages. When taught in this way, those young students, relying on the skilled and proficient teacher, can learn the craft quickly. In this analogy, the Blessed Buddha should be understood as the teacher; the three Piṭakas, which stand as the subject to be taught, should be understood as the three Vedas; the skill in conventional and ultimate teachings should be understood as the skill in local dialects; the veneyya beings, who are capable of penetrating the truth through the power of convention and the ultimate, should be understood as the young students with various local dialects; and the Blessed Buddha’s teaching through the power of convention and the ultimate should be understood as the teacher’s instruction in Tamil and so on. In this regard, it is also said:

“The Fully Enlightened One, the best of speakers, declared two truths: the conventional and the ultimate; a third is not found.”
79:
“Conventional speech is truth by reason of worldly convention; ultimate speech is truth by reason of the actual nature of phenomena. Therefore, the Teacher, the Lord of the World, who is skilled in usage, does not incur false speech even when speaking in conventional terms.” Furthermore, the Blessed Buddha teaches the discourse on persons (puggala-kathā) for eight reasons. They are: to demonstrate shame and fear (hiri-ottappa); to demonstrate that kamma is one’s own property (kammassakatā); to demonstrate the individual effort of men (paccatta-purisakāra); to demonstrate anantariya kamma; to demonstrate the divine abidings (brahmavihāra); to demonstrate past lives (pubbenivāsa); to demonstrate the purity of offerings (dakkhiṇāvisuddhi); and to not discard worldly convention (lokasammuti).

If it were taught that “the aggregates, elements, and sense bases feel shame and fear,” most people would not understand and would fall into confusion. Or they might even become hostile, asking, “What is this called ‘aggregates, elements, and sense bases feeling shame and fear’?” But when it is taught that “a woman feels shame and fear, a man, a khattiya, a brahmin, a deva, a Māra feels shame and fear,” they understand, do not fall into confusion, and do not become hostile. Therefore, the Blessed Buddha teaches the discourse on persons to demonstrate shame and fear.

The same method applies when teaching “the aggregates have kamma as their own property, the elements and sense bases have kamma as their own property.” Therefore, he also teaches the discourse on persons to demonstrate that kamma is one’s own property. The same method applies when teaching “the aggregates caused great monasteries such as Veḷuvana to be built, the elements and sense bases caused them to be built.” Similarly, the same method applies when teaching “the aggregates kill the mother, the father, the arahant; they cause the shedding of blood; they cause a schism in the Saṅgha; the elements and sense bases do so.” The same method applies when teaching “the aggregates develop loving-kindness, the elements and sense bases develop loving-kindness.” The same method applies when teaching “the aggregates remember past lives, the elements and sense bases remember them.” Therefore, the Blessed Buddha teaches the discourse on persons to demonstrate the individual effort of men, to demonstrate anantariya kamma, to demonstrate the divine abidings, and to demonstrate past lives.

If it were taught that “the aggregates receive offerings, the elements and sense bases receive them,” most people would not understand and would fall into confusion. They might even become hostile, asking, “What is this called ‘aggregates, elements, and sense bases receiving’?” But when it is taught that “persons receive,” they understand, do not fall into confusion, and do not become hostile. Therefore, the Blessed Buddha teaches the discourse on persons to demonstrate the purity of offerings.
80:
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, do not abandon worldly convention (loka-sammuti). They teach the Dhamma by relying on the designations, language, and expressions used in the world. Therefore, for the sake of not abandoning worldly convention, the Blessed One also speaks in terms of persons (puggalakathā). In this sutta as well, wishing to show the meaning to be taught by way of worldly usage, he said: "Of a single person" (ekapuggalassa), and so forth.

In that passage, "of a single person" (ekapuggalassa) means of a single being. "An aeon" (kappaṃ) means for a great aeon (mahākappa). Although this accusative case is used in the sense of continuous duration, it should be understood by way of the wandering and circling of beings in saṃsāra. "A skeleton" (aṭṭhikaṅkala) means a portion of bones. Some also read it as aṭṭhikhala, meaning a collection of bones. "A heap of bones" (aṭṭhipuñja) means a multitude of bones. "A pile of bones" (aṭṭhirāsi) is just a synonym for that same heap. However, some teachers say: "A collection lower than the height of the waist is called kaṅkala; a collection above that up to the height of a palm tree is called puñja; and a collection higher than that is called rāsi." That is merely their opinion. All these are just synonyms for a collection, brought in as a simile for the vastness of Mount Vepulla.

"If there were a collector" (sace saṃhārako assa) is said as a supposition: "if there were someone to collect and store them so they would not be scattered." "And what is collected would not perish" (sambhatañca na vinasseyya) is also said as a supposition: "if that skeleton collected by someone were not to disappear, not becoming rotten or ground to dust, but were to remain without perishing." This is the meaning here: Monks, if a single being, by way of repeated births due to kamma and defilements, were to wander and circle for a whole great aeon, there would be such a great collection of bones, as large in height and circumference as this Mount Vepulla. If there were someone to collect and store them, and if that collection were to remain without perishing (it would be this large). This method is stated by excluding beings of spontaneous birth (opapātika) who, like an extinguished lamp, have a nature of breaking up without leaving a corpse, and also excluding small beings who have no bones at all. Some teachers, however, say: "Since this method is brought in by way of supposition, if those beings also had a skeleton, this size of the heap of bones is stated together with those as well." Other teachers say: "This should not be taken so; this size was stated by the All-knowing Knowledge by delimiting the heap of bones that could actually be obtained. Therefore, the meaning should be taken only according to the method previously stated."
81:
If that skeleton were to remain without perishing, it would be in this manner. This method is taught by excluding beings of spontaneous birth who, like an extinguished lamp, have a nature of perishing without leaving a body (in a cemetery), and small beings who have no bones. Some teachers say that since this method is brought in by way of supposition, if those beings also had a skeleton, this size of the heap of bones is meant to include theirs as well. Other teachers say this should not be taken so, because this size was taught by the All-knowing Knowledge by delimiting the heap of bones that could be obtained. Therefore, the meaning should be taken only according to the method previously stated.

In the verses, "by the Great Sage" (mahesinā) refers to the Buddha, who is called "Great Sage" (mahesī) because he seeks (esati/gavesati) the great aggregates of virtue and so forth. In saying "It was said by the Great Sage," the Blessed One presents himself as if he were another, as in such passages as "Monks, the Tathāgata is possessed of the ten powers." "Vepulla" is the name of the mountain that is the most extensive and large among the five mountains surrounding the city of Rājagaha. For that reason, it is "Great." In terms of its location, it is to the north of Vulture Peak (Gijjhakūṭa). "In Giribbaja" (giribbaje) means near Rājagaha, which is also named the city of Giribbaja.

With this much, the Blessed One showed the danger in the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa) by showing that for an ordinary person (puthujjana) whose root of existence is not yet cut and who has not fully understood the Four Noble Truths for such a long time, there is this "increasing of the cemetery" (repeated death). Now, wishing to show that for the noble person (ariyapuggala) who has seen the Noble Truths, there is no such "increasing of the cemetery"—whereas for the blind ordinary person, there is such "increasing of the cemetery" because of not understanding and not penetrating those Noble Truths—he spoke the verse beginning with "And when the Noble Truths" (yato ca ariyasaccāni).

In that verse, "when" (yato) means at the time when. "Noble Truths" (ariyasaccāni): they are called "Noble" (ariya) because they are to be approached (araṇīya), and "Truths" (sacca) because of their non-erroneous nature; thus they are "Noble Truths." Alternatively, they are Noble Truths because they are the truths that make one noble. Or, they are Noble Truths because they are the truths to be penetrated by the Nobles, such as the Buddhas. Or, they are Noble Truths because they are the truths of the Noble One (the Buddha). For the Blessed One is "Noble" (ariya) because he is to be approached as a refuge by the world with its devas; since these truths were seen by him through his self-evolved knowledge (sayambhūñāṇa), they are his truths, thus "Noble Truths." "He sees with right wisdom" (sammappaññāya passati) means he sees by way of the breakthroughs of full understanding (pariññā), abandonment (pahāna), realization (sacchikiriyā), and development (bhāvanā), through the path-wisdom (maggapaññā) accompanied by insight-wisdom (vipassanā-paññā) in the right manner and through the right cause. The words "suffering" (dukkha) and so forth are the demonstration of the specific nature of the Noble Truths. Therein, it is "suffering" (dukkha) because it is the site of many afflictions and thus is loathsome, and because it is empty, being devoid of the permanence, beauty, happiness, and self imagined by fools. Because suffering arises from this cause, it is the "arising of suffering" (dukkhasamuppāda) or the "origin of suffering" (dukkhasamudaya). Because one transcends suffering through this Nibbāna, which is the object-condition, or because one transcends suffering in this Nibbāna, it is the "transcending of suffering," which is Nibbāna. It is "noble" (ariya) because it is far from defilements and because it is to be approached. It is "eightfold" (aṭṭhaṅgika) because it is possessed of the eight factors such as Right View. It is the "path" (magga) because it goes along killing the defilements, or because it is sought by those desiring Nibbāna, or because it itself seeks Nibbāna. For that very reason, it is "leading to the subsiding of suffering" (dukkhūpasamagāmī) because it leads to the peace and cessation of suffering. "When he sees with right wisdom" (yato sammappaññāya passati) is the connection (sambandha) with the preceding words.
82:
According to the words, "That person has seven times at most as the limit, wandering [in Saṃsāra]," a Noble Person who is a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna), who is a beholder of the Four Noble Truths and whose faculties are all dull, wanders and circles through successive births in existences for a maximum of seven times. There are three types of Stream-enterers based on the sharpness, mediumness, or dullness of their faculties: the One-seeder (Ekabījī), the One-who-goes-from-family-to-family (Kolaṃkola), and the One-with-seven-times-at-most (Sattakkhattuparama). Among these three, this statement "That person has seven times at most as the limit, wandering [in Saṃsāra]" is spoken with reference to the Stream-enterer whose faculties are all dull. "He becomes one who makes an end of suffering" means he is one who brings the suffering of the round of rebirths to an end, reaching its conclusion. How? Because of the destruction of all fetters, he gradually attains the Path of Arahantship (Arahattamagga) and exhausts the fetters without remainder. Thus, the teaching reaches its peak with the Fruit of Arahantship (Arahattaphala).

## The Commentary on the Fourth Sutta Ends.

## 5. Commentary on the Musāvāda Sutta

In the fifth Sutta, what is the origin (atthuppatti) of the Sutta beginning with "Ekadhammaṃ atītassa"? Great gain, honor, and respect arose for the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks, while those of the non-Buddhist ascetics (titthiyas) declined. Having lost their gain and honor, being without luster or power, and overcome by envy, they urged a female wandering ascetic named Ciñcamāṇavikā, saying, "Come, sister, accuse the ascetic Gotama with what is untrue." While the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma in the midst of the fourfold assembly, she approached and accused him with untruth. When Sakka, the King of Devas, revealed her falsehood, the great multitude shouted, "Shame on you, wretched woman! Loathsome woman!" and drove her out of the monastery. As the earth opened up, she became fuel for the flames of the Avīci hell and was reborn there. The gain and honor of the non-Buddhist ascetics declined even further. The monks raised the topic in the Dhamma hall, saying, "Friends, Ciñcamāṇavikā, by falsely accusing the Fully Enlightened Buddha, who possesses such grand virtues and is the supreme recipient of offerings, has met with great destruction." The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you sitting together now?" When they replied, "For such a reason," he said, "Monks, not only now has Ciñcamāṇavikā met with great destruction by falsely accusing me; in the past also, she met with destruction by falsely accusing me." He then related the Mahāpaduma Jātaka in detail and, continuing the teaching based on this incident, he taught this Sutta: "Ekadhammaṃ atītassa."

In that Sutta, "Ekadhammaṃ" refers to the one Dhamma known as truthful speech (vacīsacca). "Atītassa" refers to a person who stands having transgressed the boundary set by the Noble Ones—"One should speak the truth; one should not speak what is untrue"—for the purpose of establishing one in the eight types of noble speech while avoiding the eight types of ignoble speech. For such a person, there is no evil that cannot be done. Indeed, a person who is in the habit of lying commits some evil. When told, "You have done such a deed," he will cover it up only with a lie, saying, "I did not do it." One who acts in this way will surely commit any evil. He feels no shame in that evil because he has completely transgressed the boundary of truth.
83:
"Truth, friend, is not false"—this is the boundary (rule) set by the Noble Ones. A man who stands having transgressed that rule is called a "purisapuggala" (individual/person) because he is a person. For such a person, there is no evil he would not dare to do. A person who is in the habit of telling deliberate lies, after committing some evil, if told "You have done this," will hide it only with a lie, saying "I did not do it." One who acts thus is indeed capable of committing any evil; he no longer has shame or fear regarding that evil because he has already transgressed the boundary of truthfulness. Therefore, it was said: "Monks, for one who transgresses this one thing, namely, deliberate lying, there is no evil that cannot be done," and so forth.

In the verse, "Musāvādissa" refers to one who is in the habit of speaking what is false, untrue, and unreal for the purpose of making others believe it. For such a being, if out of ten words not even one is true, there is no word he would not dare to say. "Jantuno" refers to a being; a being is called "jantu" in the sense of being born. "Vitiṇṇaparalokassa" means one who has abandoned (has no regard for) the next world. Such a person does not look forward to the three types of fortune: human fortune, celestial fortune, and ultimately, the fortune of Nibbāna. "Natthi pāpaṃ" means for such a person, there is no such thing as "this evil should not be done."

## The Commentary on the Fifth Sutta Ends.

## 6. Commentary on the Dāna Sutta

In the sixth Sutta, in the word "Evañce," "evaṃ" is a particle in the sense of a simile, and "ce" is in the sense of a condition (if). "Sattā" (beings) are so called because they are particularly attached to forms and so on. "Jāneyyuṃ" means "if they should know." In the phrase "Dānasaṃvibhāgassa," "Dāna" refers to the volition (cetanā) by which one collects offerings such as alms-food and gives them to others through either compassion or reverence. "Saṃvibhāga" refers to the sharing of a portion of an object that one has taken for one's own use. "Vipākaṃ" refers to the fruit or result. "Yathāhaṃ jānāmi" should be analyzed as "just as I know." The meaning intended is this: by giving a gift even to an animal, it becomes an offering with a hundredfold benefit, producing happiness throughout a hundred existences. In this way, monks, just as I know the fruit of giving and sharing—the result of kamma—through the power of knowledge by direct perception, if these beings also knew it in the same way. "Na adatvā bhuñjeyyuṃ" means that with a stingy mind, without giving to others the things in one's possession that are fit to be used...
84:
If one has an object suitable for use, one should not consume it without giving to others, out of a mind of stinginess or by the power of craving and greed; one should consume it only after giving. The stain of stinginess—which is one of the dark states (kaṇhadhamma) that are defilements, spoilers of the mind's radiance, and characterized by an inability to tolerate sharing one's own prosperity with others—should not persist by overwhelming the minds of those beings. Alternatively, the aforementioned stinginess, along with other stains such as envy, greed, and hatred that obstruct giving, should not persist by taking hold of and overwhelming the minds of those beings so that the volition of giving (dāna-cetanā) does not arise or is not perfectly pure. For who, knowing well the fruit of giving, would allow the stain of stinginess an opportunity in their own mind?

"Whatever might be their very last morsel" is a synonym for the phrase "the last mouthful of food." The meaning is this: beings would normally sustain themselves with a certain number of morsels; if they set aside only one morsel for themselves and give all the other morsels to those in need as they come, the morsel that was set aside is called here "the last morsel." Even from that last morsel, they should not consume without sharing. If there were recipients for those beings, they should consume only after sharing and giving a portion even from that aforementioned last morsel. It means: "If they knew, as I know directly, the fruit of giving and sharing." By the words "And because..." etc., [the Buddha] establishes the intended meaning with a reason, stating that because they do not directly know the fruit of kamma, these beings do not engage in giving and sharing. In this way, it should be understood that the reason for their non-practice of other meritorious deeds and their practice of unmeritorious deeds is shown.

In the verses, "as spoken by the Great Sage" means as spoken by the Blessed One, such as "By giving a gift to an animal, a hundredfold offering is to be expected," or in this very sutta, "If beings knew thus," etc. The meaning is that the mind is known by the range of [His] knowledge as it was spoken. "The fruit of sharing" means even the fruit of sharing, let alone the fruit of giving. "As it is of great fruit" means as that fruit is great; it should be connected as "if these beings knew thus." "Having removed the stain of stinginess" means having discarded the stain of stinginess through faith in the fruit of kamma, or through special devotion, and to those Noble Ones (ariyas) who are endowed with virtues such as morality (sīla) because they are far from defilements, even a small gift given is of great fruit; thus one should praise them at the appropriate time.
85:
Through faith in the Triple Gem and especially with a clear mind, even a small gift given to Noble Ones (ariyas) who are endowed with virtues such as morality (sīla) because they are far from defilements, is of great fruit. One should give to such persons at the appropriate time.

They are called "worthy of offerings" (dakkhiṇeyya) because they produce great fruit and are worthy of noble gifts. In those dakkhiṇeyya persons who have practiced well, having given a gift—the object to be given with faith in the world beyond—so that the gift becomes a "great gift" (mahā-dāna); or, having given food to many. As to how food should be given, He said: "an offering among those worthy of offerings" (dakkhiṇeyyesu dakkhiṇam). Having passed away from this human state, the donors reach heaven by way of rebirth. Being "desirous of sensual pleasures" (kāmakāmino), because they approach through kamma the attainment of the form and wealth of the grand celestial pleasures they desired, they are endowed with all sensual pleasures and enjoy themselves as they wish, according to their liking.

## The Commentary on the Sixth Sutta is finished.

## 7. Commentary on the Mettābhāvanā Sutta

In the seventh sutta, "whatever" (yāni kānici) is an inclusive term without exception. "Meritorious actions based on acquisitions" (opadhikāni puññakiriyavatthūni) is the specification of those meritorious deeds. In that phrase, "acquisitions" (upadhi) refers to the aggregates (khandhas). They are called "opadhika" because they possess morality that causes the aggregates, or because they have the aggregates as their purpose. They produce the selfhood (attabhāva) in a prosperous existence and provide rebirth and the result of the process (pavatti-vipāka). "Meritorious actions" (puññakiriyavatthūni) are so called because they are the performance of merit and the basis for various benefits. These meritorious actions are briefly of three kinds: consisting in giving (dānamaya), consisting in morality (sīlamaya), and consisting in mental development (bhāvanāmaya). What should be said there will be made clear later in the commentary on the Book of Threes (Tika Nipāta).

"By the deliverance of mind through loving-kindness" (mettāya cetovimuttiyā) refers to the attainment of the third or fourth jhāna obtained by the power of the development of loving-kindness. For when "loving-kindness" (mettā) is mentioned, both access (upacāra) and absorption (appanā) can be obtained, but when "deliverance of mind" (cetovimutti) is mentioned, only absorption jhāna (appanā-jhāna) is obtained. That absorption jhāna is called "deliverance of mind" because of the mind's complete liberation from opposing states such as the hindrances (nīvaraṇa). "Do not equal a sixteenth part" (kalaṃ nāgghanti soḷasiṃ) means that the meritorious actions based on acquisitions do not equal even one-sixteenth of a sixteenth part of the divine abiding of loving-kindness. The meaning is this: if the fruit of the deliverance of mind through loving-kindness is divided into sixteen parts, and one of those parts is again divided into sixteen parts, the other meritorious actions based on acquisitions cannot reach or equal even that resulting portion.

"Surpassing" (abhibhuyya) means overwhelming. "Shines" (bhāsate) means it glows through purity from the causes of defilement. "Blazes" (tapati) means for that very reason it burns away opposing states. "Radiates" (virocati) means it is beautiful through the fulfillment of both. Indeed, the deliverance of mind through loving-kindness shines like the moonlight free from impurities during the waxing phase. It blazes and radiates like the sun, destroying the mass of darkness and opposing states.
86:
If one were to divide that merit into sixteen parts, one part of those sixteen would not be equaled by other meritorious actions leading to rebirth (opadhika-puññakiriyavatthu). 'Adhiggahetvā' means having surpassed or overwhelmed. 'Bhāsate' means it shines through purity from the defilements. 'Tapate' means it glows or burns intensely, dispelling all remaining opposing states due to that very purity. 'Virocati' means it is brilliant through the fulfillment of both (attainment and success). Indeed, the liberation of mind through loving-kindness (mettā-cetovimutti) is brilliant like the moonlight in the bright half of the month, which is free from impurities; it glows like the sun's heat, dispelling opposing states just as it dispels darkness; and it is brilliant like the radiance of the morning star (osadhi-tārakā).

'Seyyathāpi' is a particle used in the sense of showing a simile. 'Tārakarūpānaṃ' means of the stars. 'Candiyā' means belonging to the moon, or the moonlight. 'Vassānaṃ' means the season that is so named because of the abundance of rain. 'Pacchime māse' means in the month of Kattika. 'Saradasamaye' means in the autumn season. Indeed, in the world, the months of Assayuja and Kattika are called the 'autumn season' (sarada-utu). 'Viddhe' means cleared upwards, or distant because the clouds have gone. Therefore, the Buddha said 'vigatavalāhake' (cloudless). 'Deve' means in the sky. 'Nabhaṃ abbhussakkamāno' means ascending into the sky from the place of rising. 'Tamagataṃ' means darkness. 'Abhivihaccā' means having dispelled or struck down. 'Osadhi-tārakā' is the star called 'Osadhi' either because it carries a great radiance or because it gives strength to medicinal plants.

In this context, a question may arise: 'Why did the Blessed One single out loving-kindness as superior to other meritorious actions, even though they are similar in leading to rebirth?' The answer is: It is spoken of specifically because of its noble meaning, its faultless nature, and its being the right conduct towards beings. Indeed, these abodes, which are the meditations on loving-kindness, are noble as they constitute right conduct towards all beings. Just as the Brahmas live with faultless minds, so do the practitioners endowed with this loving-kindness live like Brahmas. Thus, these states are called 'Sublime Abodes' (brahmavihāra). Therefore, because of its noble meaning, faultless nature, and right conduct towards beings, loving-kindness alone is spoken of as superior to other meritorious actions.

Furthermore, why is loving-kindness specifically singled out? Because it is the foundation for the other Sublime Abodes and because it fulfills all wholesome states such as giving (dāna).
87:
This loving-kindness has the characteristic of promoting the welfare of beings. Its function is to bring about their benefit. Its manifestation is the removal of resentment. If it is developed and practiced frequently without limit, then the meditations on compassion (karuṇā) and so on are easily accomplished; therefore, loving-kindness is the foundation for the remaining Sublime Abodes. This is because when there is an inclination for the welfare of beings, the inability to endure their suffering, the desire for their specific successes to last long, and the state of mind that proceeds equally towards all without partiality are easily fulfilled. In this way, the Great Bodhisattvas (Mahābodhisatta), who are intent on providing for the welfare and happiness of the entire world, do not make distinctions based on superior discernment such as 'This should be given to this person, this should not be given to that person,' but give gifts (dāna) which are the cause of absolute happiness to all beings without exception. They undertake virtue (sīla) only for the sake of the welfare and happiness of those beings. They resort to renunciation (nekkhamma) for the sake of fulfilling virtue. They purify wisdom (paññā) so as not to be deluded regarding the welfare and happiness of those beings. They exert firm effort (vīriya) only for the sake of increasing welfare and happiness. Even when they have reached courage through supreme effort, they endure the various offenses of beings only with an inclination for their welfare. They do not fail in their promises, such as 'We will give this to you, we will do this.' They have unshakable determination (adhiṭṭhāna) only for the welfare and happiness of those beings. Being those who act first with unshakable loving-kindness towards those beings, they remain indifferent to their misconduct only with an inclination for their welfare. Even though they are the first to help, they do not expect any favor in return. In this way, those Bodhisattvas fulfill the perfections (pāramī) and complete all wholesome states, including the ten powers (dasabala), the four kinds of intrepidity (catu-vesārajja), the six unshared knowledges (cha-asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa), and the eighteen unique Buddha-qualities (āveṇika-buddhadhamma). Thus, to show this distinction—that loving-kindness fulfills all wholesome states such as giving—it is spoken of as superior to other merits. 

Alternatively, the great power of loving-kindness over other meritorious actions leading to rebirth should be understood through the Velāma Sutta. In that Velāma Sutta, it is stated that a gift given to one Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna) is more fruitful than the great gift of the Brahmin Velāma. Likewise, a gift to a Once-returner... a Paccekabuddha, the Blessed One, the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, the building of a monastery for the Saṅgha of the four quarters, taking refuge, and undertaking the precepts—the development of loving-kindness for even the duration of milking a cow is more fruitful than all those. As it is said: 'Householder, the Brahmin Velāma gave a great gift. If someone were to feed one Stream-enterer, this feeding would be more fruitful than that gift of Velāma... more fruitful than abstaining from drinking intoxicants is the development of a mind of loving-kindness for at least the duration of milking a cow.' Since it is a sublime (mahaggata) merit, there is no need to mention that it surpasses sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) merit. It is stated: 'Whatever sense-sphere kamma there is, that kamma does not remain or persist in the Brahma realm.'
88:
"Householder, the Brahmin named Velāma gave that gift which is called a great gift. If one were to feed a single person endowed with right view (diṭṭhisampanna), this would be of greater fruit than the gift of that Brahmin Velāma. If one were to feed a hundred persons endowed with right view... (and so on) ...one should abstain from drinking intoxicants. If one were to develop a mind of loving-kindness for even the duration of milking a cow once, this would be of greater fruit than that (observing the precepts)," thus He (the Buddha) taught (in the Aṅguttara Nikāya).

Furthermore, because it is an exalted (mahaggata) merit, there is no need to say how much more excellent this merit of loving-kindness is than the merit of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara). It has also been taught: "A limited (kāmāvacara) action does not remain there, it cannot stand there (in the exalted action)." A sense-sphere action is called limited (pamāṇakata), while an exalted action is called immeasurable (appamāṇakata) because it is developed by transcending the limits of the sense-sphere through specific (odhisa-pharaṇa) and non-specific (anodhisa-pharaṇa) pervasion. A sense-sphere action is unable to get stuck in the middle of that exalted action, nor can it overcome that action to take the opportunity to produce its own result. Rather, just as a great flood overcomes a small amount of water and takes its own place, the exalted action alone overcomes that sense-sphere action, prevents its result, and leads one to the company of the Brahmas. This is the meaning of that Pali text.

In the verses, "yo" (whoever) refers to any person, whether a householder or a monk. "Mettā" refers to the jhāna of loving-kindness. "Appamāṇa" (immeasurable) means immeasurable by way of development (bhāvanā) and by way of the object (ārammaṇa). Unlike the meditation on foulness (asubha-bhāvanā) and others, it does not take only a part of the object but is called immeasurable because it has an immeasurable object through complete and non-specific pervasion, and because of the proficiency in development.

"The fetters become thin" (tanū saṃyojanā honti) means that for one who, based on the jhāna of loving-kindness, practices insight (vipassanā) and attains the lower paths, the fetters of aversion (paṭigha-saṃyojana) and others are easily abandoned and thus become thin. Therefore, He taught: "For one who sees the destruction of the bases (upadhikkhaya)" (passato upadhikkhayaṃ). Nirvana is called "upadhikkhaya." One who develops loving-kindness sees that Nirvana with the path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa) through the realization of the truth (sacchikiriyābhisamaya).

Alternatively, "the fetters become thin" means that by means of insight which has the jhāna of loving-kindness as its proximate cause, one gradually reaches Arahatship, which is the destruction of the bases; for one who sees that Arahatship, the ten fetters especially become thin, meaning they are abandoned.

Alternatively, "the fetters become thin" means that aversion (paṭigha) and the fetters associated with aversion become thin. "For one who sees the destruction of the bases" means for one who sees the destruction of those bases of defilements such as aversion...
89:
...the destruction of which is called loving-kindness, seeing it through the power of attainment. This is how the meaning should be understood here.

Having thus shown the supreme benefit of the development of loving-kindness, which is the abandoning of defilements and the attainment of Nirvana, He now spoke the words beginning with "ekampi ce" to show other benefits. In those words, "aduṭṭhacitto" (undisturbed mind) refers to a person whose mind is not corrupted by ill-will because ill-will has been well suppressed by the power of loving-kindness. "Mettāyati" means one practices loving-kindness by way of diffusing welfare. "Kusalo" means one who has extraordinary merit, a possessor of great merit. Or, it means one who is safe because of the absence of harms such as aversion. "Tena" means by such practice of loving-kindness. In the phrase "sabbē ca pāṇē," the word "ca" is used in the sense of distinction (vyatireka). "Manasānukampaṃ" means compassionate protection with the mind.

The intended meaning is this: even loving-kindness directed towards a single being is a great mass of merit. A person with a noble and pure mind, who compassionately protects all beings with a mind diffusing welfare as if they were his own dear son, accomplishes an abundant, great, vast, and boundless merit, capable of producing a continuous result for himself even for sixty-four great aeons.

"Sattasaṇḍaṃ" means full of a multitude of beings, crowded with people. "Vijitvā" means conquering righteously, without using punishment or weapons. "Rājisayo" refers to righteous kings who are like seers (isayas). "Yajamānā" means giving gifts (dāna). "Anupariyagā" means they traveled about.

In the words beginning with "assamedhaṃ," it is said that in the time of ancient kings, there were four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu): Sassamedha, Purisamedha, Sammāpāsa, and Vācāpeyya. With these principles, kings supported and helped the people. In that context, taking a tenth part of the produced crops is called "Sassamedha." It means skill in producing crops. Giving six months' worth of rations and wages to the great warriors is called "Purisamedha." It means skill in supporting men. Issuing a loan of one thousand or two thousand units of wealth to the poor without interest for three years upon a written contract is called "Sammāpāsa." This is called "Sammāpāsa" (right bond) because it binds the people to the king's heart. Supporting people with gentle words such as "Father" or "Uncle" is called "Vācāpeyya." It means speaking pleasant words. A country supported by these four bases of sympathy becomes prosperous and flourishing. Food and drink are abundant, it is safe and free from internal strife. People live happily, making their children dance in their laps, and living with their house doors open. Because the houses have no door-panels (or are left open), they are called "apārutaghara" (open houses). This was the ancient tradition. Later, during the time of King Okkāka, the Brahmins changed these four bases of sympathy and this prosperity.
90:
People live joyfully, making their children dance in their laps, and living without closing their house doors. This way of living is called "Niraggaḷa" (unbarred) because of the absence of door-bolts (aggaḷa) at the house doors. This is the ancient tradition, the ancient nature.

Later, during the time of King Okkāka, brahmins corrupted these four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu) and the prosperity of this kingdom, turning the roots upside down, and performed five sacrifices such as Assamedha and Purisamedha. Regarding this, the Blessed One taught in the Brāhmaṇadhammiya Sutta: "A perversion occurred to those brahmins upon seeing even a tiny bit [of wealth]... Those brahmins, having composed mantras for that purpose, approached King Okkāka." (Sn 301-304).

Among those sacrifices, it is called "Assamedha" because horses are tormented and killed there. This Assamedha is the name of a sacrifice to be performed with two subsidiary sacrifices, having twenty-one sacrificial posts, terrifying due to the slaughter of nine hundred and seventy-five animals on the final day, and where all wealth and possessions are given as gifts, excluding land and people. It is called "Purisamedha" because men (humans) are tormented and killed there. This Purisamedha is the name of a sacrifice to be performed with four subsidiary sacrifices, where wealth and possessions as mentioned in the Assamedha are given as gifts, including the land. It is called "Sammāpāsa" because a peg (yoke-pin) is thrown. Having thrown the peg, which is the stick to be inserted into the yoke-hole, a sacrificial altar is made at the spot where that peg falls; it is the name of a Satra sacrifice to be performed by proceeding upstream from the place where the Sarasvatī River disappears, using portable sacrificial posts and so on. It is called "Vājapeyya" because strength-giving [liquor] is drunk there. It is the name of a sacrifice to be performed with one subsidiary sacrifice, seventeen animals, having a sacrificial post made of bael wood (beḷuva), and seventeen kinds of gifts. It is called "Niraggaḷa" because there is no door-bolt. It is the name of a specific type of Assamedha sacrifice called Sabbamedha, to be performed with nine subsidiary sacrifices, where all wealth and possessions as mentioned in the Assamedha are given as gifts, including land and people.

"Candappabhā" means by the light of the moon. "Tāraganāva sabbe" means just as all the hosts of stars do not equal even a sixteenth part of the moon's radiance, so too these sacrifices like Assamedha do not enjoy, do not reach, and are not worth even a sixteenth part of the merit of a mind of loving-kindness (mettā-citta) that is well-developed with the characteristics mentioned.
91:
Now, to show other benefits of the development of loving-kindness (mettā-bhāvanā) pertaining to the present life and the future life, the words beginning with "Yo na hanti" (Who does not kill) are spoken. In that passage, "Yo" refers to a person devoted to the development of the divine abiding of loving-kindness (mettā-brahmavihāra-bhāvanā). "Na hanti" means that by the power of that development of loving-kindness, because ill-will (byāpāda) has been driven far away, he does not harm any being, nor does he oppress them with clods of earth, sticks, and so on. "Na ghāteti" means he does not cause others to kill or oppress beings by instigating them. "Na jināti" means he does not conquer anyone through contentious speech and the like, because there is no hostility in him. Or, it means he does not cause others to lose, such as by winning a lawsuit. "Na jāpayeti" means he should not cause the loss of others' property by employing someone else. "Mettāṃso" means a portion of the mind consisting of loving-kindness. Or, it is called "mettāṃsa" because it is a component of loving-kindness in the sense of not being abandoned. "Sabba-bhūtesu" means among all living beings. Therefore, for that person who dwells in loving-kindness, there is no unwholesome enmity for any reason; there is no opposition, known as personal grudge, with any person.

Thus, in this Ekanipāta (Book of Ones), the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa) is taught in thirteen discourses in sequence and in the two Sikkhā Suttas, making fifteen discourses in total. In these four discourses—the Nīvaraṇa Sutta, Saṃyojana Sutta, Appamāda Sutta, and Atthisañcaya Sutta—both the round (vaṭṭa) and the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa) are taught. In the other discourses, however, only the round (vaṭṭa) is taught.

## The Explanation of the Seventh Discourse is finished.
## The Explanation of the Ekanipāta of the Itivuttaka
## in the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya
## named Paramatthadīpanī is finished.
92:
## 2. Dukanipāta
## 1. Paṭhamavagga
## 1. Commentary on the Dukkhavihāra Sutta

In the first sutta of the Dukanipāta, the word 'dvīhi' (by two) is a numerical delimitation. 'Dhammehi' (by states) indicates the states being delimited. 'Dvīhi dhammehi' means being associated with two unwholesome states. 'Samannāgato' means one who is endowed. 'Diṭṭheva dhamme' means in this very state of existence. 'Dukkhaṃ viharati' means living miserably in all four postures due to the suffering of defilements as well as physical and mental suffering. 'Savighātaṃ' means being accompanied by distress of mind and distress of body. 'Saupāyāsaṃ' means being accompanied by despair through the power of intense exhaustion, such as the despair of defilements and physical fatigue. 'Saparilāhaṃ' means being accompanied by feverishness, both the fever of defilements and the fever of the body. 'Kāyassa bhedā' means due to the relinquishing of the acquired aggregates (upādinnakhandha). 'Paraṃ maraṇā' means in the taking up of new aggregates immediately after that. Alternatively, 'Kāyassa bhedā' means due to the cutting off of the life faculty (jīvitindriya). 'Paraṃ maraṇā' means after the death-consciousness (cuti). 'Duggati pāṭikaṅkhā' means one of the four planes of misery, known as 'duggati', is to be expected; the meaning is that it will inevitably occur.

'Aguttadvāro' means one who has unguarded doors. To the question "In what respect are the doors unguarded?", the text says "in the faculties" (indriyesu). By this, the lack of restraint of the six faculties, with the mind as the sixth, is stated. One who does not know the measure in food through the power of receiving and consuming is called 'bhojane amattaññū' (immoderate in eating). Some also read it as 'indriyesu aguttadvāratāya bhojane amattaññutāya'.

How is there an unguarded door in the faculties, and how is there a guarded door? In reality, there is neither restraint nor non-restraint in the eye faculty (cakkhundriya). Indeed, neither mindfulness nor forgetfulness arises depending on the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda). However, when a visual object comes into the range of the eye, the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) arises and ceases twice. When it ceases, the functional mind-element (kiriyā-manodhātu), performing the function of adverting (āvajjana), arises and ceases. After that, the eye-consciousness (cakkhu-viññāṇa) performs the function of seeing; then the resultant mind-element (vipāka-manodhātu) performs the function of receiving (sampaṭicchana); then the resultant rootless mind-consciousness-element (vipāka-ahetuka-manoviññāṇadhātu) performs the function of investigating (santīraṇa); then the functional rootless mind-consciousness-element (kiriyā-ahetuka-manoviññāṇadhātu) arises and ceases while performing the function of determining (vottabbana). Immediately after that, the impulsion (javana) runs. Nevertheless, neither at the time of the life-continuum nor at the time of adverting and so on...
93:
...nor at any other time does restraint or non-restraint exist. But at the moment of impulsion (javana), if immorality, forgetfulness, ignorance (aññāṇa), impatience, or laziness arises, then there is non-restraint (asaṃvara). Even though it occurs in this way at the moment of impulsion, it is called "non-restraint in the eye-door."

Why? Because when that non-restraint exists, the door is unguarded, the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is unguarded, and the process-consciousnesses (vīthicitta) such as adverting are also unguarded. For example, if the four gates of a city are not closed but left open, even if the doors of the inner houses, chambers, and rooms are well-secured, all the goods within the city remain unprotected and unguarded. Thieves entering through the city gates can carry away whatever they desire. In the same way, when immorality and so on arise at the moment of impulsion, if that non-restraint exists, the door is unguarded, and the life-continuum and process-consciousnesses such as adverting are also unguarded.

When that non-restraint is absent and virtue and so on arise at the moment of impulsion, the door is guarded, and the life-continuum and process-consciousnesses such as adverting are also guarded. For example, if the city gates are closed, even if the inner house doors and so on are not closed, all the goods within the city remain well-protected and well-guarded. For when the city gates are shut, there is no entry for thieves. In the same way, when virtue and so on arise at the moment of impulsion, the door, the life-continuum, and the process-consciousnesses such as adverting are also guarded. Therefore, even though it arises at the moment of impulsion, it is called "restraint in the eye-door." The same method applies to the remaining doors. Thus, unguarded doors and guarded doors in the faculties should be understood.

How is one immoderate in eating (amattaññū), and how is one moderate (mattaññū)? A person who is highly ambitious (mahiccha) does not know the measure in receiving requisites. A highly ambitious person is like a peddler (kacchapuṭa) who takes ornaments in his hands, puts as much as is appropriate into his pocket, and while the public is watching, shouts out, "Take this one, take that one!" In the same way, such a person advertises even a small amount of their own virtue, learning, or the qualities of ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), or even just the fact of living in the forest, so that the public may know. After advertising in this way, they accept requisites brought even by cartloads without saying "Enough." Three things cannot be filled: fire with fuel, the ocean with water, and a highly ambitious person with requisites.

"A mass of fire, the ocean, and a highly ambitious person—these three cannot be filled even if many requisites are given."
94:
A person of great desire is unable to take even the milk of the mother who gave him birth (in the proper measure). Such a person does not bring about gains that have not yet arisen and falls away from gains that have already arisen. Thus, first of all, he is one who does not know the measure in receiving.

Whosoever consumes even rightfully and fairly obtained food with greed, infatuation, and obsession, without seeing the danger and without the wisdom of escape—behaving like one of the [types of] brahmins such as those who lick their hands, those who strip off their clothes, those who roll about [while eating], those who eat like crows, or those who eat until they must vomit—consuming as much as desired until the stomach is overflowing in an improper way, and then dwells devoted to the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of reclining, and the pleasure of sloth. This person is called one who does not know the measure (amattaññū) in consumption.

Whosoever reflects: "Even if the gift is abundant, if the donor wishes to give only a little, he takes only a little according to the donor's wish. If the gift is small, but the donor wishes to give much, he takes only a little according to the measure of the gift. If the gift is abundant and the donor also wishes to give much, he takes only what is appropriate to the measure, knowing his own capacity." Thus, he knows the measure in receiving. Furthermore, he reflects: "He consumes food wisely and reflectively, not for fun, not for intoxication..." and so on, and "He consumes the obtained alms-food without greed, infatuation, or obsession, seeing the danger and possessing the wisdom of escape." By reflecting in this way and knowing through the wisdom of reflection, he becomes one who knows the measure in eating by virtue of knowing the measure in consumption, which is the partaking of food. This person is called one who knows the measure (mattaññū) in eating. In this way, immoderation and moderation in eating should be understood.

In the verses, among the terms beginning with "cakkhu" (eye): it is called 'cakkhu' because it experiences (cak khati) visible forms. It enjoys visible forms, or it is as if it points out what is even and uneven; thus it is defined as 'cakkhu'. It is called 'sota' (ear) because it hears. It is called 'ghāna' (nose) because it smells. The essence of food, which is the cause of life, is called 'jīvita' (life); because it calls out to that life, it is called 'jivhā' (tongue). It is called 'kāya' (body) because it is the site of the arising of loathsome unwholesome states. It is called 'mano' (mind) because it knows (manate). However, the ancient teachers said it is 'mano' because it measures (munāti); it is defined as 'mano' because it knows the object as if measuring with a vessel or weighing with a great scale. Thus, first of all, the meaning of the terms should be understood here.

According to the nature of the meaning, the eye (cakkhu) is of two kinds: the fleshly eye (maṃsacakkhu) and the wisdom eye (paññācakkhu). Among these, the wisdom eye is of five kinds: the Buddha-eye (Buddhacakkhu), the all-seeing eye (Samantacakkhu), the eye of knowledge (Ñāṇacakkhu), the divine eye (Dibbacakkhu), and the Dhamma-eye (Dhammacakkhu). Among these, [the passage] "I saw..."
95:
"...monks, when I was looking at the world with the Buddha-eye, I saw," this is called the Buddha-eye (Buddhacakkhu). "Omniscience is called the all-seeing eye," this is called the all-seeing eye (Samantacakkhu). "The eye of knowledge arose," this is called the eye of knowledge (Ñāṇacakkhu). "Monks, I saw with the divine eye, which is purified," this is called the divine eye (Dibbacakkhu). "The dustless, stainless Dhamma-eye arose," this refers to the Dhamma-eye (Dhammacakkhu), which consists of the three lower paths.

The fleshly eye (maṃsacakkhu) is also of two kinds: the composite eye (sasambhāracakkhu) and the sensitive eye (pasādacakkhu). Among these, the mass of flesh situated in the eye socket, bounded above by the brow bone, on both sides by the corners of the eyes, inside by the brain, and outside by the eyelashes, [is the sasambhāracakkhu]. In brief, there are fourteen constituents: the four great elements, color, smell, taste, nutritive essence, fluid (sambhava), shape, life-faculty (jīvita-rūpa), sex-faculty (bhāva-rūpa), body-sensitivity (kāya-pasāda), and eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda). In detail, the four great elements and the six dependent on them—color, smell, taste, nutritive essence, shape, and fluid—make forty because they are produced by four causes. The four—life-faculty, sex-faculty, body-sensitivity, and eye-sensitivity—are produced solely by kamma. Thus, by virtue of these forty-four material phenomena, there are forty-four constituents. In the world, people perceive the white, round, thick, wide, and extensive part as the 'eye', but they do not know the true eye; they only perceive the physical mass which is the base as the 'eye'. That mass of flesh is situated in the eye socket, bound by the cord of the sinews and the brain. In that mass of flesh, there are white, black, and red parts. There are also the elements of earth, water, fire, and air. That mass of flesh is white due to the abundance of phlegm, black due to the abundance of bile, red due to the abundance of blood, stiff due to the abundance of the earth element, trickling due to the abundance of the water element, burning due to the abundance of the fire element, and moving due to the abundance of the air element. This is called the composite eye (sasambhāracakkhu). However, the sensitivity (pasāda) that is dependent on and connected to this composite eye, which arises depending on the four great elements, is called the sensitive eye (pasādacakkhu). This eye-sensitivity functions as the base (vatthu) and the door (dvāra) for eye-consciousness and so on, as appropriate.

Regarding the ear and so on, the ear (sota) is of two kinds: the divine ear (dibbasota) and the fleshly ear (maṃsasota). Here, "With the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing that of humans, he hears both sounds," this is called the divine ear. The fleshly ear is also of two kinds: the composite ear (sasambhārasota) and the sensitive ear (pasādasota); all this should be understood in the same manner as described for the eye. The same applies to the nose (ghāna) and the tongue (jivhā). The body (kāya) is of many kinds, such as the body of motion (copanakāya), the body born of action (karajakāya), the collective body (samūhakāya), and the sensitive body (pasādakāya). Among those many types of bodies—
96:
“The wise are restrained in body, and also restrained in speech” (as stated in the Dhammapada).

This kāya (mentioned in the above verse) is called copanakāya (the body in motion). This kāya in the passage “He creates another body from this body” (from the Dīgha Nikāya and Paṭisambhidāmagga) is called karajakāya (the physical body). Samūhakāya (the aggregate body), however, appears in many ways through the power of aggregates such as consciousness. Thus, in passages such as “Friends, these six are the groups of consciousness,” the aggregate of consciousness is spoken of. In “six groups of contact,” the aggregate of contact etc. (is spoken of). Likewise, in “tranquillity of body, lightness of body,” the aggregate of feeling etc. are meant. In “Here, a certain monk repeatedly contemplates the aggregate of earth as impermanent, the aggregate of water, the aggregate of fire, the aggregate of air, the aggregate of hair, the aggregate of body hair,” the aggregate of earth etc. is meant. This kāya in “having touched a tangible with the body” is called pasādakāya (the sensitive body). In this (Bhikkhu Sutta) too, only pasādakāya should be understood. It functions as the physical base and door for body-consciousness etc., as appropriate. Regarding the term mano (mind), although it refers to all consciousness, here the door-function is intended; therefore, the bhavaṅga (life-continuum) along with āvajjana (adverting) which acts as a door should be understood.

“For which bhikkhu these doors are unguarded” means for whichever monk these doors, with the mind as the sixth, are not closed with the door-panel of mindfulness because of falling into negligence by abandoning mindfulness. “In food... he attains” means that monk, through the aforementioned method of not knowing moderation in food and being without restraint of the faculties, attains suffering in every way: physical suffering in the present through diseases etc., physical suffering in the future belonging to the woeful states, and mental suffering through the burning of defilements like lust etc., and through the exhaustion of desires. Because it is so, such a person, with a body and mind burning with the two-fold fire of suffering in this world and the next, lives only in suffering at all times, whether by day or by night; for that person, there is no possibility of living happily, and it goes without saying that he cannot transcend the suffering of the round of rebirths.

## The Commentary on the First Sutta is finished.
97:
## 2. Sukhavihāra Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, the meaning should be understood by the opposite of the method stated (in the previous sutta).

## The Commentary on the Second Sutta is finished.

## 3. Tapanīya Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the third sutta, “tapanīyā” means they are called tapanīya because they cause burning, oppression, and harassment both in this present life and in the future life. Alternatively, they are called tapanīya because they are conducive to harm by producing and strengthening that suffering in the present life and the future life. Or else, one burns because of that [action]; thus it is “tapanaṃ,” meaning remorse or regret (vippaṭisāra); they are called tapanīya because they are conducive to being the cause of that [remorse].

“Akatakalyāṇo” means one is called akatakalyāṇa because he has not performed good, auspicious merit. The remaining two terms are just synonyms for that term. Indeed, merit is called “kalyāṇa” (auspicious) in the sense of being good because of its benefit in the present and happiness in the future; it is called “kusala” (wholesome) in the sense of shaking off contemptible things; and it is called “bhīruttāṇa” (protection for the fearful) in the sense of protecting those who fear suffering and those who fear the round of rebirths.

“Katapāpo” means one is called katapāpa because he has accumulated and performed base evil. The remaining two terms are just synonyms for that term. Unwholesome action is called “pāpa” (evil) in the sense of being base; it is called “ludda” (terrible) because of its fierce nature at the moment of its own occurrence and at the moment of its result; and it is called “kibbisa” (fault/sin) because of its state of being corrupted by defilements.

Thus, the Blessed One, having pointed out in brief by way of dhammādhiṭṭhāna (teaching in terms of dhammas) that “two things are tormenting,” then explained in detail by way of puggalādhiṭṭhāna (teaching in terms of persons) the unperformed wholesome dhammas and the performed unwholesome dhammas. Now, wishing to show their tormenting nature, he said, “He burns thinking, ‘I have not done good,’ and he also burns thinking, ‘I have done evil.’” The meaning is that he burns, burns with regret, and sorrows with the intense burning of the mind.

In the verses, “duccarita” (misconduct) is so called because it is badly practiced or because it is made putrid by defilements. Misconduct performed by the body or occurring from the body is “kāyaduccarita” (bodily misconduct). Verbal and mental misconduct should also be understood in this same way. These bodily misconducts etc. are intended as those that have reached the course of action (kammapatha). Therefore, referring to the group of unwholesome states that have not reached the course of action, he said, “yañcaññaṃ dosasañhitaṃ.” Its meaning is: whatever other unwholesome [action] that does not technically receive the name of bodily action etc. because it has not reached the status of a course of action, but is associated with fault because it is mixed with defilements like lust etc.—having done that too.

“Nirayaṃ” (hell) is the name given to all woeful states because of the sense of being devoid of delight or the sense of being without pleasure...
98:
Alternatively, because of being devoid of happiness, such a person reaches suffering that is devoid of delight in all states of existence, both happy and unhappy; this is how the meaning should be understood in this text.

In this sutta, regarding the distressing nature of bodily misconduct, the stories of Nanda the Ogre, Nanda the Youth, Nanda the Butcher, and the two brothers should be told. It is said that those two brothers killed a cow and made two portions of the meat. Then the younger brother said to the elder, "I have many children; please give me these intestines." The elder brother replied, "All the meat has already been divided into two portions; what more do you want to take?" and he struck him, causing his death. When he turned back and saw that his younger brother was dead, the thought arose, "I have indeed committed a grave deed; I have killed my brother for no reason." Then, powerful remorse (vippaṭisāra) arose in him. Whether standing or sitting, he reflected only on that unwholesome deed; he found no delight of mind, and the food he ate, drank, or chewed did not provide nourishment to his body, which became mere skin and bones.

Then a Thera asked him, "Lay follower, you are extremely thin, being mere skin and bones; what kind of illness do you have, or have you committed some distressing deed?" He replied, "Yes, Bhante," and related the whole matter. Then the Thera said, "Lay follower, you have committed a grave deed; you have offended against one who should not be offended." That person, having died with that very kamma, was reborn in hell. Regarding the distressing nature of verbal misconduct, the stories of King Suppabuddha the Sakyan, Kokālika, Ciñcamāṇavikā, and others should be told. Regarding the distressing nature of mental misconduct, the stories of Ukkalajayabhañña and others should be told.

## The Commentary on the Third Sutta is finished.

## 4. Atapanīyasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the fourth sutta, the meaning should be understood as the reverse of what was stated in the third sutta.

## The Commentary on the Fourth Sutta is finished.

## 5. Paṭhamasīlasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the fifth sutta, regarding the phrase "pāpakena ca sīlena" (with evil morality), it is said that what is called evil morality is the lack of restraint (asaṃvara) that causes the destruction of virtue. In that statement, if lack of restraint is indeed not morality, then why is that lack of restraint called morality because of the state of being immoral? In this matter, the intention is as follows: Just as in the world, what has not been seen is said to be "seen," or as one says, "drink this syrup" which has never been drunk before, so too in this context, immorality and lack of restraint are referred to as "morality." Alternatively, what unwholesome things are called morality? Because it was taught, "Thapati, what are unwholesome moralities? Unwholesome bodily action, unwholesome verbal action, and evil livelihood," the name "morality" (sīla) indeed exists even for unwholesome states. Therefore, all habitual conduct that exists as a natural state by the power of constant practice is called "morality." In that context, because of the sense of producing what is not good, whatever unwholesome deed is inferior, the Buddha taught "pāpakena sīlena" with reference to that unwholesome deed. Alternatively, all views that are evil views are indeed evil. Specifically, the three views: the view of non-causality (ahetukadiṭṭhi), the view of non-action (akiriyadiṭṭhi)...
99:
Just as in the world, what has not been seen is called "seen," or an immoral person is called "moral," so too in this context, immorality and lack of restraint should be referred to as "morality." Alternatively, because of the word of the Buddha, "Thapati, what are unwholesome moralities? Unwholesome bodily action, unwholesome verbal action, and evil livelihood," the name "morality" indeed exists even for unwholesome states. Therefore, all habitual conduct that has become a natural state by the power of repeated practice is called "morality." In that context, because of the sense of producing what is not good, whatever unwholesome deed is inferior, the Buddha taught "with evil morality" with reference to that unwholesome deed. Regarding "with evil view," all wrong views (micchādiṭṭhi) are indeed evil. Specifically, however, these three views—the view of non-causality (ahetukadiṭṭhi), the view of non-action (akiriyadiṭṭhi), and the nihilistic view (natthikadiṭṭhi)—are even more evil. Between those two, a person endowed with evil morality is one who is ruined in effort (payoga-vipanna), and a person endowed with evil view is one who is ruined in disposition (āsaya-vipanna). Thus, a person ruined in both effort and disposition is certainly one who goes to hell. Therefore, the Buddha taught: "Monks, a person endowed with these two qualities is placed in hell as if carried and dropped there." In this sutta, the phrase "endowed with these two qualities" should be understood as a descriptive statement of characteristics, not a direct scriptural designation. For example, in the world, it is said, "If these people should be afflicted by disease, this medicine should be given to them." In other similar cases, the same method should be understood. "Duppañño" means a person without wisdom.

## The Commentary on the Fifth Sutta is finished.

## 6. Dutiyasīlasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the sixth sutta, "with good morality" (bhaddakena ca sīlena) refers to the fourfold morality of purification (catupārisuddhi-sīla), such as good bodily conduct. Because of its nature as unbroken morality, it is itself auspicious and brings about auspicious qualities such as tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā); therefore, it is called "good" (bhaddaka). "With good view" (bhaddikāya ca diṭṭhiyā) means being endowed with the knowledge of the ownership of deeds (kammassakatā-ñāṇa) and the right view of the path of action (kammapatha-sammādiṭṭhi). In that context, through good morality, one becomes accomplished in effort (payoga-sampanna), and through good view, one becomes accomplished in disposition (āsaya-sampanna). Thus, a person accomplished in both effort and disposition is one who goes to heaven. Therefore, the Buddha taught: "Monks, a person endowed with these two qualities is placed in heaven as if carried and dropped there." "Sappañño" means a person with wisdom. The remaining words are easily understood.

## The Commentary on the Sixth Sutta is finished.
100:
## 7. Commentary on the Ātāpī Sutta

In the seventh sutta, regarding the term 'anātāpī': 'ātāpa' refers to the effort (vīriya) in the sense of burning away the defilements (kilesa). One who possesses this effort is called 'ātāpī'. One who does not possess it is 'anātāpī'. This means a lazy person who is devoid of right effort (sammappadhāna).

Fear of evil is called 'ottappa'. One who possesses this ottappa is called 'ottāpī'. One who does not possess it is 'anottāpī', meaning one who is devoid of moral dread (ottappa). Alternatively, 'anātāpa' is laziness (kosajja), which is the opposite of ardor (ātāpa). One who has that laziness is 'anātāpī'. 'Anottappa' is described as: "He does not dread what should be dreaded; he does not dread the arrival of evil, unwholesome states." One who possesses that state is 'anottāpī'. In this context, the meaning should be understood in this way.

'Abhabbo' means an unworthy or incapable person. 'Sambodhāya' means for the sake of the Noble Path (ariya magga). 'Nibbānāya' means for the sake of the Great Deathless Nibbāna, which is the absolute pacification of defilements. 'Anuttarassa yogakkhemassa' refers to the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala). It is called 'anuttara' (unsurpassed) because there is no state higher than it, and it is called 'yogakkhema' (security from the yokes) because it is safe and fearless, being unassailed by the four yokes (yoga). 'Adhigamāya' means for the sake of attainment.

'Ātāpī' means one who possesses energy (vīriya). Such a person is 'ātāpī' because they have the habit of truly burning away defilements by being endowed with the arousal of energy as described: "He dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the acquisition of wholesome states; he is firm, of steady valor, and does not cast off the burden concerning wholesome states." 'Ottāpī' means one who has the habit of being fearful because they are endowed with moral dread (ottappa) as described: "He dreads what should be dreaded; he dreads the arrival of evil, unwholesome states." This very person is called 'ottāpī'. Because it is inseparable from that moral dread, he is also endowed with moral shame (hiri). Therefore, being endowed with shame and dread (hiri-ottappa), he sees fear even in the slightest faults and fulfills the precepts (sīla) completely. In this way, his perfection of virtue (sīla-sampadā) is shown.

By the term 'ātāpī', through the illustration of the burning of defilements, his engagement in the development of tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) is shown. Since the aforementioned energy cannot exist without faith (saddhā), mindfulness (sati), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (paññā), the five faculties (indriya) beginning with faith, which mature liberation (vimutti), are already implied by meaning. When those faculties are fulfilled, the six perceptions (saññā) that are part of penetration (nibbedha-bhāgiya)—namely, the perception of impermanence (anicca-saññā), the perception of suffering in the impermanent, the perception of non-self in suffering, the perception of abandonment (pahāna-saññā), the perception of dispassion (virāga-saññā), and the perception of cessation (nirodha-saññā)—are also already accomplished. Thus, for one endowed with these two qualities...
101:
To show the capability of attaining the Path, Fruit, and Nibbāna through the fulfillment of mundane virtue, concentration, and wisdom, the Buddha said: "Ātāpī ca kho... pe... adhigamāya."

In the verses, 'kusīto' (lazy) refers to one who is associated with despicable, evil, unwholesome states known as wrong thoughts (micchā-vitakka), namely: sensual thought (kāma-vitakka), ill-will thought (byāpāda-vitakka), and harmful thought (vihiṃsā-vitakka). Or, he is called 'kusīto' because he sinks (sīdati) away from right practice in a despicable manner (by substituting the letter 'd' with 't'). 'Hīnavīriyo' means one who lacks energy, one who is devoid of exerting energy in all four postures. He is full of sloth and torpor (thina-middha-bahulo) because of the constant occurrence of mental laziness (thina), which has the nature of being oppressed by a lack of effort, and physical laziness (middha), which has the nature of inability and exhaustion.

He is called 'ahiriko' (shameless) because he lacks 'hiri', which has the characteristic of loathing evil, and is instead endowed with its opposite, 'ahirika'. He is called 'anādaro' (disrespectful) because he lacks respect for right practice due to the very absence of shame, dread, and energy. In both cases, he is called 'anādaro' because of the twofold action regarding both the Dhamma and the person. 'Phuṭṭhuṃ' means to touch (to attain). 'Sambodhimuttamaṃ' means he is incapable of attaining the supreme Arahantship known as Sambodhi.

'Satimā' (mindful) means one who is mindful by virtue of being capable of remembering things done and said long ago, and by being associated with the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). 'Nipako' (wise) means one who is prudent because he is endowed with the wisdom known as clear comprehension (sampajañña) occurring in seven instances, and the wisdom of maintaining the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). 'Jhāyī' (meditative) means one who meditates by means of the two types of jhana: meditation on an object (ārammaṇūpanijjhāna) and meditation on characteristics (lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna). 'Appamatto' (heedful) means one who is diligent in the development of the meditation subject by the method of "purifying the mind from hindering states (nīvaraṇa) through walking and sitting throughout the day."

'Saṃyojanaṃ jātijarāya chetvā' means having cut from the root—by means of uprooting latent tendencies (anusaya)—the group of ten defilements such as sensual lust (kāmarāga), which are called 'fetters' (saṃyojana) because they bind beings to birth and old age. Alternatively, 'saṃyojanaṃ jātijarāya chetvā' means having cut the bond of birth and old age. For if the fetters have not been cut for someone, there is no cutting or uprooting of birth and old age for him. But if those fetters have been cut for someone, birth and old age are also already cut because the cause has been uprooted. Therefore, only one who cuts the fetters also cuts birth and old age. Thus, the Buddha said: "Saṃyojanaṃ..."
102:
"Cutting off birth and old age" (jātijarāya chetvā) means that in this very life, one should reach the unsurpassed Enlightenment (Sambodhi); one should reach (attain) the highest Path of Arahatship (Arahatta-magga) or the Fruition of Arahatship (Arahatta-phala).

## The Commentary on the Seventh Sutta is finished.

## 8. Commentary on the First Nakuhaṇa Sutta

In the eighth sutta, in the word "nayidaṃ," "na" is a particle (nipāta) having the sense of negation, and it should be connected with the word "vussati"; the letter "ya" is a euphonic junction (sandhi). The word "idaṃ" is a mere particle in such passages as: "Monks, once I was staying at Ukkaṭṭhā, in the Subhaga Grove at the foot of the royal Sal tree" (Ekamidāhaṃ, bhikkhave, samayaṃ ukkaṭṭhāyaṃ viharāmi subhagavane sālarājamūle). In such passages as: "Monks, this aforementioned virtue, which is present and evident, is only a trifle, a matter of little value, a mere matter of virtue" (Idaṃ kho taṃ, bhikkhave, appamattakaṃ oramattakaṃ sīlamattakaṃ), it appears in the sense of the aforementioned thing that is near and evident.

In such verses as:
"This is that Jetavana, frequented by the assembly of seers,
Where the King of Dhamma resided, which gives me joy."
(Idañhi taṃ jetavanaṃ, isisaṅghanisevitaṃ,
āvutthaṃ dhammarājena, pītisañjananaṃ mama.)
It appears in the sense of something near and evident that is about to be mentioned. In this sutta also, it should be understood only in the sense of something near and evident that is about to be mentioned.

The word "Brahmacariya" (holy life) is used as in these verses:
"O Naga king, what is your vow? What is your holy life (brahmacariya)?
By the result of what well-practiced merit has this attainment of psychic power, splendor, strength, and energy come to be?
And why is this great mansion of yours?

I and my wife were donors in the world of men, possessing faith;
At that time, my house was like a well or a pond,
And recluses and brahmins were well-satisfied.

O wise one, that satisfying of recluses and brahmins was my vow; that merit was my holy life (brahmacariya);
This attainment of psychic power, splendor, strength, and energy is the result of that well-practiced holy life;
And this great mansion of mine has arisen."
103:
In this Puṇṇaka Jātaka, (the word brahmacariya) appears in the sense of almsgiving (dāna).

"By what kind of holy life does your hand give whatever is desired? By what kind of holy life does your hand flow with sweet flavor? By what kind of holy life of yours is the fruit of merit fulfilled in your hand?

By such a holy life, the hand gives whatever is desired; by such a holy life, the hand flows with sweet flavor; by such a holy life of mine, the fruit of merit is fulfilled in my hand."
In this Aṅkura Petavatthu, (the word brahmacariya) appears in the sense of service (veyyāvacca).

"Monks, this was the holy life called Tittiriya (the practice of the partridges) in the past."
In this Tittira Jātaka, it appears in the sense of the five precepts of virtue (pañcasīla).

"Pañcasikha, that holy life does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation... it leads only to rebirth in the Brahma-world."
In this Mahāgovinda Sutta, it appears in the sense of the four sublime states (brahmavihāra).

"Others will be those who practice unholy conduct (sexual intercourse); we shall be those who practice the holy life (abstaining from low sexual conduct) in this Dispensation."
In the Sallekha Sutta, it appears in the sense of abstinence from sexual intercourse (methunavirati).

"We do not transgress against our wives,
Nor do our wives transgress against us;
Apart from those wives, we practice the holy life,
Therefore, the young in our family do not die."
In the Mahādhammapāla Jātaka, it appears in the sense of contentment with one's own wife (sadārasantosa).

"Sāriputta, I know that I have practiced the holy life endowed with four factors; I was one of great energy."
In the Lomahaṃsa Sutta, it appears in the sense of energy (vīriya).

"By a low holy life, one is born in the khattiya clan;
By a middling one, one reaches the state of a deity;
By a superior one, one is purified."
In the Nemi Jātaka, it appears in the sense of the eightfold Uposatha performed by way of self-restraint.

"Pañcasikha, this holy life leads certainly to disenchantment, to dispassion... this is the Noble Eightfold Path."
