In the same Mahāgovinda Sutta, it appears in the sense of the Noble Path (Ariya-magga).

"This holy life (the Dispensation) is successful, prosperous, widespread, known by many, become popular, and well-proclaimed as far as there are gods and men."
In the Pāsādika Sutta, it appears in the sense of the entire Dispensation (Sāsana), which is the summary of the three trainings (sikkhattaya). In this context also, it refers to the Noble Path and the Dispensation.
104:
"Vussati" means it is lived, it is practiced. "For the purpose of deceiving the people" means for the purpose of making the world of beings, the people, marvel, thinking, "Oh, the venerable one is indeed virtuous, possessed of duties, of few desires, contented, of great psychic power, and of great majesty," and so on. "For the purpose of getting the people to talk" means for the purpose of making people with confident minds say, "Giving to a venerable one of such a nature will be of great fruit," and asking, "What do you need? What should be brought?"

"For the purpose of the benefit of gain, honor, and fame" means for that benefit which is the gain of the four requisites mentioned as the benefit of virtue in the passage: "Monks, if a monk should desire, 'May I be a receiver of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick,' he should be a perfecter of the virtues" (M. i. 65); and honor, which is characterized by the respectful giving of the four requisites and by respect, esteem, and reverence; and fame, which is the sound of high praise such as "He is possessed of virtue, learned, a bearer of what he has heard, and of aroused energy," which is the benefit in the present life for those living the holy life. "So that people may know me thus" means it should be connected as: this holy life is not lived for the purpose of being praised by the power of the qualities truly present in oneself, thinking, "While living the holy life in this way, let people know me and esteem me as 'This one is virtuous, of good character,'" and so on.

However, some teachers say: "For the purpose of deceiving the people" means for the purpose of making the people marvel through the three bases of deception—scheming, talk, and the use of requisites—by one who has evil desires and is overcome by longing. "For the purpose of getting the people to talk" means for the purpose of talking to people by way of indirect talk, hinting, and so on, for the sake of requisites by one who has evil desires. "For the purpose of the benefit of gain, honor, and fame" means for the purpose of producing the arising of benefits known as gain, honor, and fame, because of the importance given to gain and so on by one who has evil desires. "So that people may know me thus" means this holy life is not lived by one who has evil desires with the intention of being esteemed for qualities he does not possess, thinking, "Let people know me thus." This is how they state the meaning here. However, the former meaning is more essential.

In the phrase "Atha kho," "atha" is a particle in the sense of "another purpose," and "kho" is in the sense of emphasis (certainty). Therefore, it shows that "But, monks, this holy life is lived for another purpose than deception and so on." Now, wishing to show that purpose, he said, "For the purpose of restraint..." and so on.
105:
He said, "And for the purpose of abandoning" (pahānatthañca). In that passage (beginning with "saṃvaratthañceva"), restraint is of five kinds: restraint of the Pātimokkha, restraint of mindfulness, restraint of knowledge, restraint of patience, and restraint of energy.

Among those five, this restraint that comes by way of the method beginning with "He is endowed, well-endowed with this restraint of the Pātimokkha" (Vibh. 511) is called restraint of the Pātimokkha. That restraint of the Pātimokkha is also called restraint of virtue (sīlasaṃvara). This restraint that comes as "He guards the eye-faculty, he practices restraint over the eye-faculty" (D. i. 213, etc.) is called restraint of mindfulness (satisaṃvara).

"Whatever streams there are in the world, O Ajita (said the Blessed One),
Mindfulness is their dam;
I call mindfulness the restraint of the streams,
By wisdom they are shut off." (Sn. 1041) —

This restraint that comes thus is called restraint of knowledge (ñāṇasaṃvara). This restraint that comes by way of the method beginning with "He is one who endures cold and heat" (M. i. 24, etc.) is called restraint of patience (khantisaṃvara). This restraint that comes by way of the method beginning with "He does not tolerate an arisen sensual thought (but abandons it)" (M. i. 26, etc.) is called restraint of energy (vīriyasaṃvara).

In terms of ultimate reality, however, they are the volitions (cetanā) and abstinences (virati) that occur by way of abandoning killing and so on, and by way of performing major and minor duties. In brief, all restraint of body and speech is restraint of virtue. In detail, the non-transgression of the seven classes of offenses is restraint of virtue. Mindfulness itself is restraint of mindfulness; or else, the wholesome aggregates in which mindfulness is predominant are restraint of mindfulness. Knowledge itself is restraint of knowledge. Non-hatred occurring by way of endurance is restraint of patience; or else, the wholesome aggregates occurring thus with non-hatred as the predominant factor are restraint of patience; some teachers say it is wisdom. Energy itself occurring by way of not tolerating sensual thoughts and so on is restraint of energy.

Among those five, the first is to be understood as restraint because it shuts out immorality such as bodily misconduct; the second because it shuts out forgetfulness; the third because it shuts out ignorance; the fourth because it shuts out impatience; and the fifth because it shuts out laziness. Thus, "saṃvaratthaṃ" means for the purpose of this restraint, for the purpose of accomplishing restraint.

Abandoning (pahāna) is also of five kinds: abandoning by substitution of opposites (tadaṅgapahāna), abandoning by suppression (vikkhambhanapahāna), abandoning by eradication (samucchedapahāna), abandoning by tranquilization (paṭippassaddhipahāna), and abandoning by escape (nissaraṇapahāna). Regarding those five kinds of abandoning, what should be said has already been stated below in the explanation of the first sutta of the Ekakanipāta. Of those five kinds of abandoning, in such and such a manner...
106:
The term 'pahānatthaṃ' is used for the purpose of the five kinds of abandoning (pahāna), either in the sense of relinquishing defilements such as greed, etc., or in the sense of transcending them. It means for the purpose of accomplishing abandonment. Between these two, it is said that through restraint (saṃvara), the entry of defilements into the mental continuum is prevented; through abandoning (pahāna), the defilements that have entered are blocked and uprooted. However, it should be understood that both are fulfilled by both as appropriate. Indeed, the dhammas such as virtue (sīla) are called 'saṃvara' because they restrain, and 'pahāna' because they abandon.

In the verses, 'anītiham': 'Īti' refers to calamities (upaddava)—both those belonging to this life and the next. Because it destroys, eliminates, and abandons those calamities, it is called 'ītiham'; because it is without such 'ītiham', it is 'anītiham'. This refers to the holy life of the Dispensation (sāsana-brahmacariya) and the holy life of the Path (magga-brahmacariya). Alternatively, 'ītihas' are defilements (upakkilesa) such as craving, because they occur, proceed, and go along with harmful things. Since there are no such 'ītihas' here, it is 'anītiham'. Or, 'ītihas' are the sectarian doctrines (titthiya-samaya) in the sense mentioned above; because it is the opposite of those, this Dispensation is 'anītiham'. There is also a reading 'anitiha'. Its meaning: 'itiha' is doubt (vicikicchā) because of the state of taking things in various ways among the dhammas. Since it accomplishes the state of being free from doubt for those practicing according to the instruction as proclaimed by the Fully Enlightened One, there is no 'itiha' (doubt) here, thus it is 'anitiha'. It means 'not depending on another' (aparappaccaya). Indeed, it is said: 'to be personally realized by the wise' and 'beyond the sphere of reasoning'. However, for the sake of ease in reciting the verse, they recite it with a long vowel (dīgha) as 'anītiham'.

'Nibbānogadhagāmī' means going to the shore, the foundation, known as Nibbāna. Since it has the taste of liberation (vimuttirasa), it means it leads certainly to Nibbāna. That Blessed One, who fulfilled the thirty perfections, destroyed all defilements, and fully awakened to the unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment, taught that holy life which leads to the plunge into Nibbāna. Alternatively, the Noble Path is called 'nibbānogadha'. This is because without that Path, plunging into Nibbāna is impossible, and because that Path does not occur without taking Nibbāna as its object. Since it leads certainly to that Path which plunges into Nibbāna, it is 'nibbānogadhagāmī'. Alternatively, 'nibbānogadhagāminaṃ' refers to the holy life of the Path that goes into the interior of Nibbāna; because it occurs and proceeds only within Nibbāna by making Nibbāna its object. 'Mahattehi' means by those with great bodies, with noble intentions. The Buddhas and other Noble Ones are called 'mahesi' because they seek (esanti) the great Nibbāna or the great aggregates of virtue, etc. It is the practice followed by those Noble Ones. 'Yathā buddhena desitaṃ' means just as it was taught by Me, the Fully Enlightened One, regarding the things to be directly known, etc., exactly as they are to be directly known, etc.; thus those who...
107:
...practice this holy life of the Path and the holy life of the Dispensation for the sake of that Path. Those persons, following the instruction of Me, the Teacher, who advises them appropriately regarding the benefits in this life and the next, and acting according to the Dispensation, will make an end—a limit, a non-occurrence—to the entire suffering of the round (vaṭṭa-dukkha), or they will realize Nibbāna, the end of suffering.

## The Commentary on the Eighth Sutta is finished.

## 9. Dutiya-nakuhana Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the ninth sutta, 'abhiññatthaṃ' means for the purpose of knowing all phenomena without distortion through superior knowledge, by way of distinguishing the wholesome, etc., and by way of distinguishing the aggregates, etc. 'Pariññatthaṃ' means for the purpose of fully understanding the phenomena belonging to the three planes as "This is suffering," etc., and for the purpose of transcending them. Between these two, knowing the things to be directly known (abhijānanā) has the Four Noble Truths as its domain. As for knowing the things to be fully understood (parijānanā), although it has the Truth of Suffering as its object, it cannot occur without the realizations of abandoning (pahāna), realization (sacchikiriyā), and development (bhāvanā); therefore, it should be understood that abandoning, etc., are also included here. The rest is exactly as explained in the preceding sutta.

## The Commentary on the Ninth Sutta is finished.

## 10. Somanassa Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the tenth sutta, in the term 'sukhasomanassabahulo', 'sukha' is bodily pleasure and 'somanassa' is mental pleasure. Therefore, one in whom bodily and mental pleasure occur frequently is called 'one abounding in happiness and joy' (sukhasomanassabahulo). 'Yoni' (origin/source): in passages such as "Sāriputta, there are these four origins (yoniyo)," etc., 'yoni' refers to the group of aggregates. In passages such as "Bhūmija, this is the cause (yoni) for the attainment of the fruit," etc., 'yoni' means cause. In "I do not call him a brahmin [merely] because of his origin (yonija) or being born from a mother," and "The karma-born winds turn him upside down with feet up and head down and bring him to the mother's birth canal (yonimukha)," etc., it refers to the urinary tract/birth canal. In this sutta, however, 'cause' is intended.
108:
In this sutta, the cause is intended. The term 'āraddha' refers to states that are initiated, exerted, fulfilled, or accomplished.

In the phrase 'āsavānaṃ khayāya' (for the destruction of the taints), they are called 'āsavas' because they flow or occur. This means they flow or arise from the eye... and from the mind. Alternatively, they are called 'āsavas' because they flow or occur up to the stage of gotrabhū (change-of-lineage) in terms of states (dhamma), and up to the bhavagga (highest point of existence) in terms of location (okāsa). It means they occur by taking these states and this location within. For this prefix 'ā' has the sense of 'making within' (antokaraṇa). They are also called 'āsavas' in the sense of being long-matured, like madirā (spirituous liquor) and the like. In the world, liquors such as madirā that have been matured for a long time are called 'āsavas'. If they are called 'āsavas' due to long maturation, then only these states such as greed (lobha) and so on deserve to be called 'āsavas'. For has the Blessed One not said: 'Monks, a first point of ignorance (avijjā) is not evident, such that one could say: Before this, ignorance did not exist'? They are also called 'āsavas' because they produce or bring forth the long suffering of the round of rebirths (saṃsāra). The previous definitions are suitable for those suttas where the defilements (kilesas) are called 'āsavas'. The last definition is also suitable for kamma. Not only kamma and defilements are called 'āsavas', but indeed various kinds of afflictions (upaddava) are also called 'āsavas'. In the Abhidhamma, it is said: 'There are four taints: the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava), the taint of existence (bhavāsava), the taint of views (diṭṭhāsava), and the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava)'; thus defilements such as sensual lust (kāmarāga) are called 'āsavas'. In the Suttas also, in the passage: 'Cunda, I do not teach the Dhamma only for the restraint of taints belonging to the present life,' the defilements that are the roots of dispute are meant by 'āsavas'.

'That kamma by which there would be rebirth as a deva, or a gandhabba, or a bird;
By which one would go to the state of a yakkha, or go to the state of a human;
Those taints (kamma) of mine are destroyed, demolished, and abolished.'

Here, kamma pertaining to the three planes and the remaining unwholesome states are meant. In the passage: 'For the restraint of taints belonging to the present life, and for the warding off of taints belonging to the future life,' it refers to various afflictions such as harming others, remorse, killing, and imprisonment, as well as the suffering of the woeful states.

In the Vinaya, those taints appear in two ways: 'For the restraint of taints belonging to the present life, and for the warding off of taints belonging to the future life.' In the Saḷāyatana Saṃyutta, they appear in three ways: 'Friend, there are these three taints: the taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, and the taint of ignorance.' In the Suttas also, they appear in three ways. In the Abhidhamma, those same three appear as four, together with the taint of views. In the Āsīvisūpama Sutta, they appear in five ways: 'Monks, there are taints leading to hell, taints leading to the animal realm, taints leading to the realm of hungry ghosts, taints leading to the human world, and taints leading to the deva world.' In these five, only kamma is intended as 'āsava'. In the Chakka Nipāta, they appear in six ways, such as: 'Taints to be abandoned by restraint,' and so on. In the Sabbāsava Sutta, those same six appear as seven, together with states such as those to be abandoned by seeing.
109:
The term 'taint of ignorance' (avijjāsava) appears in three ways (in the Saṃyutta Nikāya). Likewise in other Suttas. In the Abhidhamma, however, those same three appear as four, together with the taint of views (diṭṭhāsava). In the Nibbedhikapariyāya Sutta, they appear in five ways: 'Monks, there are taints leading to hell, taints leading to the animal realm, taints leading to the realm of hungry ghosts, taints leading to the human world, and taints leading to the deva world.' In this context, only kamma is intended as 'āsava'. In the Chakka Nipāta, they appear in six ways, such as: 'Monks, there are taints to be abandoned by restraint,' and so on. In the Sabbāsava Sutta, those same six appear as seven, together with states to be abandoned by seeing (dassana-pahātabba). In this Abhidhamma method, however, it should be understood that the four taints are intended.

Regarding the word 'khayāya': the destruction of the taints according to their nature is called 'āsavānaṃ khaya', meaning their exhaustion, passing away, breaking up, disintegration, impermanence, and disappearance. In the passage: 'Monks, I say the destruction of the taints is for one who knows and sees,' the mode of the taints being exhausted, their state of non-existence, and their absolute non-arising is called 'āsavakkhaya'.

'For the trainee (sekha) who is practicing, following the straight path, the first knowledge arises in the destruction (the path of Arahantship), and immediately after that, the final knowledge (the fruit of Arahantship).' In this verse, the Noble Path is called 'āsavakkhaya'. In the passage: 'By the destruction of the taints, one becomes a recluse,' the Fruit (of Arahantship) is called 'āsavakkhaya'.

'For one who always looks for others' faults and is prone to disparaging, his taints grow; he is far from the destruction of the taints (Nibbāna).' In this verse, Nibbāna is called 'āsavakkhaya'. In this context, however, 'āsavānaṃ khayāya' is said with reference to the Fruit of Arahantship, meaning for the sake of the Fruit of Arahantship.

'Saṃvejanīyesu ṭhānesu' means in the grounds for urgency (saṃvegavatthu) such as birth and so on, which produce spiritual urgency (saṃvega). These eight—birth, aging, sickness, death, suffering in the woeful states, suffering rooted in the round of rebirths in the past, suffering rooted in the round of rebirths in the future, and suffering rooted in the search for food in the present—are the grounds for urgency called saṃvejanīya-ṭṭhāna. Furthermore: 'The world-habitation is burning (with the fire of defilements), it is departing (towards death), it has entered upon a wrong path; the world is being led away (towards aging and death), it is unstable, the world is without protection, without a master...'
110:
"The world is without ownership, one must go leaving everything behind; the world is deficient, insatiable, a slave to craving"—these and other such teachings should be understood in this sutta as grounds for spiritual urgency (saṃvejanīyaṭṭhāna). By "through spiritual urgency" (saṃvejanena) is meant the urgency called fear that arises based on the objects of urgency such as birth and so forth. In terms of ultimate meaning, however, spiritual urgency (saṃvega) is knowledge (ñāṇa) accompanied by moral dread (ottappa).

"For one who has spiritual urgency" (saṃviggassa) means for one in whom spiritual urgency has arisen due to the various kinds of suffering such as birth, by way of descent into the womb and so forth. There is also a reading "saṃvejitvā." "Through wise exertion" (yoniso padhānena) means through exertion by way of means, through right effort. That right effort is called "exertion" (padhāna) because it is the means by which unwholesome states are abandoned and wholesome states reach fulfillment through development, and because it accomplishes the state of excellence.

In that context, through spiritual urgency, not seeing any protection, shelter, or refuge in existences and so forth, not clinging to those existences, with a mind unattached, and being turned away from and disillusioned with the opposite of that [Nibbāna], one indeed becomes one who slopes toward Nibbāna, inclines toward Nibbāna, and leans toward Nibbāna. That person, by relying on a good friend (kalyāṇamitta), being abundant in wise attention (yoniso manasikāra), having pure intention and application, and being intensely devoted to tranquility and insight (samatha-vipassanā), becomes weary of all conditioned things (saṅkhāra), becomes dispassionate, and arouses insight. Between those two, in that he is abundant in wise attention, has pure intention and application, and is intensely devoted to tranquility and insight, by that effort, it should be understood that he has an abundance of happiness and joy even in the present life. In that he, established in tranquility, is intensely devoted to insight, becomes weary of all conditioned things, becomes dispassionate, and arouses insight, by that arousal, it should be understood that his wise effort for the destruction of the taints (āsava) has reached completion.

In the verses, "saṃvizzetheva" means one should indeed be stirred, one should indeed cultivate spiritual urgency. There is also a reading "saṃvizzitvāna." It means having become one who has spiritual urgency in the manner described. "The wise one" (paṇḍito) means a person of wisdom, referring to one with triple-rooted rebirth-linking (tihetukapaṭisandhi). "Having clearly seen with wisdom" (paññāya samavekkhiya) means having properly contemplated the objects of spiritual urgency with wisdom by way of their presence. Alternatively, it means having properly contemplated with wisdom. All the remaining words have clear meanings.

## The Explanation of the Tenth Sutta is finished.
## Thus, in the Commentary on the Itivuttaka named Paramatthadīpanī,
## The Explanation of the First Chapter of the Book of the Twos is finished.
111:
## 2. Second Chapter (Dutiya Vagga)
## 1. Explanation of the Vitakka Sutta

In the first sutta of the second chapter, in the passage beginning with "Tathāgataṃ, bhikkhave," the word "Tathāgata" is first seen applied to the conventional designation of a being, the Fully Enlightened Buddha, and so forth. Among those, in passages such as "A Tathāgata exists after death" (hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā), it appears as a conventional designation for a being.

In passages such as "The Tathāgata, honored by gods and humans, we revere the Buddha; may there be safety" (tathāgataṃ devamanussapūjitaṃ, buddhaṃ namassāma suvatthi hotu), it appears in reference to the Fully Enlightened Buddha.

In passages such as "The Tathāgata, honored by gods and humans, we revere the Dhamma; may there be safety" (tathāgataṃ devamanussapūjitaṃ, dhammaṃ namassāma suvatthi hotu), it appears in reference to the Dhamma.

In passages such as "The Tathāgata, honored by gods and humans, we revere the Saṅgha; may there be safety" (tathāgataṃ devamanussapūjitaṃ, saṅghaṃ namassāma suvatthi hotu), it appears in reference to the Saṅgha.

In this sutta, however, it refers to the Fully Enlightened Buddha. Therefore, in this context, the Blessed One is called "Tathāgata" for eight reasons. What are the eight? He is the Tathāgata because he has come in the same way (tathā āgato); he is the Tathāgata because he has gone in the same way (tathā gato); he is the Tathāgata because he has arrived at the true characteristics (tathalakkhaṇaṃ āgato); he is the Tathāgata because he has fully awakened to true things as they really are (tathadhamme yāthāvato abhisambuddho); he is the Tathāgata because of seeing truly (tathadassitāya); he is the Tathāgata because of speaking truly (tathavāditāya); he is the Tathāgata because of acting truly (tathākāritāya); and he is the Tathāgata in the sense of overcoming everything (abhibhavanaṭṭhena).

How is the Blessed One the Tathāgata because he has come in the same way? Just as by whatever aspiration (abhinīhāra) he fulfilled the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramī), and fulfilled the perfections of virtue, renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truthfulness, determination, loving-kindness, and equanimity—having fulfilled these ten perfections, ten intermediate perfections, and ten ultimate perfections, thus thirty perfections—and having sacrificed the five great sacrifices (mahāpariccāga), namely, the sacrifice of limbs (aṅgapariccāga), the sacrifice of life (attapariccāga), the sacrifice of wealth (dhanapariccāga), the sacrifice of wife (dārapariccāga), and the sacrifice of kingdom (rajjapariccāga), just as the Fully Enlightened Buddhas such as Vipassī...
112:
Just as the Buddhas such as Vipassī and others have come, so too has our Blessed One come. Therefore, He is called the 'Tathāgata' (Thus Come). With reference to this meaning, it was said:

"Just as in this world, the Sages such as Vipassī and others came to the state of omniscience,
In that very same way, this Sakyan Sage has also come;
Therefore, the One endowed with the five-fold vision is called 'Tathāgata'."

Thus, because He has come in the same manner as the previous Buddhas such as Vipassī, He is called 'Tathāgata'.

In what way is He called 'Tathāgata' because He has gone in the same manner as those previous Buddhas? Just as the Buddhas such as Vipassī, immediately upon being born, stood on the earth with level feet and, facing the north, went forward with a stride of seven steps, so too did our Blessed One go. Therefore, He is called 'Tathāgata' (Thus Gone). With reference to this meaning, it was said:

"Just as the Lord of Beings, immediately upon being born,
With level feet touched the earth,
That Gotama took seven strides,
And the deities held a white parasol over Him.

Having gone those seven strides, that Gotama
Looked equally in all directions;
Like a lion standing on a mountain peak,
He uttered a speech endowed with eight qualities."

Thus, because He has gone in the same manner as those previous Buddhas, He is called 'Tathāgata'.

In what way is He called 'Tathāgata' because He has arrived at the true characteristics? He has arrived, by way of the path of knowledge, at the individual characteristics (salakkhaṇa) and the common characteristics (sāmaññalakkhaṇa) of all material and immaterial phenomena, which are true (tatha) and not false (avitatha); He has reached and understood them without contradiction. Therefore, He is called 'Tathāgata'. With reference to this meaning, it was said:

"Since the Protector has arrived through knowledge
At the individual and common characteristics of all phenomena,
Which are indeed true,
Therefore, He is called 'Tathāgata'."

Thus, because He has arrived at the true characteristics, He is called 'Tathāgata'.

In what way is He called 'Tathāgata' because He has fully awakened to the true realities as they really are? The true realities (tathadhamma) are the Four Noble Truths. As the Blessed One said: "Monks, these four things are true, not false, not otherwise." Thus, the detail should be made. "Monks, what are the four? This is the Noble Truth of Suffering," and so forth. Monks, this Truth of Suffering and the others are true, not false, not otherwise. The Blessed One has fully awakened to these four truths. Therefore, because He has fully awakened to the true realities, He is called 'Tathāgata'. Indeed, in this context, the word 'gata' has the meaning of 'fully awakened' (abhisambuddha). Thus, because He has fully awakened to the true realities without distortion, He is called 'Tathāgata'.

In what way is He called 'Tathāgata' because He is one who sees truly? In the world with its devas, among the generation of beings with its recluses and brahmins, its devas and humans, in the immeasurable world systems...
113:
...those realities are true, not false, not otherwise. What are the four? Monks, "This is the Noble Truth of Suffering," and so forth, as preached in detail. Monks, this Truth of Suffering and the others are true, not false, not otherwise. And the Blessed One has fully awakened to them; therefore, because of His full awakening to the truths, He is the 'Tathāgata'. For here, the word 'gata' has the meaning of 'fully awakened'. Thus, because He has fully awakened to the true realities as they really are, He is called 'Tathāgata'.

In what way is He called 'Tathāgata' because He sees truly? Whatever visible object (rūpārammaṇa) comes into the range of the eye-door of immeasurable beings in immeasurable world systems... in the world with its devas and humans, the Blessed One knows and sees that in every aspect. To the Blessed One who thus knows and sees, whether by way of the desirable and so forth, or by way of the terms obtained among the seen, heard, sensed, and cognized, when that visible object is analyzed by various names, or by the thirteen sections, or by the fifty-two methods—such as "What is that form which is the base of visible form (rūpāyatana)? It is that form which, depending on the four great elements, is a color-brightness, visible, and impinging, whether blue, yellow, etc."—it is only true (tatha), there is no falsehood. This same method applies to sounds and so forth that come into the range of the ear-door and other doors. For this was said by the Blessed One:

"Monks, whatever in the world with its devas... with its devas and humans, is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, reached, sought after, and examined by the mind, all that I know... all that I have fully realized; that is known to the Tathāgata, but the Tathāgata does not take His stand upon it."

Thus, because He sees truly, He is called 'Tathāgata'. In this context, the occurrence of the word 'Tathāgata' in the sense of 'seeing truly' should be understood.

In what way is He called 'Tathāgata' because He speaks truly? From the night the Blessed One fully awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment until the night He attained Parinibbāna in the Nibbāna element without remainder, during this interval of forty-five years, whatever the Blessed One spoke, such as the Sutta, Geyya, and so forth, all of it is pure, complete, crushing the intoxication of lust and so forth, uniform, true, and not false. Therefore, He said:

"Cunda, from the night the Tathāgata fully awakens to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment until the night He attains Parinibbāna in the Nibbāna element without remainder, whatever He speaks, utters, or points out in this interval, all that is just true, and not otherwise."

It is true; in this context, the word 'gata' has the meaning of 'knowing specifically'. Because He speaks truly in such a manner...
114:
Whatever the Blessed One speaks, utters, or points out in this interval, all that is just so and not otherwise. Therefore, he is called 'Tathāgata'.

Here, the word 'gata' has the meaning of 'gada' (speaking). Thus, because of speaking truly, he is 'Tathāgata'. Alternatively, 'āgadana' is 'āgada', meaning 'speech'. Because the Blessed One has true, unerring speech, by changing the letter 'da' to 'ta', the formation of the word 'Tathāgata' should be understood.

How is he 'Tathāgata' because of acting truly? The Blessed One's speech conforms to his bodily actions, and his bodily actions conform to his speech. Therefore, as he speaks, so he acts; as he acts, so he speaks. For such a one, as his speech is, so his bodily action proceeds. And as his bodily action is, so his speech proceeds; thus he is 'Tathāgata'. Hence it was said: "Monks, as the Tathāgata speaks, so he acts; as he acts, so he speaks. Thus, because he acts as he speaks and speaks as he acts, he is called Tathāgata." Thus, he is 'Tathāgata' because of acting truly.

How is he 'Tathāgata' in the sense of overcoming? Because the Blessed One, from the highest peak of existence above to the Avīci hell below, and across the boundless world systems, overcomes all beings by virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. There is no measure or comparison for him. Indeed, he is incomparable, immeasurable, supreme, the god beyond gods of the devas, the Sakka beyond Sakkas, the Brahmā beyond Brahmās, the most excellent of all beings. Therefore, he is 'Tathāgata'. Hence it was said—
"Monks, in the world with its devas... among humans, the Tathāgata is the overcomer, the unvanquished, the one who sees everything, the wielder of power. Therefore, he is called Tathāgata."

The word formation here is: 'Agada' (medicine) like 'agada' refers to the elegance of the teaching and the greatness of merit. For this reason, just as a powerful physician overcomes snakes with divine medicine, he overcomes all proponents of other views and the world with its devas. Thus, in overcoming the entire world, because he possesses the aforementioned true and unerring 'agada' (medicine/power), by changing 'da' to 'ta', he should be known as 'Tathāgata'. Thus, he is 'Tathāgata' in the sense of overcoming.
115:
Alternatively, he is 'Tathāgata' because he has arrived at the true nature; he is 'Tathāgata' because he knows the true nature. In this context, he is 'Tathāgata' because he has arrived at—that is, understood—the entire world through the full understanding of investigation (tīraṇapariññā). He is 'Tathāgata' because he has arrived at—that is, transcended—the origin of the world (samudaya) through the full understanding of abandoning (pahānapariññā). He is 'Tathāgata' because he has arrived at—that is, attained—the cessation of the world (nirodha) through realization. He is 'Tathāgata' because he has arrived at—that is, practiced—the path leading to the cessation of the world (magga) through true practice.

This matter was spoken by the Blessed One thus: "Monks, the world has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata is detached from the world. Monks, the origin of the world has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; the origin of the world has been abandoned by the Tathāgata. Monks, the cessation of the world has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; the cessation of the world has been realized by the Tathāgata. Monks, the path leading to the cessation of the world has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; the path leading to the cessation of the world has been developed by the Tathāgata. Monks, whatever is seen, heard, sensed, or known in the world with its devas... all that has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata. Therefore, he is called Tathāgata."

The Blessed One is also called 'Tathāgata' for eight other reasons: because he arrived through true resolution; because he practiced through true great compassion; because he arrived at the true Noble Path-knowledges; because he arrived at the true practice; because he is distinguished in such a manner; because he has such a mode of occurrence; because he arose through true knowledges; and because of the state of having arrived in a true manner.

How is he 'Tathāgata' because he arrived through true resolution? The Blessed One, when he was the hermit Sumedha, at the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara:
"Humanity, the perfection of the male sex, the possession of sufficient cause, the sight of the Teacher,
The state of a monk, the possession of virtues, extreme dedication, and strong desire—
When these eight things are combined, the aspiration for Buddhahood succeeds."
Thus fulfilling the aspiration (abhinihāra) endowed with eight factors as spoken, he made the great resolution and vow: "Having crossed over myself, I will cross over the world of devas and humans; having been liberated, I will liberate others; having been tamed, I will tame others; having attained relief, I will provide relief; having attained peace, I will bring peace; having become pure, I will purify others; having known, I will make others know."
116:
“I, having become pure from the defilements, shall make others pure; I, having known the Four Noble Truths, shall make others know them” — thus the Great Vow (Mahāpaṭiññā) was made. It is also said:

“What is the use of me crossing over alone, a man showing his strength? Having reached Omniscience, I shall ferry across the world with its devas.”

“By this extraordinary merit I have performed towards the Supreme Man (Dīpaṅkara Buddha), having reached Omniscience, I shall rescue many people.”

“Having cut the stream of Saṃsāra, having destroyed the three realms of existence, having boarded the ship of the Dhamma, I shall ferry across the world with its devas.”

“What is the use of me realizing the Dhamma here in an unknown form (as an Arahant)? Having reached Omniscience, I shall truly become a Buddha in the world with its devas.” (Bv. 55-58).

That true Great Vow is the cause for the selection, reflection, and undertaking of all the qualities that make a Buddha (Buddhakara-dhamma). The Lord of the World, without failing that vow, fulfilled the thirty perfections such as the Perfection of Giving (Dāna-pāramī) respectfully, continuously, and without remainder for four asankheyyas and a hundred thousand aeons. He made the five great sacrifices such as the sacrifice of limbs, developed the four resolutions such as the Resolution of Truth (Saccādhiṭṭhāna), and accumulated the requisites of merit and knowledge (puñña-ñāṇa-sambhāra). Elevating his previous efforts, previous conduct, preaching of the Dhamma, and conduct for the benefit of relatives, he brought the conduct of wisdom (buddhi-cariyā) to its peak and realized the unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi). Therefore, for that Blessed One alone, that Great Vow is true, not false, and not otherwise. Not even a hair's breadth of that Blessed One's vow is false. Because it is true, these twenty-four Buddhas, from Dīpaṅkara, Koṇḍañña, Maṅgala, and so on, up to Kassapa the Blessed One, appearing in succession, gave the prophecy to that Bodhisatta: “He will become a Buddha.” Thus, having received the prophecy in the presence of twenty-four Buddhas and having obtained the benefits to be obtained by Bodhisattas who have made their resolution (abhinīhāra), he came. Because he reached and attained Buddhahood according to that aforementioned true Great Vow, he is called “Tathāgata.” Thus, he is “Tathāgata” because he came (āgata) according to the truth (tathā).

How is he “Tathāgata” because he has gone (gata) according to the truth? The Lord of the World has Great Compassion (Mahākaruṇā). Seeing the multitude of beings beset by the great mass of suffering through that compassion—
117:
“There is no other refuge for this multitude of beings but me; I myself, being liberated from this suffering of Saṃsāra, shall liberate those beings.” With a mind thus well-exerted, he made the Great Resolution (Mahābhinihāra). Having made it, and striving for the welfare of the entire world in accordance with his aspiration, he practiced the extremely difficult austerities (dukkara-cariyā), which cause terror even to those who merely hear of them, without regard for his own body or life. Just as the practice of Great Bodhisattas does not belong to the side of decline, defilement, or mere stability, but rather belongs only to the side of further distinction, so practicing in that way, he gradually fulfilled the requisites of enlightenment (bodhi-sambhāra) without remainder and reached Omniscience, which penetrates the Four Noble Truths.

Even after becoming a Buddha, with a heart constantly urged by that Great Compassion, he renounced the delight in seclusion and the supreme, peaceful bliss of liberation (vimokkha-sukha). Disregarding the various perversions such as honor or contempt shown by the foolish people in the world, he completed the Buddha's duties (Buddha-kicca) without remainder by disciplining beings to be trained (veneyya). In this context, the manner of the Blessed One's intense entry into Great Compassion for beings will be made clear later. Just as the Lord of the World, having become a Buddha, has Great Compassion for beings, so he had it at the time of the Great Resolution as a Bodhisatta. Thus, because of the similarity in all places and at all times, that compassion is truly true, not false, and not otherwise. Therefore, because he went (gata) or practiced for the welfare of the entire world through that true Great Compassion, which has the same flavor towards all beings in those three stages, he is called “Tathāgata.” Thus, he is “Tathāgata” because he has gone (gata) according to the truth (tathā).

How is he “Tathāgata” because he has come (āgata) to the true (tathā) things? The true things (tathā) are the four types of Knowledge of the Noble Path (ariya-magga-ñāṇa). These Path-knowledges encompass all that should be known as “This is suffering, this is the origin of suffering, this is the cessation of suffering, this is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.” They are the causes of both the occurrence and the cessation [of suffering]. They are true, not false, and not otherwise, because they do not fail in the individual essence and characteristic of things, occurring in an unerring manner, known as the penetration without delusion into the Four Noble Truths—namely, the meanings of suffering such as oppression, being conditioned, burning, and change; the meanings of origin such as accumulation, source, bondage, and hindrance; the meanings of cessation such as escape, seclusion, being unconditioned, and deathlessness; the meanings of the path such as leading out, cause, seeing, and dominance; and the divisions of those truths—obtained by the total cutting off of the defiled side which obstructs the realization of the true nature of things.
118:
The Blessed One reached and attained these true dhammas by himself, without being led by others. Therefore, because he has come to the truth (tathāni āgato), he is called 'Tathāgata'.

Just as the path-knowledges (magga-ñāṇa) are clearly explained, so too should the Blessed One's unobstructed knowledges in the three periods of time, the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), the four intrepidities (vesārajja), the knowledges defining the five destinations (gati), the six uncommon knowledges (asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa), the knowledges clarifying the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), the knowledges clarifying the eight path factors (maggaṅga), the nine knowledges of the successive meditative attainments (anupubbavihārasamāpatti), and the ten powers (dasabala) be clearly explained.

Among those knowledges, this is the explanation: In the countless world systems (loka-dhātu), regarding the countless beings divided by various grades such as inferior and so on, one should know the past aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu), along with their specific states such as nature and function, and their names and clans associated with the aggregates. Also, regarding material phenomena (rūpa-dhamma) that are inanimate (anindriyabaddha), extremely subtle, hidden, or in distant regions, there exist specific qualities such as color, shape, smell, taste, and touch of those produced by conditions, along with their respective specific causes. In all these matters, the Blessed One's knowledge proceeds as an immediate perception, without attachment or obstruction, like an emblic myrobalan (āmalaka) placed on the palm of the hand. It is the same regarding the future and the present. These are called the unobstructed knowledges in the three periods of time. Accordingly, it is said: "The Buddha, the Blessed One, has unobstructed knowledge of the past; the Buddha, the Blessed One, has unobstructed knowledge of the future; the Buddha, the Blessed One, has unobstructed knowledge of the present."

Furthermore, these knowledges are true (tathāni) because they do not deviate from the nature, essence (rasa), and characteristics of the dhammas in those respective instances; they are not false, nor are they otherwise. The Blessed One attained these knowledges through his self-evolved knowledge (sayambhū-ñāṇa). Thus, because he has come to the truth, he is called 'Tathāgata'.

Likewise, there are four analytical insights: the analytical insight of meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā), the analytical insight of dhamma (dhamma-paṭisambhidā), the analytical insight of language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā), and the analytical insight of perspicuity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā). Among these four, the knowledge that reaches the distinctions in meaning, which is capable of performing the noting, clarifying, and defining of the distinctions of meaning, is called attha-paṭisambhidā. The knowledge that reaches the distinctions in dhamma, which is capable of performing the noting, clarifying, and defining of the distinctions of dhamma, is called dhamma-paṭisambhidā. The knowledge that reaches the distinctions in linguistic expression, which is capable of performing the noting, clarifying, and defining of the distinctions of linguistic expression, is called nirutti-paṭisambhidā.
119:
The knowledge that reaches the distinctions in perspicuity, which is capable of performing the noting, clarifying, and defining of the distinctions of perspicuity, is called paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā. For it is said: "Knowledge of the meaning is attha-paṭisambhidā; knowledge of the dhamma is dhamma-paṭisambhidā; knowledge of the linguistic expression (nirutti-abhilāpa) of those dhammas is nirutti-paṭisambhidā; knowledge of the knowledges is paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā" (in the Vibhaṅga).

In this context, briefly, the result of a cause is called 'attha' (meaning/result) because it is to be known and reached by following the cause. In detail, however, these five things are called 'attha': whatever is produced by conditions (paccayuppanna), Nibbāna, the meaning of what is spoken, resultant consciousness (vipāka), and functional consciousness (kiriya). For one who contemplates that attha, the knowledge that reaches the distinctions in that attha is called attha-paṭisambhidā. 'Dhamma', briefly, is the cause. That cause is called 'dhamma' because it ordains, produces, and brings about various results. In detail, however, these five things are called 'dhamma': any cause that produces a result, the Noble Path (ariya-magga), the spoken text (pāḷi), the wholesome (kusala), and the unwholesome (akusala). For one who contemplates that dhamma, the knowledge that reaches the distinctions in that dhamma is called dhamma-paṭisambhidā.

It is also said: "Knowledge of suffering (dukkha) is attha-paṭisambhidā; knowledge of the origin of suffering (samudaya) is dhamma-paṭisambhidā; knowledge of the cessation of suffering (nirodha) is attha-paṭisambhidā; knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering (paṭipadā) is dhamma-paṭisambhidā."

Alternatively, knowledge of the cause is dhamma-paṭisambhidā; knowledge of the result of the cause is attha-paṭisambhidā. Knowledge of those dhammas that are born, become, well-born, produced, newly produced, and manifested is attha-paṭisambhidā. Knowledge of those dhammas because of which those [results] are born, become, well-born, produced, newly produced, and manifested is dhamma-paṭisambhidā. Knowledge of aging and death (jarā-maraṇa) is attha-paṭisambhidā; knowledge of the origin of aging and death is dhamma-paṭisambhidā. Knowledge of the cessation of aging and death is attha-paṭisambhidā; knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of aging and death is dhamma-paṭisambhidā. Knowledge of birth (jāti), existence (bhava), clinging (upādāna), craving (taṇhā), feeling (vedanā), contact (phassa), the six sense bases (saḷāyatana), mentality-materiality (nāmarūpa), consciousness (viññāṇa), and volitional formations (saṅkhāra) is attha-paṭisambhidā; knowledge of the origin of volitional formations is dhamma-paṭisambhidā. Knowledge of the cessation of volitional formations is attha-paṭisambhidā; knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of volitional formations is dhamma-paṭisambhidā.
120:
In this Dispensation, a monk knows the Dhamma—the Sutta, Geyya ... Vedalla. This monk is said to have attained the Dhamma-paṭisambhidā (Analytical Knowledge of the Dhamma). That monk knows the meaning of each of those spoken texts: 'This is the meaning of this statement; this is the meaning of that statement.' This monk is said to have attained the Attha-paṭisambhidā (Analytical Knowledge of Meaning).

Which states are wholesome? At a time when a wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere has arisen, accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge, having a form as object ... or a mental phenomenon as object, or whatever object it may be; at that time there is contact ... there is non-distraction (avikkhepa). These states are wholesome. Knowledge regarding these states is called Dhamma-paṭisambhidā. Knowledge regarding the result (vipāka) of those states is called Attha-paṭisambhidā. Thus, the detail should be understood in this manner.

There is the expression of the nature, the unerring usage, and the speech regarding that result (attha) and that cause (dhamma). In that speech known as Sabhāva-nirutti, the knowledge that distinguishes—using the Māgadha language, which is the root language of all beings—saying 'This is the natural expression, this is not the natural expression,' is called Nirutti-paṭisambhidā (Analytical Knowledge of Language). For one who contemplates by making an object of all the aforementioned knowledges as they occur in detail by way of object, function, etc., the knowledge that distinguishes within that knowledge is called Paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā (Analytical Knowledge of Perspicuity). Thus, these four analytical knowledges were attained by the Blessed One himself. Because they occur in an unerring and non-perverted manner within their respective domains of meaning, cause, etc., they are 'thus' (tatha), not false, and not otherwise. In this way also, the Blessed One is the Tathāgata because he has come to (āgata) these 'thus' (tatha) truths.

Likewise, whatever is to be known, all that has been known, seen, attained, and fully awakened to by the Blessed One in every aspect. For indeed, the things to be known with higher knowledge (abhiññeyya) have been known by him as things to be known with higher knowledge. The things to be fully understood (pariññeyya) have been known by him as things to be fully understood. The things to be abandoned (pahātabba) have been known by him as things to be abandoned. The things to be realized (sacchikātabba) have been known by him as things to be realized. The things to be developed (bhāvetabba) have been known by him as things to be developed. Therefore, there is no ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, or Brahmā who is able to justly challenge the Blessed One, saying, 'These things have not been fully awakened to by you.'

Whatever is to be abandoned, all that was abandoned by the Blessed One without remainder at the foot of the Bodhi tree, made into a state that will not arise again. There is no further task to be done for the abandoning of what has been abandoned.
121:
Indeed, he possesses the knowledges of self-confidence (vesārajja-ñāṇa). For the Blessed One has abandoned, cut off, and uprooted the 1,500 defilements along with their residual tendencies (vāsanā), including greed, hatred, delusion, perverted attention, lack of shame (ahirika), lack of moral dread (anottappa), sloth and torpor (thina-middha), anger, enmity, contempt, domineering, envy, avarice, deceit, fraud, obstinacy, impetuosity, conceit, arrogance, intoxication, negligence, the three unwholesome roots, misconduct, uneven perception, stains, thought (vitakka), proliferation (papañca), seeking, craving, the four perversions (vipariyāsa), taints (āsava), ties (gantha), floods (ogha), yokes (yoga), wrong paths (agati), clinging to craving, the five delights (abhinandana), hindrances (nīvaraṇa), mental barrenness (cetokhila), mental shackles, the six roots of dispute, the seven underlying tendencies (anusaya), the eight wrongnesses (micchatta), the nine grounds for resentment, those rooted in craving, the ten unwholesome courses of action, the twenty-one wrong ways of seeking, the sixty-two views, and the one hundred and eight varieties of craving. Therefore, there is no one—ascetic, Brahmā, or anyone else—who can justly challenge the Blessed One, saying, 'These defilements have not been abandoned by you.'

The Blessed One has taught those obstructive states (antarāyika-dhamma) consisting of kamma, result, defilements, disparaging the Noble Ones, and transgressing the rules. These states are indeed sufficient to cause an obstacle. Therefore, there is no one... who can justly challenge the Blessed One, saying, 'Those things taught by you do not constitute an obstacle for one who indulges in them.'

The Blessed One has taught the unsurpassed Dhamma that leads out of suffering (niyyāna-dhamma), which is comprised of virtue, concentration, and wisdom, categorized into seven groups and thirty-seven factors, preceded by the Noble Path, for the purpose of escaping the suffering of the round (vaṭṭa-dukkha) without remainder. This Dhamma indeed leads one who practices it out of the suffering of the round. Therefore, there is no one... who can justly challenge the Blessed One, saying, 'The Dhamma leading out of suffering taught by you does not lead out [of suffering].' Thus, it is taught in detail: 'To you who claim to be a Perfectly Enlightened One, these things are not fully awakened to,' and so on. In this way, these four knowledges of self-confidence of the Blessed One, which occur in an unerring manner because they make known the non-falsity of his own excellence in knowledge, abandonment, and teaching, are 'thus' (tatha), not false, and not otherwise. Because he has reached these four 'thus' knowledges of self-confidence, the Blessed One is called Tathāgata.

There are five destinations (gati): the hell realm (niraya-gati), the animal realm, the peta realm, the human realm, and the deva realm. Among these five destinations, the eight great hells such as Sañjīva, the sixteen prominent hells (ussada-niraya) such as Kukkula, and the Lokantarika hell are called Niraya because they are purely of the nature of suffering and have no pleasantness (nirassāda). They are also called Gati because they are destinations to be reached by one's own kamma.
122:
It is the destination of hell (nirayagati). Even the hells of intense darkness and cold are included within this nirayagati. Worms, maggots, insects, snakes, scorpions, lice, birds, dogs, jackals, and so forth are called animals (tiracchāna) because of their horizontal movement. These very beings are the destination; thus, it is the animal destination (tiracchānagati). Those such as the hungry ghosts (petas) afflicted by hunger and thirst, those who subsist on what is given by others, and those who are constantly burning, are called petas because they are far removed from manifest happiness due to the abundance of suffering. These very beings are the destination; thus, it is the peta destination (petagati). Asuras such as the Kālakañjikas are also included within this peta destination. Those dwelling in the four great islands such as Jambudīpa, along with those dwelling in the small islands, are called humans (manussa) because of the loftiness (or intensity) of their minds. These very beings are the destination; thus, it is the human destination (manussagati). These twenty-six groups of deities, from the Cātumahārājika realm up to the realm of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception, are called gods (deva) because they sport and shine with their own psychic power and majesty. These very beings are the destination; thus, it is the deva destination (devagati).

Since these destinations are specific distinctions of the rebirth-process (upapatti-bhava) produced by various kammas, in the ultimate sense, they are merely resultant mental aggregates (vipāka-nāma-khandha) and kamma-born matter (kaṭattā-rūpa). Regarding these destinations, the Buddha's knowledge arises by way of discerning the specific cause and effect, such as: 'This particular destination arises because of this particular kamma; due to the specific conditions of that kamma, these groups of beings are thus divided and distinguished.' Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Sāriputta, there are these five destinations. Which five? Hell, the animal realm, the peta realm, humans, and gods. Sāriputta, I know hell, and the path leading to hell, and the practice leading to hell; and I also know how one who has practiced accordingly, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in the plane of misery, the bad destination, the lower world, in hell,' and so forth.

Because these knowledges of the Blessed One occur in their respective objects in an unerring manner, they are true (tatha), not false, and not otherwise. Because he has arrived at (āgata) such truths (tatha), the Blessed One is called the Tathāgata.

Likewise, the Blessed One’s knowledge of the higher and lower faculties (indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa) is that which arises through wisdom, manifesting distinctions such as those with little dust in their eyes and those with much dust, by understanding the presence or absence of faith and so forth in beings. For it has been said: 'A person with faith has little dust; a person without faith has much dust,' and so forth in detail.
123:
'This person has little dust in their eyes; this person has eternalist views; this person has annihilationist views; this person is established in conforming patience (anulomika-khanti); this person is established in knowledge according to reality; this person has an inclination for sensuality, not for renunciation; this person has an inclination for renunciation, not for sensuality,' and so forth. Also, 'In this person, sensual lust has reached extreme strength, but not aversion; in this person, aversion has reached extreme strength, but not sensual lust,' and so forth. Also, 'In this person, meritorious formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra) are predominant, not demeritorious or imperturbable formations; in this person, demeritorious formations are predominant, not meritorious or imperturbable formations; in this person, imperturbable formations (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra) are predominant, not meritorious or demeritorious formations. In this person, bodily good conduct is predominant; in this person, verbal good conduct is predominant; in this person, mental good conduct is predominant. This person has low inclinations; this person has noble inclinations; this person is possessed of the obstruction of kamma; this person is possessed of the obstruction of defilement; this person is possessed of the obstruction of result; this person is not possessed of the obstruction of kamma, nor of defilement, nor of result.' Thus, the Blessed One’s knowledge of the inclinations and underlying tendencies (āsayānusaya-ñāṇa) occurs in a manner that manifests the inclinations and so forth of beings according to reality. With reference to this knowledge, it was said: 'Here, the Tathāgata knows the inclinations of beings, knows their underlying tendencies, knows their temperaments, knows their dispositions, and knows which beings are capable or incapable of liberation,' and so forth.

Furthermore, there is the Blessed One’s knowledge of the Twin Miracle (yamaka-pāṭihāriya-ñāṇa), which produces various psychic transformations not shared by others, such as the issuing of a mass of fire and a stream of water from the upper body, the lower body, the front, and the back; from the right and left eyes, ears, nostrils, shoulders, sides, hands, and feet; from the fingers and the intervals between the fingers; and from the hairs and the pores of the skin. With reference to this knowledge, it was said: 'Here, the Tathāgata performs the Twin Miracle, which is not shared with the disciples. From the upper body, a mass of fire issues; from the lower body, a stream of water issues. From the lower body, a mass of fire issues; from the upper body, a stream of water issues,' and so forth.
124:
The knowledge that is the cause for the Blessed One’s entry into Great Compassion, which arises through various methods out of the desire to lead out the multitude of beings oppressed by many painful states such as lust and birth, is called the Knowledge of the Attainment of Great Compassion (mahākaruṇāsamāpattiñāṇa). As it is said: “What is the Tathāgata’s Knowledge of the Attainment of Great Compassion? Great compassion descends upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, as they behold beings in many ways. Great compassion descends upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, as they behold that ‘the world is ablaze’...” and so on, it is analyzed and taught in eighty-nine ways.

Furthermore, the Blessed One’s knowledge which is capable of realizing all things—the entire dhammadhātu, all that is to be known, the conditioned and the unconditioned—in all their aspects without the instruction of others, which functions in connection with whatever is desired, and which is not shared by others, is called Omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa) because it penetrates and realizes the conditioned, the unconditioned, and conventional truths in their entirety. Because it proceeds without attachment and without obstruction in that realization, it is also called Unobstructed Knowledge (anāvaraṇañāṇa). This is a brief summary here; the details will be made clear later. Thus, these six uncommon knowledges (asādhāraṇañāṇa) of the Blessed One are true (tatha), unerring (avitatha), and not otherwise (ananyathā), because they proceed in an undistorted manner and do not fail in their respective domains. In this way too, the Blessed One is the Tathāgata because he has arrived at these true knowledges.

Likewise: “Monks, there are these seven factors of enlightenment: the mindfulness factor of enlightenment, the investigation-of-states factor of enlightenment, the energy factor of enlightenment, the rapture factor of enlightenment, the tranquility factor of enlightenment, the concentration factor of enlightenment, and the equanimity factor of enlightenment.” Thus, in terms of their individual nature, there is a collection of states beginning with mindfulness which arises at the moment of the supramundane path and acts as the opposite of many afflictions such as sluggishness, restlessness, stagnation, exertion, devotion to sensual pleasures, devotion to self-mortification, and the views of annihilationism and eternalism. By this collection of states, the noble disciple awakens (bujjhati), rises from the sleep of defilements, or penetrates the Four Truths, or realizes Nibbāna itself; therefore, that collection of states is called “Enlightenment” (bodhi). Because they are the factors of that enlightenment, they are called “Factors of Enlightenment” (bojjhaṅga). Or, because the noble disciple awakens by means of the aforementioned collection of states, he is called “Enlightenment” (bodhi). Because they are the factors of that enlightenment, they are called “Factors of Enlightenment” (bojjhaṅga). In this way...
125:
In terms of general characteristics (sāmaññalakkhaṇa) and specific characteristics (visesalakkhaṇa): the mindfulness factor of enlightenment has the characteristic of establishing [co-nascent states]; the investigation-of-states factor of enlightenment has the characteristic of investigating states; the energy factor of enlightenment has the characteristic of uplifting [co-nascent states]; the rapture factor of enlightenment has the characteristic of pervading the body with sublime materialities; the tranquility factor of enlightenment has the characteristic of calming the body and mind; the concentration factor of enlightenment has the characteristic of non-distraction; and the equanimity factor of enlightenment has the characteristic of neutrality toward associated states. Thus is it by way of specific characteristics.

“Therein, what is the mindfulness factor of enlightenment? Here, a monk is mindful, possessed of the highest mindfulness and prudence; he is one who remembers and recollects what was done and said long ago,” and so on. This shows their simultaneous occurrence at a single moment by way of mutual assistance among the seven factors of enlightenment. “Therein, what is the mindfulness factor of enlightenment? There is mindfulness regarding internal states, there is mindfulness regarding external states,” and so on. This shows the occurrence of their objective manifestation. “Monks, here a monk develops the mindfulness factor of enlightenment which is dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, and results in relinquishment,” and so on. This shows the method of development (bhāvanā). “Therein, what are the seven factors of enlightenment? Here, at the time a monk develops supramundane jhāna... at that time there are the seven factors of enlightenment: the mindfulness factor of enlightenment... the equanimity factor of enlightenment. Therein, what is the mindfulness factor of enlightenment? That which is mindfulness, recollection,” and so on. In this way, the Blessed One’s knowledges that clarify the factors of enlightenment, which proceed in various ways through ninety-six thousand methods, are true, unerring, and not otherwise, because they do not fail in their respective meanings. In this way too, because he has realized true things, the Blessed One is called Tathāgata.

Likewise: “In that context, what is the Noble Truth of the Way Leading to the Cessation of Suffering? It is this Noble Eightfold Path, namely: Right View... Right Concentration.” Thus is it by way of its individual nature. It is called “Noble” (ariya) because it is far from all defilements, because it makes one a noble one, and because it causes the attainment of the noble fruit. It is called “Eightfold” (aṭṭhaṅgika) because it has eight factors and because it is the certain cause for the attainment of Nibbāna. It is called “Path” (magga) because it goes along killing the defilements, because it is sought by those who desire the goal, or because it seeks Nibbāna itself. Thus is it by way of general characteristics.

Right View has the characteristic of seeing rightly; Right Intention has the characteristic of directing co-nascent states toward the object; Right Speech has the characteristic of rightly embracing [co-nascent states]; Right Action has the characteristic of rightly originating [co-nascent states]; Right Livelihood has the characteristic of rightly purifying [co-nascent states]; Right Effort has the characteristic of rightly uplifting [co-nascent states]; Right Mindfulness has the characteristic of rightly establishing [co-nascent states]; and Right Concentration has the characteristic of rightly non-distracting. Thus is it by way of specific characteristics.

Right View abandons other defilements along with its opposite, Wrong View; it takes Nibbāna as its object; and by destroying the delusion that covers that object, it sees the associated states without confusion. Likewise, Right Intention and the others also abandon Wrong Intention and so on; they take the Truth of Cessation as their object; and they also perform the functions of directing, embracing, originating, purifying, uplifting, establishing, and non-distracting of the co-nascent states. Thus, by way of various functions...
126:
Right mindfulness has the characteristic of establishing well; right concentration has the characteristic of non-distraction. Thus, it should be understood by way of specific characteristics. First, Right View abandons wrong view along with its opposing defilements; it takes Nibbāna as its object; by destroying the delusion that covers it, it sees the associated states without confusion. Likewise, Right Intention and the others abandon wrong intention and so forth, take the truth of cessation as their object, and perform the functions of applying, grasping, originating, purifying, supporting, establishing, and steadying the conascent states. Thus, it should be understood by way of the analysis of functions.

In the preliminary stage, Right View occurs at various moments and has distinct objects such as suffering; however, at the moment of the Path, it occurs in a single moment, taking only Nibbāna as its object, and by way of function, it receives four names such as 'knowledge regarding suffering.' Right Intention and the others also have various moments and various objects in the preliminary stage, but at the moment of the Path, they have a single moment and a single object. Among those path factors, Right Intention receives three names by way of function, such as 'intention of renunciation.' The three factors beginning with Right Speech are both abstinences and volitions in the preliminary stage according to the analysis such as 'abstaining from false speech,' but at the moment of the Path, they are only abstinences. Right Effort and Right Mindfulness receive four names each by way of the functions of the Right Strivings and the Foundations of Mindfulness. Right Concentration, however, even at the moment of the Path, is diverse by way of the first jhana and so forth. Thus, it should be understood by way of the analysis of occurrence in the preliminary and subsequent stages.

By way of the method of cultivation, such as 'Here, monks, a monk develops Right View based on seclusion,' and by way of the analysis of the eighty-four thousand methods, such as 'Among those, what is the Eightfold Path? Here, monks, at the time when one develops supramundane jhana... when there is the painful practice and slow intuition, at that time the Eightfold Path exists—Right View, Right Intention,' all the Blessed One's knowledges that explain the Noble Path, which have arisen in many ways, are true, unfailing, and not otherwise, because their meaning is unerring. In this way, the Blessed One is the Tathāgata because He has arrived at these truths.

Likewise, the Blessed One's knowledges regarding the successive attainments from the attainment of the first jhana to the attainment of cessation—in the sense of being dwelt in and attained in sequence, by way of accomplishment and reviewing, and by way of appropriate association—are true, unfailing, and not otherwise, because of the realization of those benefits. In this way, the Blessed One is the Tathāgata because He has arrived at these truths. Likewise, 'This is for this person...'
127:
Knowing without distortion that 'this is the cause, this is not the cause' regarding the cause and non-cause of various results; knowing according to reality and without remainder the specific results of the undertaking of kamma of various beings, distinguished by the past and so forth; knowing according to reality the distinction between kamma with taints and kamma without taints even at the moment of exertion for various beings, such as 'this is the practice leading to hell... this is the practice leading to Nibbāna'; knowing the diversity of elements according to reality in the manner of 'because this element is predominant, this distinction arises in this continuity of phenomena,' as well as the various and diverse natures of the aggregates and sense bases, such as clung-to and not-clung-to; knowing the sharpness and dullness of the faculties such as faith; knowing the jhānas, liberations, and so forth, along with their defilements; knowing without remainder the continuity of aggregates lived in the past throughout the immeasurable births of beings, along with their connections to those births; knowing the passing away and rebirth along with distinctions such as inferior and so forth; and knowing the Four Noble Truths in the manner previously stated, such as 'this is suffering'—these Ten Powers of the Blessed One are true (tatha), unerring (avitatha), and not otherwise (anaññatha), because they penetrate their respective objects without fail, accomplish the desired meaning, and exist according to reality.

It has also been said: 'Here, the Tathāgata understands according to reality the cause as cause and the non-cause as non-cause,' and so forth.

Thus, because he has arrived at (āgata) these true (tatha) things, the Blessed One is called 'Tathāgata'.

Just as by the power of those knowledges, so too by the power of the special wisdoms that are not shared with others and have infinite and immeasurable divisions, such as the knowledge explaining the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), right efforts (sammappadhāna), and so forth, the Blessed One has arrived at (āgata) and attained those true knowledges; thus he is called 'Tathāgata'. In this way also, because he has arrived at true things, he is called 'Tathāgata'.

In what way is he called 'Tathāgata' because he has gone to (gata) or attained a true goal? There are the Blessed One's birth (abhijāti), his enlightenment through the penetration of the Four Noble Truths (abhisambodhi), his proclamation of the Dhamma and Vinaya (dhamma-vinaya-paññapana), and his Parinibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without remainder of the results of kamma. These things are true (tatha). What is meant by this? These goals were first aspired to and set in motion by the Lord of the World (Lokanātha). Because of the certain accomplishment of those goals, because they are unerring, and because they exist in a sense that is not distorted, they are true, unerring, and not otherwise.

To elaborate further—this Blessed One, while being a Bodhisatta, fulfilled the causes for all-knowing Buddhahood in the manner stated, such as the fulfillment of the thirty perfections. While residing in the Tusita heaven, having heard the 'Buddha-uproar' (Buddha-kolāhala) announcing 'A Buddha will arise,' the devas dwelling in the ten thousand world-systems gathered together, approached him, and requested: 'O Great Hero, the time has come for you; take conception in your mother's womb. Cross the world of devas and humans over the flood of saṃsāra; realize the deathless Nibbāna.' Having been thus requested, and with the preceding omens having appeared, he made the five great observations and decided, 'Now is the time for me to be born in the human world and become a Buddha.' On the full moon day of Āsāḷha, he took conception in the womb of Queen Mahāmāyā in the Sakyan clan. For ten months, he was attended to by devas and humans with great protection, and on the full moon day of Visākha, he arrived at birth in the Lumbinī Sal grove.

Furthermore, at the moment of the Bodhisatta's birth, just as at the moment of his conception, the thirty-two great omens became manifest. This ten thousand world-element shook from top to bottom; it shook like a water-wheel and like a potter's wheel. Immeasurable radiance became manifest throughout the ten thousand world-systems.
128:
Having fulfilled the perfections and residing in the Tusita heaven, upon hearing the "Buddha-uproar" (Buddha-kolāhala), the deities and Brahmas from ten thousand world-systems assembled and approached him, requesting:

"O Great Hero, the time has come for you. Please take conception in a mother's womb. Saving the world including the devas, may you realize the Deathless state (Amata)."

Being thus requested, the Bodhisatta, seeing the omens that had arisen, made the Five Great Observations (Mahāvilokana) and thought, "Now I shall be born in the human world and attain Enlightenment." On the full moon day of Āsāḷha, he took conception in the womb of Queen Mahāmāyā of the Sakyan royal clan. For ten months, he was protected with great care by devas and humans, and at the time of dawn on the full moon day of Visākha, he was born.

At the moment of his birth, just as at the moment of his conception, the thirty-two omens appeared. This ten-thousandfold world-system shook violently. An immeasurable light spread throughout the ten thousand world-systems. As if wishing to see the glory of the Bodhisatta, the blind regained their sight. The deaf heard sounds. The mute were able to speak. The hunchbacked became straight-bodied. The lame regained the ability to walk. All beings in bondage were freed from shackles and other restraints. In all the hells, the fires were extinguished. In the realm of hungry ghosts (peta-visaya), hunger and thirst were appeased. There was no fear for animals. The diseases of all beings were cured. All beings spoke pleasant words. Horses neighed with sweet sounds. Elephants trumpeted. All musical instruments produced their own sounds spontaneously. The ornaments of humans, such as bracelets, produced sweet sounds without being struck. All directions became clear. A gentle, cool breeze blew, bringing happiness to beings. An unseasonable great rain fell. Water gushed out from the earth and flowed. Birds gave up flying in the sky. Rivers stood still without flowing. The water in the great ocean became sweet. While the sun, free from defilements, was shining brightly, all the stars in the sky also shone. Excluding the formless (arūpāvacara) Brahmas, all other devas, Brahmas, and all hell-beings became visible to one another. Trees, walls, doors, and rocky mountains became unobstructed and open. There was no passing away or rebirth of beings. Overpowering all unpleasant odors, divine fragrances wafted. All fruit-bearing trees became laden with fruit. The great ocean was everywhere covered with five-colored lotuses.
129:
All kinds of flowers, both land-based and water-based, bloomed. On the trunks of trees, trunk-lotuses bloomed; on the branches, branch-lotuses; and on the vines, vine-lotuses bloomed. Breaking through the surface of the earth and rock, stalk-lotuses (daṇḍapaduma) emerged, appearing in seven successive layers. Hanging lotuses appeared in the sky. A rain of flowers fell all around. Celestial musical instruments played in the sky. The entire ten-thousandfold world-system became like a mass of flowers released in a ball, like a bouquet of flowers being turned, or like a decorated seat of flowers. It became a single mass of flowers, like a spreading yak-tail fan, perfumed with the scent of flowers, incense, and fragrances, reaching the pinnacle of supreme beauty. These omens were the signs for the attainment of many special qualities to be achieved later. This birth, characterized by many such wonders, was for the sake of that Supreme Enlightenment (Abhisambodhi) desired by the Bodhisatta. Because of the certain accomplishment of that Supreme Enlightenment, it happened exactly so—true, unerring, and not otherwise.

Furthermore, there were those to be guided (veneyya) among his relatives who were fit for the Buddha's instruction; all of them, without exception, were personally disciplined by the Blessed One. There were also those to be guided by the disciples (sāvaka-veneyya) and those to be guided by the Dhamma (dhamma-veneyya); they were disciplined by the disciples and others, and they have reached or will reach discipline (vinaya). For the sake of this benefit, the Blessed One aspired to Supreme Enlightenment. Because of the certain accomplishment of that benefit, the Supreme Enlightenment is true, unerring, and not otherwise.

In another way, whatever nature of the things to be known (ñeyyadhamma) should be understood, the Blessed One has fully awakened to each of those natures without distortion and without remainder, through his own knowledge which is connected to mere reflection, like an emblic myrobalan (āmalaka) placed in the palm of the hand. In this way too, the Supreme Enlightenment is true, unerring, and not otherwise.

Furthermore, having well observed the various ways in which those various teachings should be taught, and the dispositions (āsaya), latent tendencies (anusaya), temperaments (carita), and inclinations (adhimutti) of those various beings, the Blessed One disciplined the beings to be guided and led them to the Noble Plane (ariyabhūmi). He did this without abandoning the natural law (dhammatā), without overstepping the sequence of speech which is mere conventional usage (vohāra) and the method of designation (paññatti), while making the nature of things clear, and instructing according to the fault, according to the inclination, and according to the Dhamma.
