Thus, the proclamation of the Dhamma and Vinaya is also true, unerring, and not otherwise, because it accomplishes that benefit of the Blessed One and because it is a statement of what is real.
130:
Furthermore, the Blessed One has attained the element of the Great Deathless Nibbāna (amata-mahā-nibbāna-dhātu), which is free from the nature of materiality and mentality such as contact and feeling beginning with earth; which transcends the nature of the world, whether in the state of disintegration or otherwise; which is not to be illuminated by any light because it is free from association with darkness; which is devoid of destinations (gati) and so forth precisely because of the absence of worldly nature; which is unestablished and objectless. It is also called 'Anupādisesa' (without remainder of grasping) because of the absence of even a trace of the objects of grasping known as the aggregates (khandha) or the defilements. With reference to this state called Anupādisesa, it was said: "Monks, there is that sphere where there is neither earth, nor water, nor fire, nor air; where there is no sphere of infinite space, no sphere of infinite consciousness, no sphere of nothingness, no sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; where there is neither this world, nor the next world, nor both sun and moon. Monks, I say that there is no coming to that sphere, no going from it, no staying, no passing away, and no rebirth. It is unestablished, non-evolving, and objectless; this alone is the end of suffering."

That element of the Great Deathless Nibbāna, being the cessation of all aggregates of grasping, the stilling of all formations (saṅkhāra), the relinquishing of all acquisitions (upadhi), the calming of all suffering, the total uprooting of all attachments (ālaya), the cutting off of all rounds of rebirth (vaṭṭa), and having the characteristic of absolute peace—is 'True' (tathā) because its nature as described never deviates at any time; it is unerring and not otherwise. Thus, because he has truly approached (upagata), understood (adhigata), practiced (paṭipanna), and reached (patta) the states beginning with his birth, he is called 'Tathāgata'. In this way, the Blessed One is 'Tathāgata' because he has gone (gata) in a true (tathā) manner.

How is he 'Tathāgata' because he is of such a nature (tathā-vidha)? Just as the previous Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas were of such a nature, so too is this Blessed One of such a nature. What is meant? Those Blessed Ones were [of such a nature] by way of the virtue of the Path, the virtue of the Fruit, and all mundane and supramundane virtue; by the concentration of the Path, the concentration of the Fruit, and all mundane and supramundane concentration; by the wisdom of the Path, the wisdom of the Fruit, and all mundane and supramundane wisdom; by the two trillion four hundred thousand crores of meditative attainments (samāpatti-vihāra) to be enjoyed daily; and briefly, by way of liberation through substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-vimutti), liberation by suppression (vikkhambhana-vimutti), liberation by eradication (samuccheda-vimutti), liberation by tranquilization (paṭippassaddhi-vimutti), and liberation by escape (nissaraṇa-vimutti); and in detail, by all the qualities of omniscience (sabbaññuta-guṇa) which have infinite and immeasurable divisions and inconceivable power...
131:
Our Blessed One is also of such a nature. For all the Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas, there might be differences in these five aspects: lifespan, body size, lineage, ascetic practices, and radiance. However, there is no difference whatsoever in the purifications such as the purification of virtue (sīla-visuddhi), in the practice of serenity and insight (samatha-vipassanā), or in the qualities realized by themselves. Rather, those Blessed Buddhas are indistinguishable from one another, like gold split in the middle. Therefore, just as the previous Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas were of such a nature, so too is this Blessed One of such a nature. Being of such a nature, he is called 'Tathāgata'. Here, the word 'gata' has the meaning of 'vidha' (manner/way). For this reason, people in the world use the word 'gata' joined with 'vidha' in the sense of 'pakāra' (manner).

How is he 'Tathāgata' because his occurrence is true (tathā-pavattika)? Because he is endowed with the power of psychic potency (iddhi) that is not shared with others, because he has reached the highest perfection in the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) such as the discrimination of meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā), and because he has obtained unobstructed knowledge (anāvaraṇa-ñāṇa), there is no obstruction anywhere to the Blessed One's bodily occurrences and so forth. Thus, his occurrence (gata/gamana)—the occurrence of body, speech, and mind—proceeds according to his wish. Therefore, he is called 'Tathāgata'. In this way, because his occurrence is in that manner, he is called 'Tathāgata'.

How is he 'Tathāgata' because he has not gone (agata) by way of [wrong] truths? While fulfilling the requisites of enlightenment (bodhi-sambhāra), that which is called occurrence contrary to that [fulfillment] (gata) does not exist for this Blessed One; thus he is 'Agata' (not gone). That state of not having gone [wrongly] occurs through the true knowledges (tathā-ñāṇa) that proceed by way of reflecting on the disadvantages and advantages in relation to meanness (macchariya) and the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramī), and so forth. Therefore, because he has not gone [wrongly] due to those true knowledges, he is called 'Tathāgata'.

Alternatively, the going (gata) into the five destinations (gati), which is called the occurrence of the formations of defilements (kilesābhisaṅkhāra) or the occurrence of the aggregates (khandha), does not exist for this Blessed One; thus he is 'Agata'. This state of not going, through the attainment of Nibbāna with remainder (sa-upādisesa) and Nibbāna without remainder (an-upādisesa), occurs through the true knowledges of the Noble Path (ariya-magga-ñāṇa). In this way, because the Blessed One has not gone [into rebirth] due to the true knowledges of the Noble Path, he is called 'Tathāgata'.

How is he 'Tathāgata' by way of the state of being a Tathāgata (tathāgata-bhāva)? 'Tathāgata-bhāvena' means by the nature of a Tathāgata, because of [its] existence. If it is asked, 'What is this Tathāgata, by whose existence the Blessed One is called Tathāgata?', it is the True Dhamma (Saddhamma). For the True Dhamma, which is the Noble Path, must first be gone to (be known) by the power of serenity and insight joined together (yuganaddha-samatha-vipassanā), uprooting the entire side of defilements by way of abandonment by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna)...
132:
It is so. The Fruition-dhamma (phala-dhamma) occurs in that manner, just as it is to be reached by way of abandonment through subsiding (paṭippassaddhippahāna) in accordance with its respective Path. As for the Dhamma of Nibbāna, it leads to the cessation of all suffering in the round of rebirth (vaṭṭadukkha) just as it is penetrated by wisdom; because it is realized in that manner by the Buddhas and others, it is called 'Tathāgata'. The Dhamma of scriptural study (pariyatti-dhamma) is also called 'Tathāgata' because it was taught by our Blessed One in that manner, just as it was set forth by previous Buddhas by way of Sutta, Geyya, etc., and by way of manifesting the arising [of phenomena], in accordance with the inclinations (āsaya) and so forth of those to be tamed (veneyya). Or, it is called 'Tathāgata' because it is understood (gata) by the disciples of the Blessed One just as it was taught by the Blessed One. Thus, the entire True Dhamma (saddhamma) is called 'Tathāgata'. Therefore, Sakka, the king of devas, said: 'We worship the Tathāgata Dhamma, honored by devas and humans; may there be well-being.' Because that True Dhamma exists in the Blessed One, the Blessed One is called 'Tathāgata'.

Just like the Dhamma, the Noble Saṅgha (ariya-saṅgha) is also called 'Tathāgata' because they have reached (gata) those respective Paths in that manner (tathā), having placed at the forefront the practice of serenity and insight (samatha-vipassanā) of the preliminary stage, which is extremely pure, by those practicing for their own benefit and the benefit of others. Or, it is called 'Tathāgata' because they know in that manner and teach in that manner, just as the methods of the Truths, Dependent Origination, etc., were taught by the Blessed One. Therefore, Sakka, the king of devas, said: 'We worship the Tathāgata Saṅgha, honored by devas and humans; may there be well-being.' Because that Noble Saṅgha, who are his disciples, exists in the Blessed One, the Blessed One is called 'Tathāgata'. Thus, he is 'Tathāgata' by virtue of being the Tathāgata.

This statement is merely a brief indication of the Blessed One's nature as the Tathāgata. In every respect, however, only a Tathāgata could praise the Tathāgata-nature of a Tathāgata. This term 'Tathāgata' is of great meaning, of great scope, and of a vast range. Just like the term 'heedfulness' (appamāda), a Dhamma-teacher who adduces the Word of the Buddha from the Three Piṭakas by way of reason and meaning should not be said to have 'plunged into what is not the way'.

In this regard, it is said:
Just as the previous Great Sages (Mahesino) in the world,
The Munis, arrived here at the state of omniscience,
So too has this Sakyan Sage (Sakyamunī) arrived;
Therefore, the One with Vision (Cakkhumā) is called 'Tathāgata'.
133:
Just as the Conquerors (Jina) of old, having abandoned the stains of sensuality and so forth without remainder, arrived [at the goal] through concentration and knowledge, so too has the Sakyan Sage, the bearer of radiance, arrived. Because he has arrived like the previous Buddhas, he is known as 'Tathāgata'.

This Pre-eminent of the Sakyans (Sakyapuṅgava), the Conqueror, has arrived through self-enlightened knowledge (sayambhūñāṇa) at the true (tatha) nature of the elements, bases, and so forth, by way of the distinction between individual and general characteristics. Because he has known them thus according to the truth, the Pre-eminent of the Sakyans is called 'Tathāgata'.

The One with Universal Vision (Samantacakkhu) has clearly realized the true (tatha) Four Noble Truths and likewise specific conditionality (idappaccayatā) in every respect, through the method [of discovery] without being led by others. Because he has known them thus according to the truth, the Conqueror is called 'Tathāgata'.

In the numerous world systems (lokadhātu), among the diverse objects such as visible forms and so forth within the range of the Conqueror, his vision is only of the truth (tatha). Because he sees thus according to the truth, the All-seeing One is called 'Tathāgata'.

Because the Blessed One speaks the Dhamma only according to the truth (tatha), and he himself acts in accordance with his own words, and he dwells having overcome the world through his virtues [such as virtue and concentration], for that reason also, the Leader of the World is called 'Tathāgata'.

Having fully understood the world and the origin of the world according to the truth in every respect, he has transcended the world. He has arrived at Nibbāna through personal realization and has arrived at the Noble Eightfold Path. Because he has arrived at the true Dhamma, he is called 'Tathāgata'.

Because he has arrived at Buddhahood just as he vowed in every respect for the welfare of the world, and because he always acts for the welfare of the world with unwavering compassion, for that reason also, the Conqueror is called 'Tathāgata'.
134:
Because He has arrived at the knowledge of objects as they truly are, without deviation, according to their nature,
Therefore, He is called the Tathāgata.
Because He has arrived at the state of Abhijāti and so forth, just as the previous Buddhas did, in order to fulfill that benefit,
Therefore, He is also called the Tathāgata.

In whatever manner those former Great Sages (Mahesī) lived, such as through virtue, concentration, and so forth,
In that same manner, this Supreme Person also lives.
Because His speech occurs exactly as He intends, and because His mind is in accordance with that speech,
That Supreme Person is called the Tathāgata.

For that Blessed One who sees the end of existence, while He was fulfilling the perfections,
Because of His non-deviating knowledge of the perfections, there was no opposition to the requisites of enlightenment (bodhisambhāra), nor was there any [further] becoming in saṃsāra.
Therefore, the Blessed One, who is free from returning to existence, is called the Tathāgata.

Just as the defilements to be abandoned are abandoned by a certain kind of abandonment, by such abandonment the Great Sage’s noble Dhamma is established.
By that path, the Noble Group (the Saṅgha) also arises for the Blessed One.
Because He is endowed with such noble Dhamma and such a noble Group, the Blessed One, who is the Leader of the three worlds of beings, is called the Tathāgata.

In the phrase "Arahaṃ Sammāsambuddhaṃ," the meaning of the word "Araha" has already been explained below. He is called "Sammāsambuddha" because He has realized all dhammas rightly and by Himself. This means that whatever is to be known (ñeyya), He has personally penetrated and realized all of it in all its aspects and without deviation. By this term, it is shown that He has attained Omniscience (Sabbaññutañāṇa), also known as Unobstructed Knowledge (Anāvaraṇañāṇa), which is capable of knowing all dhammas in all their aspects without the instruction of others, and which functions according to His wish.

If it is asked, "Are not Omniscience and Unobstructed Knowledge different? If they are not different, would it not contradict the statement that the six uncommon knowledges are the Buddha's knowledges?"—it does not contradict. This is because a single knowledge is described in two ways to show its uncommon nature in relation to others, based on the different ways it functions upon its objects. Indeed, that single knowledge is called Omniscience because its objects are the conditioned (saṅkhata), the unconditioned (asaṅkhata), and conventional dhammas (sammuti) without exception; and it is called Unobstructed Knowledge because it functions without attachment, there being no obstruction regarding those objects. As stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga—
135:
“It is Omniscience because it knows all conditioned and unconditioned things without exception. It is Unobstructed Knowledge because there is no obstruction therein,” and so forth (Paṭi. M. 1.119).

Therefore, it should be definitely understood that there is no difference between these two knowledges in terms of meaning. Otherwise, if they were considered different, it would follow that Omniscience and Unobstructed Knowledge would be disconnected from each other, and they would not have all dhammas as their object. This is because there is not even a grain of obstruction in the Blessed One's knowledge. If Unobstructed Knowledge could not take all dhammas as its object, then in whatever area that knowledge did not reach, an obstruction would exist, and thus the state of being 'unobstructed' (anāvaraṇa) would itself be impossible.

Alternatively, even if Unobstructed Knowledge were distinct from Omniscience, in this context, Omniscience itself is intended by the term 'Unobstructed Knowledge' because it functions without hindrance in all things. It is only through the attainment of that Omniscience that the Blessed One is called Omniscient (Sabbaññū), All-Knower (Sabbavidū), and Fully Self-Enlightened (Sammāsambuddha); He is not called so merely because of realizing all dhammas in a single moment. Thus, it is said in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: “This designation 'Buddha' is a realization-based designation of the Blessed Buddhas, attained at the root of the Bodhi tree along with the acquisition of Omniscience; this designation culminates in the Fruit of Arahantship.” Indeed, because He attained the knowledge capable of realizing all dhammas, the ability to penetrate all dhammas without exception arose within the Blessed One's continuity.

Here, a question arises: “When this knowledge occurs, does it occur upon all objects at once, or does it occur sequentially?” Regarding this question, what should be considered? If [the knowledge] were to occur upon all objects at once, then when conditioned dhammas—divided into past, future, present, internal, external, etc.—along with unconditioned and conventional dhammas appear all together, there would be no realization of the objects through analytical distinction, like a person looking at a painting from a distance. If that were the case, it would follow that all dhammas would become objects of the Blessed One's knowledge in an indistinct form, just as all dhammas appear as 'non-self' (anattā) to those practicing insight (vipassanā) through the aspect of non-self.

Some teachers also say: “The knowledge of the Buddhas occurs at all times, free from conceptualization, having the stable characteristic (ṭhitalakkhaṇa) of all knowable dhammas as its object. Therefore, those Buddhas are called All-Knowers (Sabbavidū). For this reason, the statement 'The Great One (Nāga) is concentrated while walking, and concentrated while standing' is well-said.” However, their statement also cannot escape the faults mentioned above. This is because if the object is only the stable characteristic, then since past, future, and conventional dhammas do not possess such a stable characteristic, [it would imply the Buddha's knowledge only takes a portion as its object].
136:
The Blessed One's knowledge would [then] have only a partial range. Therefore, the statement that [his] knowledge occurs only once [for all objects] is not fitting.

If it is said that knowledge occurs sequentially for all objects, that too is not fitting. Why? Because if the objects of knowledge (ñeyya), which are infinitely diverse by way of birth, plane, nature, etc., and by way of direction, place, time, etc., are grasped sequentially, it is impossible to penetrate them without remainder because the objects of knowledge are limitless.

Some teachers say: "Because the meaning is unerring (non-contradictory), the Blessed One is omniscient by directly perceiving a portion of the objects of knowledge and then determining and resolving that the rest are also like this. And that knowledge is not inferential (anumāna) because there is no doubt; in the world, only knowledge associated with doubt is called inferential." This statement of those teachers is also not fitting. Why? Because when all meanings are not directly perceived, it is impossible to directly perceive a portion of the objects of knowledge and determine/resolve that the rest are also like this. For whatever is "the rest" is not directly perceived. If those remaining things were also directly perceived, their state of being "the rest" would no longer exist. Therefore, all this is without reason. Why? Because it is a reflection on what is not one's range (avisaya-vicāra). Indeed, the Blessed One said:
"Monks, the range of a Buddha (Buddha-visaya) is inconceivable; it should not be thought about. One who thinks about it would reap madness and frustration." (Aṅguttara Nikāya, Catukka Nipāta, Acinteyya Sutta).

The conclusion here is: Whatever the Blessed One wishes to know, whether in its entirety or a part, knowledge occurs there directly (paccakkha) because of its unobstructed functioning. There is also constant concentration (samādhi) because of the absence of distraction. Since all objects to be known are not "non-range" (avisaya), it is not that the functioning of that knowledge is not connected to his wish; indeed, it should be accepted as connected to his wish. For it was said: "All phenomena are connected to the advertence (āvajjana) of the Buddha, the Blessed One, connected to his wish, connected to his attention (manasikāra), connected to the arising of his thought." The Blessed One's knowledge of past and future objects is also purely direct (paccakkha) because it is free from grasping through inference (anumāna), tradition (āgama), or logic (takka).

An objection might be raised here: "When he wishes to know everything, then because of having all objects as the object at once, the Blessed One's knowledge would occur in an indistinct manner without specific differentiation; therefore, does it not fail to escape the aforementioned faults?" If such an objection is made, it should be answered that it should not be so objected. Why? Because that knowledge has been purified. That fault has been cleared by the scriptural text: "The range of a Buddha is inconceivable." Otherwise, if it occurred similarly to the knowledge of ordinary people, the knowledge of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, would not be inconceivable. Therefore—
137:
Even when taking all phenomena as an object, that knowledge occurs by making those phenomena well-defined, as if taking a single phenomenon as an object—this point is inconceivable (acinteyya) here. As far as the objects of knowledge (ñeyya) extend, so far does the knowledge extend; as far as the knowledge extends, so far do the objects of knowledge extend. Knowledge has the objects of knowledge as its limit; the objects of knowledge have knowledge as their limit. In this way, whether collectively or individually, all at once or sequentially, because he knows all phenomena rightly and by himself according to his wish, the Blessed One is called the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha). To that Perfectly Enlightened One (I pay homage).

'Dve vitakkā' means two kinds of right thoughts (sammā-vitakka). Among them, it is called 'thought' (vitakka) because one thinks by means of this state, or it thinks by itself, or it is just the act of thinking. It has the characteristic of directing the mind onto the object, the function of striking and impinging on the object repeatedly, and is manifested as the bringing of the mind to the object. Because of the difference in objects, it is spoken of as two, saying 'two thoughts.' 'Samudācaranti' means they occur and circulate evenly, rightly, upwards and upwards, within their bounds. For this [prefix 'ā'] has the meaning of a limit/bound; because of the connection with that, the phrase 'tathāgataṃ arahantaṃ sammāsambuddhaṃ' uses the accusative case in the sense of possession (sāmī). This is what is meant: In the range of the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, [these thoughts] occur and circulate evenly, rightly, without overstepping each other's bounds, upwards and upwards, frequently and repeatedly.

What is their object? What is their bound? And how do they occur upwards and upwards, frequently, repeatedly, and constantly without overstepping that bound? It is said: They are these two thoughts—the thought of safety (khema-vitakka) and the thought of seclusion (paviveka-vitakka). Among them, the thought of safety is first found to be particularly associated with the Blessed One's compassion (karuṇā); it is also found associated with loving-kindness (mettā) and empathetic joy (muditā). Therefore, that thought of safety should be understood as the precursor to and associated with the attainment of Great Compassion (mahākaruṇā-samāpatti) and the attainments of loving-kindness, etc. The thought of seclusion, however, should be understood as the precursor to and associated with the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti); it is also found by way of the divine abidings (dibba-vihāra), etc. Thus, 'thought' is their object. Therefore, even though they occur frequently in a single continuity (santāna), because they circulate only in their own objects from time to time, there is no [exceeding of] bounds, nor is there any confusion in their occurrence.

Among them, the thought of safety should be manifested by the Blessed One's descent into compassion, etc. The thought of seclusion should be manifested by the attainments (samāpatti). Herein, this is the manifestation: 'This world is born into heat, overwhelmed by suffering,' etc.—by seeing the state of the world of beings being burnt by the fires of lust (rāga), etc., it is spoken of in the preliminary stage of the attainment of Great Compassion, and also in the attainment itself by way of the first absorption (jhāna). Indeed, this was said (in the Paṭisambhidāmagga): 'The descent of the Buddhas' Great Compassion upon beings, seeing them in many ways...'
138:
Great compassion descends upon the Buddhas, the Exalted Ones, who observe beings in many ways. Great compassion descends upon the Buddhas, the Exalted Ones, as they see that the world of beings is burning with the fires of lust and so forth.

The world is striving in various affairs, moving to and fro through aging and death, and has entered upon the wrong path of false views. The world is unstable and is being led away [to death]; the world is unprotected and has no master; the world has nothing of its own, for one must go leaving everything behind. The world is ever-deficient, insatiable, and a slave to craving.

The beings living in the world have no protector other than themselves; they have no shelter, no refuge, and are truly refugeless. The world is distracted and unpeaceful. The beings living in the world are pierced by many thorns such as lust and so forth. They are obstructed and shrouded by the darkness of ignorance and surrounded by the cage of defilements. The beings living in the world, having reached ignorance, are as if inside an eggshell, covered by the membrane of ignorance, and are as tangled as a ball of thread bitten by mice, like a spider's web, or like muñja and babbaja grass. Great compassion descends upon the Buddhas who see that beings cannot transcend the cycle of birth and death (saṃsāra), the states of deprivation, the unhappy destinations, and the perdition.

Beings are smeared with the poisonous venom of ignorance, mired in the mud of defilements, and entangled in the knots of lust, hatred, and delusion.

They are fastened by the harness of craving, covered by the net of craving, swept away by the flood of craving, bound by the fetters of craving, followed by the underlying tendency of craving, tormented by the fever of craving, and intensely burned by the heat of craving.

They are fastened by the harness of wrong views, covered by the net of wrong views, swept away by the flood of wrong views, bound by the fetters of wrong views, followed by the underlying tendency of wrong views, tormented by the fever of wrong views, and intensely burned by the heat of wrong views.

Rebirth follows them, aging follows them, sickness oppresses them, death strikes them down, and they are established in suffering.

They are trapped by craving, surrounded by the wall of aging, encircled by the snare of death, and bound by great bonds. The beings living in the world are bound by the bonds of lust, hatred, and delusion, and by the bonds of pride, wrong views, defilements, and misconduct. They have entered upon a very narrow and difficult path, are obstructed by great obstacles, have fallen into a great precipice, have entered upon a great wilderness, have entered upon the great cycle of birth and death, are revolving repeatedly in great danger, and are mired in a great swamp.
139:
The world of beings is oppressed [by dangers]. The world of beings is burning with the fire of lust, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion; and with rebirth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. The world of beings is held fast by the hand of birth and led toward the dangers of aging and death. Being without protection, it is constantly tormented. It is like a thief who has received the king's punishment. It is manifest as one bound by the fetters of guilt and standing at the place of execution. The world of beings, having no refuge, has reached a state of extreme pitiableness. It is greatly oppressed by suffering and has been tormented for a long time. It is constantly attached and constantly thirsting with craving.

It is blind, eyeless, and its eye [of wisdom] is destroyed. Without anyone to point out its welfare, it runs onto the wrong path of false views. Having strayed from the straight path of the Middle Way, it has entered into the four great floods.

It is oppressed by the two views of eternalism and annihilationism. It practices wrongly through the three types of misconduct. It is joined with the four yokes. It is tied by the four ties. It is intensely grasped by the four types of clinging. It repeatedly ascends to the five destinations. It is lustful for the five cords of sensual pleasure. It is covered by the five hindrances. It is prone to dispute through the six roots of contention. It is lustful for the six bodies of craving. It is oppressed by the six types of wrong views. It is followed by the seven underlying tendencies. It is joined with the seven fetters. It is uplifted by the seven types of pride. It revolves repeatedly through the eight worldly conditions. It is fixed in the eight wrongnesses. It is corrupted by the eight defects of man. It is oppressed by the nine grounds for resentment. It is uplifted by the nine types of pride. It is lustful for the nine things rooted in craving. It is defiled by the ten bases of defilement. It is oppressed by the ten grounds for resentment. It is possessed of the ten courses of unwholesome action. It is joined with the ten fetters. It is fixed in the ten wrongnesses. It is possessed of wrong view based on ten objects. It is possessed of extremist view based on ten objects. It is delayed by the one hundred and eight mental proliferations of craving. Great compassion descends upon the Buddhas, the Exalted Ones, who see the Four Noble Truths, as they observe that the world of beings is thus oppressed by the sixty-two types of wrong views.

I have crossed over [the cycle of birth and death], but the world has not crossed over. I am liberated [from bonds], but the world is not liberated. I am tamed, but the world is not tamed. I am stilled,
140:
“In the world, the multitude is untamed, but I alone am peaceful. In the world, the multitude is not peaceful, but I alone have found relief. In the world, the multitude has not found relief, but I alone am extinguished. In the world, the multitude is not extinguished. Indeed, having crossed over [the ocean of saṃsāra], I am able to help others cross; having been freed [from the bonds of defilements], I am able to free others; having been tamed, I am able to tame others; having become peaceful, I am able to bring peace to others; having found relief, I am able to give relief to others; having been extinguished, I am able to lead others to extinction.” Thus, Great Compassion (mahākaruṇā) descends upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, as they behold sentient beings.

In this very manner, the descent of the Blessed One’s loving-kindness (mettā) toward sentient beings should also be explained. Indeed, mettā also occurs by bringing happiness—which is the opposite of the suffering that is the object of compassion—near to sentient beings. Thus, in this context, the thought of non-ill will (abyāpāda-vitakka) and the thought of non-cruelty (avihiṃsā-vitakka) are called the thought of safety (khema-vitakka). The thought of seclusion (paviveka-vitakka), however, is the thought of renunciation (nekkhamma-vitakka) itself. The occurrence of that thought of seclusion should be understood by way of reflection on the first jhāna, which is the preliminary stage of the divine abidings (dibba-vihāra) and noble abidings (ariya-vihāra).

In that regard, the Blessed One possesses two million four hundred thousand crores (2.4 trillion) of meditative attainments (samāpatti-vihāra) for daily use. The knowledge that occurs as a precursor to those meditative attainments, following the course of concentration and the course of knowledge, is called the Great Diamond Knowledge (mahāvajira-ñāṇa) which ranges over two million four hundred thousand crores of attainments. By the power of those meditative attainments, the frequent occurrence of the thought of seclusion in the Blessed One should be understood. This meaning should also be understood through the Mahāsaccaka Sutta. For it was said therein by the Blessed One:

“Agnivessana, I establish, settle, and steady my mind internally in that same preceding sign of concentration (samādhi-nimitta) in which I constantly dwell.”

Indeed, when Saccaka the son of the Nigaṇṭhas thought, “The ascetic Gotama is handsome, pleasing to behold, with well-set gums, a thin tongue, and sweet speech; I think he wanders about charming the assembly with all these. But there is no one-pointedness of mind (samādhi) in him who wanders about so much for the sake of convincing others,” the Blessed One brought forth this Mahāsaccaka Sutta to demonstrate—like catching a thief with the stolen goods—that: “Agnivessana, the Tathāgata does not wander about for the sake of convincing others by charming the assembly. He teaches the Dhamma to assemblies as far as the limits of the world-system (cakkavāḷa). Unattached and unstained, He dwells alone, devoted to the fruit of the attainment of the void (suññatā-phala-samāpatti).”
141:
The Blessed One, at the moment the audience cries 'Sādhu' or when He reflects on the Dhamma, first determines the time and enters the Fruit Attainment (phala-samāpatti) during every in-breath and out-breath. While the sound of 'Sādhu' has not yet ceased and upon the conclusion of the reflection on the Dhamma, He emerges from the attainment and preaches the Dhamma from where He stands. Because the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) of the Buddhas is swift, they can enter attainments during every in-breath and out-breath. Thus, by the power of the aforementioned attainments along with their preliminary stages, the frequent occurrence of the thought of safety (khema-vitakka) and the thought of seclusion (paviveka-vitakka) in the Blessed One should be understood.

In that regard, by the power of the thought of non-ill will and the thought of non-cruelty, which abandon the defilements such as the thought of ill will and the thought of cruelty, there is no fear from any source; thus, one endowed with those qualities dwells having attained safety (khema). Because of such dwelling, there is only safety and fearlessness for everyone at all times. Therefore, that twofold thought is called the thought of safety (khema-vitakka) because it brings about safety for both [oneself and others]. Furthermore, by the power of the thought of renunciation (nekkhamma-vitakka), which is for the sake of abandoning defilements such as the thought of sensual desire, the three types of seclusion—namely, bodily seclusion (kāya-viveka), mental seclusion (citta-viveka), and seclusion from the substrata (upadhi-viveka)—as well as the five types of seclusion—namely, seclusion by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-viveka), seclusion by suppression (vikkhambhana-viveka), seclusion by eradication (samuccheda-viveka), seclusion by tranquilization (paṭippassaddhi-viveka), and seclusion by escape (nissaraṇa-viveka)—reach fulfillment. That thought of renunciation is called the thought of seclusion (paviveka-vitakka) because it is a thought accompanied by seclusion according to its object and its association. Although these two thoughts have distinct spheres in this way, they arise to assist each other for those who are beginners in meditation. Just as the thought of seclusion helps the thought of safety to arise if it has not arisen, and to increase and expand if it has arisen, so too does the thought of safety assist the thought of seclusion. Indeed, without secluded body and mind, the abidings of loving-kindness and so forth cannot occur; and without the abandoning of ill will and so forth, mental seclusion and so forth are impossible. Therefore, these states should be seen as being of great mutual assistance. For the Blessed One, however, who has entirely abandoned all defilements, these thoughts of safety and seclusion bring about welfare and happiness for the sake of the world's benefit even in the mere duration of an in-breath and out-breath. Thus, they should be understood as 'the thought of safety' and 'the thought of seclusion' in connection.

To explain in detail the two thoughts thus summarized, He said the words beginning with 'abyāpajjhārāmo'. In that context, 'abyāpajjha' means not causing suffering to anyone. Because that state of non-affliction is delightful, it is called 'ārāma'. Therefore, it is called 'abyāpajjhārāma' because of delighting in the state of non-affliction by way of practicing and frequenting it.
142:
Because non-affliction (avyāpajjha) of anyone is his great delight, he is called 'avyāpajjhārāma' (one who delights in non-affliction). Because he delights in that non-affliction and is constantly devoted to it through practice, he is called 'avyāpajjharata' (one who rejoices in non-affliction). 'Esevā' means 'eso eva' (he himself). 'Iriyāyā' means by action, by the application of body and speech. 'I do not harm anyone' means that he does not harm or cause suffering to any being, whether they are 'trembling' beings (tasa)—those who tremble due to association with craving, fear, etc., among the lowly and so forth—or 'stable' beings (thāvara)—those who are firm and steady because they are free from all defilements and thus do not tremble. The Blessed One, who possesses the disposition of compassion and frequently enters the attainment of great compassion, spoke thus in accordance with his own most cherished disposition of compassion. By speaking in this way, he demonstrates the thought of non-cruelty (avihiṃsā-vitakka) and the thought of non-ill-will (avyāpāda-vitakka).

This is the intended meaning: "While I, practicing well in this manner with this posture and this practice, and dwelling in such meditative attainments, accept the respect, honor, esteem, veneration, and offerings made by those desiring merit, I do not harm any being. On the contrary, I promote only their welfare and happiness, categorized as the mundane, the supramundane, and the ultimate goal."

"Whatever unwholesome state is abandoned" means that all the 1,500 varieties of defilements and other infinite unwholesome states associated with them were abandoned and uprooted by me at the foot of the Bodhi tree. By this statement, among the types of seclusion (paviveka), he shows 'seclusion by escape' (nissaraṇa-viveka), which is the pinnacle, along with 'seclusion by eradication' (samuccheda-viveka) and 'seclusion by tranquilization' (paṭippassaddhi-viveka). Some teachers also extract 'seclusion by substitution of opposites' (tadaṅga-viveka) and 'seclusion by suppression' (vikkhambhana-viveka) here. This is because the Blessed One spoke here of his own exhaustion of defilements along with the practice to be attained (āgamanīya-paṭipadā).

Thus, the Blessed One, having now brought his disposition for seclusion—cultivated throughout immeasurable aeons—to its pinnacle along with the disposition for escape, and having entered the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti) associated with that disposition, manifests the destruction of his own defilements through the method of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā). For whatever purpose the Teacher raised these two thoughts in this sutta, he now speaks the words beginning with "Tasmātiha, bhikkhave" to show that purpose. The Blessed One began this teaching to lead the monks into those thoughts by showing his own frequent practice of these two thoughts.

In that context, "tasmā" means: because for me, who delights in non-affliction and seclusion, only thoughts of safety and thoughts of seclusion frequently occur; therefore. "Tiha" is merely a particle.
144:
He is called **Asayhasāhī** because he subdues and overcomes the five Māras, which others cannot endure or bear; and because he carries out the Buddha's duties (Buddhakicca), which others cannot perform, by understanding the distinctions of dispositions (anusaya), temperaments, and so forth, and by instructing veneyya beings according to their needs regarding present, future, and ultimate benefits; or because he is well-practiced in those Buddha's duties. In the phrase 'samudācaranti naṃ', 'naṃ' is merely a particle, or it means 'that Tathāgata'.

He is called **Tamonuda** because he dispels the darkness of delusion (moha) known as 'tamas' within his own continuity and that of others. He is called **Pāragata** because he has gone to the further shore, which is Nibbāna. Alternatively, he is called **Pāragata** because he has reached the end of the great aspiration (mahābhinīhāra) that arose through the method of 'having been liberated, I shall liberate others,' or because he has reached the end of the entire suffering of Saṃsāra and all the qualities of omniscience. To that Buddha who dispels the darkness of delusion, who has reached the further shore, and who is therefore **Pattipatta**—having attained all the qualities such as virtue (sīla) and the ten powers (dasabala-ñāṇa) that are to be attained by the Fully Enlightened Buddhas—(thoughts occurred).

He is called **Vasimā** because he possesses the supreme mastery (vasībhāva) of adverting (āvajjana) and so forth in jhāna and other states according to his wish, and the mental mastery known as noble psychic power (ariyiddhi) which is not shared with others. He is called **Anāsava** because of the absence of all taints (āsavas) such as the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava). He is called **Visantara** because he has vomited out the unevenness (visama) such as bodily unevenness, or because he has crossed over all the filth of defilements known as poison (visa), or because he has personally crossed over the poison of the entire round of suffering and enables others to cross. He is called **Muni** because he is liberated from defilements in the fruit of Arahatship, which is the end of craving, or in Nibbāna; or because he has reached both and is pre-eminently endowed with the knowledge known as 'mona' or with bodily sagehood (kāya-moneyya) and so forth.

Sages (munis) are of many kinds: the householder sage (agāriya-muni), the homeless sage (anagāriya-muni), the learner sage (sekkha-muni), the adept sage (asekkha-muni), the silent sage (pacceka-muni), and the sage of sages (munimuni). Among them, a layperson who has attained the fruit and understands the Dispensation is a householder sage. A monk of such a kind is a homeless sage. The seven types of learners (sekkhas) are learner sages. One whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) is an adept sage. A Silent Buddha (Pacceka-buddha) is a silent sage. The Fully Enlightened Buddha (Sammāsambuddha) is the sage of sages (munimuni). In this context, only the sage of sages is intended. He is called **Antimadehadhārī** because he bears his final body, as there will be no further rebirth in the future. He is called **Mārañjaha** because he has completely abandoned the Māra of defilements and so forth. For that very reason, he is called **Pāragū**, one who has gone to the further shore of all aging (jarā), such as the manifest aging, by attaining Nibbāna without remainder through the absolute cutting off of the cause of aging. Here, by mentioning aging (jarā) as the head, it should be understood that he has gone to the further shore of birth (jāti), death (maraṇa), sorrow (soka), and so forth. It is said that 'two thoughts occurred simultaneously to that Tathāgata who is of such a nature.'

After the Blessed One had indicated the two thoughts with the first verse and shown the thought of seclusion (paviveka-vitakka) with the second verse, he now began to show the thought of safety (khema-vitakka).
145:
Thus, the Blessed One, having pointed out the two kinds of thought with the first verse, and having shown the thought of seclusion (paviveka-vitakka) with the second verse, now spoke the third verse beginning with 'Sele yathā' to show the thought of safety (khema-vitakka). In that verse, 'Sele yathā pabbatamuddhaniṭṭhito' means as if standing on the peak of a solid mountain made of rock. Indeed, for one standing on such a mountain peak, there is no need for such tasks as craning or stretching the neck upwards. 'Tathūpamaṃ' means having a similar comparison, like a rocky mountain. The summary of the meaning here is: Just as a man with vision standing on the peak of a rocky mountain would see the multitude of people all around, even so, the Blessed One, who is of excellent wisdom and who sees all around with the Eye of All-Knowledge (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), having ascended the palace made of Dhamma and wisdom, being himself free from sorrow, looks upon, reflects on, and examines the multitude of beings, the body of beings, who are immersed in sorrow and overwhelmed by birth and old age.

The meaning here is: Suppose a large field is made at the foot of a mountain, and huts are built on the ridges of those fields where fires are lit at night, and there is thick darkness consisting of four factors. A man with vision standing on the peak of that mountain, looking down at the ground, would see neither the fields, nor the ridges, nor the huts, nor the people sleeping there; he would see only the flames of the fires in the huts. In the same way, to the Tathāgata who has ascended the Dhamma palace and looks upon the multitude of beings, those beings who have not performed merit do not come into the range of the Buddha's knowledge even if they are sitting on the right side in the same monastery; they are like arrows shot at night. However, those teachable persons (veneyya-puggala) who have performed merit come into the range of his knowledge even if they are far away. They are as distinct as fire or the Himālaya mountains. This has also been said: 'The good shine from afar like the Himālaya mountains; the wicked are not seen here, like arrows shot at night.' Thus, in this sutta and in these verses, the Blessed One showed himself as if he were another person.

## The Commentary on the First Sutta is Finished.

## 2. Desanāsutta-vaṇṇanā

In the second sutta, regarding the word 'pariyāyena', the word 'pariyāya' occurs in the sense of 'teaching' (desanā) in such places as 'Remember this sutta as the Madhupiṇḍika-pariyāya.' In the passage 'Atthi pariyāyo,' it occurs in the sense of 'cause' (kāraṇa). In other contexts, it occurs in the sense of 'instruction' (ovāda) or 'turn/sequence' (vāra). In this sutta, however, it occurs in the sense of 'cause' or 'turn'. Among those meanings: Monks, the teachings of the Tathāgata are twofold; those teachings occur by way of cause or by way of turn as appropriate. This is the meaning of this Pali. Indeed, the Blessed One, according to his own wish, sometimes [preaches], 'These dhammas are wholesome dhammas.'
146:
The word "pariyāya" occurs in the sense of "reason" (kāraṇa) in such passages as: "Brahmin, if one speaking rightly of me were to say, 'The ascetic Gotama is a teacher of non-action (akiriyavāda)'" and so forth. It occurs in the sense of "turn" (vāra) in such passages as: "Ānanda, whose turn is it today to exhort the bhikkhunīs?" and so forth.

In this sutta, however, it is appropriate in both the sense of "turn" and "reason." Therefore, the meaning here is: "Monks, the two Dhamma teachings of the Tathāgata occur appropriately either by way of reason or by way of turn." The Blessed One, in accordance with the inclinations of those to be tamed, sometimes teaches the Dhamma by distinguishing between wholesome and unwholesome states, saying: "These states are wholesome, these states are unwholesome. These states are blameworthy, these states are blameless. These states are to be cultivated, these states are not to be cultivated," and so forth. Wishing to define them without mixing wholesome states with unwholesome states, he teaches the Dhamma: "See evil as evil." Sometimes, revealing the danger (ādīnava), he teaches the Dhamma: "Monks, the taking of life, when practiced, developed, and cultivated, leads to hell, leads to the animal realm, leads to the realm of hungry ghosts. The lightest consequence of taking life is that it leads to a short lifespan," and so forth. Wishing to engage them in revulsion (nibbidā) and so forth towards evil, he teaches the Dhamma: "Be revulsed, be dispassionate."

"Bhavanti" means they are, they occur. "See evil as evil" means one should see all unwholesome states as low or inferior because they bring harm and suffering in both the present life and the future. In that context, "be revulsed" (nibbindatha) means: seeing with right wisdom the various dangers in those unwholesome states—such as "it is called 'pāpa' (evil) because it is of an extremely low nature; it is called 'akusala' (unwholesome) because it arises from lack of skill; it is called 'saṅkilesika' (defiling) because it destroys the natural radiance and clarity of the mind; it is called 'ponobbhavika' (leading to rebirth) because it repeatedly produces the suffering of existence; it is called 'sadaratha' (with distress) because it occurs along with distress and fever; it is called 'dukkhavipāka' (having suffering as its result) because it ripens only into suffering; it is called 'āyatiṃ jātijarāmaraṇiya' (leading to future birth, aging, and death) because it produces birth, aging, and death in the future for an immeasurable time; it is capable of destroying all welfare and happiness"—and seeing the benefits of abandoning that unwholesome state, one should become revulsed, reaching a state of revulsion.

Being revulsed, by developing insight (vipassanā) and attaining the Noble Path (ariya magga), be dispassionate towards evil and be liberated. Or, be dispassionate by way of the dispassion of eradication (samuccheda-virāga) through the Path, and then be liberated by way of the liberation of tranquilization (paṭippassaddhi-vimutti) through the Fruit (phala). Alternatively, "pāpa" is so called because it is low. What does this mean? Because of its nature as impermanent, suffering, and so forth, the Noble Ones...
147:
...it is called "pāpa" (evil) because it leads to the loathsome suffering of the round (vaṭṭa-dukkha). What is that suffering of the round? It is the collection of phenomena occurring in the three planes of existence. Seeing it as low in the sense already mentioned, and developing insight into those phenomena of the three planes as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a boil, as a dart, as a calamity, as an affliction, and so forth, be revulsed. "Ayaṃ dutiyā" (This is the second) means: starting from the first statement which clearly explains the harm and disadvantage as it truly is, and then analyzing further, this Dhamma teaching is the second Dhamma teaching.

In the verses, "Buddhassa" means of the Omniscient Buddha (Sabbaññu Buddha). "Sabbabhūtānukampino" means of the one whose nature is to be compassionate towards all beings with great compassion (mahākaruṇā). "Pariyāyavacanaṃ" means a teaching given by way of a method or turn. "Passa" (See!) is either an address to the assembly or spoken with reference to the leader of the assembly. Some, however, say: "The Blessed One said 'Passa' referring only to himself." "Tattha" means in that low, unwholesome state; "be dispassionate" means abandon lust (rāga). The rest is as already explained.

## The Commentary on the Second Sutta is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Vijjā Sutta

In the third sutta, "pubbaṅgamā" (precursor) means the primary cause, being the forerunner in two ways: by way of conascence (sahajāta) and by way of decisive support (upanissaya). Indeed, there is no arising of the unwholesome without ignorance (avijjā). "Samāpattiyā" means for the sake of attaining, for the sake of acquiring its nature, for the sake of occurrence. In that occurrence of the unwholesome, the nature of decisive support (upanissaya) for unwholesome states is seen through the concealing of danger, through being the cause of unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra), and through the state of not being abandoned.

Thus, because they are the basis for sufferings such as sickness and death, all destinations (gati) are here called "bad destinations" (duggati). Alternatively, destinations corrupted by defilements such as lust, being the occurrences of body, speech, and mind, are called "bad destinations"; these are bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct. "Asmiṃ loke" means in this world or in the human destination. "Paramhi ca" means in other destinations besides that. "Avijjāmūlikā sabbā" means all those failures of misconduct have ignorance as their precursor in the manner stated, and thus they have ignorance as their root. "Icchālobhasamussayā" means accumulated and built up by desire (icchā), characterized by seeking an object not yet obtained, and by greed (lobha), characterized by attachment to an object already obtained.
148:
"Yato" means because of the cause of ignorance, being veiled by ignorance. "Pāpiccho" (one of evil desire) refers to one who, being covered by ignorance, does not see the danger of evil desire and acts with pretension (koha) and the like by imagining non-existent virtues. It should be understood that excessive greed (atricchatā) is also included within greed (lobha). "Anādaro" (disrespectful) means being devoid of respect toward fellow practitioners (sabrahmacārī) due to the absence of moral dread (ottappa), which is the sovereign of the world. "Tato" means because of those causes: ignorance, evil desire, lack of shame (ahiri), and lack of moral dread (anottappa). "Pasavati" means accumulating evil (pāpa) such as bodily misconduct. "Tena apāyaṃ gacchati" means that through such accumulated evil, one goes to or is reborn in the planes of misery (apāya) such as hell.

"Tasmā" means because those factors like ignorance are the root of all misconduct and the cause of all bad destinations and defilements. Therefore, "abandoning desire (icchā), greed (lobha), and ignorance (avijjā)"—and by the word "ca" (and), also lack of shame and lack of moral dread—means abandoning them by way of eradication (samuccheda). How does one abandon them? As stated in "producing knowledge (vijjā)," it is by making an effort through the sequence of insight (vipassanā) and the sequence of the path (magga) to produce the knowledge of the path of Arahantship (arahattamagga-vijjā) within one's own continuity. "Sabbā duggatiyo" (all bad destinations) means one should abandon or transcend all bad destinations known as misconduct, or all five destinations (gati) because they are the basis for the suffering of the round (vaṭṭadukkha). This is because by abandoning the round of defilements (kilesavaṭṭa), the round of kamma (kammavaṭṭa) and the round of results (vipākavaṭṭa) are also abandoned.

## The Commentary on the Third Sutta is finished.
## The Commentary on the First Recitation Section (Bhāṇavāra) is finished.
## 4. Commentary on the Paññāparihīna Sutta

In the fourth sutta, "suparihīnā" means thoroughly bereft or diminished. "Ye ariyāya paññāya parihīnā" (those who are bereft of noble wisdom) refers to those beings who are bereft of pure insight wisdom (vipassanā-paññā) and path wisdom (magga-paññā). These wisdoms are "noble" (ariya) because they stand far from defilements through the penetration of the rise and fall of the five aggregates and the penetration of the Four Noble Truths. Such beings are great losers, being utterly bereft of both mundane and supramundane attainments. Who are they? They are those possessed of kamma-obstructions (kammāvaraṇa). Because they are fixed in wrongness (micchatta-niyata), they are definitely bereft, incomplete, and great losers. Therefore, it is said, "a bad destination is to be expected (duggati pāṭikaṅkhā)." Those possessed of result-obstructions (vipākāvaraṇa) are also bereft. Alternatively, those who are not bereft on the side of the wholesome...
149:
...are those free from the three types of obstructions (āvaraṇa), possessing right view and endowed with the knowledge that kamma is one's own (kammassakata-ñāṇa). The rest should be understood according to the method already described.

In the verses, "paññāyā" is a word in the ablative case (nissakkavacana), meaning "due to falling away from insight knowledge and path knowledge." Or it is in the genitive case (sāmivacana), meaning "due to the falling away of the aforementioned knowledge." Here, "falling away" (parihāna) simply means the non-arising of the knowledge that ought to be produced. "Niviṭṭhaṃ nāmarūpasmiṃ" (settled in name-and-form) means being attached to and obsessed with the group of five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandha) known as name-and-form, through the power of craving (taṇhā) and view (diṭṭhi), thinking "this is mine," and so on. Because of that very obsession, one thinks, "This alone is the truth, all else is empty." In the phrase "sadevake loke," the case ending should be transformed.

Thus, after showing the side of defilement (saṃkilesapakkhā) with the first verse, the Buddha spoke the verse beginning with "Paññā hi seṭṭhā lokasmiṃ" (Wisdom is indeed supreme in the world) to declare the power of wisdom. This shows that while the round of defilements (kilesavaṭṭa) continues through the obsessions and imaginings regarding name-and-form when wisdom does not arise, the round is cut off when wisdom does arise.

In that verse, "lokasmiṃ" means in the world of formations (saṅkhāraloka). Just as the Perfectly Enlightened One is supreme among beings, there is no quality (dhamma) equal to wisdom among formations. Wholesome states have wisdom as their chief (paññuttarā); when wisdom is accomplished, all blameless states are indeed accomplished. Thus it is said: "For one of right view, right intention originates," and so on. The wisdom intended here is praised as "supreme." To show how that wisdom functions, the phrase "ယာယံ နိဗ္ဗေဓဂါမိနီ" (yāyaṃ nibbedhagါminī - which is penetrative) etc., is spoken. Its meaning is: this wisdom is "penetrative" (nibbedhagāminī) because it proceeds by piercing and breaking through the mass of greed and so on, which had never been pierced or broken before. By means of this wisdom, one correctly knows and realizes Nibbāna and Arahantship—the end and exhaustion of birth (jāti), which is the first arising of the aggregates, and its cause, the kamma-process (kammabhava), within the various realms of existence, origins, destinations, stations of consciousness, and abodes of beings. This path wisdom coupled with insight (sahavipassanā magga-paññā) is supreme in the world.

Now, wishing to praise the Arahants who are endowed with the power of wisdom described above, the Buddha spoke the final verse: "Tesaṃ devā manussā ca" (To them, gods and humans...). Its meaning is: to those who are "Awakened" (sambuddha) through the realization of the Four Truths, having completed the sixteen tasks such as full understanding (pariññā) regarding the Four Noble Truths; to those who are "mindful" (satimataṃ) having reached the abundance of mindfulness; to those of "joyous wisdom" (hāsapaññānaṃ) because they have reached the abundance of wisdom by utterly uprooting delusion (sammoha) as described; or to those of joyous wisdom because they have much joy and gladness from the fulfillment of virtue etc. in the preliminary stage up to the realization of Nibbāna... to those who bear their final body, having exhausted all fetters of existence (bhavasaṃyojana), both gods and humans long to approach. Thus, the commentary on the Paññā Sutta is finished.
150:
Starting from the fulfillment of virtue and so on, up to the realization of Nibbāna, because of the abundance of joy, gladness, satisfaction, and rapture, the Arahants—who possess joyful wisdom and who bear their final body because all fetters of existence have been entirely exhausted—are yearned for and loved by both devas and humans. Desiring to attain that state, they think: "How wonderful! The power of wisdom is truly great. If only we, being of such a nature, could also cross over all suffering like this!"

## The Commentary on the Fourth Sutta is finished.

## 5. Commentary on the Sukkadhamma Sutta

In the fifth sutta, "sukka" (bright/pure) does not mean bright in color; rather, they are bright by way of accomplished purity, as they lead to a state of supreme purification. By their own nature, all wholesome states (kusala dhamma) are indeed bright because they are the opposite of the dark states (akusala). Due to the arising of those wholesome states, the mind becomes radiant and completely pure. "Dhammā" refers to wholesome states. "Lokaṃ" refers to the world of beings. "Pālenti" means they protect by establishing boundaries through support and maintenance.

In the phrase "hiri ca ottappañca," "hiri" (moral shame) is so called because one is ashamed of what should be shamed, or because one feels shame through this quality. Thus it has been said: "That which is ashamed of what should be shamed, ashamed of falling into evil and unwholesome states—this is called hiri." "Ottappa" (moral dread) is so called because one dreads what should be dreaded, or because one feels dread through this quality. Thus it has been said: "That which dreads what should be dreaded, dreads falling into evil and unwholesome states—this is called ottappa."

Among those two, hiri is internally-arisen, while ottappa is externally-arisen. Hiri is self-governed, while ottappa is world-governed. Hiri is established in the nature of shame, while ottappa is established in the nature of fear. Hiri has the characteristic of respect, while ottappa has the characteristic of fearing blame and seeing danger.

Among such hiri and ottappa, one arouses internally-arisen hiri through four reasons: by reflecting on one's birth (lineage), by reflecting on one's age, by reflecting on one's heroism, and by reflecting on one's great learning. How? "Doing evil is not the work of those well-born; it is only the work of those of low birth, such as fishermen and the like. For someone well-born like me, it is not proper to do this act." Thus, by first reflecting on one's birth, one who does not commit evil acts such as killing living beings arouses shame. Likewise... regarding oneself...
151:
...arouses shame (hiri). Likewise, reflecting on one's age: "Doing evil is an act to be done by the young; for someone established in an age like mine, it is not proper to do this evil deed." Thus, reflecting on age, one who does not commit evil acts such as killing living beings arouses shame. Likewise, reflecting on heroism: "Doing evil is the work of those of a weak nature; for someone endowed with heroism like me, it is not proper to do this evil deed." Thus, reflecting on heroism, one who does not commit evil acts such as killing living beings arouses shame. Likewise, reflecting on great learning: "Doing evil is the work of the blind and foolish, not of the wise; for a wise and learned person like me, it is not proper to do this evil deed." Thus, reflecting on great learning, one who does not commit evil acts such as killing living beings arouses shame. In this way, one arouses internally-arisen (ajjhatta-samuṭṭhāna) hiri through these four reasons. Having aroused it, one introduces shame into one's mind and no longer commits evil deeds. Such shame is called hiri with an internal origin.

How is ottappa (moral dread) called externally-arisen (bahiddhā-samuṭṭhāna)? Reflecting: "If you commit an evil deed, you will be censured among the four assemblies," and "The wise will censure you, just as a city-dweller avoids filth; you will be shunned by the virtuous. O monk, how could you dare to do evil?" Thus, through externally-arisen dread, one does not commit evil deeds. Such dread is called ottappa with an external origin.

How is hiri called self-governed (attādhipateyya)? Here, a certain clansman, making himself the chief and authority, thinks: "For someone like me who has gone forth out of faith, who is learned and a proponent of dhuta practices, it is not proper to do an evil deed," and thus does not commit evil. Such shame is called attādhipateyya hiri. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "He, making himself the authority, abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome; he abandons the blameworthy and develops the blameless; he maintains himself in purity."

How is ottappa called world-governed (lokādhipateyya)? Here, a certain clansman, making the world the chief and authority, does not commit evil. As the Blessed One said: "Indeed, this world of beings is vast. In this vast world of beings, there are recluses and brahmins who possess psychic power, the divine eye, and knowledge of others' minds. They can see from afar, and though they are near, they are not apparent; they can know the minds of others with their own minds. They will know me thus: 'O friends, look at this clansman; though he has entered from the lay life into the monkhood out of faith, he lives mingled with evil, unwholesome states.'" Thus he reflects. There are also deities who possess psychic power, the divine eye, and knowledge of others' minds. Those deities can see from afar, and though they are near, they are not apparent; they can know the thoughts in the minds of others with their own minds.
152:
Those who know the minds of others see even from afar; though they are near, they are not seen (by the ordinary eye); they know the minds of others with their own minds. They will know me thus: 'Look, sirs, at this clansman; having gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, he lives entangled with evil, unwholesome states.' There are devas who possess psychic power, the divine eye, and knowledge of others' minds. They see even from afar; though they are near, they are not seen; they know the minds of others with their own minds. They will know me thus: 'Look, sirs, at this clansman; having gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, he lives entangled with evil, unwholesome states.' That person, making the world his authority, abandons the unwholesome (Aṅguttara Nikāya, 3.40).

Such is the fear of wrongdoing governed by the world (lokādhipateyya ottappa).

In the phrase 'established in the nature of shame,' shame means the mode of loathing; the state established by that nature of loathing unwholesome states is called hiri. Fear means the fear of the states of deprivation (apāya); the state established by that nature of fearing the states of deprivation is called ottappa. These two become manifest in the avoidance of evil. In this regard, for example, suppose there are two iron balls: one is cold but smeared with excrement, and the other is hot and glowing. Just as a wise person does not pick up the cold one because of disgust at the excrement, and does not pick up the other because of the fear of being burnt; even so, a wise person does not do evil because of disgust through shame (hiri), and does not do evil because of fear of the states of deprivation through ottappa. Thus, hiri is established in the nature of shame, and ottappa is established in the nature of fear.

How is it that hiri has the characteristic of respect and deference, while ottappa has the characteristic of seeing fear and dread in faults? Some person, through four reasons—reflection on the greatness of one's birth, reflection on the greatness of the Teacher, reflection on the greatness of the inheritance, and reflection on the greatness of one's fellow practitioners—arouses hiri characterized by respect and deference toward those reasons and does not do evil. Another person, through four reasons—fear of self-reproach, fear of others' reproach, fear of punishment, and fear of an unfortunate destination—fearing faults and seeing them as a danger, arouses ottappa characterized by seeing fear and dread in faults and does not do evil. Here, the internal origin and so forth of hiri and ottappa are stated according to their manifestation in various places, but they are never separated from each other. Indeed, there is no loathing without fear, nor is there fear of evil without loathing.
153:
Monks, if these two bright states did not protect the world; monks, if these two blameless states did not guard the world, if there were no world-protectors. In this world, 'This is my mother' would not be known by way of respect and honor; 'This is my mother' would not be found. The same method applies to the remaining terms. 'Maternal aunt' means the mother's sister. 'Uncle's wife' means the wife of a maternal uncle. 'Wives of teachers' means the wives of those in the position of teachers, such as the wives of elder uncles, younger uncles, elder brothers, and so forth. There would be confusion with them or a breaking of boundaries.

The Buddha shows the analogy with the words 'like goats and sheep.' These animals do not know 'This is my mother' or 'This is my maternal aunt' by way of respect and honor; they even behave wrongly toward the very source (the mother) from which they were born. Therefore, wishing to bring an analogy, he cited goats, sheep, and so forth. The summary of the meaning here is: Just as animals like goats and sheep, being devoid of hiri and ottappa, do not perceive 'mother' and so forth, and live with broken boundaries and confusion everywhere; even so, if these world-protecting states did not exist in this human world, people would live with confusion everywhere. But because these world-protecting states do protect the world, there is no such confusion.

In the verses, in the phrase 'yeseṃ ce hiri-ottappaṃ,' the word 'ce' is a mere particle. For those beings in whom hiri and ottappa are never found at any time. Those beings, because they perform actions that lead to the cutting off of the roots of wholesome states, or because of the absence of hiri and ottappa which are the foundation of wholesome actions, have 'deviated from the bright roots' (vokkantā sukkamūlā) because they stand having turned away and receded from the wholesome. The meaning is that because they have the nature of being born and dying again and again, they reach birth and death and cannot transcend saṃsāra.

'Yeseñca hiri-ottappaṃ' means for those beings of pure wisdom, these states of hiri and ottappa stand well-approached at all times, day and night, during the times of being a junior, middle-seated, or senior monk. Loathing and fearing evil, they abandon evil by way of 'abandoning by substitution of opposites' (tadaṅga) and so forth. 'Virūḷhabrahmacariyā' means they have reached growth and increase in the holy life of the Dispensation (sāsana-brahmacariya) and the holy life of the Path (magga-brahmacariya). They are 'peaceful' (santa) because all defilements have been stilled by the attainment of the highest path (Arahattamagga), or because they possess peaceful qualities. They are 'those for whom renewed existence is exhausted' (khīṇapunabbhavā) because they have ended renewed existence.

## The Explanation of the Fifth Sutta is finished.
154:
## 6. Commentary on the Ajāta Sutta

In the sixth sutta, what is the origin (uppatti) of the sutta beginning with "Atthi, bhikkhave"? It is said that one day, the Blessed One, having illustrated the faults of Saṃsāra through various methods, delivered a Dhamma discourse related to Nibbāna in terms of the cessation of that Saṃsāra and so forth. At that time, this thought occurred to the monks: "The Blessed One has taught this Saṃsāra as having causes, along with causal factors such as ignorance (avijjā) and so on. However, he has not stated any cause for Nibbāna, which is the cessation of Saṃsāra. How then can such an uncaused Nibbāna be found as a true ultimate reality (paramattha)?"

Then, the Blessed One spoke this sutta by the power of an inspired utterance (udāna) with a surge of joy, for the purpose of dispelling the doubts of those monks; for the purpose of destroying the false views of those outside the dispensation who hold wrong views, such as the Lokāyatikas, who wrongly assume that "In this world, the word 'Nibbāna, Nibbāna' used by recluses and brahmins is merely a matter of words, for Nibbāna does not exist in the ultimate sense because its nature cannot be found"; for the purpose of showing the actual existence of the deathless Great Nibbāna in the ultimate sense; and for the purpose of showing its possession of power, such as being the escape from Saṃsāra. For this reason, this sutta is also recited in the Udāna Pāḷi.

In that sutta, "atthi" means it exists, it is found by wisdom in the ultimate sense. The terms "ajata" (unborn), "abhūta" (unbecome), "akata" (unmade), and "asaṅkhata" (unconditioned) are all synonyms of one another. Alternatively, it is "ajata" because it is not born or produced by the harmony of causes known as root-causes (hetu-paccaya) and contributing conditions (paccaya-paccaya), unlike feelings (vedanā) and so forth. It is "abhūta" because it has not become, manifested, or arisen spontaneously without a cause. Because it is thus unborn (ajata) and unbecome (abhūta), it is "akata" because it is not made by any cause whatsoever. The nature of being born, become, and made belongs only to conditioned things (saṅkhata-dhamma) such as mind and matter (nāmarūpa), and not to Nibbāna, which has an unconditioned nature; to show this, it is called "asaṅkhata."

Alternatively, in reverse, that which is made by causes coming together is called "saṅkhata"; that which is not so made and is devoid of the characteristics of the conditioned is called "asaṅkhata." When the state of being produced by many causes is thus refuted, should there be a doubt that "perhaps it is made by a single cause," it is called "akata" to show that it is not made by any cause. Even though it is without conditions, should there be a doubt that "perhaps this has become or manifested spontaneously," it is called "abhūta" to dispel that doubt. It is called "ajata" to show that this state of being unconditioned, unmade, and unbecome is due to its nature of being entirely unborn in every respect. Thus, the purposefulness of all these four terms should be understood.
155:
Thus the Blessed One, having stated the existence of Nibbāna in the ultimate sense by saying, "Monks, there is the unborn, the unbecome, the unmade, the unconditioned," spoke the words beginning with "Monks, if this were not so" to show the reason for it. The summary of those words is: Monks, if this unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu) characterized by being unborn and so forth did not exist, then in this world, the escape from the mass of conditioned things (saṅkhāragata) known as the five aggregates of form and so forth—which are characterized by being born and so forth—namely, the cessation of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) without remainder, would not be apparent, would not be obtainable, and would not be possible. Indeed, the factors of the Noble Path, such as Right View (Sammādiṭṭhi) and so forth, which arise taking Nibbāna as their object, eradicate the defilements (kilesa) without remainder. Therefore, in this Nibbāna, the non-occurrence, the departure, and the escape from all the suffering of the round of rebirth are evident.

Having thus shown the existence of Nibbāna through the method of exclusion (vyatireka), he now spoke the words beginning with "But since" (yasmā ca kho) to show it through the method of inclusion (anvaya). Those words have the meaning already stated. Furthermore, in this regard, the existence of the Nibbāna element in the ultimate sense has been taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One, who has compassion for the entire world, through many sutta passages such as: "There are unconditioned states, there are unconditioned states (Dhammasaṅgaṇī); Monks, there is that sphere where there is no earth (Udāna); This state, too, is hard to see, namely the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions (Mahāvagga, Majjhima Nikāya); Monks, I will teach you the unconditioned and the path leading to the unconditioned (Saṃyutta Nikāya)," and also by this sutta, "Monks, there is the unborn." Therefore, Nibbāna should not be rejected.

Regarding that Nibbāna, even for the wise who have not yet realized it for themselves, there is no doubt or uncertainty at all. As for those individuals who lack wisdom, for the purpose of dispelling their doubts, this is the logical investigation by way of clarifying the meaning: Just as an escape is evident which is the opposite of, and free from the nature of, the sense-sphere (kāma) and the form-sphere (rūpa)—which have the nature of being fully understood and have something superior to them—so too, there must be an escape which is the opposite of, and free from the nature of, all conditioned things (saṅkhata-dhamma) that have such a nature. That which is this escape is the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu).

What more can be said? Neither insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) nor conformity knowledge (anuloma-ñāṇa), which take conditioned things as their object, are able to abandon defilements by way of eradication (samuccheda). Similarly, the knowledge in the first jhāna and so forth, which takes conventional truth (sammuti-sacca) as its object, abandons defilements only by way of suppression (vikkhambhana); it cannot abandon them by way of eradication. Thus, because the knowledge that takes conditioned things as its object and the knowledge that takes conventional truth as its object are incapable of the abandonment of defilements by eradication, the Noble Path knowledge (ariyamagga-ñāṇa), which performs the abandonment of those defilements by eradication, must have an object that is opposite in nature to both of those...
156:
That nature should be the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu). Likewise, the statement, "Monks, there is the unborn, the unbecome, the unmade, the unconditioned," is a statement showing the existence of Nibbāna in the ultimate sense, because it was spoken by the Blessed One as an unerring meaning. What is spoken by the Blessed One is known as the ultimate truth with an unerring meaning. For example, the statement: "All formations are impermanent, all formations are suffering, all phenomena are non-self."

Likewise, the word 'Nibbāna' in certain contexts has a true ultimate object, just as the word 'lion' (sīha) has a metaphorical usage (upacāra) due to its proximity. Alternatively, the unconditioned element exists in the ultimate sense because it has a nature liberated from the transformations of the conditioned, which are contrary to it, just like the earth element (pathavī-dhātu) or feeling (vedanā). In this way and by such methods, the existence of the unconditioned element in the ultimate sense should be understood through reasoning.

In the verses, "jāta" (born) means 'born' in the sense of being produced; it means having reached the characteristic of birth. "Bhūta" (become) means 'become' in the sense of coming into being; it means having arisen without having existed before. "Samuppanna" (arisen) means arisen together with its co-arisen factors, or arisen along with associated phenomena. "Kata" (made) means produced by causes and conditions. "Saṅkhata" (conditioned) means 'conditioned' because it is made by those very causes coming together and meeting. All these are designations for what is produced by conditions. It is "addhuva" (impermanent) because it is devoid of a permanent essence and so forth. It is "jarāmaraṇasaṅghāta" (a mass of aging and death) because it is inevitably intertwined with aging and death. Some also read it as "jarāmaraṇasaṅghaṭṭa," meaning oppressed and afflicted by aging and death. It is "roganīḷa" (a nest of diseases) because it is the nesting place for many diseases such as eye diseases.
