It is "pabhaṅgura" (fragile) because it has the nature of tending towards destruction, both by its own nature and by external effort.

It is "āhārannettippabhava" (originating from nutriment and the lead of craving) because the four types of nutriment and the 'lead' (netti) known as craving are its source and origin. Alternatively, every condition is called 'nutriment' (āhāra). However, here, since craving is already taken by the word 'netti', phenomena other than craving should be understood as 'āhāra'. Therefore, it is "āhārannettippabhava" because nutriment and the lead of craving are its origin. Or, nutriment itself is called 'netti' in the sense of leading or causing to proceed; thus also it is "āhārannettippabhava". "Not fit to be delighted in" means that the collection of the five aggregates of clinging, which thus proceeds dependent on conditions and is therefore impermanent and suffering, is not fit to be delighted in or relished through craving and wrong view.
157:
The "escape" (nissaraṇa) from that sakkāya (the five aggregates of clinging) mentioned as "born, become," etc., is the peaceful state. It is peaceful because of the absence of defilements such as greed, which have an unpeaceful nature, and the absence of all formations; because of the nature of their stilling; and because of its praiseworthy nature. It is "atakkāvacara" (beyond the sphere of reasoning) because it is not the object of speculative knowledge. It is "dhuva" (stable) in the sense of being permanent. Because it is thus permanent, it is "ajāta" (unborn) and "asamuppanna" (unproduced). It is "asoka" (sorrowless) because of the absence of the causes of sorrow. It is "viraja" (stainless) because the dust of greed and so forth has been removed. It is "pada" (the state) because it is to be attained by those oppressed by the suffering of saṃsāra. It is the "cessation of suffering phenomena" (nirodha) because it is the cause for the cessation of suffering phenomena such as birth. It is the "stilling of formations" (saṅkhārūpasama) because it is the cause for the stilling of all formations. Because it is the stilling of formations, it is "sukha" (happiness) because it is ultimate bliss. Thus, with all these terms, the Blessed One praises only the deathless Great Nibbāna. In this way, the Blessed One explained Nibbāna by way of exclusion (vyatireka) in the first verse, and by way of inclusion (anvaya) in the second verse.

## The Commentary on the Sixth Sutta is Finished.

## 7. Nibbānadhātusutta-vaṇṇanā

In the seventh sutta, "dvemā" should be resolved as "dve imā". Craving is called "vāna". It is called "Nibbāna" because of the escape from that craving, or because there is no craving in this state, or because craving no longer exists when this state is attained. That Nibbāna itself is called "dhātu" (element) in the sense of being non-living and non-soul, and in the sense of bearing its own nature. Therefore, it is called "Nibbāna-dhātu". Although that Nibbāna-dhātu has no division in the ultimate sense, it is known through figurative designations (pariyāya). Aiming at those figurative divisions, the Blessed One said, "Monks, there are these two Nibbāna elements," and to show the intended divisions, He said "saupādisesā" (with residue remaining) and so forth. Therein, "upādi" (clinging/fuel) refers to the five aggregates, because they are clung to as a result of craving and so forth. "Upādisesa" means that only the upādi (aggregates) remain. "Saupādisesā" means that which exists together with the remaining aggregates. "Anupādisesā" means the absence of that upādi.

"Arahaṃ" means one who is far from defilements, or one who has distant defilements. This was indeed spoken by the Blessed One:
"And how, monks, is a monk an Arahant? Monks, for that monk, evil unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, ..."
158:
...[Evil unwholesome states] that are accompanied by distress, result in suffering, and are causes for future rebirth, aging, and death, are far removed. "Monks, in this way, a monk is called 'Arahaṃ' (Worthy One/Free from defilements)," so it was said [by the Buddha].

'Khīṇāsavo' means that for the Arahant, the four taints (āsava) such as the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava) have been exhausted, completely cut off, abandoned, subsided, are no longer liable to arise, and have been burnt by the fire of knowledge; therefore, he is called 'Khīṇāsavo'.

'Vusitavā' means he has lived, resided, and dwelt in the respected communal life, in the Noble Path, and in the ten noble dwellings (ariyavāsa); he has completed the residence and practiced the conduct; therefore, he is called 'Vusitavā'.

'Katakaraṇīyo' means that starting from the virtuous worldling up to the seven types of trainees (sekha), they perform what is to be done through the four paths. For the Arahant, however, all that was to be done has been done and completed; there is nothing further to be done for the sake of reaching the end of suffering (Nibbāna); therefore, he is called 'Katakaraṇīyo'. This was also said: "For that monk who is well-liberated and of peaceful mind, there is no further accumulation of what has been done, and there is nothing more to be done."

'Ohitabhāro' refers to the three burdens: the burden of the aggregates (khandha-bhāra), the burden of defilements (kilesa-bhāra), and the burden of volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra-bhāra). For that person, these three burdens have been laid down, cast off, and dropped; therefore, he is called 'Ohitabhāro'.

'Anuppattasadattho' means one who has reached his own goal. In the word 'sakattha', the letter 'k' is replaced by 'd'. Because he has reached his own goal through this path, he is called 'Anuppattasadattho'. 'His own goal' (sadattha) should be understood as the fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala). That fruit of Arahantship is called 'sakattha' (one's own goal) because it is bound to oneself, because it does not abandon oneself, because it is one's own supreme purpose, and because it is one's own benefit.

'Parikkhīṇabhavasaṃyojano' refers to the fetters of sensual lust, aversion, conceit, views, doubt, adherence to rules and rituals, lust for existence, envy, stinginess, and ignorance. These are called fetters of existence because they occur in the seven types of existence or because they bind and tie existence to existence. For the Arahant, these fetters are exhausted, abandoned, and burnt by the fire of knowledge; therefore, he is called 'Parikkhīṇabhavasaṃyojano'.

In the phrase 'Sammadññā vimutto', 'sammadññā' means having known rightly. This means: having known, distinguished, weighed, and made clear the meaning of the aggregates as a group, the meaning of the sense bases as a location, the meaning of the elements as voidness, the meaning of suffering as oppression, the meaning of the origin as source, the meaning of cessation as peace, the meaning of the path as seeing, or the various aspects such as "all formations are impermanent" according to reality. 'Vimutto' means two kinds...
159:
Liberations are of two kinds: liberation of the mind (citta-vimutti) and Nibbāna. Indeed, because the Arahant is liberated from all defilements, he is liberated through the liberation of the mind and is also liberated in Nibbāna. Therefore, he is called "one liberated through right knowledge."

As long as the kamma that is the cause for the final existence of that Arahant is not yet exhausted, the five sense faculties such as the eye faculty continue to remain. 'Aviaghātattā' means because they have not yet ceased through the cessation of non-arising. That Arahant experiences desirable (iṭṭha) and undesirable (aniṭṭha) objects such as visible forms. Through those doors, he experiences pleasure and pain which are the results (vipāka) [of past kamma].

Having shown the Nibbāna element with residue remaining (sa-upādisesa nibbānadhātu) to this extent, the phrase "Tassa yo" etc., is now stated to further illustrate the Nibbāna element with residue remaining. Therein, "tassa" refers to that Arahant who has residue remaining. "Yo rāgakkhayo" means the state of exhaustion of lust, its absence, and its absolute non-arising. This method applies to the remaining terms as well. To this extent, it is shown that the exhaustion of lust etc., is the Nibbāna element with residue remaining.

"Idheva" means in this very existence (attabhāva). "Sabbavedayitāni" refers to all indeterminate (abyākata) feelings such as pleasure. Wholesome and unwholesome feelings, however, were abandoned previously. "Anabhinanditāni" refers to feelings that are not delighted in by craving etc. "Sītibhavissanti" means they will become cool through absolute pacification and the subsiding of the distress of formations (saṅkhāra-daratha). It means they will cease through the cessation that leaves no further rebirth. Not only feelings, but all five aggregates in the continuity of the Arahant will cease; the teaching is given using feeling as the heading.

In the verses, "cakkhumatā" refers to the Buddha who is endowed with the five eyes: the Buddha-eye, the Dhamma-eye, the divine-eye, the wisdom-eye, and the all-seeing eye. "Anissitena" refers to the person who does not depend on any state through the dependence of craving and views, or who is not bound by the bonds of lust etc. "Tādinā" refers to being endowed with the quality of "Suchness" (tādi-lakkhaṇa), which is the single nature towards all desirable and undesirable objects by way of six-factored equanimity (chaḷaṅgupekkhā). "Diṭṭhadhammikā" refers to the states occurring in this very existence. "Bhavanettisaṅkhayā" is due to the exhaustion of craving that leads to existence. "Samparāyikā" refers to the states occurring in the future life after the breaking up of the aggregates. "Yamhi" means in which Nibbāna element without residue remaining (anupādisesa nibbāna). In the word "bhavāni", although the gender is changed, it means that the existences of rebirth (upapatti-bhava) cease entirely without remainder and do not proceed further.
160:
"Te" refers to those Arahants whose minds are thus liberated. "Dhammasārādhigama" means attaining the essence of the Dhamma, which is the fruit of Arahatship, the core of this Dispensation, or because it possesses the essence of liberation. "Khaya" means they greatly delight in Nibbāna, which is the destruction of lust and so on. Alternatively, Nibbāna is called "Dhammasāra" (the essence of dhammas) because of its permanent and noble nature. It is also said: "Among all dhammas, Nibbāna (detachment) is the best; detachment is declared to be the foremost among them." Because of attaining that essence of Dhamma, they delight in the Nibbāna element without residue (anupādisesa-nibbāna), which is the destruction of all formations. "Pahaṃsu" means they have abandoned. "Te" is merely a particle. The rest is as previously explained.

## The Commentary on the Seventh Sutta is finished.

## 8. Paṭisallāna Sutta Commentary

In the eighth sutta, "paṭisallānarāmā" refers to "paṭisallāna," which is the act of withdrawing from various beings and formations to dwell in seclusion. It means living alone, frequenting suitable places, and bodily seclusion (kāyaviveka). Because they love and cherish such seclusion, they are called "paṭisallānarāmā." There is also a variant reading "paṭisallānārāmā." They are called "paṭisallānārāmā" because they have seclusion as their "ārāma" (pleasurable resort) in which they should delight. "Viharatha" means "dwell as such persons." They are called "paṭisallānarata" because they delight and rejoice in seclusion.

By these words, the practice of wakefulness (jāgariyānuyoga) and bodily seclusion (vūpakaṭṭhakāyatā), which is the basis for that wakefulness, are shown. The practice of wakefulness cannot exist without these qualities: restraint in virtue, guarding the sense doors, moderation in eating, and mindfulness and clear comprehension. Therefore, it should be understood that these qualities are also implicitly mentioned here.

"Ajjhattaṃ cetosamathamanuyuttā" means being constantly devoted to one's own internal tranquility of mind (samatha). The two terms "ajjhattaṃ" and "attano" have the same meaning, differing only in phrasing. Although the word "samathaṃ" is in the sense of the locative case (bhummattha), it is used in the accusative case (upayogavacana) due to its association with the word "anu." "Anirākatajjhānā" means those who do not discard jhāna from their own continuity, or those who do not let jhāna perish. "Nirākata" means discarding or perishing. It is similar to the usage in texts such as "thambhaṃ niraṅkatvā nivātavuttī" (having discarded pride, he is of humble conduct). "Vipassanāya samannāgatā" means being endowed with the seven types of insight (anupassanā). The seven types of insight are:
161:
Contemplation of impermanence, contemplation of suffering, contemplation of non-self, contemplation of disenchantment, contemplation of dispassion, contemplation of cessation, and contemplation of relinquishment. These seven types of insight have been explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga. "Brūhetāro suññāgārānaṃ" means those who cultivate empty places. Here, "suññāgārānaṃ" refers to any secluded place suitable for the practice of meditation. Monks who take up a meditation subject through tranquility and insight, enter an empty place day and night, and dwell there devoted to meditation, should be known as "cultivators of empty places." However, even those meditators dwelling in single-story mansions and the like who enter into jhāna should also be known as "cultivators of empty places."

In this sutta, the bodily seclusion prescribed by the words "Bhikkhus, dwell delighting in seclusion, rejoicing in seclusion" is only for one with pure virtue, not for one without virtue or with impure virtue, because for such a person, there is no withdrawal of the mind from visual objects and so on. Thus, it is said that purification of virtue (sīla-visuddhi) is implicitly shown. By the two terms "ajjhattaṃ cetosamathamanuyuttā anirākatajjhānā," the development of concentration (samādhi-bhāvanā) is shown, and by the term "vipassanāya samannāgatā," the development of wisdom (paññā-bhāvanā) is shown. Thus, the three mundane trainings (lokiya-sikkhā) are presented.

Now, to show the inevitable fruit for one established in those trainings, the words beginning with "paṭisallānarāmānaṃ" are spoken. Therein, "brūhetānaṃ" means "of those who cultivate." "Dvinnaṃ phalānaṃ" refers to the third fruit (the fruit of non-returning) and the fourth fruit (the fruit of Arahatship). "Pāṭikaṅkha" means what is to be expected or what will inevitably occur. "Aññā" refers to the fruit of Arahatship. It is called "aññā" (final knowledge) because it knows without overstepping the boundaries known by the lower path-knowledges, and because it is complete knowledge with no further duty to know. "Sati vā upādisese" means if there is a residue of defilements that cannot yet be abandoned. When knowledge is not yet mature, those defilements that should be abandoned by mature knowledge remain unabandoned. Referring to this, it is said, "sati vā upādisese." If defilements remain, the formations of the aggregates (khandhābhisaṅkhāra) will certainly persist. Thus, in this sutta, two states are shown: the fruit of non-returning and the fruit of Arahatship. As in this sutta, so it should be understood in the next two suttas.

In the verses, "ye santacittā" refers to those practitioners (yogāvacara) whose minds are peaceful because their defilements have been calmed through substitution (tadaṅga) and suppression (vikkhambhana). "Nepakkaṃ" is called wisdom (paññā), and because they are endowed with that wisdom, they are "nipakā" (prudent). By this, their knowledge in maintaining the meditation subject is shown.
162:
They are called 'mindful' (satimanto) because they possess mindfulness which is the cause for not abandoning the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) while standing, sitting, and so forth. They are called 'meditators' (jhāyino) by way of jhāna characterized by close contemplation of the object. Having previously contemplated the danger in objective sensuality (vatthu-kāma) and subjective sensuality (kilesa-kāma) with such thoughts as 'Sensual pleasures are like a skeleton,' they are without desire for them and, having abandoned them, they make the attained access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) or absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi) the basis. Then, having grasped mentality-materiality (nāmarūpa) and its causes, they rightly practice insight (vipassanā) on the five aggregates as impermanent (anicca) and so forth, without deviation, through the sequence of comprehension of groups (kalāpa-sammasana) and so on.

'Delighting in diligence' (appamādarata) means they greatly delight in non-negligence in the aforementioned practices of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). They spend their time day and night only with diligence in those practices. 'Santā' means those who are peaceful. There is also a variant reading 'sattā', meaning persons. They are accustomed to seeing danger in negligence (pamāda), such as rebirth in hell. Such persons are incapable of falling away from the states of serenity and insight or from the paths and fruits (magga-phala). Indeed, they do not fall away from the states of serenity and insight they have already reached, and they attain those higher states they have not yet reached. They are in the very presence of Nibbāna and final Nibbāna without clinging (anupādā-parinibbāna). Before long, they will attain that Nibbāna.

## The Commentary on the Eighth Sutta is Finished.

## 9. Sikkhanisaṃsasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the ninth sutta, the Sikkhanisaṃsa Sutta, in the word 'sikkhanisaṃsā', it is called 'training' (sikkhā) because it should be trained in. That training is threefold: the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā), the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā), and the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā). For these persons, only these three trainings are the benefit (ānisamsa), not gain, honor, or fame. Therefore, they are called those for whom training is the benefit. 'Viharatha' means dwell as those for whom training is the benefit. The meaning is: dwell as those who habitually see the benefit in the three trainings, rightly perceiving only the benefit to be obtained through those trainings. 'Paññuttarā' means that among those trainings, the wisdom known as the training in higher wisdom is supreme, chief, and distinguished for them; thus they are called 'paññuttarā'. Those who dwell as ones for whom training is the benefit become those with superior wisdom.
163:
"Vimuttisārā" means they are called so because liberation (vimutti), known as the fruit of arahantship (arahattaphala), is their essence (sāra). The meaning is that they stand having taken only the aforementioned liberation as the essence. Those who dwell with the training as their benefit and with wisdom as supreme do not long for any special form of existence (bhava); rather, desiring the end of existence (vibhava), they rely on liberation alone as the essence. "Satādhipateyyā" means they are called so because mindfulness (sati), which acts as the chief, is their governing factor (adhipateyya). "Adhipati" is the same as "adhipateyya." It means they have minds well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) and are devoted to the development of serenity and insight, beginning with the contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā), etc.

Alternatively: "O bhikkhus, dwell making the practice of the threefold training your only benefit when you have obtained the rare opportunity (khana). While dwelling thus, dwell as those for whom wisdom is supreme, being endowed with supramundane wisdom (lokuttara-paññā). Being such, dwell as those for whom liberation is the essence, for whom Nibbāna is the essence, and for whom there is no other essence besides Nibbāna. The means for becoming so is to dwell with mindfulness as the governing factor. Be fully devoted to the development of the foundations of mindfulness. Or, dwell with a mind protected by mindfulness in all things." This is how the meaning should be understood here. Thus, the Blessed One, wishing to urge the bhikkhus toward the three trainings, showed in brief how they should be trained in and how they reach fulfillment. Now, showing the special fruit for those who practice according to the instruction, and wishing to manifest the non-emptiness of that practice, he spoke the verse beginning with "Sikkhānisaṃsānaṃ." Its meaning is as already stated.

In the verses, "Paripuṇṇasikkha" (one with perfected training) refers to an asekha person whose training is purified by the attainment of the highest fruit. "Apahānadhamma": here, "pahānadhamma" (perishable states) refers to the unstable (kuppa) liberations. Indeed, "pahānadhamma" means a state of decline, an unstable state. "Not a state of decline" is "apahānadhamma," a stable state (akuppadhamma). There is also a Pali reading "appahānadhamma," which has the same meaning. "Khayanto" means destruction itself is the end. It refers to Nibbāna, which is the end of the destruction of birth (jāti). Or, "khaya" means death; it refers only to Nibbāna as the end of the destruction of birth. Because of seeing that Nibbāna, one is a "Jātikhayantadassī" (seer of the end of birth).

"Tasmā" means: because the benefit of fulfilling the training is the arrival at Nibbāna, which is the end of aging; therefore. "Sadā" means at all times. "Jhānarata" means they delight in both kinds of jhāna: contemplation of characteristics (lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna) and contemplation of the object (ārammaṇūpanijjhāna). Because of delighting in jhāna...
164:
Thus they have a concentrated mind. "Overcoming Māra with his army" (māraṃ sasenaṃ abhibhuyya) means subduing the fourfold Māra without remainder, along with the army of defilements and the army of misfortune. Indeed, defilements are called the "army" because they act as associates in the destruction of virtues by Devaputta-māra. Similarly, misfortunes such as disease are the army of Maccu-māra. As it was said:

"Sensual pleasures are your first army, discontent is called the second;
Hunger and thirst are your third, craving is called the fourth.

Sloth and torpor are your fifth, fear is called the sixth;
Doubt is your seventh, hypocrisy and obstinacy are the eighth.

Gain, renown, honor, and whatever fame is falsely obtained;
And whoever exalts oneself and disparages others.

This, Namuci, is your army, the striker of the Dark One (Kaṇha);
The one who is not a hero cannot conquer it, but having conquered it, one gains happiness."

In another way, it was said: "The task should be ardently done this very day, who knows if death will come tomorrow? Indeed, there is no making a deal with Death and his great army."

"Become those who have gone to the further shore of birth and death" (bhavatha jātimaraṇassa pāragā) means become those who reach Nibbāna, which is the further shore of birth and death.

## The Commentary on the Ninth Sutta is finished.

## 10. Commentary on the Jāgariya Sutta

In the tenth sutta, "jāgaro" means one who is awake, a wakeful person who is free from sleep and devoted to wakefulness, meaning one who is intensely and continuously applied to the attention of the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) throughout the day and night. For this has been said:

"And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu devoted to wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night? Here, bhikkhus, during the day, a bhikkhu purifies his mind from obstructive qualities (nīvaraṇa) by walking and sitting. During the first watch of the night..."
165:
...by walking and sitting, he purifies his mind from obstructive qualities. During the middle watch of the night, he lies down on his right side in the lion's posture (sīhaseyya), placing one foot on the other, mindful and clearly comprehending, having fixed his mind on the thought of rising. Having risen in the last watch of the night, he purifies his mind from obstructive qualities by walking and sitting. In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is devoted to wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night."

The word 'ca' (and) has the sense of conjunction; by that 'ca', it connects the states such as being mindful which will be mentioned. 'Assa' means 'should be' or 'would be'. They also read "The wakeful bhikkhu should dwell" (jāgaro ca bhikkhu vihareyya).

He is called 'sato' (mindful) because of not abandoning the meditation subject at all places and at all times through the non-lapse of mindfulness. He is 'sampajāno' (clearly comprehending) by the power of the fourfold clear comprehension which occurs in the seven bases (or for the sake of beings). 'Samāhito' means having a well-concentrated and one-pointed mind through access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) and absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi). 'Pamudito' means one who has much joy because of seeing the benefits of the practice, the attainment of successive higher distinctions, and seeing that the undertaking of energy is not in vain. 'Vippasanno' means one who is thoroughly serene due to the abundance of faith in the three trainings which constitute the practice, and in the Teacher who taught the practice. In all terms, it should be connected with 'assa' (should be) or 'vihareyya' (should dwell).

In that context, "Kālavipassī ca kusalesu dhammesu" means an insight-practitioner at that time, or one who practices insight according to the proper time in that application of the meditation subject. What is meant? Having established insight and investigating by way of group-contemplation (kalāpa-sammasana) etc., avoiding the seven unsuitable (asappāya) things such as dwellings and resorting to the suitable ones, not falling into stagnation in between, with a mind directed towards Nibbāna, noting the concentrated state of the mind, respectfully and continuously proceeding with the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā) etc.—at the time when the insight-mind is sluggish, he should be an insight-practitioner according to the proper time in the wholesome, faultless factors of enlightenment known as investigation of states (dhamma-vicaya), energy (vīriya), and joy (pīti). But at the time when the mind is restless, he should be an insight-practitioner according to the proper time in the wholesome, faultless factors of enlightenment known as tranquility (passaddhi), concentration (samādhi), and equanimity (upekkhā). However, the mindfulness factor of enlightenment (sati-sambojjhaṅga) is desired in all instances. For this has been said: "Bhikkhus, I say that mindfulness is useful in all things."

By this much, having shown wakefulness (jāgariya) through the teaching based on a person (puggalādhiṭṭhāna), he now reveals the qualities by which the devotion to wakefulness is accomplished. Thus, the Blessed One, having shown the practice to be investigated along with the qualities that are beneficial in brief to the bhikkhu who has undertaken insight, now, wishing to show the state of the person practicing in such a manner whose practice is not yet finished...
166:
In this way, the Blessed One, having briefly shown the practice of contemplation along with the beneficial qualities to the monk who has undertaken insight, now speaks the words beginning with 'To the vigilant monk, O bhikkhus,' in order to show that the practice of one who practices in such a manner is not in vain.

In that passage, the firm establishment of mindfulness and clear comprehension in the devotion to wakefulness is beneficial in all circumstances and brings about joy and confidence. In that meditation practice, what is called 'insight at the right time' (kāla-vipassanā) is the reaching of maturity in the nascent stage of insight (i.e., becoming mundane insight). Indeed, when insight-knowledge, freed from defilements and having entered the right path, proceeds sharply and courageously, great joy and confidence arise in the yogi. Because of that joy and confidence, one is in the very presence of attaining the distinction. This has also been stated:

'Whenever one contemplates the rise and fall of the aggregates, one attains joy and delight; that is the Deathless for those who know it.'
'The monk who is full of joy and has confidence in the Buddha's Teaching would reach the peaceful state, the bliss of the stilling of formations.'

In the verses, 'Being vigilant, listen to this' means: listen while being devoted to wakefulness, associated with qualities such as mindfulness and clear comprehension, for the purpose of truly awakening from the sleep of negligence and the sleep of ignorance. 'Let those who are asleep awaken' means: you who are asleep, having fallen into the aforementioned sleep, should awaken from it through the practice of diligence, gathering the faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment by the power of devotion to wakefulness, and making an effort in insight. Alternatively, 'being vigilant' refers to the signs of wakefulness. In the phrase 'listen to this,' what are those words? He said, 'Let those who are asleep awaken,' and so on. Therein, 'those who are asleep' refers to those sleeping with the sleep of defilements; may you awaken with the awakening of the Noble Path. 'Wakefulness is better than sleep'—this is the statement showing the reason for awakening. Because the aforementioned wakefulness is better for a man of good family who desires his own welfare than the aforementioned sleep, is more praiseworthy, and brings about welfare and happiness, therefore, awaken. 'There is no fear for the vigilant'—this is the demonstration of the benefits therein. For one who is vigilant, being endowed with the qualities of wakefulness such as faith and so on, and does not fall into the sleep of negligence, there is no fear of self-reproach, fear of reproach by others, fear of punishment, fear of woeful states, or any fear of the round of rebirths caused by birth and so on.
167:
'At the right time' (kālena) means at the time when suitable lodgings and so on are obtained. The word 'so' is merely a particle. 'Rightly investigating the Dhamma' (sammā dhammaṃ parivīmaṃsamāno) means contemplating by investigating from all sides and in every aspect, using the proper method so that weariness (nibbida), dispassion (virāga), and so on arise regarding the phenomena of the three planes which are the objects of insight. 'Unified' (ekodibhūta) refers to concentration (samādhi) called 'ekodi' because it arises as singular and noble. One in whom such unified concentration has arisen or been produced is 'ekodibhūta.' Here, the word 'bhūta' should be understood as being placed at the end, similar to words like 'aggiahita.' Alternatively, one is 'ekodibhūta' because one has reached the state of being singular and noble. In this context, 'ekodi' is intended as Path-concentration (magga-samādhi). In the word 'concentrated' (samāhito), however, insight-concentration along with foundation-jhana concentration is intended.

Alternatively, 'at the right time' (kālena) means at the time of the penetration of the Path. 'Rightly investigating the Dhamma' means investigating the Dhamma of the Four Truths well by way of full understanding (pariññā), realization (abhisamaya), and so on, realizing them through a single realization. 'Unified' (ekodibhūta) refers to the Right Effort (sammappadhāna) which accomplishes the four tasks, called 'ekodi' because it arises as singular, noble, or without a companion. The meaning of 'that unified state has arisen' is entirely the same as before. 'He should destroy the darkness' (vihane tamaṃ so) means that such a noble disciple should completely destroy or cut off the darkness of ignorance with the Path of Arahatship.

Thus, the Blessed One, having shown that the practice is not in vain, now speaks the concluding verse beginning with 'Therefore indeed' (tasmā have) to firmly exhort one to that practice. Therein, 'therefore' (tasmā) means: because through vigilance, through the non-lapse of mindfulness and so on, the development of tranquility and insight reaches fulfillment, and the Noble Path gradually appears, and because of the appearance of that Noble Path, all fears of the round of rebirths no longer exist for that person—for that reason, it is said 'therefore.' 'Indeed' (have) means certainly or firmly. 'Should resort to' (bhajetha) means one should associate with. A monk who thus resorts to wakefulness and is endowed with qualities such as the effort that burns up defilements (ātāpī), having broken the fetters, would reach the unsurpassed enlightenment, which is known as the knowledge of the highest fruit (aggaphala-ñāṇa), and above which there is nothing higher. The rest is as previously explained.

## The Commentary on the Tenth Sutta is finished.

## 11. Āpāyikasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the eleventh sutta, 'those destined for the state of deprivation' (āpāyikā) means they will be reborn in the states of deprivation (apāya). Among those, they are called 'hell-beings' (nerayikā) because they will be reborn in hell (niraya). 'Without abandoning this' (idamappahāya) means without abandoning the two kinds of evil conduct that will now be mentioned; it means without relinquishing the speech, mind, and views that proceed by way of such practice and such grasping.
168:
The term 'Abrahmacārī' is defined as follows: one who practices the noble life is a 'Brahmacārī,' or one who possesses noble conduct is a 'Brahmacārī.' One who is not a 'Brahmacārī' is an 'Abrahmacārī,' which refers to an immoral person who merely resembles a noble practitioner. 'Brahmacāripatiñño' means making a claim such as 'I am a noble practitioner.' 'Paripuṇṇaṃ' means complete and flawless, such as being unbroken. 'Parisuddhaṃ' means pure due to the absence of the defilements of corruption. 'Amūlakena' means without a basis such as seeing; it is free from the grounds of accusation like seeing, hearing, or suspecting. 'Abrahmacariyena' means by an ignoble practice. 'Anuddhaṃseti' means to destroy, accuse, or revile with a Pārājika offense while knowing 'this person is pure.' 

In the verses, 'Abhūtavādī' refers to one who accuses another by telling a baseless and empty lie without seeing any fault in the other. 'Katvā' refers to one who, having done an evil deed, says 'I did not do this.' Both of these people, having gone from this world to the next, become equal in their destination because they both go to hell. Among them, only the destination is determined, not the lifespan. Having done much evil, one is cooked in hell for a long time; having done a little evil, one is cooked for only a short time. Since the karma of both is base, it is said, 'Men of base karma [are equal] in the hereafter.' The word 'parattha' (in the hereafter) should be connected with the preceding word 'pecca' (having passed away)—meaning, having gone to the next life, those of base karma are equal. 

Thus, the Blessed One, having shown the result of lying through false accusation and through the concealment of actual faults, now spoke two verses for the purpose of causing spiritual urgency (saṃvega) by showing the result of evil conduct to the many wicked monks living in that place. In those verses, 'Kāsāvakaṇṭhā' refers to those whose necks are wrapped in cloth dyed with astringent juice (saffron robes). 'Pāpadhammā' means those of evil nature. 'Asaññatā' means those lacking restraint in body and so forth. 'Pāpā' means such wicked persons who, having been reborn due to evil deeds, experience great suffering according to the method stated in the Lakkhaṇasaṃyutta: 'His body is ablaze, glowing, and flaming; his outer robe (saṅghāṭi) is also ablaze,' and so on. 

The summary meaning of the third verse is: It is better and more excellent for an immoral person, who is unrestrained in body and so forth, to eat a red-hot iron ball like a mass of fire, than to accept and eat the alms-food given out of faith by the country-folk while claiming 'I am a monk.' Why is that?
169:
Because of the reason of eating that iron ball, only his single physical existence (attabhāva) would be consumed. However, an immoral person who consumes the four requisites given out of faith would be reborn in hell for many hundreds of births.

## The Commentary on the Eleventh Sutta is finished.

## 12. Diṭṭhigata Sutta Commentary

In the twelfth sutta, regarding the phrase 'dvīhi diṭṭhigatehi,' it should be understood that views themselves are called 'diṭṭhigata,' as in the passages 'gūthagataṃ muttagataṃ' (gone to dung, gone to urine). Or, because they are merely the occurrences of views, being void of the grasped mode, they are called 'diṭṭhigata.' By those 'diṭṭhigata,' 'pariyuṭṭhitā' means overwhelmed or obstructed. The word 'pariyuṭṭhāna' has the sense of obstruction, as in the passage 'robbers obstructed the path.' 'Devā' refers to deities by rebirth (upapatti-deva). They are called 'devā' because they play and delight in the most excellent sense pleasures and in meditative absorptions (jhāna), etc., or because they reach and obtain their desired goals through psychic power.

They are called 'manussā' (humans) because of the loftiness of their minds. This is stated by way of an excellent designation, as in 'teacher of gods and humans.' 'Olīyanti eke' (some hold back) means that some gods and humans, through the state of eternalism (sassata-bhāva) which is the obsession of holding back in existences with the thought 'the self and the world are eternal,' cling, shrink back, and become contracted; they do not escape from that. 'Atidhāvanti' (they overreach) means that they do not grasp the connection between cause and effect of the phenomena which are distinct in the ultimate sense, and by grasping a variety of methods, they run here and there. Therefore, they overreach or transcend the state of being a rejected nature in the view of annihilationism—'the self and the world are annihilated; there is nothing after death'—or in the practice for the cessation of existence. In the phrase 'cakkhumanto ca passanti,' the word 'ca' is used in the sense of distinction. Deities and humans who possess the eye of wisdom through the maturation of knowledge and the perfection of previous practice, by that very eye of wisdom, do not approach the two extremes of eternalism and annihilationism, but realize the truth by seeing the middle way. They see without distortion: 'This is merely mind and matter (nāma-rūpa) dependently arisen; therefore, it is not eternal, nor is it annihilated.'

To point out such things as holding back through the designation of persons (puggalādhiṭṭhāna), the words beginning with 'kathañca, bhikkhave' were spoken. Therein, 'bhavā' refers to the sense-sphere existence (kāma-bhava), the fine-material existence (rūpa-bhava), and the immaterial existence (arūpa-bhava). There are also three other existences: existence with perception (saññī-bhava), existence without perception (asaññī-bhava), and existence with neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññīnāsaññī-bhava). There are also three other existences: one-constituent existence (ekavokāra-bhava), four-constituent existence (catuvokāra-bhava), and five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra-bhava). Because they delight in those existences, they are called 'bhavārāma.' Because they rejoice in existences, they are called 'bhavarata.' Because they are well-gladdened by existences, they are called 'bhavasammuditā.' In the phrase 'bhavanirodhāya,' 'bhavanirodha' refers to the absolute cessation and non-arising of those existences. When the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma for the escape from saṃsāra for the sake of that cessation of existence, the mind does not enter into it.
170:
There are three types of existence: existence with perception (saññībhava), existence without perception (asaññībhava), and existence with neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññīnāsaññībhava). There are another three types of existence: one-constituent existence (ekavokārabhava), four-constituent existence (catuvokārabhava), and five-constituent existence (pañcavokārabhava). They are called 'delighting in existence' (bhavārāma) because they delight and rejoice in these existences. They are called 'rejoicing in existence' (bhavarata) because they take pleasure in existences. They are called 'well-pleased with existence' (bhavasammuditā) because they are thoroughly glad in existences. 'For the cessation of existence' (bhavanirodhāya) means for the sake of the absolute cessation and non-arising of those existences. When the Dhamma leading out of suffering (niyyānika-dhamma) as proclaimed by the Tathāgata is being taught (dhamme desiyamāne), the mind does not enter or plunge in (na pakkhandati), either because of being settled in the view of permanence or because of the nature of the Dhamma being concise. It does not attain clarity or believe in that Dhamma (na pasīdati). It does not stand or resolve in that teaching (na santiṭṭhati). Thus, by attending to it as permanent, they shrink back in existences.

'Being oppressed' (aṭṭīyamānā) means seeing aging, sickness, death, etc., as well as killing, binding, cutting, etc., in existence, and being terrified; because of being endowed with these things like aging, etc., they are oppressed and made miserable by existence. 'Being ashamed' (harāyamānā) means being embarrassed. 'Being disgusted' (jigucchamānā) means seeing it as something repulsive. 'Non-existence' (vibhava) refers to the annihilation (uccheda) of existence. 'They delight' (abhinandanti) means they delight by being obsessed through the delight of craving and views. The phrase 'Since, indeed, dear lady' (yato kira bhoti), etc., is a statement showing the manner of their delight. In that phrase, 'since' (yato) means 'when'. 'Dear lady' (bhoti) is a term of address (ālapana). The phrase 'this self' (ayaṃ attā) refers to the self conceived by oneself as an agent, etc. 'Is cut off' (ucchizzati) means it is terminated. 'Perishes' (vinassati) means it is no longer seen, reaching destruction and non-existence. 'Does not exist after death' (na hoti paraṃ maraṇā) means it does not exist beyond death. 'This is peaceful' (etaṃ santaṃ) means that one's own annihilation, etc., is peaceful because of the subsiding of all existence and the subsiding of all feverish heat. Because it is peaceful, it is 'sublime' (paṇītaṃ). Because it is the true, non-perverted state, it is called 'reality' (yāthāva). In that context, the two terms 'peaceful and sublime' (santaṃ paṇītaṃ) are spoken through delight in craving. The term 'reality' (yāthāvaṃ) is spoken through delight in views. 'Thus' (evaṃ) means by attending to it as annihilation as previously mentioned.

'What has come to be' (bhūta) refers to the group of five aggregates. Those five aggregates are called 'what has come to be' because they are produced by causes and because they exist in the ultimate sense. Therefore, He said, 'Monks, see this as what has come to be.' One sees it according to its non-perverted nature, its individual characteristics (salakkhaṇa), and its common characteristics (sāmaññalakkhaṇa). This group of five aggregates is merely mind and matter (nāmarūpa). Among them, 'these states such as earth, etc., are matter; these states such as contact, etc., are mind; these are their characteristics, etc.; these such as ignorance, etc., are their causes'—thus, one sees through the vision of mind and matter along with their causes. Also, 'all these states arise without having been, and having been, they vanish; therefore they are impermanent; being impermanent, they are suffering; being suffering, they are non-self'—thus, one sees through the power of the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā), etc. By this sequence of words, the plane of insight ending with tender insight (taruṇa-vipassanā) is shown. By the term 'for weariness' (nibbidāya), strong insight (balava-vipassanā), which is weariness with the states belonging to the three planes called the five aggregates, is shown. By the term 'for dispassion' (virāgāya), the Path (magga) which is the fading away of lust is shown. By the term 'for cessation' (nirodhāya), the Path itself is shown for the sake of cessation. Alternatively, by the term 'for cessation' (nirodhāya), Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna) along with the cessation through tranquilization (paṭippassaddhi-nirodha) is shown. 'Thus, monks, those with eyes see' means that those with the eye of wisdom see the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths with the eye of Path-wisdom along with the preliminary insight.

In the verses, 'seeing what has come to be as it really is' means that the noble disciple...
171:
...means the noble disciple sees the group of five aggregates as what has come to be, according to its non-perverted nature, with Path-wisdom accompanied by insight-wisdom. By this, the realization through thorough understanding (pariññābhisamaya) is shown. By the phrase 'transcending what has come to be', the realization through development (bhāvanābhisamaya) is shown. For indeed, the Noble Path transcends the group of five aggregates by means of this Path; therefore, it is called 'transcending what has come to be'. 'In what has really come to be' (yathābhūte) means in Nibbāna, which has the nature of non-perverted truth. 'They are liberated' (vimuccanti) means they resolve or plunge in; by this, the realization through witnessing (sacchikiriyābhisamaya) is shown. 'Due to the exhaustion of craving for existence' (bhavataṇhāparikkhayā) means due to the absolute destruction and cutting off of craving for existence. By this, the abandoning of the origin (samudayappahāna) is shown.

In the verse 'He is truly one who has thoroughly understood what has come to be', the word 'truly' (save) is merely a particle. That person who has thoroughly understood what has come to be is one who has thoroughly understood the aggregates due to the exhaustion of craving for existence through the Path, which is the means of transcending what has come to be. For that very reason, he is one resolved in Nibbāna, which is the true nature. 'In various existences' (bhavābhave) means in small and large existences; or else, he is one whose craving is gone and whose defilements are broken in the seeing of annihilation, etc. The monk, due to the cutting off of the self-identity called the five aggregates of clinging, does not come to renewed existence because of non-arising in the future; he reaches only the state of being beyond designation. Thus, the Teacher concluded the teaching with the Nibbāna element without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu).

Thus, in this eleventh chapter (vagga), the round of suffering (vaṭṭa) was discussed. In the third, fourth, and fifth suttas, and in the final sutta, the round and the ending of the round (vaṭṭavivaṭṭa) were discussed. In the remaining suttas, only the ending of the round (vivaṭṭa) was discussed—so it should be understood.

## The commentary on the twelfth sutta is finished.
## In the Paramatthadīpanī, the commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya,
## the commentary on the Duka-nipāta of the Itivuttaka is finished.
